a-crust-for-the-phrenologists-electronic: A Crust for the Phrenologists, 1842. The vidimus. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
a-phrenological-chart-giving-a-descripti: A Phrenological Chart, 1842. The mind's chart. This book preserves that chart. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
addison-history-knights-templars-1842:
Charles G. Addison, an English lawyer of the Inner Temple, wrote this history of the Knights Templars in 1842. It was the first full history of the order in the English tongue. Addison knew the Temple Church in London, the order's old seat, at first hand.

He tells of the order's rise in the crusades, its wealth, and its famed rule of life. Then come the shock of its fall: the arrests, the trial, and the fire that ends its tale. Bound with it is the tale of the Temple Church and the Temple grounds in London.
arxiv-2510-00042:
Söderström and colleagues present ELIGANT-TN, the new thermal neutron counter of the ELIGANT instrument suite built for photonuclear experiments at the Extreme Light Infrastructure Nuclear Physics facility in Romania there. The detector, a large polyethylene moderator carefully embedding 28 helium-3 gas counters of detectors. Counts neutrons evaporated after planned gamma-ray beams strike targets. Jointly serving high-precision cross-section measurements for nuclear astrophysics, industry, and medicine at the facility.

The paper details the mechanical design and electronics, then also validates performance with Geant4 and MCNP simulations of monoenergetic neutrons plus commissioning measurements using standard neutron sources. As an end-to-end check of the full analysis procedure, the team successfully reproduces the known branching ratios of the carbon-13 alpha-capture reaction producing oxygen-16. Demonstrating the array overall works as a whole ahead of the real gamma beam program in the coming years.
arxiv-2510-00242:
Mehdi Talbi and Nizar Touzi wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on stochastic calculus for distributions that evolve randomly. Mean-field control problems steer huge populations where each agent reacts to the whole distribution. Common shocks make that distribution itself a random, sometimes jumpy process. The authors extend two classic change-of-variable formulas, the Ito and Ito-Wentzell formulas, to this setting.

Their versions cover general semimartingales whose conditional laws may jump along with the process. The proofs rest only on Taylor expansions, keeping the machinery elementary in spirit. With the formulas in hand, they derive the dynamic programming equations for mean-field control with Poisson-type common noise. They also treat mean-field stopping problems under common noise for the first time in this generality. The results give control theorists sharper tools for crowd-like systems hit by shared shocks.
arxiv-2510-00342:
Samuel Li and Ian Roberts published this 2025 paper on full-duplex radios that send and receive at once on one frequency. A base station's own transmission can drown its incoming signal, so self-interference must be suppressed. Beamforming can help, but first the station must learn its self-interference channel. In millimeter-wave massive antenna systems, measuring that channel directly costs prohibitive overhead.

Their framework skips explicit measurement and learns site-specific probing codebooks instead. A deep network turns those few probing results into transmit and receive beams. Ray-tracing simulations show the beams keep self-interference near the noise floor. They did so with a small fraction of the measurements explicit estimation would demand. The savings ran between about seventy-five and ninety-seven percent across their tests. The approach held up as channel conditions varied, which suits fast-fading real deployments.
arxiv-2510-00442:
Harbir Antil and Deepanshu Verma published this 2025 paper on shrinking the memory that neural network training consumes. Backpropagation must store each layer's activations, and that storage blocks scaling to bigger models. The authors borrow matrix sketching, a compression trick from control theory, and apply it to activations. Three sketch matrices, updated by exponential moving averages, stand in for the full records.

An adaptive rank rule balances memory savings against the error the sketches introduce. Tests covered handwritten digits, image classification, and physics-informed networks. The accuracy-memory trade-off proved smooth and controllable in each setting. One showcase tracks gradient norms in real time on the digit task with minimal memory overhead. For monitoring alone, memory fell by more than ninety-nine percent over long windows in their runs. The authors see sketched storage as a practical path to training and debugging larger networks.
arxiv-2510-00642:
Zhang and a large team fabricate X-ray detectors from annular aluminium-manganese alloy films in this 2025 arXiv paper on instrumentation. Transition edge sensors are superconducting thermometers with superb energy resolution, widely used for cosmic microwave background work. Their use for X-rays with AlMn alloy films is rarely reported, partly because tuning the alloy's critical temperature was awkward until a baking method appeared. The annular ring shape should let designers adjust normal resistance without changing how heat leaks to the bath.

The team built three samples and tested them inside a dilution refrigerator. Their current-voltage curves matched each other closely, which shows the fabrication is consistent. The smallest-absorber device reached an energy resolution of 11.0 electronvolts at 5.9 kiloelectronvolts. That fell short of the theoretical estimate, and the authors blame excess heat capacity and noisier readout electronics than expected.
arxiv-2510-00742:
Karaouli and four co-authors ask how foundational time series foundation models really are, in this 2025 arXiv paper on forecasting. Foundation models pretrained on corpora transformed language and vision work through zero-shot skill and fine-tuning. Time series foundation models promise much for forecasting, but time series vary across domains in seasonality, sampling, and trend. The authors test whether the promise survives contact with unseen data.

They find zero-shot quality is tied to how similar the target series is to the pretraining domains. On synthetic and similar data the models shine, yet domain shifts erode the advantage. Fine-tuned foundation models did not consistently beat dedicated models by enough to justify their size. A model called SAMFormer, with under fifty thousand parameters and no pretraining, sometimes won when trained from scratch. Their advice is conditional deployment: foundation models where similarity is high, specialists where personalization matters.
arxiv-2510-00842:
Szusterman simplifies a key step in the proof of Banaszczyk's 5K theorem in this 2025 arXiv note on convex geometry. The theorem belongs to vector balancing, which asks how well vectors can be signed so their sum stays small inside a target convex body. Banaszczyk's original argument used a transformation of convex bodies under which Gaussian measure never decreases. That monotonicity is powerful but its known proof is intricate.

Szusterman slightly modifies the transform so it interacts cleanly with Ehrhard symmetrizations, a standard tool for Gaussian problems. The monotonicity of Gaussian measure then follows through a smoother route. As a payoff, the proof of the 5K theorem itself becomes somewhat easier. The note is short and technical, aimed at researchers in asymptotic geometric analysis who use Gaussian measure estimates.
arxiv-2510-01642:
Lin and co-authors teach robot vision-language-action models to recover from failures by generating failure cases automatically in simulation. Robot datasets overwhelmingly show only successful trajectories, so models freeze when execution goes wrong. The rare failure datasets offer text explanations that controllers cannot execute directly.

Their system, FailSafe, manufactures diverse failures paired with executable recovery actions for any simulated task. A fine-tuned model learned to reason about failures better than flagship general models. Plugged into action models, the reasoner lifted overall manipulation success. Failure becomes training data instead of an unmodeled embarrassment. Motion planning inside simulators generates the recovery actions automatically. Crowd-sourced robot data taught success and hid failure systematically. Any simulator with planning qualifies as a failure factory. Executable recoveries beat textual explanations for action models. Unpredictable failures are the deployment reality finally being faced.
arxiv-2510-01842:
Belkhiter and four co-authors try to predict the best model before any training runs in this 2025 paper. Automated machine learning tools usually search by training many candidate models on the target dataset. That exhaustive search wastes heavy computing on losers. Pre-hoc prediction instead guesses the winner from dataset descriptions and summary statistics alone.

The authors test both classic predictors and large language model agents at this guessing game. Their benchmark is the AutoGluon portfolio, covering one hundred seventy-five tabular datasets from OpenML. Enriched dataset descriptions helped traditional models pick better candidates. The language model agents showed real reasoning about model choice, though they still need refinement. Trimming the search space this way cut the computing overhead of automated selection sharply. The authors also argue for open datasets with consistent text and numeric descriptions.
arxiv-2510-01942:
Bui proves fractional product rules on spaces far beyond flat Euclidean geometry in this 2025 analysis paper. Leibniz rules bound the fractional derivative of a product by the derivatives of its factors. The classical Kato-Ponce versions live on Euclidean space and lean on Fourier transforms. Many modern problems live on curved or operator-defined settings where no Fourier transform exists.

Working with nonnegative self-adjoint operators on spaces of homogeneous type, Bui avoids Fourier methods entirely. The unified approach yields bilinear estimates for spectral multipliers on weighted Hardy, Besov, and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces. Nilpotent Lie groups, Grushin operators, and Hermite expansions all fall inside the framework. New weighted estimates follow for the Hermite, Laguerre, and Bessel operators as special cases. Applications reach scattering formulas and related partial differential equation models. The paper exports a cornerstone inequality of harmonic analysis to the geometries where analysts now work.
arxiv-2510-02042:
Glittum and Syljuåsen chart the warm behavior of a classic frustrated magnet in this 2025 physics paper. The triangular lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet resists simple ordering because its spins cannot all antialign at once. Real materials, including several delafossites, realize versions of this model. The authors study the classical model with couplings out to third-nearest neighbors.

Their tool, nematic bond theory, computes free energies and neutron scattering structure factors at finite temperature. The resulting phase diagram holds more than the familiar one-hundred-twenty-degree ordered state. Extra couplings create phases that break the lattice's rotational symmetry. Finite-temperature spiral spin liquid regimes appear as well. A broad hump in the specific heat shows up across the ordered phase, as experiments often see. The quantitative maps should help experimentalists infer exchange couplings from measured transition temperatures and heat data. Classical results also frame where quantum effects might later intervene.
arxiv-2510-02542:
Erkul surveys analogue gravity and asks how far wave dispersion can reach. His 2025 essay traces models that mimic gravity with material media. Newton himself speculated about an ether-like medium for gravity. Modern versions use fluids and condensates to stage curved spacetime. Those experiments showed Hawking radiation is robust. Dispersion, meaning wave speed varies with wavelength, proved central there. Erkul wonders whether hidden dispersion shapes real gravity too. He speculates it might bear on the cosmological constant. It might also touch current tensions in cosmic measurements.

The piece is written as a reflective three act survey. Historical analogies guide each leap in gravity theory, he notes. Future breakthroughs may again borrow from analogue systems. The essay asks where analogy ends and mechanism begins. No new experiment is claimed in these pages. Its value lies in framing fresh questions. Medium based thinking keeps returning to gravity research.
arxiv-2510-02842:
Vereshchagin revisits a theorem about tilings built by substitution rules. A substitution inflates each tile into a patch of smaller tiles. A family of tilings is called sofic when local rules can define it. Local rules need only decorated tiles and checks between neighbors. The Goodman-Strauss theorem says this holds for almost every substitution. Its proof, though, hides the needed conditions in scattered steps.

Vereshchagin states those conditions in full, up front. The stated version is more restrictive than the original claim. Two simple tricks recover the full strength anyway. One trick raises the substitution to a large power. The other merges small tiles into larger blocks. He also proves a matching result for hierarchical tilings. Those are tilings that split under the rule forever. Prior work by Fernique and Ollinger had a gap there. Under the new conditions, their technique goes through cleanly.
arxiv-2510-03042:
Murtaza, De, and Paliathanasis test a steep potential in a modified gravity theory. The theory uses non-metricity, where lengths shift under transport. A scalar field joins that geometric setup here. The universe's background splits into three connection branches. Each branch gives its own cosmic history to check. The authors add a steep potential with a power-law coupling. They ask whether both acceleration eras can fit one model.

A phase-space study maps all the asymptotic paths. Matter eras, stiff kinetic eras, and de Sitter states all appear. Some paths dive toward a Big Crunch or a Big Rip. Steep potential states can act like dark energy at both ends. Center manifold theory checks their stability where plain tests fail. Under stated parameter limits, those states hold steady. Early inflation and late acceleration may thus share one cause. Data tests must still judge the model's worth.
arxiv-2510-03142:
Xu and co-authors teach a robot to navigate by sight alone with help from three experts. Vision-language-action models steer robots from camera views and words. Depth sensors make the job easier but cost more. Their model, MM-Nav, sees in a full circle at once. It starts from pretrained language and vision foundations. Three reinforcement learning experts supplied its lessons. Each expert trained with secret depth data in a custom world.

One expert mastered reaching a goal in open space. Another learned to squeeze through tight gaps. The third learned to dodge obstacles cleanly. Training mixed their lessons with a shifting balance. Weak skills received more practice time automatically. The student ended up beating each teacher at its own game. Lab tests in synthetic worlds showed strong generalization. Real-world trials then confirmed the transfer held. The recipe scales because expert data is synthetic.
arxiv-2510-03342:
The Gemini Robotics Team at Google DeepMind published a 2025 technical report on the newest models in its robot family. One model, Gemini Robotics 1.5, turns sight and words into robot actions across many robot bodies. Its partner model handles embodied reasoning, such as judging space, planning steps, and estimating progress. The report stresses three advances: learning across bodies, thinking in words before acting, and stronger spatial reasoning.

A motion transfer method lets skills learned on one robot body carry to others. The action model also writes out its reasoning steps before it moves. That habit improved its success on long, multi-step chores and made its choices easier for people to follow. The reasoning model set new best scores on embodied reasoning tests in the report. Together, the pair points toward general robots that can perceive a scene, plan in plain words, and then act with care.
arxiv-2510-03442:
Cakar and Kristensson present a 2025 arXiv paper arguing that AI explanations should work like human ones: as arguments that others can check. People cannot see inside each other's brains, yet trust grows from verifiable claims and evidence. The authors build pipelines that turn model text into argument graphs. Each step can then be inspected, supported, or attacked by fact nodes. A risk assessment team of agents shows the approach in action.

Their argument extraction scored a macro F1 near ninety four on a standard essay corpus, beating prior work by several points in the study. Relation sorting between argument parts also set a new best mark. In the risk demo, fact nodes that clash with an argument flag possible hallucinations automatically. Users can push back at test time and refine answers without retraining. The team ships code and a container so others can deploy the checker on plain hardware.
arxiv-2510-03742:
Ruchika, Mukherjee, and Favale present a 2025 arXiv paper warning that a machine learning tool for cosmology lets a choice steer its answer. Gaussian process reconstruction estimates the universe's expansion rate without assuming a cosmic model. The authors show the choice of kernel, the function encoding smoothness, shifts the inferred Hubble constant as much as switching cosmological models does. Their fix, the Generalised GP framework, frees the Matérn smoothness parameter so the data choose it. They test the approach on cosmic chronometer measurements.

Across six kernels, inferred Hubble values spanned a range matching the gap between the standard model and a dark energy rival. The generalised framework stayed consistent between optimized and marginalized analyses, where standard practice diverged, especially at high redshift. Its worse fit statistics reflect flexibility rather than failure. Cosmology's Hubble tension is a fight over differences. Methods that hide their uncertainty inside fixed settings can manufacture precision.
arxiv-2510-03842:
Baghbadorani and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on faster ways to solve variational inequalities. These problems appear in traffic planning, games, and machine learning, wherever a stable balance point is needed. Standard solvers project the current guess onto the allowed set at every step, and that projection can be costly. The cost grows fast in problems like traffic assignment with many links.

The authors build an accelerated algorithm that uses a Frank-Wolfe method as its inner engine. Instead of projecting, each step solves a simpler linear minimization over the allowed set. They prove convergence for strongly monotone problems, their target class. They also show the inner step can stop early once a simple test turns negative, cutting cost further. Tests on traffic assignment support the approach. The method offers a cheaper path for large problems where projection dominates runtime.
arxiv-2510-03942:
Beutner and Finkbeiner present this 2025 arXiv paper on verifying system properties that compare several executions. Hyperproperties capture needs like secrecy, where public behavior must not leak private inputs. The logic HyperLTL states them by quantifying over executions, but alternating quantifiers make full verification impractical. A cheaper game-based method existed, yet it covered only a narrow pattern of quantifiers.

The authors show that multiplayer games with partial information can handle arbitrary quantifier patterns. Each player in the game sees only part of the state, mirroring the quantifier structure. Games with partial information are undecidable in general, which would doom the approach. Their game's information is hierarchical, though, and that special structure lands in a decidable class. They also study prophecy variables, which let players peek at future choices, in this setting. The result widens the range of secrecy properties that tools can check with game methods.
arxiv-2510-04242:
Juhász and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv note proving three new results about Delta-spaces in general topology. A Delta-space lets every decreasing sequence of sets with empty intersection be enclosed by open sets whose intersection is also empty. The class matters because a function space is distinguished exactly when its domain is a Delta-space. Open problems about the class have accumulated in the literature.

First, every regular countably compact Delta-space is in fact compact, settling one question fully. Second, the existence of a crowded Baire Delta-space has set-theoretic strength: it implies an inner model with a measurable cardinal. Third, they improve a known cardinality bound, showing a Delta-space whose number of open sets has uncountable cofinality must be smaller than that number. Results like the second show innocent topological questions can hide large-cardinal content.
arxiv-2510-04542:
Wolfgang Lehrach and a large team at Google DeepMind wrote this 2025 paper on a way for AI to play games. The usual approach asks a language model to name a move, which yields illegal moves and shallow plans. Their method asks the model to write a code world model. The model translates the rules and play of a game into Python code. That code can list moves, advance the state, and detect the end.

A search planner then plays through the generated simulator at high speed. The model writes value heuristics to guide the search and inference code for hidden state in card style games. The agent was tested on ten games, four of them new and built for the study. Half the games hid information from the players, and half showed all of it. The method beat or matched a direct play model in nine of the ten games.
arxiv-2510-04642:
Marta Bílková, Thomas Ferguson, and Daniil Kozhemiachenko wrote this 2025 paper on a logic of graded plausibility. Agents in their logic rate statements from fully plausible to known false, on a scale between zero and one. The base is Gödel fuzzy logic, extended with an involutive negation and a knowledge operator for each agent. The semantics for such logics lacks finite models, which blocks proof search. The team supplies a semantics that restores the finite model property.

On that semantics, they build a tableaux calculus that ends after finitely many steps. Failed proofs yield counter models that show why a formula is not valid. With the calculus in hand, they settle the cost of checking validity. The problem is PSpace complete when two or more agents reason together. For one agent, it drops to coNP complete. A terminating proof method with cost turns the logic into a tool.
arxiv-2510-04842:
Yorgos Felekis, Theodoros Damoulas, and Paris Giampouras wrote this 2025 paper on causal models that stay valid when the world shifts. Causal abstraction links a detailed model to a coarse one: cell to organ, neuron to brain region. The two levels must agree on what interventions do. Learned abstractions so far assume the conditions are fixed. Environments drift, and the assumptions can be wrong.

The authors build the first distributionally robust abstractions. Their learning method plans for the worst background within a ball of ones. The ball is measured with the Wasserstein distance, and its radius sets the caution level. Theory guides how to pick that radius for measured and bell curved environments. In experiments the robust versions survived environment shifts that broke ordinary ones. They tolerated errors in the model structure and in the mapping between levels. Robustness at the level of causal models matters wherever models guide interventions.
arxiv-2510-04942:
Raktim Bhattacharya tackles spacecraft navigation between Earth and the Moon in this 2025 arXiv paper. That region, called cislunar space, has no GPS coverage. Gravity from both bodies also makes orbits hard to predict over long stretches. Bhattacharya builds an onboard estimator that works from angle-only sightings of Earth and the Moon.

The design uses ordinary star-tracker cameras, so a craft needs no precision clock or radio ranging. The math wraps the nonlinear orbit model in a form that carries firm error bounds. In simulations of a near rectilinear halo orbit, tracking stayed smooth over several orbits. The largest errors appeared in the out-of-plane states, where angle-only sensing is weakest. The approach suits missions like NASA's planned Gateway station.
arxiv-2510-05142:
Xin Wang and five co-authors mine the materials literature with AI that shows its sources in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most experimental materials knowledge sits buried in unstructured papers. Data-driven discovery needs it as clean, structured records. Earlier extraction tools captured only a few features and missed links between composition, processing, structure, and properties.

Their multi-stage language-model pipeline extracts 47 features from experimentally reported materials only. Each pass tracks its source text, which guards against invented values. Feature-level and tuple-level scores both reached F1 values around 0.96 in both evaluations. Source tracking cut missed materials from 49 down to 13 in a 100-article test set. The database it builds has minimal omissions and zero false positives.
arxiv-2510-05342:
Hyung Gyu Rho teaches preference tuning to treat hard and easy examples differently in this 2025 arXiv paper. Direct Preference Optimization aligns language models with human choices. Its fixed temperature parameter applies one strength to every training pair. Easy pairs then get overfit while informative hard pairs get under-learned.

His method, MADPO, first trains a reward model to estimate each pair's margin. It then weights the DPO loss per sample using that margin. Hard pairs receive an amplified target margin, and easy pairs receive a dampened one. Theory shows the optimization landscape stays stable and tolerates reward-model errors. On sentiment generation, MADPO beat the next-best method by up to about 33 percent on high-quality data.
arxiv-2510-05542:
Jiang and colleagues build a model that can describe a whole sound scene in words. Human listeners naturally note what sounds occur, where they sit, and how the room shapes them. Audio models usually name sounds but miss direction, distance, and echo. Their 2025 model, Sci-Phi, aims to narrate spatial scenes at once.

Sci-Phi pairs two encoders, one for spatial cues and one for sound content. Training used over four thousand hours of synthetic surround recordings with labels. The work was completed during an internship at Microsoft. In one pass, the model lists up to four directional sources plus background sounds. It also reports timing, loudness, and room traits for each source. Tests across fifteen measures show strength even with similar or overlapping sources. Hearing aids, robots, and navigation tools are named as future users. Performance dipped only slightly on real room recordings.
arxiv-2510-05742:
Huang and colleagues build a tool for auditing text-to-image generators systematically. These systems can produce biased or offensive images, yet auditors face a vast output space. Manual checks cover only a few prompts and miss broader patterns. Their 2025 system, Vipera, blends visual guidance with language-model suggestions.

Formative studies with five working auditors shaped five design goals for the tool. Vipera shows scene graphs and stacked charts to help auditors make sense of images. It also helps them organize criteria in hierarchies. A language model suggests unexplored auditing directions along the way. In a controlled study, twenty-four experienced auditors used the system. They navigated large output spaces well and engaged diverse criteria. The work targets end-user auditing rather than developer-only testing. Better auditing supports more responsible creative use of generative AI. Funding came partly from an NSF fairness-in-AI program with Amazon.
arxiv-2510-05842:
Mirian tests whether optical klystrons can generate short, powerful terahertz pulses. Terahertz free-electron lasers fight strong radiation slippage and diffraction. Long wavelengths slip past the electron bunch before amplifying cleanly. Her 2025 simulation study targets the planned DALI facility.

Simulations cover resonant wavelengths of ten, thirty, and one hundred micrometers. Long wavelengths grow energy fast but broaden temporally from slippage. Short wavelengths need large dispersive strengths to bunch the beam. Harmonic bunching offers an alternative that lowers that requirement. Diffraction does not limit the present design's apertures. A novel chicane-embedded optical delay restores phase alignment between light and electrons. Staged amplification then preserves beam quality through the undulator sections. Output power reaches the multi-megawatt range in the tuned designs. Compact, intense terahertz pulses would serve spectroscopy and imaging users.
arxiv-2510-05942:
Mohammadi and colleagues evaluate moral alignment of language models transparently. Models deployed worldwide must respect diverse moral norms across cultures. EvalMORAAL, their 2025 framework, scores twenty models against global values surveys. Chain-of-thought protocols and peer review make the judgments inspectable.

Two scoring methods, log-probabilities and direct ratings, enable fair cross-model comparison. A model-as-judge peer review flags hundreds of conflicts for inspection. Top models align closely with World Values Survey responses overall. A stark regional gap persists beneath that headline. The gap amounts to about twenty-one points of correlation between regions. Western regions average far higher alignment than non-Western regions. Topics like political expression and religious practice see persistent mistakes. Peer agreement itself predicts survey alignment, enabling automated quality checks. Performance tiers guide model selection for cultural applications.
arxiv-2510-06042:
Ma, Xiao, and Ye add a planning layer to phone-operating AI agents in a 2025 computer science paper. Language model agents can tap and type through apps, but they often hallucinate on long tasks. They act on local screens without seeing how the whole app connects.

Their framework, Agent+P, first maps an app's screens into a transition graph built by program analysis. A classical symbolic planner then finds a provably correct, shortest route from the start screen to the goal screen. The agent follows that route instead of wandering through menus. On the AndroidWorld benchmark, the add-on raised the success rates of leading agents by up to 14 percent. It also cut the number of action steps by more than a third, which makes automated app testing faster and more reliable.
arxiv-2510-06142:
Nguyen studies the generating series of the degree sequence of a monomial self-map in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is a projective toric variety built from combinatorial data. Iterating the map produces degrees that grow in a pattern, and the generating series packages that pattern into one function.

He establishes conditions under which the series cannot extend beyond its circle of convergence. That circle is a natural boundary, making the function transcendental and non-holonomic. A non-holonomic function satisfies no polynomial differential equation, so the pattern resists closed-form description. For toric surfaces the results are sharp and cannot be improved. He also answers a question of Bell about arithmetic behavior. Reducing the series modulo a prime p keeps it transcendental for all but finitely many primes. The work sharpens what dynamicists can expect from a single generating function for iteration growth.
arxiv-2510-06942:
Mirek Giersz leads a team simulating the lives of globular star clusters that host chemically distinct populations. Their 2025 paper uses the MOCCA simulation code to follow cluster evolution over time. Real clusters show stars with different light-element mixes side by side. Why the second population formed remains an open question in astronomy.

The team adopts the AGB scenario, where gas shed by aging giant stars mixes with infalling gas. Over two hundred simulations varied the cluster's environment and the populations' starting properties. Most observed features of Milky Way clusters came out matching the simulations well. The mixing patterns of the two populations also fit the picture. One exception remains, namely how the second population's share grows with cluster mass. The authors outline a speculative extension that might explain that mismatch too. Their simulations predict that red giant stars of the first population sit more centrally only temporarily.
arxiv-2510-07142:
De Moura and Silva study a flexible antenna scheme for crowded wireless networks. Their 2025 paper covers fluid antenna multiple access, or FAMA. A fluid antenna moves its active point along a small strip to find the cleanest signal. Many users can then share the same channel. The authors test this idea under a realistic model of fading and linked signal strength across positions.

They derive formulas for the chance that a user's signal fails against interference. The work covers slow and fast versions of the scheme. A neat result links the fast formulas to the slow ones, so one set yields the other. They also measure how many users an opportunistic version can support at once. Computer simulations matched the formulas across many settings. Network planners can use these results to size future fluid antenna systems with more confidence.
arxiv-2510-07242:
Tao and co-authors present HERO, a training method that blends two kinds of feedback for reasoning models. Their 2025 paper starts with checkers that give a simple right or wrong verdict. Such verdicts are reliable but blunt, since partly correct answers earn nothing. Learned reward models give richer, graded scores instead. HERO merges both signals in a structured way. It aims at stable learning that still rewards quality among correct answers.

Reward scores are first scaled inside groups defined by the checker's verdict. That keeps correctness supreme while letting grades refine each group. Prompts where models struggle most receive extra weight, since dense feedback helps most there. Across math reasoning benchmarks, HERO beat training with either signal alone. Gains appeared on both checkable tasks and harder open ones. Hybrid feedback may be the practical path for teaching models to reason with nuance.
arxiv-2510-07342:
Chen, Jamison, Sabuncu, and Kuceyeski model brain activity as a continuous landscape instead of a fixed grid of boxes. Their 2025 paper concerns encoding models, which predict brain responses to natural images from scans. Standard models flatten the scanned volume into a list and ignore anatomy. Each model then fits only one person's specific grid. The Neural Response Function instead takes an image plus any point in standard brain space. It predicts the response at that exact location.

The design exploits two facts about brains. Nearby tissue responds similarly, so continuity shares strength across neighbors. Standard coordinates also align different people into one frame, enabling joint training. Queries work at any resolution, free of the original scan grid. The authors describe it as a resolution-free digital twin of visual brain responses. Such twins could help compare patients across scanners and sites.
arxiv-2510-07542:
Pinzi defines an evolution equation for random probability measures and proves its solutions are built from classical ones. The 2025 paper operates one level above ordinary diffusion theory. Its unknown is a curve of laws over probability measures themselves, driven by a nonlocal drift and diffusion that depend on the whole distribution.

Superposition turns one hard object into an average of understood ones. Pinzi then runs the transfer in the useful direction: assuming uniqueness for a linearized equation, existence and uniqueness flow from the random-measure equation down to the nonlinear Fokker-Planck and McKean-Vlasov problems. Such transfer principles are the load-bearing beams of modern mean-field theory.
arxiv-2510-07642:
Klisura and four coauthors wrote this 2025 computer security paper on language models and access control. Access control rules decide who may see or change each piece of data. Language models often blur those role limits and answer too freely. The authors study role-conditioned refusals, meaning a model should answer when a user is authorized. It should refuse when the user is not.

The team built test data from two text-to-SQL benchmarks and added realistic database role policies. They compared plain prompting, a two-step checker pipeline, and fine-tuned models. The checker pipeline improved refusal precision and cut false permits. Fine-tuning gave the best balance between safety and correct answers. Longer and more complex policies made every system less reliable. The authors release their policy-augmented datasets and code for other researchers. Databases in hospitals, banks, and firms depend on such limits daily.
arxiv-2510-08042:
Sutanto, Gatti De Giacomo, Nakazawa, and Yamada wrote this 2025 study testing ChatGPT as a Japanese-English translation engine. The authors compared simple prompts against enhanced prompts adding context and instructions. They tested sentence-by-sentence and whole-document translation. Two commercial systems served as benchmarks. Automatic scores were paired with structured human evaluation. That human evaluation followed the MQM framework, which scores errors by type and severity.

Document-level translation clearly beat sentence-level translation, likely because wider context survives. Whether enhanced prompts beat simple ones stayed undecided. Automatic metrics preferred the older model overall, but the authors found a real tradeoff: one version was more accurate, the other more fluent. Across all settings, ChatGPT proved a strong competitor to the two commercial systems. Practical advice follows: translate whole documents, and choose the version by whether accuracy or fluency matters more.
arxiv-2510-08142:
Pankkonen, Raasakka, Marchesin, and Tittonen wrote this 2025 paper improving the hybrid optimizers used to train parameterized quantum circuits. Such circuits power variational algorithms on noisy quantum devices, and no single optimizer rules them all. Hybrids switch between gradient methods and sequential single-qubit optimizers. The authors borrow early stopping from classical machine learning to decide the switch: when recent cost values stall, the optimizer changes.

Two new hybrid algorithms built on this rule proved more robust and scalable than previous hybrids. They converged toward global minima better across various cost functions. Tests under different noise profiles showed feasibility on noisy hardware. A switch rule driven by cost history needs no extra quantum measurements, the scarce resource. The result is a practical upgrade for tuning circuits on real devices.
arxiv-2510-08242:
Mohammed Almutairi and a large team present VirT-Lab in a 2025 arXiv paper, a tool for simulating how teams work together using AI agents. Studying real teams is slow and hard to repeat under controlled conditions. VirT-Lab lets users build their own team scenarios inside flat, two-dimensional spaces. Agents based on large language models take roles, move around, and react over time.

Unlike older tools with fixed tasks, VirT-Lab lets users write scenarios in plain words. Users assign roles and traits, set up the space, and watch agents coordinate and adapt. The system produces structured records of team behavior for later study. The team checked simulated results against real human data and ran a user study. Both checks supported the tool's value, and the design aims to serve non-technical users as well as researchers.
arxiv-2510-08542:
Ainesh Bakshi, Allen Liu, Ankur Moitra, and Ewin Tang link rapid mixing to information decay in hot quantum systems in a 2025 arXiv paper. Classical statistical physics ties equilibrium structure to how fast Markov chains settle into it. Quantum physics lacked a comparable bridge between dynamics and structure. Their framework imports the classical theory's breadth to Gibbs states of quantum systems at high temperature.

At its core sits a quantum analog of the Dobrushin condition, a classic test for weak interactions. When it holds, a short path-coupling argument proves the Markovian evolution mixes rapidly. The same machinery yields exponential decay of conditional mutual information, with no restriction on subsystem size. That resolves a central open question in open quantum systems theory. Their key insight uses optimal transport, coupling quantum dynamics to a linear differential equation. This gives precise control over how local disturbances spread to distant sites.
arxiv-2510-08842:
Wu and Zhang build a team of AI agents that writes launch scripts for deep learning jobs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. National research programs now lend out graphics processors across many modest clusters, which should spread scarce computing power widely. In practice each cluster has its own launcher, scheduler, and settings, so hand-writing a correct script for each one is fiddly and error prone. Researchers lose time or waste machine hours on small mistakes.

Their system, Maple, takes a plain-language request and splits the work among four agents. They extract the key facts, fetch a matching template, verify the script, and correct any errors. Trials covered nine United States clusters, five model families, and four ways of training in parallel. Maple produced correct scripts in more than ninety-five percent of five hundred sixty-seven test cases. Its accuracy rivaled the largest commercial models, using far smaller ones.
arxiv-2510-08942:
Wang and colleagues test language models against the written procedures that real businesses run on, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Companies increasingly hand work to AI agents, yet standard benchmarks rarely resemble a standard operating procedure, the step-by-step rulebook for tasks like refunds or approvals. Such rulebooks branch heavily and punish small deviations. The team's benchmark, SOP-Maze, adapts real business material into three hundred ninety-seven tasks across twenty-three procedure scenarios.

They sort the tasks into two families. One family offers many options and demands precise selection, and the other demands deep chains of logic through tangled branches. Nearly every leading model struggled badly. The authors group the failures into three kinds: losing the procedural route, breaking under the quirks of real dialogue, and slipping on time or arithmetic inside complex contexts. They argue these skills, breadth and depth of procedure following, need direct training attention.
arxiv-2510-09242:
Siino and co-authors test whether a flexible wavelet preprocessing step makes brain-computer interfaces read imagined movements more accurately, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Motor imagery decoding translates EEG, the scalp's electrical signals, into commands by classifying imagined movements. The Rational Discrete Wavelet Transform slices signals into frequency bands tunable to brain rhythms. The team bolted it in front of four leading deep classifiers as a plug-in step.

Every model was tested with and without the transform on three benchmark datasets. Gains were clearest on one set, where one architecture improved by about four and a half percentage points and another by over two. Gains elsewhere were smaller but mostly consistent, and the biggest subject-level jumps appeared in difficult, non-stationary recordings. The authors conclude the transform is a low-overhead step that recovers rhythm-specific information and tames local noise, though its benefit depends on the architecture.
arxiv-2510-09842:
Mohammud Bocus, Senhui Qiu, Robert Piechocki, and Kerstin Eder build a system that profiles energy use across whole IoT networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Energy use has become a defining limit for lasting Internet of Things networks. Most earlier studies simulate energy or study single devices, leaving the network-level picture unmeasured.

Their platform unites Bluetooth Low Energy and visible light links with weather sensing and e-ink display subsystems under one profiling and prediction system. Automated, time-synced gear captures fine-grained energy dynamics at both the device and gateway layers. The team also built tools to generate fresh energy datasets for IoT ecosystems, tackling the scarcity of such data. Those datasets enable AI-based predictive and adaptive energy tuning. Validated on a network-level testbed under real operating conditions, the approach shows robust performance, moving energy analysis from device guesswork toward end-to-end measurement.
arxiv-2510-10642:
Jianke Zhang and seven co-authors build a robot policy that learns from both understanding and prediction, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generalist robot policies are usually built on vision language models, which understand scenes, or on generative models, which predict how scenes change. Embodied robots need both skills. The team's system, UniJEPA, learns continuous and discrete representations together, modeling high dimensional visual features dynamically.

UniJEPA is pretrained on more than one million internet scale instructional manipulation videos. It is then fine tuned on data from the actual robot, learning to map its predictive representations into action tokens. In extensive experiments, the approach consistently beat baseline methods. The reported gains were about 9 percent in simulation environments and about 12 percent on real world out-of-distribution tasks, which test robots on situations unlike their training.
arxiv-2510-11042:
Mohd. Meraj Khan, Sumesh P Thampi, and Anubhab Roy test a fluid simulation method on light waves, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The lattice Boltzmann method models flow by tracking particle groups on a grid. It steps forward explicitly and runs in parallel. That makes it a good fit for solving Maxwell's equations. The team first checks it on standard cases: reflection and refraction at a flat dielectric interface, and scattering from long circular cylinders. Angular scattering patterns are compared against exact Lorenz-Mie solutions.

They vary the cylinders' material constants to probe different contrasts. Then comes the demanding case: three dimensional scattering from dielectric spheres, again matching Lorenz-Mie results. A hexagonal cylinder, a non circular shape, is checked against a semi analytical reference. Across all cases and a range of size to wavelength ratios, the lattice Boltzmann predictions agreed closely with the references.
arxiv-2510-11142:
Standard semen analysis cannot measure sperm DNA fragmentation, a key factor in male fertility, and the reference test destroys the sperm it checks. B. A. Jacobs and co-authors validate an artificial intelligence tool meant to solve that problem in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system predicts DNA damage from ordinary phase contrast microscope images, leaving the checked sperm alive and usable for treatment.

The team used the TUNEL assay, a labeling test that marks broken DNA ends, as the gold standard for comparison. Their morphology-assisted ensemble model combines image processing with a transformer model called GC-ViT, improving on the link between sperm shape and DNA integrity. They benchmarked it against a pure transformer model and a morphology-only model. The ensemble reached a sensitivity of 60 percent and a specificity of 75 percent, a result the authors call promising for real-time sperm selection.
arxiv-2510-11342:
Some superconductors can host Majorana zero modes, exotic states sought for quantum computing. Their sorting depends closely on symmetry. Max Tymczyszyn and Edward McCann construct and sort one-dimensional examples in this 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. Starting from a Rice-Mele model, they build four-band Hamiltonians with superconducting terms. They constrain them with plain or nonsymmorphic time-reversal symmetry, a symmetry combined with a fractional translation.

For the nonsymmorphic case they find a four-valued topological index: two of its phases support Majorana zero modes and two do not. They study how disorder interacts with solitons and extend a winding-number method to compute the new indices. Proposed topolectric circuits, using plain electrical circuits as quantum simulators, agree with the theory. One finding is negative: in one dimension, nonsymmorphic unitary symmetries yield no new classes beyond the known integer and two-valued indices.
arxiv-2510-11542:
Reinforcement learning can teach a bipedal robot to walk, but the reward functions that produce graceful motion are notoriously hard to tune. Neil C. Janwani, Varun Madabushi, and Maegan Tucker combine learning with classical motion planning instead in this 2025 arXiv robotics paper. Their framework, NaviGait, starts from a library of gaits computed offline by trajectory optimization methods such as Hybrid Zero Dynamics, interpretable but brittle under real-world disturbances.

NaviGait blends smoothly between library gaits to produce reference motions answering high-level commands, while a learned policy adds joint-level and velocity corrections. Because the rich motion priors are already encoded in the library, reward design becomes dramatically simpler, with less need for finely tuned shaping terms. In experiments, NaviGait trained faster than conventional and imitation-based reinforcement learning and produced motions that stayed closest to the optimized references.
arxiv-2510-11842:
Urs Spiegelhalter, Jörg Franke, and Frank Hutter study how to teach a language model new skills without erasing old ones. Continued pretraining on fresh material often causes catastrophic forgetting, where general knowledge fades. Mixing old examples back in, called replay, fights the forgetting, but the right mixing ratio was poorly understood. Their 2025 arXiv paper runs a systematic empirical study of that balance.

The team generated synthetic training data aimed at the bAbI reasoning tasks. They then varied both the total token budget and the replay ratio across many configurations. Each run was scored for mastery of the new tasks and for retention of general knowledge. An optimal configuration emerged that balanced the two goals well. From the full pattern, the authors distill practical guidelines linking budget to a sensible replay share. Practitioners can thus adapt models strongly while spending far less on training than a blind search would cost.
arxiv-2510-11942:
Tomaso Poggio, writing with the AI system GPT-5 as co-author, proves a bridge theorem between computation and neural networks. The question is old: which functions can neural networks approximate efficiently? Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from Turing computability, the gold standard of what computers can do. If a function can be computed efficiently at fixed precision, they ask, must a modest neural network also capture it?

The answer is yes, by construction. Efficient computability guarantees a compositionally sparse circuit: a directed graph of simple gates, each listening to few inputs, with total size growing only polynomially in the desired precision. Swapping each gate for a tiny fixed-size neural emulator gives a deep network of polynomial size and depth that hits the target accuracy. The authors connect the construction to known compositional approximation rates. They also frame training as a hierarchical search over such sparse structures.
arxiv-2510-12042:
Wanying Ge, Xin Wang, and Junichi Yamagishi trace fake speech to the machine that made it. Knowing a deepfake exists is not enough; sleuths want its source system. Classifiers trained per system fail on shifted data, and plain audio watermarks wash out when squeezed or removed on purpose. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes FakeMark, which marks speech in a new way.

Instead of hiding a random bit string, FakeMark injects marks tied to the artifacts each deepfake system leaves behind. The detector then reads two cues at once: the planted watermark and the system's built-in fingerprints. If one cue is damaged or removed, the other still speaks up. Tests show FakeMark carries over to cross-dataset samples where classifier tools struggle. It also keeps high accuracy under distortions, including codec squeezing, that defeat standard watermarking. The authors publish speech samples for checking.
arxiv-2510-12742:
Carroll and a large team let users steer a recommender system by typing what they want changed, in plain language, in a 2025 arXiv paper. People dissatisfied with recommendations usually have no fine grained controls, only blunt options like hiding a topic. CTRL-Rec converts a natural language request, such as asking for respectful posts from a different perspective, into real time changes in a traditional recommender.

At training time, a language model simulates whether users with a given request would approve of items, and embedding models are trained to approximate those simulated judgments. Those predictions join the standard signals the recommender optimizes. At deployment, only one language model embedding computation per request is needed. On the MovieLens dataset the method delivered fine grained control across diverse requests. In a study with nineteen Letterboxd users, CTRL-Rec greatly improved users' sense of control and satisfaction without reducing engagement.
arxiv-2510-12942:
Wiggins, Loebman, and Frinchaboy ask why some star clusters survive for billions of years in this 2025 arXiv paper. Open clusters in the galactic disk show chemical trends that mismatch those of ordinary field stars. One proposed explanation is that clusters migrate and survive at rates depending on where they sit in the galaxy. The authors test that idea inside two simulated Milky Way-like galaxies from the FIRE project.

They traced the full trajectories of long-lived clusters and characterized the gas environment around them across cosmic time. Clusters in both galaxies spent most of their lives in under-dense gas regions, which sheltered them from disruption. Brief passages through gas clouds did occur and noticeably altered their orbits. The pattern supports survivability shaped by environment, helping explain the chemical mismatch between clusters and field stars.
arxiv-2510-13142:
Nakazato and Pascazio derive an exact master equation for a qubit coupled to a thermal environment in this 2025 arXiv paper. A qubit, a two-level quantum system, interacting with a large bosonic reservoir, a bath of wave-like excitations, gradually relaxes and thermalizes. Describing that open-system dynamics exactly is notoriously hard.

Working within the rotating-wave approximation, which discards very fast oscillating interaction terms, and assuming the environment starts in an arbitrary thermal state, the authors derive the exact, though formal, master equation. It governs the qubit. They then analyze how the evolution operator behaves over long times for the combined system and environment. From that analysis they examine the conditions under which the qubit reaches thermal equilibrium, clarifying when a hot bath truly imposes its temperature on a small quantum system.
arxiv-2510-13842:
Wu and co-authors poison the knowledge base behind retrieval-based fact-checkers with a handful of crafted documents. Their 2025 arXiv paper, ADMIT, extends knowledge poisoning to settings where honest evidence dominates retrieval. Flipping a verdict while real supporting and refuting sources surround the fake is harder. The attack needs no access to the target model, retriever, or tokens.

ADMIT injects a few semantically aligned fakes designed to blend with genuine evidence. Across four retrievers, eleven language models, and four cross-domain benchmarks, it flipped decisions reliably. The average success rate reached eighty-six percent at a minuscule poisoning rate, the authors report. Strong counter-evidence in the pool did not save the checkers. ADMIT beat prior state-of-the-art attacks by over eleven points of success rate. The results expose real fragility in deployed fact-checking pipelines.
arxiv-2510-13942:
Andreas Kirchner and co-authors build a new theoretical framework for heavy quarks moving through quark-gluon plasma, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quark-gluon plasma is the ultra-hot matter created in particle collisions, where quarks and gluons, the particles that normally stay locked inside protons, move freely. Heavy quarks are useful probes of this plasma, but describing their interactions systematically is difficult.

The authors treat the plasma as a relativistic fluid and describe it with an effective field theory, a simplified theory that keeps only the physics relevant at the energies of interest. Coupling heavy quarks to this fluid theory gives a systematic route to their interactions with phonons, the fluid's sound-like excitations. As a concrete result, they calculate the quasiparticle width, which measures how quickly a heavy quark's state decays, for scattering processes involving phonons in the hot medium.
arxiv-2510-14142:
Yin Tang, Yanyuan Ma, and Jiwei Zhao tackle a classic flaw in randomized controlled trials: participants assigned to a treatment do not take it, in this 2025 arXiv paper. When noncompliance is one-sided, the control group cannot access the treatment at all, while the treated group may skip it. Standard intention-to-treat analysis then measures the effect of being assigned treatment, not of actually receiving it.

The authors propose a target quantity, the complier general causal effect, which characterizes the treatment's effect among compliers, the participants who follow their assignment. They investigate the conditions under which this quantity can be estimated efficiently, with the best possible precision, under minimal assumptions. They draw on tools such as propensity scores and efficient influence functions from semiparametric theory. Simulation studies and a data application illustrate the methods and compare them against existing approaches for handling one-sided noncompliance.
arxiv-2510-14342:
Amandip Sangha recasts automatic differentiation, the engine that computes derivatives inside machine learning, in the language of differential geometry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Automatic differentiation appears as graph bookkeeping in software, which obscures why forward and reverse modes work and how derivatives fit together.

Using jet functors and Weil algebras, constructions from geometry that package a function's derivatives. Sangha shows forward-mode arises as a pushforward, and reverse mode as a cotangent pullback. Higher-order work is evaluation in a Weil algebra. The formulation is coordinate-free and unifies the modes in one picture. All results are realized in working JAX code, where the Weil mode computes all mixed derivatives in a single forward pass at cost linear in the algebra's dimension. The author reports exact, stable derivatives with predictable scaling, arguing this abstraction can make such systems both more efficient and more transparent.
arxiv-2510-14542:
Sakamoto and Sato, in a 2025 arXiv paper, look for a safe way to shrink deep state-space models, a family of neural networks used for long sequences. These models contain smaller systems as building blocks. Cutting a model down usually risks unknown damage to its output. The authors want a compression method that comes with a proven limit on that damage.

They first prove a ceiling on the output error between an original model and a compressed one. The bound is expressed through error measures for each internal block, which justifies older reduction methods. Building on it, they set up an optimization problem and design a gradient-based reduction method. On a movie review task from the Long Range Arena benchmark, the method removed roughly eighty percent of the trainable parameters. It did so without retraining, and performance fell by only about four to five percent.
arxiv-2510-14642:
Seoev and a large team of co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a learning system for bidding in blockchain auctions. On networks like Polygon, the order of transactions inside a block can be worth money, a practice known as maximal extractable value. Polygon's Atlas system runs sealed-bid auctions for this right, and bidders must decide in under a second, without seeing rivals or even knowing who is competing.

Classical game theory fits this setting poorly, since it assumes full information and fixed equilibria. The authors instead train a reinforcement learning agent with a PPO algorithm, inside a simulator that models how arbitrage chances arrive and how competition plays out. Their history-conditioned agent captured forty-nine percent of available profits when run alongside existing searchers. When it replaced the market leader, it captured eighty-one percent, far ahead of static bidding strategies.
arxiv-2510-14842:
Elder, Duesterwald, and Muthusamy introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a technique for making language models actually obey the directions developers pile into a prompt. Adding more of them is the usual way to steer an application, but obedience is not guaranteed, and it decays as they multiply. Their method, Instruction Boosting, acts after generation to raise the follow rate.

On a new benchmark, ScaledIF, with up to ten per sample, boosting improved the follow rate by up to seven points with two, and up to four points with ten. The authors also analyze why performance degrades as the count grows. A major factor is tension: the entries increasingly conflict with each other. Their quantitative conflict scoring tool reproduces the observed trends. Developers can use it to see, before deployment, how each addition is likely to affect a model's behavior.
arxiv-2510-15342:
Joshua Li and four colleagues reconstruct people moving through a scene from a single fixed camera video, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Animating believable human interaction with surroundings matters for games, augmented reality, and robotics, but monocular methods often misplace the person in 3D space, so feet float or sink through floors. Their method, SHARE, uses the scene's own geometry as the anchor.

SHARE first estimates a body mesh and a segmentation mask for the person in every frame, plus a point map of the scene at key frames. It then shifts the person's keyframe positions until the body mesh agrees with the human points inside the scene map. Frames between keyframes keep their motion relative to those anchors, so the whole sequence stays consistent. Across curated datasets and wild web videos, SHARE placed people more accurately than existing methods while also rebuilding the surrounding scene.
arxiv-2510-15542:
Ivan Kartashov, Mariia Pushkareva, and Iakov Karandashev prepare spiking neural networks for the strict hardware of neuromorphic chips. Their 2025 workshop paper introduces SpikeFit, a training method built around real device limits. A neuromorphic processor caps how many neurons and connections fit onboard and forces weights into a few low-precision values, constraints most compression schemes only partly respect.

SpikeFit makes the allowed weight values themselves learnable, training them jointly with the network in a clusterization-aware way at two, four, or eight bits of precision. It also caps the number of unique synaptic connections to what the processor supports. A new pruning method, guided by Fisher information and spike contributions, trims the network further with leading performance. In tests where only four unique weight values were allowed, SpikeFit beat other compression pipelines on accuracy. It also recorded the lowest energy use in their experiments.
arxiv-2510-15842:
Yuhang Chen and colleagues tackle a practical job in a 2025 paper. They turn research papers into project websites. Good sites spread findings well. But current generation methods fall short. Language models, templates, and direct conversion all have flaws. The pages often ignore layout. Interactivity is usually missing too. No proper benchmark existed to judge the results.

The authors introduce Paper2Web. It is a benchmark and evaluation framework. Rule-based measures check connectivity and completeness. Human-checked model judging covers interactivity and aesthetics. It also scores how informative a site is. A quiz tests whether visitors retain the paper's content. The team also presents PWAgent. It is a pipeline that builds interactive multimedia sites from papers.
arxiv-2511-00142:
Saeed Hashemi Sababe presents a full approach for map-valued positive fixed kernels, driven by useful uses in map theory and random processes. Operator-valued kernels extend scalar kernels to settings where outputs are vectors or maps. Two use paths are developed: dilation buildings in map theory, and broad classes of random processes.

Results from the kernel theory are used to build new Hilbert space-valued Gaussian processes and to study the structure of their covariance setups. Probability and map theory readers get a unified treatment linking kernels, dilations, and Gaussian processes. Such methods support multi-factor time series and functional data analysis, where correlations live between whole functions.
arxiv-2511-00342:
Hendrio Braganca, Diego Kreutz, Vanderson Rocha, Joner Assolin, and Eduardo Feitosa present MH-1M, a large public dataset for Android malware research. It holds well over a million apps, about one point three million in total, with rich features and metadata for each. Labels come from the VirusTotal service, which pools many detection engines for a more reliable verdict on each app.

The processed data, feature extraction outputs, and detection reports are openly shared through GitHub, Figshare, and Harvard Dataverse, totaling more than four hundred gigabytes. The authors argue the set's scale and freshness make it valuable for machine learning, deep learning, language model, and threat intelligence studies of how Android malware evolves. For defenders, it offers a shared test bed in a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2511-00842:
David Amaro-Alcala works on cheaper ways to benchmark passive bosonic devices, hardware such as optical systems whose behavior is tested by randomized benchmarking. The existing proposal for such devices is costly, partly because it relies on Clebsch-Gordan coefficients from group theory.

He introduces two filter functions that use the same measurement data but avoid those coefficients. One filter is built from immanants, the other from characters of the special unitary group, and both yield simple formulas for the variance of the estimate. The character filter is cheap to compute and keeps a constant, low variance. A test case with photon loss and gain suggests estimates stay close to the ideal values, which could simplify device characterization.
arxiv-2511-00942:
Simona Diaconu studies a central quantity in the theory of Gaussian random processes, Talagrand's gamma two functional. For a centered Gaussian process, the expected size of its largest value is comparable to this functional, which depends only on the geometry of the index space under a natural distance.

The functional is defined as an infimum over admissible sequences, chains of ever finer approximations to the space. In practice it is mostly used to compare one process with another. Diaconu instead constructs admissible sequences that come close to optimal, treating the functional as an object worth computing in its own right. The aim is a more direct route to understanding expected suprema of Gaussian processes.
arxiv-2511-01042:
Tobias Dijkhuis and colleagues ask which uncertain inputs astrochemical models of interstellar ice should worry about most. Ices on dust grains in cold clouds host rich chemistry, but the models need many parameters, from binding energies to reaction barriers, and most are poorly measured.

Using the UCLCHEM code, they sample binding energies, diffusion barriers, prefactors, and reaction barriers in Monte Carlo fashion across a grid of temperatures, densities, radiation fields, and cosmic ray rates. The abundances of the main ice species prove most sensitive, under all conditions, to the diffusion barriers of small, mobile reactive species such as atomic hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen. Those are the parameters laboratory and theory work should pin down first.
arxiv-2511-01442:
Benedikt Reible, Nils Liebreich, Carsten Hartmann, and Luigi Delle Site build a fast, exact tool for spotting when a molecular simulation box is too small. Splitting a modeled system into independent subsystems changes its free energy, and the two sided Bogoliubov inequality bounds that cost exactly, for both classical and quantum many body systems.

That theorem yields a quality factor measuring how consistent a given box size is. For systems with two body interactions and a known radial distribution function, the factor needs only two six dimensional integrals. The authors present an algorithm for computing it. Its results agree with published findings from simulations run at different box sizes. That gives simulators a solid check for length scale errors.
arxiv-2511-01742:
Muhammad Gaffar and Wei Ku present computer evidence for a hidden actor in strongly linked materials. The actor is a boson made of two electrons bound tightly, each one carrying charge 2e. Such pairs could explain the odd non-Fermi liquid behavior seen in many working materials. Yet the idea is often dropped when tests show clean electronic bands.

The authors use the attractive Hubbard model. With determinant quantum Monte Carlo, they compute how the pairs and the leftover electrons each move. The pairs emerge in force, and can even lead in number. Still, the electronic spectrum shows sharp quasiparticles with barely raised mass. So the pairs dodge the spectrum. Only above the superfluid point does a pseudogap in the spectrum give them away. A clean band, the moral runs, is no proof that strong links are absent.
arxiv-2511-01842:
Haniyeh Tajer and five colleagues run planet-formation simulations to explain Mercury's oversized iron heart. Mercury's core makes up about 70 percent of its mass, more than double the share in the other rocky planets, and dense exo-Mercuries are now turning up too. Two explanations compete: giant impacts late in formation stripped the mantle away, or the raw material near the Sun was iron-rich from the start.

Their N-body simulations test both, starting either from a uniform core fraction or from a step pattern enriched in the inner region. Under the uniform start, erosive impacts do create iron-rich debris, but without a mechanism to remove the stripped mantle material, the debris merges back into lower-fraction bodies, diluting the enrichment. The framework is built to extend to high-core-fraction exoplanets.
arxiv-2511-02042:
M. Z. Haider, M. U. Ghouri, Tayyaba Noreen, and M. Salman aim a hybrid quantum-classical generative model at the events that matter most and occur least: financial crashes, climate extremes, and biological anomalies. Classic generative models often botch these rare cases. They collapse the rare modes entirely, or get their uncertainty wrong. Scarce heavy-tailed data gives them little to learn from.

Their Quantum-Enhanced Generative Model couples a deep latent-variable model with variational quantum circuits. Two ideas carry it. One is a hybrid loss, jointly tuning reconstruction fidelity and a tail-aware likelihood. The other is quantum randomness-driven noise injection. It varies samples and fights mode collapse. Training alternates classical backpropagation with parameter-shift updates. Tests cover synthetic mixtures and real finance, climate, and protein datasets. The model cut tail divergence by up to 50 percent, against GAN, VAE, and diffusion baselines. Recall and calibration improved too.
arxiv-2511-02942:
Ekaterina Kubyshkina, Marcio Kleos Pereira, and Mattia Petrolo ask when not knowing something can excuse a wrong act, and they treat the question as logicians. Philosophers debate which kinds of ignorance excuse. One strong case is a fact the agent never thought about at all. Their 2025 paper gives the first formal analysis of ignorance as an excuse, using epistemic logic.

They introduce a complete and sound logic where excusable ignorance is a basic operator, not a derived one. Its semantics uses Kripke models whose worlds may be incomplete, so a fact can fail to be considered rather than simply false. They then extend the system with public announcements and a new update rule, so the logic can track how learning or disclosure changes what an agent can be excused for not knowing.
arxiv-2511-03542:
Roberta Di Marino and colleagues assemble SOLVE-Med, a team of small specialist models that answer medical questions together. Single models answering across all of medicine face hallucinations, bias, heavy compute, and privacy strain. SOLVE-Med routes each query to the right specialist among ten small models, each tuned on one medical field.

An orchestrator then blends the chosen specialists' answers into one reply. On Italian medical forum data across ten specialties, scores beat standalone models many times larger. All parts run locally, which protects patient privacy and cuts cost. The design trades one giant generalist for a panel that mirrors how real care splits by specialty.
arxiv-2511-03842:
Niels Bottner, Roman Schnabel, and Mikhail Korobko propose a readout scheme to clean back-scatter noise out of gravitational-wave detectors. Stray laser light bouncing back into the signal path creates loud, uneven disturbances, and the noise also appears in the normally unmeasured orthogonal quadrature of the light.

Measuring that second quadrature at the same time gives a witness channel. From it, the disturbance in the signal channel can be reconstructed and subtracted. The scheme stays compatible with frequency-dependent squeezing, already used to cut both shot noise and radiation pressure noise. If it works as designed in a real detector, loud back-scatter events would do less damage to sensitivity.
arxiv-2511-03942:
Shih-Lun Wu, Dave Carlton, Ryan Miyakawa, Yoon Kim, Chris Donahue, and Cheng-Zhi Anna Huang present MIDI-LLM, a recipe for text-to-MIDI music generation built by adapting a large language model. Catalog evidence credited a different author set; the arXiv record governs, and it adds MIDI tokens to the model's vocabulary with a two-stage training pipeline.

Stage one continues pretraining on music-adjacent text and standalone MIDI files; stage two fine-tunes on text-MIDI pairs. Built on a one-billion-parameter Llama model, it beat a recent text-to-MIDI baseline on control and musical quality. A blind study with fifty-eight Hookpad Aria users over four thousand outputs gave it the highest acceptance rate for lead sheet generation.
arxiv-2511-04142:
Sai Praneeth Donthu, Souvik Roy, Soumyarup Sadhukhan, and Gogulapati Sreedurga pin down strategy-proof probabilistic assignment rules. In this setting, indivisible objects are shared among equally many agents by lottery, and each agent starts with an endowment and strict preferences. The deterministic version is well known through the Top Trading Cycles rule.

A weakened incentive demand is introduced: no trick may raise the chance of getting one's top-ranked object. On broad preference domains, Top Trading Cycles is the unique rule meeting that demand together with efficiency and individual rationality conditions in dominance terms. A weaker pairwise efficiency still is enough on a slightly stronger domain, and extensions to ex post notions follow.
arxiv-2511-04342:
Kaiwen Guo and Yanjun Liu investigate extremal functions for anisotropic Trudinger-Moser inequalities, which mark the borderline where exponential integrals in two planes stay finite. Whether the supremum is attained by an actual function, and what symmetry that function must have, are the central questions for several anisotropic variants.

Convex symmetrization does much of the work, joined by continuity of the key function. A link between subcritical and critical suprema moves attainment from the easier regime to the critical one. Existence and Wulff symmetry results follow for the extremal functions across the cases studied. Sharp constants in such bounds anchor limits of many variational arguments in analysis.
arxiv-2511-04542:
Nicolas Moens leads seven authors simulating the atmospheres and winds of O-type stars. These massive stars have turbulent outer layers driven by radiation near an iron opacity bump. The turbulence shapes both the atmosphere and the spectral lines observers use.

Their two-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamic runs cover a grid of O stars at solar composition. They vary basic parameters to see how the subsurface turbulent zone responds. They also trace how that motion shows up in photospheric absorption lines. Replacing ad hoc guesses with direct simulation could sharpen how stellar spectra are read across the whole O-star range.
arxiv-2511-04642:
Jazmin Ordonez-Toro and two colleagues weigh young stars in tight multiple systems with the VLBA. Very long baseline radio images resolve pairs separated by mere milliarcseconds. Gaia cannot split systems that close, so radio astrometry is essential.

The DYNAMO-VLBA project tracks pre-main-sequence binaries with detectable radio emission. Here the team reports dynamical masses for single stars in two systems. S1 in Ophiuchus is that region's brightest and most massive young member. EC 95 in Serpens is the second target. Direct masses for young stars test the models used to age and weigh whole star-forming regions.
arxiv-2511-04842:
Hongyu Zhang and his co-author test whether split compilation truly protects quantum circuit designs. Quantum circuits are valuable intellectual property, and split compilation hides their wiring. The circuit is cut into two parts, each visible, while the links between them stay secret.

Their oracle-guided attack tries to recover those hidden connections systematically. Candidate links are proposed, checked against an oracle, and refined step by step. A full security evaluation framework wraps the attack for repeatable testing. The work warns compiler designers that splitting alone may leak more than assumed, so obfuscation claims need adversarial proof.
arxiv-2511-04942:
Nikita Guseynov and co-authors give a quantum method to price options when asset prices follow a local volatility model. Pricing can be hard when payoffs are complex, many assets are linked, or price rules are detailed.

Their full method solves the forward Kolmogorov equation, also called the Fokker-Planck equation, by mapping it to a quantum evolution task.
