They spell out state prep, the main run, and price read-out by a swap test. Read-out gains are a key plus of solving the forward form rather than the backward pricing form used in most past work.
arxiv-2511-05342:
D. Kynoch and co-authors report three months of dense X-ray, ultraviolet, and optical watching of the Seyfert galaxy MCG+08-11-11, with the Swift satellite plus ground telescopes. Light echoes between bands show how the hot core's glow is reprocessed by nearby matter.

The twelve light curves track each other closely. The X-ray to ultraviolet link is the strongest yet seen in a Seyfert galaxy, by the authors' count. Lags grow with wavelength, as reprocessing predicts, but the lag spectrum is far flatter than a past one, which poses a puzzle for disk models.
arxiv-2511-05442:
Frauke Andersen and co-authors present APP, a faster form of path patching for finding circuits inside a language model. Circuit discovery is a key step in mechanistic interpretability, but path patching is slow and has seen little deep use on small models.

APP first prunes the search space with a contrastive attention head method. That method, built on causal mediation ideas, scores heads by how task-bound they are and cuts the rest. With far fewer heads to test, patching runs much faster. Tests check that the found circuits still match the slow method's finds.
arxiv-2511-05542:
Jeff Brown, Andrew Kirjner, Annika Vivekananthan, and Ed Boyden ask whether large language models can proofread brain wiring maps. Making such a map, called a connectome, takes huge human effort. People must check data from imaging and machine segmentation by hand, fixing wrong splits and merges.

Their test, ConnectomeBench, grades models on three proofreading jobs. It uses expert-marked data from mouse visual cortex and the full fruit fly brain. Top models did well on naming segment types and fixing split errors, scoring far above chance. They still lagged experts and struggled to spot merge errors, so human proofreaders remain needed for now.
arxiv-2511-05642:
Justin Williams, Kishor Datta Gupta, Roy George, and Mrinmoy Sarkar show a small robot that sees, reasons, and moves at the same time using only its own hardware. Robots working where GPS fails need local, frugal intelligence. Past systems often split perception from motion or lean on cloud computing.

Their framework runs a compact vision-language model on the robot itself. The model reads the scene and reasons about it while the robot keeps moving through changing surroundings. Trials on a mobile robot checked the trade-off between compute cost, task accuracy, and response speed. The authors present the run as an early proof that small models can guide edge robots in service, disaster, and defense work.
arxiv-2511-05942:
Vladimir Kozlov and Oleg Motygin analyze when a family of water waves trades stability with the smooth flow it branches from. They study steady waves in a two-dimensional channel with a flat bottom and free surface, ignoring surface tension. The flow rotates with constant vorticity, and a branch of Stokes waves grows out of a laminar flow as the wave period varies.

The first eigenvalue along the branch stays negative. The second, small eigenvalue decides whether the exchange-of-stability principle holds, and whether the period grows or shrinks near the critical point. The authors show a critical depth splits the two signs for each vorticity. They compare that depth with the depth where a stagnation point forms, and find the order flips at a specific vorticity value.
arxiv-2511-06142:
Sizhe Tang, Jiayu Chen, and Tian Lan target a weakness of Monte Carlo Tree Search when many agents must plan together. The joint action space grows explosively as agents are added, so the search tree branches too fast to explore well. Their system, MALinZero, compresses that space before searching.

MALinZero projects joint-action returns into a low-dimensional form modeled as a contextual linear bandit problem. A new tree search rule built on linear confidence bounds then balances trying new actions against using known good ones. The authors bound the method's regret and give an approximation algorithm for picking joint actions. Tests on matrix games and the SMAC benchmarks beat model-based and model-free rivals.
arxiv-2511-06542:
Chaegeun Song, Zhong Zheng, Bing Li, and Lingzhou Xue tame categorical predictors that splinter regression data into too many tiny groups. Categories are everywhere in applied regression, and modern datasets keep adding more. Each extra category fragments the available information and drags accuracy down, so merging look-alike categories is attractive if done carefully.

Their method uses a pairwise vector fused lasso, a penalty that automatically fuses categories whose relationship with the response looks the same. The approach fits a broad family of models with general loss functions, and the authors prove it merges the right categories consistently. A practical gradient algorithm, tested on simulations and Spotify music data, improved prediction while simplifying the categories.
arxiv-2511-06642:
Renato Castro, Rodrigo Paredes, and Douglas Kahn predict which shops will actually grow after receiving a free commercial beverage cooler. In fast-moving consumer goods, placing coolers is a costly bet on future sales, and machine learning rarely guides that placement. Churn and demand models are common, but asset allocation decisions stay mostly manual.

The study follows more than three thousand traditional trade clients of a Central American brewer, with a year of sales before and after installation. Gradient boosting models, explained through SHAP values, forecast which clients clear ten, thirty, or fifty percent growth targets. The best model scored strongly at every threshold, and simulations suggest better returns plus savings from skipping clients unlikely to grow.
arxiv-2511-06742:
Adam Piaseczny, Eric Ruzomberka, Rohit Parasnis, and Christopher Brinton probe how attackers should position themselves inside decentralized federated learning. Removing the central server speeds training through device-to-device links but opens new attack surfaces. Where malicious nodes sit in the network, rather than just how many there are, had gone largely unstudied.

The authors adapt span-based and centrality-based placement strategies to this setting and propose a hybrid, MaxSpAN-FL, that randomizes where nodes sit using topology cues. across network shapes and attacker counts, the hybrid attack degraded model training more than baseline schemes. Theory explains why eigenvector centrality attacks underperform here. The results map a weakness that future defenses must close.
arxiv-2511-06842:
Lionel Levine, Haniyeh Ehsani Oskouie, Sajjad Ghiasvand, and Majid Sarrafzadeh present a method for shrinking neural networks without losing accuracy. Their approach, M2M-DC, ranks building blocks of a network by how much label-relevant information they carry and prunes the least informative ones. It then alternates short knowledge distillation phases with careful channel slicing inside each stage.

The slicing respects the shape constraints of residual connections, so pruned networks stay valid. On the CIFAR-100 image benchmark, compressed ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 models kept accuracy near their teachers while using far fewer parameters and operations. A compressed MobileNetV2 even beat its teacher by about two and a half points of accuracy, showing the recipe works across network classes.
arxiv-2511-06942:
Fangqi Dai, Xingjian Jiang, and Zizhuang Deng build a detector for text that machines have revised rather than written outright. Detectors excel at spotting fully machine-generated text but struggle with polished human drafts that a model has reworked, especially when the generating model is unknown. Their idea starts from the hypothesis that human writing has distinctive stylistic patterns a model can be tuned to prefer.

The detector, HLPD, uses a reward-based alignment process that shifts a scoring model's token distribution toward human-like writing, making it more sensitive to departures from human style. It is tested in an adversarial system where a five-dimensional prompt generator and several advanced language models create varied revision cases. Against GPT-revised text it improved detection scores greatly over the ImBD and Fast-DetectGPT baselines.
arxiv-2511-07042:
Arjo Dasgupta and five co-authors explore dipoles arranged in triangular optical ladders, a lab platform where geometric frustration amplifies long-range dipolar interactions. For mobile polarized dipolar bosons, frustration can drive a transition between a chiral superfluid, whose flow breaks mirror symmetry, and an plain two-part superfluid. The authors show this transition should be reachable at temperatures today's tests already achieve, even with the weak interactions of magnetic atoms.

They also treat pinned spin-half dipoles, realized by polar molecules in two rotational states, which emulate frustrated dipolar XXZ spin models. Tuning the strength and orientation of an outside electric field moves these systems through a rich landscape of ground states, including chiral and nematic phases, and yields striking chiral dynamics worth probing.
arxiv-2511-07342:
Lorenzo Baldi, Rainer Sinn, Máté L Telek, and Julian Weigert extend Pólya's classic theorem for certifying that a polynomial is positive. Pólya's method multiplies a homogeneous polynomial that is strictly positive on the nonnegative orthant by a high power of the sum of variables. It then simply checks that all coefficients come out positive, an easy certificate. But the method can fail when the polynomial misses certain monomials of its degree, as sparse polynomials do.

Using tools from positive toric geometry, the authors present extensions and converses of Pólya's theorem adapted to sparse polynomials, so the missing-monomial cases gain certificates of their own. They also explore an application outside pure algebra. They use these positivity certificates to study the convergence of Feynman integrals in particle physics, where knowing an integral's integrand has a definite sign matters.
arxiv-2511-07542:
Hakim Atek and a large collaboration introduce GLIMPSE, among the deepest sky surveys yet taken with the James Webb Space Telescope. The program images one lensing field for twenty to forty hours per filter across nine near-infrared bands. Gravity from a foreground cluster magnifies faint early galaxies behind it.

Depths reach fainter than magnitude thirty, exposing galaxies from the era when the universe was first lit up. Hubble imaging, ground spectroscopy, and Webb spectra support the survey. Early results already probe galaxy birth and cosmic reionization. The overview lays out design, lens models, and goals for astronomers planning follow-up work.
arxiv-2511-07642:
Rafael Pereira, Túlio Vales, and Cássio Morais extend dynamics theory to maps that return sets instead of single points. For open set-valued maps, each point maps to an open connected region. Earlier work described the combinatorial shape of the final recurrent set where motion returns.

Adding transitivity and mixing brings that framework closer to Smale spectral decomposition for ordinary maps. Such maps turn out to carry infinite topological entropy, meaning their complexity grows without bound. Transitive examples also connect to transitive Anosov diffeomorphisms, the classic chaotic systems. The results give set-valued dynamics, used in economics and control, a firmer theoretical footing.
arxiv-2511-07742:
Luan Lazzari and Kleinner Farias built a checker that catches clashes between software diagrams as modelers draw them. UML class diagrams and sequence diagrams must agree, yet students and engineers routinely let them drift apart. Teaching consistency is notoriously hard when feedback arrives late.

Harmony Validator plugs into the Papyrus modeling environment and watches editing events live. Inconsistencies are flagged and reported at the moment they appear. Event-driven checking turns consistency from an exam topic into a habit formed while drawing. Modeling courses and professional teams both gain earlier, cheaper correction of design mistakes.
arxiv-2511-07942:
Rishabh Agrawal, Yusuf Alvi, Rahul Jain, and Ashutosh Nayyar tackle imitation learning when conditions change after training. Robots often learn from expert examples because writing reward rules by hand is hard. Standard methods assume the world stays fixed, yet real shifts in dynamics can badly hurt performance.

Their balance equation approach learns only from demonstrations gathered under normal conditions, with no new interaction. It seeks a policy that does well even under the worst likely change in dynamics. Tests on continuous control tasks show stronger robustness and generalization than leading offline imitation methods, especially in disturbed settings.
arxiv-2511-08042:
J V Roig presents KAMI, a benchmark meant to judge agentic AI systems on work that resembles enterprise use. Ordinary language model tests suffer from training data contamination and ignore multi step tool use under uncertainty. Companies need rankings that predict real deployment value, not just exam style scores.

The index runs one hundred seventy thousand test items, over five and a half billion tokens, across thirty five model setups. Traditional rankings poorly predicted practical agentic results, and newer models did not always beat their predecessors. The report also examines cost against performance, model behavior patterns, and how reasoning affects token efficiency.
arxiv-2511-08242:
Waseem AlShikh and co-authors argue that AI agents should be judged by outcomes rather than by infrastructure measures such as latency or token speed. A white paper framework offers eleven task agnostic, outcome based metrics covering decision quality, autonomy, adaptability, and business value. Named examples include goal completion rate, an autonomy index, multi step task resilience, and business impact efficiency.

A large simulation compares four agent designs, from ReAct to a hybrid, across health care, finance, marketing, legal, and customer service domains. Clear trade offs emerge between designs. The hybrid agent performs most consistently, with the highest average goal completion rate in their tests.
arxiv-2511-08642:
Jingwen Fu and four co-authors design a communication system that sends only what a task needs from text, audio, and video traveling together. Bandwidth is tight and channels are noisy, so the system must squeeze out overlap between the streams without losing the details the receiving task depends on.

A two-stage variational information bottleneck does the squeezing. Each stream is first compressed alone, keeping its task-specific features, while an adversarial module trims cross-stream dependence so the streams complement rather than repeat each other. A second stage compresses the fused result and hardens it against channel distortion. On multi-modal emotion recognition tests the framework beats existing baselines on accuracy and reliability. The gains grow largest when the signal-to-noise ratio is low.
arxiv-2511-08942:
Mobin Habibpour and Fatemeh Afghah hand the strategy of household navigation to a vision-language model instead of letting it merely label what the robot sees. In object-goal navigation the robot must find a named target in an unfamiliar home, and frontier-based exploration alone wanders without a plan.

Three techniques make the model an active strategist. Structured chain-of-thought prompting draws out step-by-step reasoning about where the target likely sits. The robot's recent action history is fed back in, which keeps the agent from looping over the same ground. The model also reads top-down obstacle maps beside its first-person camera views, sharpening its spatial sense. On the HM3D, Gibson, and MP3D benchmarks the resulting paths are notably more direct and logical than earlier approaches.
arxiv-2511-09542:
Jingyang Li and Yang Chen forecast matrix and tensor time series by using the fact that most interactions are local. Each entry in such data depends mainly on a small neighborhood, like nearby grid cells in an ionosphere map. Modeling only those local interactions shrinks the model a lot.

Their Local Interaction Autoregressive approach includes a separable variant sharing row and column parts. Fitting runs through parallel least squares, with a BIC-type selector choosing each entry's neighborhood. Theory ensures consistent neighborhood recovery and bounds the fitting errors. Simulated runs confirm sharp selection and forecasts beating matrix time-series baselines. A total electron content case study recovers localized space-time patterns with improved prediction.
arxiv-2511-09942:
Mustafa Munir, Md Mostafijur Rahman, and Radu Marculescu present AdaptViG, a vision graph neural network designed to be both accurate and cheap to run. Vision graph networks are powerful, but building their graphs costs heavily. AdaptViG constructs its graph on an efficient static axial scaffold and adds a dynamic gating rule that weighs long-range connections by feature similarity, with weights decaying exponentially.

Early stages use the light gating, while the final stage uses a full global attention block for maximum feature gathering. The mid-size model reached about eighty-three percent top-one accuracy, beating a larger vision graph baseline while using eighty percent fewer parameters and far fewer operations. It also surpassed a much larger efficient transformer on segmentation and detection tasks.
arxiv-2511-10342:
Christos Charalambous, writing alone, models vaccine choices in an epidemic as driven by regret, doubt, and social norms, not by cold math alone. Agents in his model weigh payoffs, fear, and peer approval. They look ahead to regret, let trust shift with doubt, and react to three norm types: their own norms, signs of peer approval, and what peers are seen to do. A standard disease spread model runs while these choices play out.

Group results were best at a mid level of rationality: keen enough to heed risk, loose enough to adapt. Mild regret aided self-correction, while strong regret or greed shook choices loose. Mild doubt bred care, but deep doubt broke joint action. Norms filled the gaps left by thin facts, with approval signs counting most when facts were weakest.
arxiv-2511-10442:
Aarush Agarwal and four co-authors present FastGraph, a graphics-processor algorithm for quickly building nearest-neighbor graphs in low dimensions. Such graphs underpin graph neural networks, but building them can dominate the cost of a project. FastGraph targets spaces of two to ten dimensions and keeps its data resident on the graphics processor.

The method splits space into bins, tunes its own parameters, and supports gradient flow, which learning pipelines need. Benchmarks show speedups of twenty to forty times over well-known libraries such as FAISS, ANNOY, and SCANN, with almost no extra memory. The gains matter most for heavy low-dimensional jobs like particle clustering in physics, object tracking in video, and graph clustering.
arxiv-2511-10842:
Jugal Gajjar, Kaustik Ranaware, Kamalasankari Subramaniakuppusamy, and Vaibhav Gandhi present HyperComplEx, a knowledge graph embedding method built to handle many kinds of relations at once. Single-space embeddings each fail somewhere: Euclidean models flatten hierarchies, hyperbolic models mishandle symmetric relations, and plain vector models miss asymmetry.

Their framework combines hyperbolic, complex, and Euclidean spaces in one model. A learned attention mechanism chooses, for each relation type, how much each space counts, and a consistency loss keeps the spaces' predictions coherent. Tested on research knowledge graphs growing from about a thousand papers to ten million, plus standard tests, it beat strong baselines including TransE, RotatE, and ComplEx throughout. On the largest graph it led the best baseline by a clear margin while keeping inference fast.
arxiv-2511-11042:
Michael Farber, Stefan Kurz, and Mathias Pillin develop math tools for robots and other systems that must move while their surroundings keep changing. A fixed setting is easier to plan for, but real settings shift during motion. The authors use layered space maps, called fibrations, to model how a system's options sit inside a changing world.

They treat two cases. When future changes are known ahead, planning costs no more than in a fixed setting. When changes cannot be foreseen, the system must react from live measures of state and speed. For that case they define a reaction mechanism, a local lifting rule that generalizes a classic connection idea, with examples.
arxiv-2511-11442:
Martin Gray, Celine Guervilly, and Graeme Sarson simulate fingering convection in rotating planetary cores, where layered liquid metal sits at the top of the core. Their setup has a stable temperature gradient but an unstable composition gradient, a case tied to Mercury. Because heat and composition diffuse at very unlike rates, narrow fingers of sinking and rising fluid form and stir the layer.

In a rotating spherical shell, the main finger mode forms narrow, elongated structures that tilt from the rotation axis toward gravity as stratification strengthens. Fingers stay laminar, with widths set by thermal stratification, not rotation. Secondary large-scale flows, from zonal winds to gyres, arise across most settings.
arxiv-2511-11642:
Matheus Duzi, Paul Szeptycki, and Walter Tholen bring Fraïssé theory, the model-theoretic machinery for building universal homogeneous structures, into the study of abstract two-player games. Recent generalizations of the theory to category-theoretic settings make the move possible.

For the class of finite games considered, an infinitely countable game exists that is both universal for the class and ultrahomogeneous, meaning its symmetries are as rich as possible. Odd features of the game categories clash with the usual framework, so weaker categorical properties are formulated that still produce a Fraïssé limit. The result extends a classic construction technique to games, where universal objects were far from obvious.
arxiv-2511-11742:
Desmond J. Higham, Francesco Hrobat, and Francesco Tudisco extend the friendship paradox, the fact that your friends have more friends than you do on average, to arbitrary attributes measured through network centrality. Such paradoxes shape social science and epidemic modeling, where sampling friends biases what you observe.

Using linear algebra, the authors find when a generalized paradox must occur, comparing two averaging styles that go back to Feld's 1991 work: global and local. For global averaging, walk-based centralities such as Katz centrality always produce the paradox, and nonbacktracking eigenvector centrality does too. Counterexamples for other centralities mark the boundary, showing the paradox is common but not automatic.
arxiv-2511-11842:
Lucas Fenaux, Christopher Srinivasa, and Florian Kerschbaum study a tension inside responsible AI: transparency helps users trust a system, but it may also help attackers fool it. Their test bed is transferable adversarial examples, where an attacker crafts inputs on a surrogate model to deceive a defender's model.

Nine attacks across one hundred eighty-one models show attackers succeed more when they match the defender's choice of defended or undefended model, meaning secrecy about defenses carries real value. Game theory then formalizes when openness pays and when obscurity protects. The result complicates any simple claim that more transparency is always safer, and gives deployers a strategic frame for disclosure decisions.
arxiv-2511-12042:
Soham Bhattacharyya and Omkar Sridhar derive formulas for gravitational waves from pairs of compact objects on eccentric orbits whose spins are tilted. Tilted spins make the orbital plane and the spins precess, or wobble, over time. Closed formulas that include both eccentricity and precessing spins at once had been missing.

The authors use the fact that orbit, precession and energy loss run on different timescales, and average over the precession to remove direct time terms. From that they obtain analytic phase formulas through the second post-Newtonian order, with eccentricity treated as a small quantity. They also extend a standard waveform model to include spin precession.
arxiv-2511-12142:
Seokwon Song, Minsu Park and Gunhee Kim present MAVIS, a benchmark for judging whether AI answers to visual questions cite their sources well. Good attribution lets users check each claim, but past work focused on text alone. MAVIS tests systems that must grasp the intent behind a visual question, find multimodal evidence, and answer at length with citations.

The dataset holds a large set of visual question cases, each answer tagged with fact-level links to text or image documents. New measures score how informative, grounded and fluent answers are, and they match human judgments well. Findings show multimodal search helps fluency, but image sources are grounded more weakly than text.
arxiv-2511-12342:
Sajjad Pakdamansavoji, Kumar Vaibhav Jha, Baher Abdulhai and James H Elder test whether traffic at intersections is better analyzed on the ground plane than in the camera image. Turning movement counts guide signal timing, traffic management and city planning. Vision systems usually track vehicles in image coordinates, which distort distance and direction.

The authors project detected vehicles from roadside cameras down onto the ground plane, giving real-world coordinates. For a single camera, that change improves both trajectory classification and turning counts. Weak fusion of projections from several cameras improves accuracy further. Their conclusion is plain: analyze traffic where it actually moves, on the ground.
arxiv-2511-12542:
Caixing Gu, Meng Li and Pan Ma characterize when products of block Hankel and Toeplitz operators are compact, a question rooted in the Sarason problem for operators on analytic function spaces. Hankel and Toeplitz operators are structured maps tied to a symbol function, and their block versions act on vector-valued functions on the unit disk. Compactness of a product is a subtle property of the symbols.

The authors describe it through harmonic extensions of the symbols and through Douglas algebras generated by them. They also answer completely when the product of a block Hankel operator with a block Toeplitz operator is itself a block Hankel operator, a structural question that complements the compactness result.
arxiv-2511-12742:
Zhongteng Cai, Yaxuan Wang, Yang Liu, and Xueru Zhang study what happens when diffusion models train on their own output. As synthetic images flood the internet, later models learn from earlier models' work, and this self-consuming loop can destabilize training or collapse the model's variety. The usual fixes, hoarding old real data or adding fresh human-labeled data, are costly. The authors instead examine the geometry of the model's latent space across generations of this recycling.

They find the structure of latent representations from synthetic data steadily degrades. Their fix, Latent Space Filtering, removes the least realistic synthetic examples from mixed training sets before reuse. Across several real-world datasets, filtering beat existing baselines and held off model collapse without extra training cost or human annotation. A supporting theory links the observed latent-space decay to the collapse itself. A cheap hygiene rule for training on web data follows.
arxiv-2511-12942:
Aritro Pathak proves that the elliptic measure doubles nicely for operators whose drift blows up near the boundary in an averaged sense. The elliptic measure tracks how boundary values influence solutions of an elliptic equation. A doubling property, where enlarging a boundary ball at most multiplies the measure by a controlled factor, is basic to its analysis. Earlier results assumed the drift was pointwise small. Pathak only needs smallness on average over Whitney cubes, a Carleson-type condition on the drift's size.

The results hold in one-sided chord-arc domains and are new even for the half-space. Along the way he proves Hardy inequalities in domains whose boundaries are Ahlfors-David regular, using a stopping time argument. The work connects to recent results on Dirichlet problems in rough domains.
arxiv-2511-20042:
The ATLAS Collaboration hunts higgsinos hiding in nearly invisible particle decays. Their 2025 paper uses Large Hadron Collider collision data. Higgsinos are hypothetical partners of the Higgs boson. Compressed spectra mean parent and child masses nearly match. Decay products then emerge with very little momentum.

The dataset holds 140 inverse femtobarns at thirteen tera-electronvolts. Events need an energetic jet plus large missing momentum. At least one soft charged track must appear. For tiny mass gaps, higgsinos decay into soft pions. Displaced tracks betray their slightly longer lifetimes there. For larger gaps, soft electrons or muons appear instead. Neural network taggers spot those faint leptons. No excess over Standard Model predictions appeared anywhere. Chargino masses below 126 GeV are now excluded. That holds for mass splittings between 0.3 and 2 GeV. These are the first ATLAS limits in this region. They surpass the older LEP experiment bounds.
arxiv-2511-20142:
Epalle, Ramière, Latu, and Lebon scale contact mechanics simulations across a thousand cores. Their 2025 paper combines adaptive mesh refinement with parallel computing. Contact between deformable bodies is stubbornly nonlinear and non-smooth. Fine meshes are needed only near the contact zone. Refining everywhere wastes enormous computing power.

Their algorithm pairs contact nodes directly, node to node. A penalty method enforces the contact constraints. Non-conforming h-refinement sharpens quadrilateral and hexahedral meshes locally. An estimate-mark-refine loop decides where refinement pays. Paired contact nodes are kept on the same MPI process. That placement slashes communication between parallel tasks. Super-parametric elements preserve curved surfaces during refinement. Even coarse starting meshes detect contact zones well. Hertzian contact problems in 2D and 3D validated accuracy. Strong scaling held up to 1,024 cores in tests. Problems with tens of millions of unknowns become feasible.
arxiv-2511-20242:
Gao, Li, Wang, and colleagues listen for radio pulses from suspected neutron stars. Their 2025 paper reports targeted searches of thirty-one binary candidates. Optical surveys flagged these stars as possible neutron star hosts. The binaries are detached, with no gas flowing between partners. Radio pulses would confirm the compact objects directly.

Three giant telescopes shared the observing campaign. FAST, Green Bank, and TianMa covered the targets. Total observing time reached about forty-seven hours. Neither steady pulses nor single bursts were detected. Flux limits sank far below typical known pulsars. FAST reached roughly four microjanskys for periodic signals. Single-pulse limits sat near ten millijanskys there. Beaming geometry likely explains the silence best. The radio beams may simply miss Earth. Extreme age offers another explanation. Stars older than ten billion years may go radio-quiet. Confirming old detached neutron stars stays hard.
arxiv-2511-20442:
Boutet de Monvel, Karpenko, Shepelsky, and Zielinski solve a wave equation on a ring. Their 2025 paper treats the periodic Camassa-Holm equation. That equation models shallow water waves with peaked crests. Integrable equations admit exact solution machinery called inverse scattering. The Riemann-Hilbert approach recasts the inverse step in a neat form. Periodic boundary conditions complicate the standard machinery.

The authors develop the Fokas unified transform for this setting. Solutions are written through a linked Riemann-Hilbert problem. Its data come from spectral functions of the initial state. The classical transform was built for fading data on a line. Finite spans and half-lines needed the unified extension. Spectral analysis of the Lax pair drives the construction. Both Lax equations are analyzed together, not one by one. The result extends exact methods to a natural geometry. Periodic waves recur in coastal and laboratory settings alike.
arxiv-2511-20842:
Narayan Budhathoki and colleagues measure in 2025 how thinning high-purity germanium, the crystal behind radiation detectors, strangles its charge carriers. Using Hall-effect tests at room temperature, they tracked electron and hole mobility in home-grown crystals thinned from 2.7 mm down to 7 micrometres, the first such study on detector-grade bulk material. Mobility collapses as the crystal thins, in an extended-exponential pattern.

That length ran from 6 to 50 micrometres across samples. Weighing models, the team shows the culprit is not Fuchs-Sondheimer surface scattering, the classical suspect, but electrostatic depletion: surface fields eat into the conducting channel, shrinking its effective thickness. Their design rule follows. Keep the device at least about three times that length thick, roughly 3 tau, and most bulk transport survives; go thinner and it falls off a cliff. The lengths give design benchmarks for ultrathin germanium devices.
arxiv-2511-20942:
Rahul Dass and colleagues upgrade in 2025 Ivy, an AI coach for procedural skills, so its explanations carry real structure instead of fluent shallowness. A good explanation must show causality, how steps depend on state; teleology, why steps serve the goal; and decomposition, how problems split into subgoals. Ivy pairs a language model with symbolic Task-Method-Knowledge models that encode those causal transitions, goal hierarchies, and decompositions. The symbolic layer constrains what the model may generate.

Ivy was deployed in Spring 2025 in an online graduate AI course at a large United States university. The team compared constrained Ivy against plain GPT and a retrieval-augmented GPT, using expert and independent annotations across the three dimensions. Symbolic constraints consistently improved the structural quality of explanations, especially for how and why questions. The authors present the hybrid as a scalable pattern for education systems that must teach transferable skill, not just steps.
arxiv-2511-21442:
Alheydis Geiger and Francesca Zaffalon define a new geometric space and explore its borders in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. The Grassmannian collects all linear subspaces of a given size inside a bigger space, a master object for moduli problems. Their self-projecting Grassmannian is the irreducible subvariety whose subspaces obey a generalized self-duality, a symmetry between a subspace and its dual that earlier work imposed only in a stricter form.

Geiger and Zaffalon relate their space to classical landmarks, including moduli spaces of pointed curves of genus g, and to other natural subvarieties of the Grassmannian. They then translate self-projectivity into combinatorics, introducing self-projecting matroids, the discrete skeletons of these configurations. Computational experiments probe the realization spaces of those matroids inside the new variety, checking which abstract patterns actual geometry can build. The paper opens a fresh meeting point for geometry, combinatorics, and moduli theory.
arxiv-2511-21642:
Pablo Rocha proves bounds for convolution operators on a flexible scale of Hardy spaces, in a 2025 harmonic analysis paper. The spaces are built over ball quasi-Banach function spaces, a broad family unifying many classical scales. His operators are convolutions with kernels of fractional type. The key hypothesis is a Fefferman–Stein vector-valued maximal inequality for the powered Hardy–Littlewood maximal operator, plus a bound on the associated space.

Under those assumptions, Rocha shows the zero-order map sends the Hardy space into the function space and into itself, with bounds intact. With extra assumptions, the fractional operators of positive order map between two different spaces in the family, on both space and Hardy levels. Classical consequences follow: singular integrals and the Riesz potential satisfy the same estimates. A bonus result gives an off-diagonal Fefferman–Stein inequality for the fractional maximal operator.
arxiv-2511-21942:
Quintarelli and colleagues argue ethical rules for data cannot be one-size-fits-all, because the right rule depends on context. A rule against using gender or age in decisions is standard, yet 'women and children first' in a shipwreck evacuation is accepted practice. Their work proposes a conceptual model that lets data managers state both the context and the ethical requirements explicitly, in advance, before data reaches a learning system.

The model has two tree structures. The Context Dimensions Tree describes possible situations as combinations of dimension values, while the Ethical Requirements Tree encodes rules about fairness, diversity, privacy, and transparency needed in each context. Together they guide dataset tailoring per situation, choosing among existing bias-removal methods rather than applying one blindly. They flag the philosophical hard part, separating beliefs from their technical measures, as the key open challenge.
arxiv-2511-22242:
Yu, Song, Sun, and colleagues make best-of-many sampling affordable for image diffusion. Test-time scaling for text-to-image models means generating from many noise seeds and keeping the reward model's favorite. Each candidate must be fully denoised before it can be scored, burning the budget on losers. TTSnap prunes weak candidates mid-generation; the catch is that reward models trained on clean images rank half-denoised estimates inconsistently, so early pruning throws away winners.

The team trains noise-aware reward models by self-distillation, aligning each intermediate estimate's reward with the final clean image's. They use a curriculum that shifts gradually from clean to noisy inputs, and add a metric tracking reward alignment against budget use. The approach improves performance by over 16 percent over methods at fixed compute, explores more seeds per budget, and stacks additively with post-training and local test-time optimization techniques.
arxiv-2511-22842:
Panayiotou and colleagues argue causal machine learning has an evaluation problem, and build a machine to fix it. Methods estimating intervention and counterfactual effects feed high-stakes decisions in medicine and policy. Yet they are typically tested on a handful of hand-crafted or semi-synthetic datasets whose hidden assumptions flatter particular methods and do not generalise. Real counterfactual ground truth is unobservable, so synthetic benchmarks are unavoidable; the question is how honestly they're made.

CausalProfiler randomly samples models, data, queries, and ground truths from an explicitly declared Space of Interest, specifying which model classes, query types, and data regimes an evaluation covers. It is the first random synthetic benchmark generator with coverage guarantees and transparent assumptions spanning causal reasoning's three levels: observation, intervention, counterfactual. Evaluating several state-of-the-art methods with it, they show performance varies substantially across spaces of interest, exposing failure modes fixed benchmarks conceal.
arxiv-2511-22942:
Li and colleagues studied how women find and judge body management advice, meaning tips on weight, diet, and appearance, on a female-dominant social media platform in China. Earlier research mostly looked at health tools built by experts or at people with medical concerns. So the team focused instead on ordinary users who go looking for this information on their own each day.

They interviewed 18 users and found that choices were shaped by consumerism, by how popular a poster was, and by whether content felt authentic, rather than by evidence alone. Users also struggled to tell reliable methods from unreliable ones, and browsing often fed body anxiety instead of easing it. The authors close with design ideas for platforms, such as clearer signals of trust, that could support healthier and more reliable engagement with this kind of content.
arxiv-2511-23142:
Kastrati and colleagues show that a neural audio codec, software that compresses sound into discrete tokens, can be repurposed to compress EEG, the brain-wave recordings used in epilepsy and sleep medicine. The two signals differ in sampling rate, channel layout, and scale, and EEG data are scarce and privacy-sensitive. So training a dedicated codec from scratch is hard, which makes the audio head start valuable.

By remapping EEG into the framing the DAC codec expects, they reuse its pretrained encoder-decoder directly. Fine-tuning on EEG beats training from scratch on both fidelity and generalization in their tests. Their multi-channel extension, DAC-MC, adds attention-based mixing across electrodes with channel-specific decoding. On the TUH Abnormal and Epilepsy datasets, the adapted codecs preserved clinically relevant structure, as judged by spectrogram reconstruction loss and by how well downstream classifiers performed on the compressed signals.
arxiv-2512-00442:
Directly imaging an exoplanet means catching its faint light beside a blinding host star. Suvinay Goyal and co-authors analyze post-processing algorithms for exoplanet detection with a photonic lantern nuller in 2025. The nuller suppresses starlight so the planet can be characterized.

The team studies angular-differential post-processing, which uses the sky's rotation to separate planet signal from starlight residue. Detailed characterization of atmospheres and surface features is the long-term prize. Better algorithms squeeze more science from the same telescope time, which is precious on the large observatories that run these instruments. A photonic lantern routes starlight into fibers, where the nulling is performed. Angular differential imaging is a proven technique the authors adapt to this instrument.
arxiv-2512-00542:
False vacuum decay describes how a universe trapped in a metastable state might tunnel to a lower one. Luchang Jin and Joshua Swaim present a non-perturbative method for computing quantum tunneling rates in 2025. They use lattice Monte Carlo simulations in imaginary time.

To recover real-time results, the authors construct an implicit decay amplitude inspired by Fermi's golden rule, with spectral reconstruction. Non-perturbative lattice methods can reach regimes where analytic approximations fail. Tunneling rates matter from cosmology, where vacuum decay could end a universe, to condensed matter systems that mimic the same mathematics. Imaginary time is a standard trick that turns quantum tunneling into a statistical problem.
arxiv-2512-00642:
Protein function prediction tools are powerful black boxes, and their opacity slows adoption in drug discovery. Ananya Krishna, Valentina Simon, and Arjan Kohli demystify DeepFRI in 2025, weighing interpretability against accuracy. DeepFRI is a leading graph convolutional network tool for predicting protein function.

The authors evaluate it with explainability techniques including GradCAM, excitation backpropagation, and PGExplainer, plus adversarial robustness tests. Adoption of such methods depends on verifying their findings before targets are chosen. The study shows what explanation tools can and cannot certify about a model that proposes drug targets. Explainability techniques disagree with each other often enough that using several is prudent. Adversarial tests check whether the explanations survive deliberate attempts to fool them. For drug teams, the gain is a check they can run at low cost. If a tool's hot spots jump at small tricks, its claims should be read with care.
arxiv-2512-00742:
K Kevin Feng, Tae Soo Kim, Rock Yuren Pang, Faria Huq, Tal August, and Amy Zhang wrote a 2025 paper on governing AI agents. Their focus is the user interface. Agents that act on their own over long stretches can cause real harm if they go wrong. Most guardrail plans target the system under the hood, such as prompt filters or agent ID cards.

Feng and coauthors look instead at the interface, the screens and controls a person actually sees and touches. A well built interface could let users set limits, check actions, and step in early. Their work maps what interface design can add to agent safety.
arxiv-2512-01042:
Amartya Chakrabortty, Georges Griso, and Julia Orlik analyze a reinforced thin plate in a 2025 applied math paper. Their setting is linearized elasticity, the small-deformation theory of solid materials. The plate is thin and composite, with small rigid rectangular plates spread across it in a periodic mosaic pattern.

Between neighboring rigid plates sits an elastic beam, thinner than the spacing between plates. The authors homogenize the structure, deriving an effective model that captures the mosaic's overall behavior without tracking every tile. Effective models like this help engineers design stiff, light panels and predict how they bend under load.
arxiv-2512-01142:
Roman Geiko and Georgii Shuklin classify a family of quantum error-correcting codes in a 2025 paper. Stabilizer codes protect quantum information by spreading it across many qudits, units that hold more than two states. Translation-invariant codes repeat the same pattern across a lattice, which makes them natural for physical hardware.

The authors develop a framework for classifying invertible such codes, up to condensation and stabilization with simple codes. They generalize the Pauli groups of local unitaries for qudits on cubic lattices, then analyze stabilizer Hamiltonians built from them. A clean classification tells builders which codes are genuinely new.
arxiv-2512-01242:
Zirui Zhao, Boye Niu, David Hsu, and Wee Sun Lee study abstract visual composition in a 2025 paper. In abstract compositions, identity comes from how a few geometric primitives are arranged: their positions, symmetry, and topology. Texture and photorealistic detail barely matter, which makes these images a clean test of spatial understanding.

Their generative method combines adversarial training with Gumbel Monte Carlo tree search. The search explores arrangements of parts, while the adversarial critic judges plausibility. Abstract composition isolates the structural side of image generation that photo-trained models often fudge. Progress here could help design tools that think in shapes.
arxiv-2512-01342:
Chenting Wang and co-authors build base models for video that skip text labels. Most strong video models learn from text paired with clips. Those texts are often made by machines and miss much of the scene. Motion, shape, and cause can be lost.

Masked video modeling learns from the frames alone. It hides parts of a clip and learns to fill them in. That path has lagged text-based paths on broad tasks. The team built InternVideo-Next to close that gap. A strong text-free model would cut the cost of labels and learn more from raw film.
arxiv-2512-01642:
Carsten Denker and co-authors image a solar active region just before huge flares. Region NOAA 14274 made some of the strongest flares of the current solar cycle. Two giant flares hit on back-to-back days in November 2025. Catching the calm before such storms is rare.

Their mosaic uses speckle-restored images from the GREGOR telescope in Tenerife. The HiFI+ imager gives high spatial detail across a wide field. Sharp maps of the pre-flare state show where stress built up. That helps test what triggers the largest solar eruptions.
arxiv-2512-01742:
Jobst Ziebell studies Wetterich's equation for Radon measures on locally convex spaces. The equation drives flows of effective average actions in field theory. It is used widely to probe quantum field traits. Its domain and boundary terms need care in infinite dimensions.

Ziebell shows the equation holds for Radon measures under set conditions. The effective action's domain is the Lusin affine kernel of the measure. Firm ground in this generality supports functional renormalization work on complex field theories where standard spaces fail. Locally convex spaces cover most function spaces physics uses, so the result's scope reaches far past the toy cases that motivated it.
arxiv-2512-01942:
Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment about a being that measures tiny thermal motions and turns them into usable energy. Rémi Goerlich and four co-authors build a real, microscopic version in 2025: an information engine shaped like a compressible piston, filled with a warm colloidal suspension.

By measuring the random degrees of freedom of the particles inside, the engine extracts energy from a heat bath that is in equilibrium. This first paper of the series concentrates on the universal features the engine shows while in equilibrium. Such tabletop demons let physicists test the deep link between information and thermodynamics with real measurements.
arxiv-2512-02042:
Some equations ask for functions defined on the whole complex plane. The functions must meet a Fermat-like rule that mixes their rates of change with shifted copies of themselves. Sujoy Majumder and Debabrata Pramanik study such equations in 2025. They hunt for solutions that are not constant.

Fermat-type equations are known for having very few solutions. Often the point is to prove that none exist beyond the trivial ones. The authors work with functions of several complex inputs, and with shifts in all of them at once. Their results add to a long effort to map which such equations admit solutions worth the name.
arxiv-2512-02242:
Phase transitions, like water boiling, look like sudden jumps, but their roots may be pure geometry. Loris Di Cairano argues in 2025 that thermodynamics can be built from the intrinsic geometry of phase space alone, without assuming an ensemble of copies of the system.

In that formulation, the ensemble emerges from the geometry instead of being postulated. Phase transitions are encoded in the shape of the constant-energy surface, and entropy follows from a deterministic equation fed by curvature. A geometric account of entropy could unify how physicists think about systems as different as gases and magnets.
arxiv-2512-02342:
Gradient descent needs a step size, and the Polyak rule sets it adaptively from the gap to the best possible loss. Dimitris Oikonomou and Nicolas Loizou extend in 2025 the stochastic Polyak step size to non-smooth problems, safeguarding it so performance stays robust without unrealistic assumptions.

The stochastic version had earned a strong record on smooth problems, including deep network training, but non-smooth extensions leaned on interpolation assumptions or tiny gradients. A safeguarded variant aims to work where losses have kinks, as many real objectives do. Step-size rules that need no hand tuning save enormous effort across optimization practice.
arxiv-2512-02742:
Maddalena Bin and a large team track how a protein drifts through supercooled sugar alcohol mixtures. Cryopreservation by vitrification, turning a solution to glass, needs deep knowledge of how biological fluids move when very cold. The team follows ferritin, a large iron storing protein, in glycerol water mixtures.

X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy watches the motion at tiny scales. The results test the Stokes-Einstein relation, which links diffusion to viscosity and often fails in supercooled liquids. Knowing when that law breaks helps design preservation recipes that keep cells and tissues alive. Cold glass states guard cells well, but only if the mix is right, and this work shows one way to tell.
arxiv-2512-03042:
Michael Ofengenden and three co-authors benchmark AI agents that edit real PowerPoint files on command. Reliable editing of real slides under natural language instructions is the skill tested. Rendering slides as images or generating fresh decks misses the in place editing users actually need.

PPTArena covers one hundred decks, more than two thousand slides, and over eight hundred targeted edits. Edits span text, charts, tables, animations, and master level styles. A hard, realistic benchmark shows which agents office workers could trust with real presentations today. Real decks with real flaws are the test that counts. Toy decks hide the traps that real office work sets for a bot each day on the job.
arxiv-2512-03242:
A good pricing model should also mean fair losses for insurers. C. Evans Hedges links model quality to loss ratio in this 2025 work. The loss ratio compares what an insurer pays out to what it takes in.

Hedges derives a closed-form formula for that link. It connects the correlation between predicted and actual losses to the expected loss ratio. The author calls it the first such analytical relationship. Insurers could use it to judge a model's business value before putting it into pricing. Pricing teams could use the formula in model reviews required by regulators.
arxiv-2512-03342:
Hypergraphs link many items at once, and they need good fingerprints. Peter Brooksbank and Clara Chaplin introduce new invariants for them in this 2025 work. An invariant is a value that stays the same when a structure is relabeled.

To each linear transformation they attach a function that maps uniform hypergraphs to vector spaces. The family is parameterized, so users can tune it. Good invariants help tell structures apart in math and computer science. They may aid work in coding, design theory, and data analysis. Vector-space fingerprints can be computed fast, which helps search over large hypergraph sets.
arxiv-2512-03642:
Achinthya Bheemaguli, Penghao Xiao, and Gopalakrishnan Gautam benchmark five foundation machine-learned potentials at predicting how hard ions hop through battery materials. That hop barrier decides charging speed, and computing it properly with quantum methods is slow. Their 2025 study races the learned models against density functional references.

MACE-MP-0 and Orb-v3 posted the lowest barrier errors across diverse battery chemistries. Two models sorted good from bad ionic conductors correctly more than four times in five. Their intermediate pathway snapshots also beat standard interpolation as starting guesses for the expensive quantum refinement in most structures. Fast screening of candidate battery materials is the intended payoff.
arxiv-2512-04042:
Cool, swollen stars near the end of their lives often shine unevenly, and polarised light can expose that lopsidedness even when telescopes cannot resolve them. Richard Ignace and colleagues model such polarisation in a 2025 stellar astrophysics preprint. The complication is that interstellar dust between us and the star adds its own polarisation, which cannot always be subtracted away.

The team builds a hybrid spectrum combining Rayleigh scattering from the star, with its steep wavelength dependence, and a Serkowski-law contribution from interstellar dust. Mixing the two flattens the expected slope, so a naive reading would misjudge the star. When the star varies, shorter wavelengths swing most where Rayleigh scattering dominates. If the two polarisation directions sit at right angles, strange slopes appear over narrow ranges. The authors apply the thinking to the variable carbon star R Sculptoris.
arxiv-2512-04342:
Ryan Wollaeger, Jim Morel, Kendra Long, Mathew Cleveland, and Robert Lowrie derive a cleaner equation for how light spreads through hot, moving matter. Their setting is a flat one-dimensional slab, and they track photon flow from a fixed lab frame. The result gives the radiation energy density as seen moving with the matter. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses careful asymptotic scaling to dodge flaws in older shortcuts.

Older work scaled the problem as if the matter stood still, which can spawn unphysical glitches at high speeds. This team scales in the lab frame and makes no guess about how fast matter moves. Photon direction stays continuous rather than split into fixed bins. The final drift-diffusion equation carries a heat term that matches the standard semi-relativistic form. As speed nears light speed, it eases into pure flow. Early tests check the equation in reachable cases.
arxiv-2512-05142:
Anil Kumar Yadav and five co-authors test a modified-gravity route that ends up imitating the standard model. They start from a theory that blends geometry with the trace of matter's energy. They then impose a special condition — density plus pressure equals zero. Under it, the theory's expansion history collapses onto the familiar model with a cosmological constant. The team derives what the theory must look like for that trick to work.

They then fit the model's remaining parameters against cosmic chronometers, baryon acoustic oscillations, and supernova data. Two independent pipelines do the fitting: a standard Bayesian sampling method and a neural-network emulator as a cross-check. The two agree, and the model reproduces observations with standard-looking parameter values. The authors are candid that, since the background mimics the standard model by construction, the approach does not resolve the tensions over expansion rate or clumpiness.
arxiv-2512-05242:
Uwe Borghoff, Mark Minas, and Jannis Schopp study how students actually use generative artificial intelligence while learning to build software. In a university programming project, teams collaboratively developed computer games. The authors tracked AI assistance across the phases of development: where it helped most, what tasks it suited, and where students ran into trouble. The rapid arrival of these tools forces software engineering education to adapt, and project courses are a natural laboratory.

Building on those observations, the team examines a repository-aware assistant — a locally run large language model that answers with retrieval from the project's own documentation and source code. They analyze its behaviour qualitatively, probing parameter sensitivity and common failure modes. The findings clarify what context-aware support does well and badly in a real course, and they inform how curricula can integrate AI help meaningfully and responsibly rather than banning or ignoring it.
arxiv-2512-06042:
Ashish Hooda and five co-authors build a machine that rewrites code without changing what it does, then use it to stress test the detectors that judge code sameness. Clone detection decides whether two code fragments mean the same thing. Real code gets refactored and reformatted, changing appearance, not meaning. Auto-SPT automates the making of such semantic preserving transformations, using large language models to invent them and write strong implementations.

A formal analysis shows diversity gives composition its power. Empirically, Auto-SPT's transformations are more diverse than prior approaches, and they significantly degrade state of the art clone detectors, exposing how brittle the detectors' notion of sameness is. Training on its data produces detectors robust to adversarial rewriting. The work closes the clean code gap from both sides.
arxiv-2512-06142:
Clément Maria and Hoel Queffelec bring representation theory to bear on one of knot theory's workhorse computations. The HOMFLY-PT polynomial is among the strongest knot invariants. Computing it runs through braids and the Hecke representation. Their fast algorithm exploits the representation's algebraic rigidity.

It powers a parameterized HOMFLY-PT method. Paired with Garside theory, it becomes a search engine for braids with trivial representations. Several are found. The five strand representation modulo two is not faithful, a new fact. The paper sharpens the tool and maps its blind spot.
arxiv-2512-06242:
Ian Hayes, Larissa Meinicke, and Cliff Jones set out rules for proving that programs with loops and self calling parts behave well when many parts run at once. When threads run side by side, each must cope with steps the others take in between its own. Their method rests on rely guarantee reasoning, where each part states what it counts on from the rest and what it promises in return.

The authors treat a self calling program as a fixed point, a definition that solves itself, and build laws for such points. Loops then fall out of the same laws, since a loop can be seen as the same kind of fixed point. They do not assume that reading a value happens in one instant step. All rules are checked by machine. The result is a shared base for proofs about loops and recursive code in real software.
arxiv-2512-06342:
Deep Mondal and three co authors explore a family of thin carbon nitrogen sheets shaped like tiny dumbbells, hunting for states where electric flow is guarded by topology. Such guarded states can carry current along edges without loss, a prize for future electronics. The sheets in this family pair a known carbon nitride layer with added partner atoms, giving six forms with fair prospects of being made.

Using first principles sums, the team shows that spin orbit effects open a gap in these sheets and that an applied electric field can tune that gap. Marks of a topological phase show up in the bend of the electron waves and in a computed index. Cut into ribbons, the sheets can be read through a classic chain model, where pattern twists reveal yet more guarded phases. The study maps a fresh material family for low loss devices.
arxiv-2512-06442:
Xuanyu Peng, John Regehr, Loris D'Antoni, and their co authors automate a fragile part of compiler building. Compilers reason about code with abstract transformers, small rules that say what an instruction does to a summary of program values. Rules that are unsound have caused real miscompilations in major compilers, and after decades of work, hundreds of instructions in the LLVM system still lack such rules.

Their framework, NiceToMeetYou, synthesizes the rules instead of asking humans to write them. The trick is to build each rule as the meet, the tight joining, of many simpler sound rules, each new one filling a gap in precision left by the last. No hand drawn sketches are needed, so the process can run in bulk. Each rule is then checked by translation into a solver dialect. The aim is compilers whose optimizing steps rest on sound, precise, fast rules.
arxiv-2512-06842:
Fedor Temnikov and co-authors study a family of magnetic crystals built from copper, iron, and rhenium arranged in a doubled pattern of sites. These materials stay magnetic at unusually high temperatures for their class, and the exact temperature shifts a lot with the extra element placed in the gaps. Using first-principles computer calculations, the team maps the electronic structure and asks which atomic interactions drive the magnetism.

Their answer centers on the rhenium states and how full those states are. The exchange between neighboring magnetic atoms turns out to oppose alignment, yet the overall ground state still settles into a mixed pattern called ferrimagnetism. Plugging the computed interactions into a reaction-field theory gives ordering temperatures close to measured values. That agreement supports the proposed picture and helps explain why swapping the gap element tunes the material so strongly.
arxiv-2512-07042:
D Fargion questions a record-breaking neutrino reported by the ARCA detector array in the deep sea. The event, KM3-230213A, appeared to carry an energy near two hundred peta-electron volts, the highest ever claimed for a neutrino. Fargion notes a problem: larger detectors that have watched longer, IceCube and the Auger array. Have set limits that such an event seems to violate, and downward tracks like it are strangely scarce.

His proposed resolution is instrumental. An array floating and bending in deep water might sometimes misjudge its own geometry, pointing a track in a wrong, more horizontal direction. The supposed cosmic neutrino could then be a steeper atmospheric muon bundle, or a single charmed event, in disguise. If instead such events are re-observed and confirmed, Fargion argues, they would open a guaranteed new astronomy based on tau neutrinos.
arxiv-2512-07142:
Tanay Arora and Christof Teuscher hunt for winning tickets: the sparse subnetworks hidden inside a big neural network that can train to full accuracy alone. Finding them by the classic rewinding method works but costs a fortune in repeated training. Cheap shortcuts that prune at the start, judging each weight on its own, fail sanity checks and lose accuracy exactly where sparsity bites hardest. The authors blame that first-order myopia, which ignores how weights depend on each other.

Their Concrete Ticket Search treats ticket-finding as one whole optimization problem, using a smooth relaxation of the yes-no choice for each weight and a balancing scheme to steer sparsity. Among a family of objectives inspired by knowledge distillation, matching the dense network's outputs under a reverse divergence measure worked best.
arxiv-2512-07442:
Richard Sear and Patrick Warren wrote this 2025 physics paper on trapping tiny charged objects in water. The objects range from small particles to large molecules such as DNA. The trap needs nothing fancier than a salt gradient, which a dissolving crystal can supply.

Inside the gradient, two forces fight over each particle. Diffusiophoresis pulls particles toward one end, while plain diffusion spreads them out. The balance sets a trap only micrometres wide. The authors give simple models for how the trapped crowd settles down. At steady state, particle density follows a power law in the salt level. The exponent in that law is a ratio of two rates for each trapped kind. Bigger particles have far larger ratios, so salt gradients catch them easily. The models help labs plan cheap ways to hold and sort tiny matter.
arxiv-2512-07842:
Daniele Avitabile, Gabriel Lord, and Khadija Meddouni wrote this 2025 neuroscience paper. Cortical activity shifts with sleep, movement, and decisions, and its rhythms are easy to record. Local field potentials capture those rhythms from the living brain.

The scientific task is tying the recorded rhythm to the dynamics beneath it. The team models a sleeping mouse's cortex from such recordings. Their model is a discretized Wilson-Cowan Amari neural field, a classic of the field. A data assimilation method then fits the model to the signal. State and parameters are estimated together, in a Bayesian joint framework. The approach is first proven on synthetic measurements with known answers. It then runs on a published real dataset from the literature. Findings suggest the method can recover what stimulus the cortex received. It infers that hidden input while matching the observed signal well.
arxiv-2512-08042:
Chandler Timm C Doloriel, Habib Ullah, Kristian Hovde Liland, Fadi Al Machot, and Ngai Man Cheung, computer vision researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their goal is universal deepfake detection, spotting images from any generator, including ones the detector has never seen. They also want detection cheap enough for large scale screening, in line with green artificial intelligence goals.

Instead of leaning on spatial features or huge pretrained models, they train detectors with masking in the frequency domain, plus random masking and geometric changes. Frequency masking generalized best across generators, for both GAN and diffusion made images. The method also held up under heavy model pruning, keeping accuracy while shrinking the detector. The authors argue this is a practical step toward deepfake screening that is both broad and resource conscious, and they release code and models.
arxiv-2512-08142:
Amy de Castro and Hyesuk Lee, applied mathematicians, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about coupling fluid flow with a porous elastic solid. Such fluid poroelastic interaction appears in tissues, soils, and filters. Their model joins time dependent Stokes flow for the fluid with the Biot equations for the porous structure, using Lagrange multipliers to enforce the coupling.

The authors develop the formulation in detail, with three multipliers handling the interface conditions. They prove the combined problem is well posed in both semi discrete and fully discrete form, and they prove stability for the fully discrete system. The payoff is practical as well as theoretical. Because the multipliers carry the coupling, the fluid and solid parts can later be solved separately in a partitioned scheme. That decoupled approach is promised for a follow up paper, with the present results as its foundation.
arxiv-2512-08442:
A S Dyatlov, D M Dolgintsev, V V Gerasimov, and a team of accelerator physicists in Russia posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They generate ultraviolet laser light twisted with high orbital angular momentum, a corkscrew structure in the beam. Such vortex beams are needed to produce twisted electron beams by photoemission inside radio frequency photoinjectors, the electron sources of modern accelerators.

Three custom optical elements, built into a working photoinjector beamline, do the shaping at a wavelength in the deep ultraviolet. A spiral phase plate made a pure vortex mode carrying a large angular momentum, with high conversion efficiency. Binary axicons produced near parallel Bessel like beams mixing several angular momentum states. A reflective fork grating gave flexible access to lower values and a handy diagnostic. The team checked the beams with cylindrical lens conversion and radial analysis, showing practical control over twisted ultraviolet light.
arxiv-2512-08642:
Shengkui Ye and Kejia Zhu prove a result about the fundamental group of the space left after removing a plane curve from the complex projective plane. They cover all algebraic curves of degree at most five. For each such curve, they show the group is linear and virtually polyfree.

Those two properties place strong structure on the group and limit how complex it can be. As a direct result, the authors settle an open question on residual finiteness for these groups in full. Readers get a short, focused proof paper whose value lies in closing a case that had remained open for low degree curves.
arxiv-2512-09342:
Momoka Fujikawa and Masamune Oguri measure how stars and dark matter are distributed inside early-type galaxies, using weak gravitational lensing. A galaxy's gravity bends light from background sources. Stacking the signals from many galaxies reveals the mass profile more clearly than one system allows.

The team used data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey on the Subaru Telescope, stacking luminous red galaxies across a range of stellar masses. Their lensing profiles reach deep toward galaxy centers and are fitted with a two-part model, one component for stars and one for dark matter. For galaxies around a hundred billion solar masses in stars, the fits prefer dark matter distributions with a central core rather than a sharp cusp. That suggests stronger feedback from stars and black holes than most simulations predict. The study pins down the relation between stellar mass and halo mass using lensing alone.
arxiv-2512-09542:
Francis Granger and colleagues apply cathodoluminescence, light emitted when an electron beam strikes a material, to a semiconductor quantum dot inside a nanowire that emits single photons. Single-photon sources are key for quantum communication, and studying them well matters. Cathodoluminescence inside a scanning electron microscope is normally used for imaging and spectroscopy.

The team shows it can do more: it can also measure the correlation function that checks the source's single-photon purity. By steering the electron beam carefully, they minimize stray luminescence from the surroundings. At cryogenic temperatures, the heating caused by the beam, read from the phonon sidebands of the emission, stayed close to that of ordinary non-resonant optical excitation. The authors conclude that cathodoluminescence is an efficient, versatile tool in the search for new single-photon sources, able to image, take spectra, and verify quantum light quality in one instrument.
arxiv-2512-09642:
Stephen Thomas and Pasqua D'Ambra present a low-synchronization technique for the dense linear systems that arise inside communication-avoiding Krylov solvers. Those are iterative methods used for huge sparse problems on supercomputers. Such solvers reduce how often processors must talk to each other, but each outer iteration still requires solving a Gram system, and synchronization is a bottleneck at scale.

Their approach uses forward Gauss-Seidel sweeps, exploiting the structure of Gram matrices built from Chebyshev polynomial bases. They show one sweep is mathematically equivalent to modified Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization in the energy norm. They supply backward error bounds. For weak scaling on AMD graphics processors, a few dozen sweeps preserved scalability up to sixty-four GPUs with problems exceeding seven hundred million unknowns. They extend the idea to the coarse-grid solves inside algebraic multigrid methods, removing the need to assemble or factor dense coarse operators.
arxiv-2512-09842:
Jonathan Hickman explains the Kakeya conjecture, a problem about how tightly lines pointing in many directions can be packed into a small space. In the plane the question proved manageable and was settled in the nineteen seventies. In three dimensions it resisted attack for decades. It fell only recently, in work by Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl that Hickman calls monumental. His note accompanies an American Mathematical Society talk and tells where the problem came from.

Much of the story runs through Fourier analysis, the mathematics of waves and frequencies, where Kakeya sets have deep classical connections. Hickman traces those links to show why analysts regard the problem as central rather than curious. He finishes by sketching elements of the Wang and Zahl proof. The aim is a feel for the stakes: a plain question about lines that governs hard problems elsewhere in analysis.
arxiv-2512-10042:
Jongmin Lee, Meiqi Sun, and Pieter Abbeel introduce SEMDICE, an algorithm that teaches a reinforcement learning agent to explore widely before any real task appears. In unsupervised pretraining, no reward is available. A good prior policy should visit states as evenly as possible, maximizing the entropy of its long run state distribution. Earlier methods learn from fresh interaction or approximate the objective indirectly. SEMDICE works off policy: it computes the entropy maximizing policy directly from an arbitrary logged dataset, optimizing within the space of stationary distributions itself.

The result is a single stationary Markov policy that spreads its visits as the objective demands. In experiments, SEMDICE beat baseline algorithms at maximizing state entropy. It also adapted fastest to downstream tasks among the state entropy methods compared. The work was presented at ICLR 2025.
arxiv-2512-10342:
Shresth Grover and colleagues introduce CoSPlan, a benchmark that tests whether vision language models can plan with pictures, not just words. Their paper notes that model planning has mostly been judged on text tasks. While real choices often depend on what a scene looks like and how it changes step by step.

CoSPlan asks a model to turn a starting scene into a goal scene across four tasks, including maze navigation, block rearrangement, and object reorganization. Each task hides a wrong action that the model must spot and fix, so simply describing the end state earns nothing. Leading models struggled even with chain-of-thought reasoning. But the authors' scene graph method, which turns images into text maps and updates them step by step, improved results here and on related tests.
arxiv-2512-10442:
Helena Del Río studies a stability question in functional analysis about operators between Banach spaces, focusing on those that strongly expose their range. Results of Bollobás type say that if an operator almost attains a certain extreme behaviour, a nearby operator attains it exactly. Her paper asks for which pairs of spaces that guarantee holds for this class of operators.

She gives fresh characterisations of uniform convexity, in both real and complex forms, through this property, including pairs built from the classical L1, L-infinity, and c0 spaces. One headline result says the pair with L1 works exactly when the target space is uniformly convex. She also uncovers pairs where the property holds over the complex numbers but fails for the underlying real spaces, treats compact and finite-rank operators, and closes with open problems.
arxiv-2512-10642:
Mykhailo Rakov and co-authors test how much disorder a quantum link model can take before its phases collapse. Their system is a U(1) quantum link model arranged on a ladder, a strip of two rails with rungs. And it hosts a symmetry-protected topological phase alongside an ordinary massive phase, with Ising-style transitions between regimes.

Finite-size scaling shows every transition they found matches the Ising universality class, with the expected critical exponent and central charge. A naive reading of the Harris criterion predicts disorder should destroy that clean criticality, yet it does not. Disorder on the rungs alone leaves the transitions standing until it grows quite strong. Disorder along the legs kills the massive phase's criticality, while the topological phase at zero mass survives gentle disorder. Field-theory arguments explain the pattern, a reassuring result for building such phases in messy real devices.
arxiv-2512-10842:
Are Austad and co-authors put distances on the maps between quantum systems. Completely positive maps are the legitimate transformations of quantum states. And a good metric on them should respect quantum information practice, in particular stability under adding unused systems and a chaining property for composed maps. Their construction imports seminorms from noncommutative geometry, the field that treats algebras as spaces.

The key tool is an infinite-dimensional C-star-algebraic analogue of the Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism, which trades a map for a state on a doubled system. Under suitable conditions, the metrics induced this way provably satisfy stability and chaining. The authors also show how to generate such metrics from native noncommutative geometry. One route uses external Kasparov products of spectral triples. This ties the distance between quantum channels to deep constructions in geometry. The study runs to thirty-four pages.
arxiv-2512-10942:
Delong Chen and co-authors build a vision-language model that predicts meanings instead of words. Ordinary models generate text token by token; VL-JEPA, built on the joint embedding predictive architecture, predicts continuous embeddings of the target text instead. Working in an abstract representation space makes the model focus on task-relevant semantics and shrug off surface differences in phrasing.

In a strictly controlled comparison, same vision encoder and same training data, VL-JEPA beat standard token-space training while carrying half the trainable parameters. A light text decoder is called only when words are actually needed, and selective decoding cut decoding operations nearly threefold at similar quality. The same embedding space supports open-vocabulary classification, text-to-video retrieval, and visual question answering with no architectural change.
