And across sixteen video classification and retrieval datasets it passed CLIP, SigLIP2, and the Perception Encoder.
arxiv-2512-11042:
C. Marconcini and a large team present new James Webb observations of NGC 1068, a nearby galaxy with an active central black hole. Combining mid infrared data from MIRI with optical data, they trace the multi phase gas around the nucleus and its clash with outflows and a radio jet. Dense clumps appear along the jet edges where the wind compresses gas.

Detailed modelling shows that different emission lines trace different gas components moving at different speeds, a split confirmed by photoionisation analysis. Much of the outflowing mass sits in a dusty component that optical lines alone miss. The authors favour a two stage acceleration picture, with the wind carrying away millions of solar masses of ionised gas and stirring the surrounding material.
arxiv-2512-11142:
Shin-Rong Tsai, Hsi-Yu Schive, and Matthew Turk present libyt, a library that lets astrophysics simulations analyse their data while they run, instead of saving huge files to disk first. At modern scales, writing and rereading data has become a major bottleneck. libyt connects simulation codes directly to the yt analysis toolkit, Python, and Jupyter notebooks.

The open source C library can run Python analysis routines automatically or hand researchers an interactive prompt mid simulation. It handles patch based adaptive mesh data in memory with little overhead, and existing post processing scripts convert to in situ use with only two lines changed. The team demonstrates integration with two major simulation codes on problems from supernovae and dwarf galaxies to dark matter and shock tubes. Performance, limits around data redistribution, and comparisons with older workflows are discussed in detail.
arxiv-2512-11242:
Lillian Hughes Wyatt and colleagues create shallow nitrogen vacancy centres in diamond with unusually precise control, aiming at better quantum sensors. These defects, a nitrogen atom beside a missing carbon, can sense magnetic fields at the nanoscale, but only if they sit close to the surface without losing coherence. The usual method, blasting ions into diamond, places them unevenly.

Instead, the team added nitrogen during diamond growth in a thin layer, a technique called delta doping. Depth confinement improved twofold over low energy implantation, and the density of centres could be tuned deliberately. The resulting defects stayed sensitive, with coherence limited mainly by interactions among the centres themselves. To prove their worth, the team imaged magnetism in thin flakes of a two dimensional magnet. The control should enable advances from tiny magnetic resonance measurements to entanglement enhanced sensing.
arxiv-2512-11542:
Hossein Shahabadi and fellow authors run the first full comparison of visual autoregressive image generators against diffusion models on compositional faithfulness. That is, whether a picture in fact contains the objects, traits, and relations the prompt asked for. Diffusion systems dominate text to image research, while the newer token building family, which builds images token by token at growing scales, had gone largely unexamined on this skill.

Six systems were benchmarked on two full testing suites covering colour and trait binding, spatial relations, counting, and complex multi object prompts. The largest such model achieved the strongest overall part by part matching. Its smaller sibling matched or beat bigger diffusion models in several categories, an attractive efficiency trade off. Two older diffusion systems showed persistent weaknesses in trait sensitive and spatial tasks. The study sets unified baselines for comparing the two families as compositional generation matures.
arxiv-2512-11742:
M Gomes, A C Lehum, and A J da Silva sort out what really makes the electric charge grow with energy when gravity joins the story. They study massless QED, the theory of light and electrons, tied to a scale free quadratic theory of gravity. Two ways to read the running charge give seeming rival answers.

At one loop the team computes the photon self energy with care for soft, low energy effects. High energy log terms are the same in all gauges and set the true running. Soft logs from gravity look similar but carry no such meaning. In the gravity sector the high energy logs cancel out. So gravity, in this form, does not shift the charge running at one loop.
arxiv-2512-11842:
Trevor McClain and Rahul Bhadani study stop and go traffic waves on a ring road through the lens of dynamics. Human drivers in the model follow the IDM car following rules. One car can instead run Followerstopper, a controller built to smooth flow.

Simulations show steady flow is unstable with human style drivers alone; waves emerge on their own. Swapping in a single Followerstopper car restores calm, even flow at safe speed. Adding a known reaction delay makes waves start sooner, as expected. Yet the one controlled car still blocks wave formation under delay. The study backs a hopeful claim: a pinch of automation can tame phantom jams for everyone on the road.
arxiv-2512-12042:
Philipp Habicht and co-authors test whether language models can grade car voice assistants for contextual sense. In car question answering systems answer drivers out loud; a good answer must respect the request, the place, and the moment. Human grading is slow and costly.

The team forges test utterances paired with correct replies and replies seeded with known faults. Thirteen models from OpenAI, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Meta grade them under four prompting styles. DeepSeek-R1 hit an F1 of 0.99 at 0.002 dollars per check. DeepSeek-V3 gave the best cost and speed balance. Small plain models gained most from fancy prompting, while reasoning models led overall. LLM grading looks ready to replace much human review here.
arxiv-2512-12142:
Björn Lütjens and co-authors build MeltwaterBench, a benchmark and model for mapping Greenland surface meltwater in fine detail. Meltwater patterns reveal how the ice sheet is failing, and satellites can see them. Existing maps trade off sharpness in space against sharpness in time.

Their deep learning model fuses radar, passive microwave, climate model output, and elevation data into daily maps at 100 meter detail over Helheim Glacier, 2017 to 2023. Against radar derived ground truth it scores 95 percent accuracy, over ten points above climate model only and passive microwave only maps. A simple radar running window still hits 90 percent. The aligned data set is public for method comparisons.
arxiv-2512-12442:
Haoyu Li, Isaac J Michaud, Ayan Biswas, and Han-Wei Shen speed up uncertainty maps for Gaussian process models in a 2025 paper. Gaussian process regression stores large simulation data compactly and carries uncertainty with it. Rebuilding values from such models is costly, and classic tools like probabilistic marching cubes are slower still at high resolution.

Their method splits space into a hierarchy and rebuilds only regions where a level crossing might occur. For each region they compute an upper bound on crossing probability from the kernel and saved samples, guiding where to refine. Tests on varied data sets show accurate probability fields at low computing cost, aiding fast visual analysis.
arxiv-2512-12542:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim introduce a degenerate version of the Euler-Seidel matrix method in a 2025 math paper. The classic method links a starting number sequence to its final sequence through generating functions, using Seidel's formula. Adding a parameter called lambda deforms the recurrence, in the style of degenerate special numbers that soften classic formulas into families.

Their generalized method proves conversion formulas from lambda based binomial identities and gives a degenerate Seidel formula for exponential generating functions. They apply the results to degenerate Bell and Fubini numbers and polynomials, two sequence families tied to set partitions and ordered structures. New counting identities follow from the framework.
arxiv-2512-13042:
Tomohiro Okuma, Kei-ichi Watanabe, and Ken-ichi Yoshida prove a variant of Rohr's vanishing theorem in algebraic geometry. Their setting is a normal surface singularity, a point where a surface fails to be smooth, studied through a resolution that replaces the point with a curve.

Their theorem gives a condition under which the size of a cohomology group for invertible sheaves meets a natural lower bound exactly. They apply it to bound the normal reduction number of the local ring. One result caps that number at the arithmetic genus plus one. For a special class they call almost cone singularities, they prove a sharper bound.
arxiv-2512-13142:
Anika Sharma and co-authors introduce behavioral coherence evaluation, a design-time test for language models used in sensitive domains. They focus on reproductive health, where a reply can sound kind while quietly reinforcing harmful ideas, such as that secrecy is safest or support is scarce.

Using an established abortion stigma scale, they had five models answer questionnaires as 627 personas, then asked five experts to review flagged patterns. Models scored personas as lower on self-judgment but higher on fear of others' judgment than the reference sample. Most also defaulted to extreme secrecy. Experts stressed that disclosure advice depends on safety, legal risk, and trusted support.
arxiv-2512-13242:
Sebastiaan ten Haaf and co-authors probe ground state degeneracies in a Fermi-Hubbard model with superconducting correlations, realized in small arrays of hybrid quantum dots. Such arrays can host exotic states, including the Majorana bound states sought for quantum computing. Strong on-site repulsion in the dots makes the model realistic.

For two sites, they find robust zero-bias peaks that signal a strongly degenerate spectrum, hosting emergent Majorana Kramers pairs or parafermions. For three sites, the pattern changes: matched sweet spots lift the degeneracy, though tuning a phase difference can restore it. Those restored states proved fragile to detuning, a caution for scaling up.
arxiv-2512-13342:
Sheikh Shakil Akhtar, Pranabendu Misra, and Geevarghese Philip study space efficient algorithms for parameterized problems, hard problems attacked by isolating one small parameter that controls the difficulty. Many classic solutions save time by using large amounts of memory. On memory-limited devices, or for huge inputs, that trade breaks down.

Their work asks which parameterized problems admit algorithms that stay thrifty with space while keeping the parameter based running time. Such results matter for streaming and embedded settings where data cannot all be stored. The paper develops tools for designing and analyzing low-space parameterized algorithms, clarifying where memory can be squeezed without losing the speed edge that parameterization gives.
arxiv-2512-13442:
Khawla Elhadri, Jorg Schlotterer, and Christin Seifert present XNNTab, a neural network for tabular data that stays interpretable. In fields where explanations matter, users often pick decision trees or linear models over stronger but opaque networks. XNNTab aims to remove that forced choice.

The network first learns rich nonlinear feature representations. A sparse autoencoder then splits them into single-concept features, called monosemantic features. Each is assigned a human readable concept, making the final prediction intrinsically explainable. In their tests, XNNTab beat other interpretable models and matched the predictive performance of its non-interpretable counterparts, showing accuracy and transparency can coexist on tabular tasks.
arxiv-2512-13542:
Tom Anders, Hiten Kothari, and R. Michael Buehrer test whether deep learning can spot a signal whose traits are unknown. The task matters in radar, sonar, location work, and wireless links, where a signal must be found in white noise. When the signal traits are unknown, no best detector exists in the classic sense.

The authors train two learning models on raw signal data and test them on three signal types. They compare the results with classic methods and with a matched filter, which knows the signal in full. They also train one model on a mixed data set and test it across all signal types, aiming for high detection at a fixed false alarm rate.
arxiv-2512-13842:
Daniel Green and Kshitij Gupta recast light scalar fields in de Sitter space as a quantum walk. The local physics of such fields is well described by classical random walks, through stochastic inflation. Recent work derived that frame from quantum field theory and the renormalization group, with corrections order by order.

That classical picture is incomplete, notably for the tail of the fluctuation distribution, where quantum dynamics should matter. Using exact renormalization group methods, the authors derive an evolution equation for the reduced density matrix of long wavelength fields. That master equation maps light fields directly to quantum walk models. They show how it reduces to stochastic inflation and how higher corrections arise, with divergences absorbed by dynamical renormalization.
arxiv-2512-14642:
Himadri Singh Raghav and four coauthors present an energy efficient neural network chip in a 2025 paper. Artificial intelligence workloads in video processing and high resolution sensing need strong compute on tight energy budgets, above all for battery powered edge devices.

Their mixed signal chip uses adiabatic capacitive circuits, a design that recovers charge to save energy, built in 130 nm CMOS technology. With 16 single cycle multiply accumulate engines in a dual layer design, it classifies 8 by 8 one bit images into four classes. Accuracy tops 95 percent, within 2.7 percent of a software version. Energy use falls by a factor between 2.1 and 6.8 versus an equivalent CMOS capacitive design.
arxiv-2512-14742:
Tan Le, Van Le, and Sachin Shetty propose a layered defense for open radio access networks, the modular 5G systems known as O-RAN. Splitting the network into parts from many vendors gives operators more data and more choice, but it also opens more paths for attack. Their 2025 technical report answers with quantum assisted machine learning.

The defense runs in three layers: spotting anomalies, confirming intrusions, and sorting attacks into types, each matched to a layer of network data. Quantum feature encodings feed deep and ensemble classifiers, tested on both synthetic and real network records. The authors report near perfect accuracy and high recall, plus checks meant to show the system stays understandable and ready for use in live network controllers.
arxiv-2512-14842:
Sameer Dambal, Yu Zhang, Eric R. Bittner, and Pavan Hosur turn a nuisance into a tool. Noise is the main enemy of today's small quantum computers, scrambling their states before work is done. Yet making a Gibbs state, a standard thermal state used in many tasks, turns out to be a job noise can help with.

Guided by the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis, the team shows noise speeds up settling into thermal balance. In tests on a spin chain, a hard to settle model thermalized about 3.5 times faster with noise present. A model that would never settle on its own reached a thermal state only because of noise. Since checking a local Gibbs state is easy, the trick offers a handy shortcut for near term machines.
arxiv-2512-14942:
Théo Reymermier and five coauthors report early results from proANUBIS, a prototype detector hunting particles that travel far before decaying. Such long lived particles appear in many theories that try to explain dark matter, which the Standard Model cannot describe. The full ANUBIS detector would watch the cavern of the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.

The prototype has collected data inside that cavern since 2024, covering 104 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions from Run 3. The team projects how sensitive the full detector could be to sample theories, including Higgs portal models and heavy neutral leptons. They also show the prototype's first results and how it helps measure the background noise the real detector must beat. The study is a step toward a new window on rare, slow decaying particles.
arxiv-2512-15442:
Neeraj Sarna, Yuanyuan Li, and Michael von Gablenz study a legal risk of image generators in a 2025 paper. Such models can memorize training images and reproduce them, and those images may be under copyright. That creates legal and financial risk for both users and developers of the tools.

The authors test whether careful prompting can lower that risk. They combine chain of thought prompting and task instruction prompting with negative prompting and prompt rewriting. Experiments across several models measure how close outputs come to a copyrighted image and how well they still match the user request. The results show how well each mix works as model size and complexity change.
arxiv-2512-15742:
Jeff Smith presents SHARe-KAN, a post training compression method for vision Kolmogorov Arnold Networks, in a 2025 paper, dated December 10. These networks store a dense spline grid on every edge, inflating prediction heads more than 140 fold over a comparable MLP and making inference memory bound on edge chips. Standard pruning collapses their accuracy.

SHARe-KAN compresses spline coefficients through a gain shape bias decomposition with a shared codebook, and a companion runtime maps that codebook into on chip memory. On PASCAL VOC detection it reaches 9.3 times storage compression at a 2 point accuracy cost, with no retraining. At 50 task heads, storage falls from 2.9 gigabytes to 211 megabytes.
arxiv-2512-15842:
Markus Niese and co authors report time resolved charge detection in quantum dots made from molybdenum disulfide in a 2025 paper. Quantum dots in transition metal dichalcogenides are candidates for quantum information devices. Reading their charge state is hard when the dots couple so weakly to leads that direct current falls below detection limits.

An integrated charge detector next to the gate defined dots solves that problem. The team watches a crossover from two weakly coupled single dots to a strongly coupled double dot. In the weak regime they still read dot occupation and reach the few electron limit. Large band gaps slow tunneling enough to resolve single events, enabling future spin and valley to charge conversion.
arxiv-2512-15942:
S. Pintus and A. Crepieux compute edge current and its noise in two dimensional topological superconductors in a 2025 paper. Edge states in such materials can carry current, and their fluctuations may reveal the topological character of the bulk. The team uses T-matrix and Green function techniques to separate chiral from non chiral behavior.

Current vanishes for non chiral edge states and is nonzero for chiral ones, while edge noise is nonzero either way. In toy models, the noise tracks the Chern number closely: it appears only when that number is nonzero, and bulk noise peaks when it changes. In an extended Qi Wu Zhang model, edge noise instead follows the Zak phase.
arxiv-2512-16042:
T Flaulhabe and nine co-authors study a star cluster in research shared on arXiv in 2025, accepted by the Astrophysical Journal. Open clusters are natural labs for testing how stars age and how the galaxy builds its elements. Their target, IC 2714, holds eight red giant stars previously listed as members, one of which is oddly rich in lithium.

Using high-resolution spectra plus Gaia satellite data, the team measured abundances for 23 chemical species, from lithium and carbon to rare earth elements. They give the fullest chemical portrait of the cluster yet, plus carbon isotope ratios for seven stars. Star number 087 stands out with high lithium and faster spin. Two other giants, numbers 028 and 034, may not belong to the cluster at all.
arxiv-2512-16142:
Hoel Queffelec, Anne-Laure Thiel, and Emmanuel Wagner link two areas of algebra in work posted to arXiv in 2025. Bridgeland stability conditions sort the objects of a triangulated category by a kind of slope, and come with a natural distance measure. The authors use that structure to build extriangulated categories, a setting that blends exact and triangulated behavior.

They then study the Grothendieck groups of these new structures, which are algebraic summaries of their building blocks. The motivation comes from knot theory: the Khovanov-Seidel categorification of the Burau representation. From that construction one can extract the Lawrence-Krammer-Bigelow representation of braid groups. Both representations are faithful, meaning they capture braids without loss, and the authors' framework helps relate the two through stability conditions.
arxiv-2512-16242:
Smritikana Patra, Soumyajit Pal, and Ranendu Adhikary prove a quantum foundations result in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Nonlocality, Einstein's spooky action, can be shown by breaking a Bell inequality or by a logical paradox like Hardy's. Self-testing uses observed statistics alone to certify exactly which quantum state and measurements a lab must have used.

For two parties, the two routes behave differently in the geometry of allowed correlations. The authors show three parties break that pattern. The correlation reaching the best Hardy success probability also self-tests the famous GHZ state and its measurements. It sits on the no-signaling boundary yet is an exposed corner point of the quantum set, and it matches the correlation that maximally violates the Mermin inequality. A robust version survives small experimental imperfections.
arxiv-2512-16642:
Mahdi Sonbolestan and Ali Gholami speed up a hard imaging task in seismology called full waveform inversion, where sound-like waves are used to map what lies underground. A strong variant uses Lagrange multipliers as source extensions, which guards against cycle skipping and speeds convergence.

The costly step is undoing blur with a huge data-space Hessian matrix. Past fixes ran costly inner loops that each needed two wave solves per source. The new method builds receiver-side Green functions in time, forms the Hessian in the frequency domain for all needed tones at once, and inverts it directly. Tests show large savings in compute cost.
arxiv-2512-16842:
Yuxin Ray Song and a large team release OpenTouch, the first in-the-wild data set that pairs first-person video with full-hand touch. Hands are our main link to the physical world, yet head-worn video rarely knows when, where, or how hard contact happens.

OpenTouch holds 5.1 hours of synced video, touch, and pose data, plus 2,900 curated clips with rich text notes. The team builds retrieval and classification tests on it to probe how touch grounds seeing and acting. Touch proved a compact but strong cue for grasp understanding, tightened cross-modal links, and could be pulled reliably from wild video queries. The set aims to aid robot learning and embodied perception.
arxiv-2512-17142:
Johannes Lohmann asks whether early-warning signals can tell a full collapse of the Atlantic overturning circulation from a partial one. Climate models project a slowdown, and some see an irreversible drop, but the warming threshold is deeply uncertain.

Warning signals read generic statistical shifts as a steady state nears a saddle-node tipping point. Lohmann builds a conceptual model with two regions tipping in sequence, shutting deep water formation one by one. Only very near each tip does the system follow the expected form, so trends differ by observable. That ambiguity makes it hard to say which collapse type comes next, or when, from signals alone.
arxiv-2512-17242:
Chuanhong Gao and three co-authors use chaos as a probe of a black hole whose electric field follows nonlinear rules. They track Lyapunov exponents, numbers that show how fast nearby particle paths split apart, for both light-like and charged particles circling the hole. The aim is to see whether chaos can flag a phase transition, a sudden change of state.

Their results say it can: the exponents shift in step with the transition. They also test a proposed chaos bound, a cap on how chaotic a system may be. Breaks of that cap show up in the stable branch of a small black hole during the transition. Breaks appear in other cases too, with or without a transition.
arxiv-2512-17442:
Jan Hutter and four co-authors rerun and stress-test BSARec, a shopping recommender that tracks the order of a user's clicks. Its core Transformer acts like a smoothing filter, muting the fast signal spikes that mark sudden short-term interests. BSARec adds a Fourier layer to boost those spikes back up, but no one had checked the claim in depth.

The rerun confirms BSARec beats rivals on some data sets, not all. A new score for how spiky a user's history is let the team grade methods per user group. Swapping in wavelet tools gained almost nothing, and plain shortcut connections matched the fancy signal methods. Padding choice mattered most: filling gaps with varied values helped a lot, while constant padding blunted the spike booster.
arxiv-2512-17742:
Qinglin Ma and three co-authors explain why the faintest, most spread-out galaxies huddle together more than expected. Ultra-diffuse galaxies are dim dwarfs smeared over a wide area, and surveys found them clustering oddly strongly. One suspect was halo spin bias: galaxies in fast-spinning dark matter halos might cluster by spin, not just by mass.

In a large cosmic simulation, the team shows the effect hinges on how spin is counted. Count every particle near a halo and high-spin halos cluster more; count only bound particles and the trend flips for small halos. Halos in crowded regions carry many unbound passersby, which inflates their spin tally. Tying galaxy puffiness to that tally reproduces the odd clustering inside standard cosmology, no exotic dark matter required.
arxiv-2512-17942:
Bin Xu, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep K. S. Gupta build a digital twin system meant to keep up with fast, risky events. A twin mirrors a real system in real time, but edge devices near the action have tight limits on speed and memory. Their setting includes tasks like avoiding mid air collisions.

The team moved the twin's neural parts, including memory cells and dense layers, onto an FPGA chip built for parallel work. The result reacts five times faster than a typical human response time. That margin shows twins can ride along on small hardware in places where a slow answer would be unsafe.
arxiv-2512-18042: Nguyen N. Hung surveys recent work on the conductor of finite group characters. A character is a basic building block in the study of a group's symmetry patterns. The conductor is a number attached to such a block. The review maps how results in this area link to each other. It also ties them to wider questions in the representation theory of finite groups. Open problems are flagged along the way, so readers can see both what is known and what remains unsolved.
arxiv-2512-18142:
Sofia Z. Sheikh leads a fifteen author team listening to 3I/ATLAS, the third known visitor from another star system, found in July 2025. If other minds send probes as we sent Voyager, a passing object could carry a radio voice. The team aimed the Allen Telescope Array at the object across 1 to 9 gigahertz.

In 7.25 hours they logged nearly 74 million narrowband blips, then cut earthly interference by tone and drift, and checked the last 211 by eye. None merited a second look. The silence caps any steady beacon on the object at about 10 to 110 watts over the ranges scanned, a firm bound for this rare guest.
arxiv-2512-18642:
Abdessatar Souissi and Amenallah Andolsi connect quantum machine learning with many-body physics in a 2025 paper. They apply hidden quantum Markov models to the AKLT state, a famous example of a symmetry-protected topological phase. In their construction, the visible system is a spin-1 chain, which emerges from a hidden spin-1/2 layer through a well-defined quantum emission step.

The authors show that the hidden Markov dynamics capture maximal entanglement through channels tied to the AKLT state. They also show that the topological order imposes a covariance structure on the decoding channels used to read the observations. The framework offers a new bridge between learning models and topological order, with possible uses in quantum information.
arxiv-2512-18842:
Aleksandr Fedchin and three co-authors bring proof to parallel programming. The Message Passing Interface, MPI, coordinates supercomputer jobs split across many processors, and a single mismatched message can hang the whole run. Their library, DafnyMPI, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and due in the Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages, lets programmers prove MPI code correct.

Rather than inventing a new logic, they extend Dafny, a language built for verified sequential programs, with concurrent reasoning. Users declare the message topology up front. They then prove that calls like MPI_ISEND and MPI_WAIT meet their stated rules, and those rules ensure freedom from deadlock. The team also verifies that the code matches its intent, terminates, and uses buffers safely. Three classic partial differential equation solvers are verified as demonstrations, a step toward trustworthy high-performance software.
arxiv-2512-18942:
Alexander Kruchkov studies how quantum correlations bend in imaginary time, and what limits that bending must obey. Correlation functions describe how a quantum system remembers itself; their curvature in imaginary time reveals built-in timescales. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, starts with topological phases, where quantum geometry reshapes the decay of correlations into patterns beyond plain exponential falloff.

He then proves a bound on correlation curvature that holds for all interacting systems in thermal equilibrium. He connects it to the leading invariants of memory function theory. The result frames imaginary-time curvature as a sturdy probe: measure how correlations curve, and you learn the system's built-in clock speeds without disturbing it. Such probes matter for characterizing quantum materials and simulators where direct timing experiments are out of reach.
arxiv-2512-19542:
Jibril Ben Achour, Adolfo Cisterna, and Mokhtar Hassaine build exact solutions for lopsided compact objects living in an expanding universe. Most known cosmological compact objects are perfect spheres; real ones spin and bulge. Kerr-de Sitter and Thakurta's solution are rare exceptions in a thin literature.

A new solution-generating technique produces nonstationary, axisymmetric solutions of the Einstein equations with a self-interacting scalar field. From it comes the first exact dynamical, axisymmetric compact object set in an FLRW cosmology. The mean curvature vector then extends trapping-horizon analysis beyond spheres, letting the authors chart where trapped and anti-trapped regions form as the object evolves.
arxiv-2512-19642:
Blaise Goutéraux, David Ramirez, and Clément Supiot study what quantum jitter does to a nearly frozen black hole. Their object is the near-extremal Reissner-Nordström black hole in anti-de Sitter space, whose near-horizon region is governed by a Schwarzian theory. That same theory is known to fix a long-standing puzzle in black hole entropy, and exact results exist for its quantum-corrected correlation functions.

Borrowing those exact results, the team computes how bulk quantum fluctuations change the shear correlators of the dual state at low temperature. In the hydrodynamic regime, the fluctuations push shear viscosity upward, safely preserving a famous lower bound on viscosity relative to entropy. Outside that regime, they lift gapless modes that classical calculations had left at zero temperature.
arxiv-2512-19742:
Md Shakhrul Iman Siam, Ishtiaque Ahmed Showmik, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu put a conversational agent in charge of recognizing human activity. Activity recognition from wearable sensors feeds healthcare and smart-environment applications, but classic classifiers output bare labels that users cannot interrogate. Their large multimodal agent wraps recognition in a language model, adding reasoning and question-answering on top of classification.

The framework was evaluated on three widely used datasets, HHAR, Shoaib, and MotionSense. Classification accuracy stayed comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while the agent could explain its judgments and respond to follow-up questions in plain language. The authors frame the contribution as closing the gap between technical sensor outputs and insights a person can actually use.
arxiv-2512-19842:
Andrea Sordello and nine co-authors built Holoscope, an open platform for watching Internet attacks. Good watch needs many sensors spread across networks. Telescopes record traffic no one asked for. Honeypots invite contact on purpose. Holoscope makes both kinds easy to set up and run. Its cloud-native build rests on K3s and WireGuard. Those give safe links and self-serve sign-up for new sensors.

The design is modular and set by code. It supports live control of sensors, self-recovery after faults, and data handling after capture. It works even on modest hardware. The team runs it across schools and cloud networks in Europe and Brazil. That gives one shared view of large attack waves. The work is set to appear in IEEE Communications Magazine.
arxiv-2512-19942:
Leon Ofman and five co-authors report a space-weather event caught in the act, high above the Sun. The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability grows when plasma layers slide past each other too fast. Too fast means past the local Alfvén speed. The boundary then rolls into waves and vortices, which feed turbulence. The effect had been seen low in the corona. Its vortex stage high up had never been seen.

On 16 February 2024, two spacecraft watched it happen. SOHO and STEREO-A saw large waves grow between six and fourteen solar radii. A fast eruption passed, and the waves rolled fully open. A second eruption in the same spot helped them grow. Field data from Parker Solar Probe confirm the speed beat the local Alfvén speed. The authors say the event is rare for a reason. It needs stretched field lines, thin plasma, and strong shear at once.
arxiv-2512-20042:
Nguyen Lam Phu Quy leads a six-author team writing captions that know what a photograph is about, not just what it shows. Real captions for journalism, education, and archives need event background, timing, outcomes, and named entities, none of which pixels alone reveal. Their system description, built for the EVENTA Grand Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2025, bolts external knowledge onto a captioning pipeline.

Similar images are retrieved with two vision-language encoders, reranked by classical feature matching for geometric alignment, and mined for context from related articles by semantic search. A fine-tuned Qwen3 model, adapted with QLoRA, then merges that context with draft captions from an instruction-tuned BLIP model. On the OpenEvents v1 dataset the pipeline produced significantly more informative, event-enriched captions than traditional methods.
arxiv-2512-20442:
Yakob Kahane gives a new proof of a twenty-year-old conjecture in commutative algebra. Watanabe and Yoshida proposed a lower bound for the Hilbert-Kunz multiplicity of local rings in 2005. Meng recently settled it with analytic methods, while another group recast the problem using Ehrhart theory, the combinatorics of lattice points in polytopes.

That recasting reduced the conjecture to one inequality about a shifted Ehrhart polynomial of a zigzag poset. Kahane completes the programme with a new explicit formula for the coefficients of that shifted polynomial. In generating-function form, the formula appears as a Hadamard product of the Euler numbers' exponential generating function with an explicit algebraic function. The conjecture now has a fully combinatorial proof.
arxiv-2512-20542:
Yerko Torres-Nova proves reciprocity rules for a widened family of Dedekind sums. Classic Dedekind sums, built from sawtooth functions, satisfy a famous reciprocity law linking number theory with shapes. Torres-Nova attaches sums to general absolutely continuous functions and asks what symmetry survives.

Periodic Bernoulli functions receive special treatment, extending the classic Dedekind-Rademacher formula. The method extends an integral approach and leans on Fourier analysis. For polynomial-type functions, the resulting law acquires a spatial reading through conical zeta values, special values tied to cones in lattices. The work continues a long tradition of squeezing number facts out of such laws, where a sum over one modulus is traded for a sum over another.
arxiv-2512-20642:
Francesco Banelli, Antonio Terpin, Alan Bonomi, and Raffaello D'Andrea build a gym for measuring fluid motion. Particle image methods and optical flow quantify flow fields in experiments, but scattered software and mismatched interfaces make methods hard to compare or rerun. Flow Gym standardizes the whole pipeline.

Classic and learning-based methods plug into one interface for building, testing, training, and use. The approach ships JAX versions and wrappers, modular pre- and post-processing, and works with OpenCV and PyTorch versions. The same workflow runs on synthetic data for testing and on live experimental data for real-time use. Hardware acceleration comes from JAX underneath. The goal is lowering the barrier between a published method and a working laboratory tool.
arxiv-2512-20842:
Ratchaphat Nakarachinda, Lunchakorn Tannukij, Pitayuth Wongjun, and Tanapat Deesuwan model a two-horizon black hole as a pair of linked qubits. A Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole has both a black hole horizon and a cosmic horizon, and its heat behavior remains mysterious. Treating each horizon as one qubit lets quantum information tools enter the problem.

By matching the entropy of each horizon subsystem to qubit entropies, they built density matrices for the parts and the whole. The model behaves as two correlated qubits, as hoped. One surprise appeared: gravity seems to force a minimum correlation stronger than the standard Araki-Lieb bound allows for ordinary qubit pairs.
arxiv-2512-21142:
Bruno Camino, Scott Woodley, and two co-authors turn a neutral-atom quantum machine into a materials sampler. The test material is nitrogen-doped graphene. Formation energies from density functional theory are fitted onto a Rydberg-atom Hamiltonian with on-site and distance-dependent pair terms, so the atom array mimics dopant layouts. One obstacle dominates: the hardware's largest energy scale is a hundred times smaller than the material's pair interaction.

A one-parameter rescaling bridges the gap, making the hardware sample Boltzmann-like weights for the material at a rescaled effective temperature, and tying the global laser detuning to the chemical potential. A complete count confirms the scheme on a 28-site flake, and Monte Carlo checks on 78 sites confirm the sampler favors low-energy configurations. Quantum annealers gain a credible route to thermodynamic materials questions.
arxiv-2512-21342:
After a geomagnetic storm drains the inner magnetosphere, the plasmasphere slowly refills with ions from below, and Jaden Fitzpatrick, Kausik Chatterjee, and Naomi Maruyama upgrade a simulation of that recovery. Their earlier multi-ion flux-corrected transport model assumed a fixed temperature along each magnetic flux tube. The new version lets electron temperature evolve on its own, driven by the electron energy equation.

With temperature varying in space and time, the pressure and electric-field forces steering the ions come out more realistic. The model still shows hydrogen dominating the refill, oxygen ions mattering early, and hydrogen and helium coupling during the shift between two refilling stages. Tests across two magnetic shells hold up, supporting future three-dimensional versions.
arxiv-2512-21642:
Yongwoo Choi, Ahmad Jafar Arifi, Ho-Meoyng Choi, and Chueng-Ryong Ji build a self-consistent light-front quark model of the kaon, the meson made of an up quark and a strange antiquark. The model describes the kaon's internal structure, probed through form factors and parton distributions.

Based on the Bakamjian-Thomas construction, the model uses one invariant mass consistently in the matrix elements and Lorentz structures. That consistency enforces four-momentum conservation at the meson-quark vertex and makes observables independent of the current component used. The authors demonstrate this uniqueness for the electromagnetic form factor. In the scalar channel, two common definitions prove not interchangeable inside the model. With a Gaussian wave function they compute the full set of unpolarized transverse-momentum-dependent distributions, finding an exact Gaussian leading shape and systematic higher-twist hierarchies. They also evolve the valence parton distributions and report Mellin moments.
arxiv-2512-21842:
Baorong Huang and Ali Asiri present AlignAR, a generative method for aligning Arabic and English sentences in parallel texts, together with a new dataset. Parallel corpora power machine translation research and teaching, but Arabic-English resources are scarce, and most existing ones contain only simple one-to-one sentence mappings.

The new dataset pairs simple legal texts with complex literary ones. The authors show that easy datasets cannot discriminate between alignment methods: everyone looks good on them. Their hard subset deliberately reduces one-to-one mappings, exposing where traditional alignment methods break. A large-language-model-based approach proved far more robust there, reaching an F1 score of about eighty-five percent, an improvement of nearly nine points over earlier methods. The work argues that benchmarks must include messy, many-to-many alignments to measure real progress. Both the datasets and the code are released openly for other researchers.
arxiv-2512-22042:
Priestley duality for distributive lattices has an order-compactification theory, and its Esakia counterpart, tied to intuitionistic logic's semantics, needed work. Rodrigo Nicolau Almeida, Guram Bezhanishvili, and Nick Bezhanishvili present Esakia order-compactifications and locate them within the general Priestley theory.

They prove an analog of Dwinger's theorem, characterizing Esakia order-compactifications through special rings of upsets. This produces locally Esakia spaces, and for these they show that taking the largest Esakia order-compactification is functorial, an analog of Banaschewski's theorem. The work extends the duality-theoretic toolkit connecting topology, order, and non-classical logic.
arxiv-2512-22142:
Leyang Xue and five co-authors argue that idle edge devices, phones, desktops, and local machines, could help train foundation models now trained almost only in big cloud data centers. Earlier edge training systems lagged behind cloud performance and scaled poorly. They also strained device memory or drowned in communication costs. Devices joining and leaving, and their wide variety, made things worse.

Their system, Cleave, exploits an asymmetry in matrix multiplication. Inputs sent down to devices are much larger than the partial results sent back up. That matches networks whose download speed far exceeds upload speed. Splitting training into independent sub-tasks lets one scheduling scheme handle memory, communication, and churn together. Cleave matched cloud-level training speed, beat prior edge systems several-fold, and scaled to thousands of devices.
arxiv-2512-22242:
Shaurya Gaur and six co-authors audit AI risk models for lung cancer screening, checking whether the models treat demographic groups fairly. Screening high-risk people with yearly low-dose CT scans saves lives but strains radiology capacity, so AI help is attractive. The team applied the JustEFAB framework's thinking about confounders and ethically significant bias to two deep learning models, Sybil and Venkadesh21, plus the PanCan2b logistic model.

Both deep models were trained on the United States National Lung Screening Trial and tested on held-out data from it. Sybil scored women noticeably higher than men in discrimination accuracy. At a fixed specificity, Venkadesh21 was much less sensitive for Black participants than for White participants. Available clinical factors did not explain the gaps, so the authors classify them as unfair biases needing monitoring.
arxiv-2512-22442:
Cattalyya Nuengsigkapian presents HiFi-RAG, the winning closed-source system in the text-to-text static evaluation of the MMU-RAGent NeurIPS 2025 competition. Open-domain retrieval-augmented generation suffers when retrieved documents contain irrelevant material and when answers drift from the user's intent. HiFi-RAG attacks both problems with hierarchical content filtering and a two-pass generation pipeline.

The fast, cheaper Gemini 2.5 Flash model handles query formulation, filtering, and citation attribution, while Gemini 2.5 Pro is reserved for final answer generation. On the competition validation set, the system improved over the baseline by about twenty percent in ROUGE-L. On a custom test set of questions needing knowledge after January 2025, it beat the parametric baseline by over fifty-seven percent in the same measure.
arxiv-2512-22542:
Tingyu Zhao and eight co-authors study how networks grow when newcomers aim imperfectly. In classic preferential attachment, new nodes link to popular current ones. Their model adds local flexibility: the newcomer connects to a uniformly random node near the intended target, the target itself included. Social friendships and the budding quantum internet both show this kind of near-miss attachment.

Through simulations and rigorous stochastic analysis, the flexibility turns out to change global behavior qualitatively. With superlinear attachment, a layered hierarchy emerges and no stationary degree distribution exists. With linear or sublinear attachment, a stationary distribution exists but decays strictly faster than in the Barabási-Albert model. The authors place the results in a 2D phase diagram of growth models with redirection.
arxiv-2512-22942:
Anwesha Chakraborty, Lucas Hackl, and Mario Kieburg predict how much entanglement a typical quantum state carries when a global spin symmetry is enforced. Take a lattice of spin-half particles, pick a random pure state with fixed total spin and zero magnetization, and ask for the average entanglement entropy between two halves. Without symmetry this is the classic Page curve problem; the SU(2) symmetry reshapes the answer.

Using random matrix methods, the authors derive the average entropy up to constant order in the system volume for subsystems under half the lattice size. Alongside the leading volume-law term, they prove a finite-size correction growing like half the logarithm of the volume, which traces back to how Clebsch-Gordan coefficients scale. The constant term is computed and reflects angular momentum coupling inside the magnetization blocks. The result extends Page-type formulas to non-Abelian symmetry sectors at arbitrary spin densities.
arxiv-2512-23042:
Ryousuke Yamada and co-authors ask whether three-dimensional scene understanding can be learned without any real 3D scans. Collecting scanned scenes is slow and expensive, while ordinary walkthrough videos, like real-estate tours, are everywhere online. The team reconstructs point clouds from such unlabeled videos with an off-the-shelf feed-forward model, building a dataset called RoomTours with nearly fifty thousand generated scenes.

On that synthetic data they train LAM3C, a self-supervised framework using Laplacian-aware multi-level clustering with Sinkhorn-Knopp balancing. A noise-regularized loss keeps features smooth over local geometry and stable when the reconstructed clouds are imperfect, as generated data always is. Despite never seeing a real scan, the method beat earlier self-supervised approaches on indoor semantic and instance segmentation. The authors present unlabeled video as an abundant, cheap source of training signal for 3D representation learning.
arxiv-2512-23142:
Mingzhen Shao and Sarang Joshi challenge a piece of conventional wisdom about deep learning for medical image registration. Learning-based registration, which warps one scan onto another, was assumed fragile under domain shift, and robustness was chased with ever larger training sets. Shao and Joshi argue the opposite: these models are naturally resistant to domain shift because they estimate deformation from local features rather than the image's global appearance.

To isolate that mechanism they built UniReg, which separates feature extraction from deformation estimation, using fixed pretrained extractors feeding a UNet deformation network. Trained on a single dataset, UniReg matched optimization-based methods across domains and imaging modalities. The analysis also pins down why ordinary convolutional models do fail under modality shift: biases absorbed from the training dataset in the early convolutional layers. The design lesson is to protect domain-invariant local features when choosing registration backbones.
arxiv-2512-23342:
Mirza Karamehmedović, Pierre Maréchal, Martin Carøe, and Lara Baalbaki generalize deconvolution, the art of undoing a blur. Classical deconvolution assumes one fixed blurring kernel everywhere, but many imaging problems blur unevenly across the scene. Their framework allows a pseudodifferential solution operator whose symbol varies with both position and frequency, which translates into images whose sharpness can vary across space while keeping one global stability promise.

The theory also allows fairly general convolution kernels, widening the class of forward models covered. Consistency, convergence, and stability results are proved, together with convergence rates, so the new method comes with the same kind of backing as the classical one. Examples back the analysis and show the advantages of letting sharpness adapt across space. The authors position the framework for imaging tasks where a single uniform sharpness is the wrong goal.
arxiv-2512-23442:
Ruriko Yoshida and Zhiwen Wang solve a practical tuning problem for density estimation on the space of phylogenetic trees. A kernel density estimator smooths data points into a probability landscape, and its quality hinges on the bandwidth, the smoothing width. Over tree space, the authors work with a tropical version of the estimator built on the tropical symmetric distance, and they need a way to pick that bandwidth.

Their choice is likelihood cross-validation, and they derive the optimal solution for the best-fit bandwidth it selects for the tropical estimator. In simulations under the multispecies coalescent model, cross-validation's bandwidth beat the nearest-neighbor estimate on both accuracy and computation time. The method is applied to genomic data from the Apicomplexa, the parasite group that includes the malaria agent. The paper gives practitioners of phylogenetic density estimation a bandwidth rule with a formula rather than a heuristic.
arxiv-2512-23642:
Nayan Sharma and Ajay Tripathi model a three-level atomic system arranged in a closed loop, where a special phase, fixed by gauge invariance, is imprinted on a structured light beam. The beam is a Laguerre-Gaussian probe, whose intensity pattern can form bright and dark lobes. In the weak-probe limit, the output intensity mixes ordinary absorption, a scattering term, and an interference term that depends on the loop phase.

Rotating that interference term lets arbitrary phases be read off the lobe pattern. The authors connect the effect to the Berry phase, the geometric phase the system's dark states collect while moving around a toroidal parameter space, visible as fringe shifts that open systems lack. They argue the scheme is feasible with cold atoms or solid-state platforms, offering a testbed for geometric phases in quantum optics.
arxiv-2512-23842:
Daniel Aronoff, Robert Townsend, and Madars Virza propose a way to unclog the market for repurchase agreements, the short-term secured loans, called repos, that lubricate the financial system. After the 2008 crisis, accounting rules forced intermediary banks to record repo assets on their balance sheets, while a new leverage ratio capped total recorded assets. Together the rules sharply limit how much repo banks can intermediate.

Regulators answered by mandating central clearing of Treasury trades, which nets positions multilaterally but moves counterparty risk onto the clearinghouse, distorting monitoring incentives and adding fees. RepoMech, the authors' method, achieves the same multilateral netting of repo trades without shifting counterparty risk at all, preserving the original risk relationships between the trading parties. The paper presents the method as a market-design fix that reduces balance-sheet impact while avoiding the clearinghouse's side effects.
arxiv-2512-24242:
Jack Allsop, Ander Lamaison, Richard Lang, and Silas Rathke set degree thresholds in hypergraphs. Their graphs are 3-uniform, so each edge joins three vertices. The question is when a minimum vertex degree forces global structure. Two kinds of structure are at stake. One is a tight spanning component. The other is a spanning copy of any given surface.

The main results give sharp thresholds for both. A degree near half of all pairs forces a spanning component. A degree near five ninths forces any surface. Both bounds are asymptotically optimal. No weaker condition can work in general. The work extends an earlier result by four other authors. Those authors had settled the matching question for minimum codegree. Vertex degree is the harder, more natural measure here.
arxiv-2512-24742:
Xiang Liu, Yimin Zhou, Jinxiang Wang, and co-authors introduce Splatwizard, a benchmark toolkit built for compressing 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. That rendering method creates fast new views of a scene, but many compression variants now compete without a shared test. Older benchmarks miss traits such as rendering speed, memory use, and geometric accuracy.

Splatwizard offers an easy framework for adding new compression models and applying leading techniques in one pipeline. Rate and distortion trade-offs can be compared on common ground. Readers in computer graphics get a standardized way to judge which splatting compression methods truly save space without losing quality or speed.
arxiv-2512-24942:
Ivan Ahumada, Max Badcott, and James Edwards extend Worldline Monte Carlo simulation to systems of many quantum particles. The method simulates Feynman's path integral by sampling worldlines, the paths particles trace in imaginary time. They show how to generate any number of worldlines from the free kinetic part and how to add interactions between worldlines in the ensemble.

Tests cover two and three particle systems with long-range Coulomb-like forces and separate external fields, in various spatial dimensions. Computational physics readers get a validated multi-particle path integral tool. Worldline methods can handle strong interactions where perturbation theory struggles, so extending them beyond one particle widens their reach.
arxiv-2512-25042:
Yan Chen and Lihua Lei study compound estimation for many binomial means at once, a problem behind measuring mobility across census tracts, disease prevalence across countries, and click rates across demographic groups. Reporting each plain average is simple but noisy when samples or means are small. Empirical Bayes methods borrow information across tasks to raise average accuracy, yet need assumptions that can fail.

Compound estimation aims for guarantees that hold broadly while still borrowing strength. Statistics readers get methods for the common many-small-estimates problem. Better small-area estimates matter because policy and product decisions are often made exactly where data is thinnest.
arxiv-2601-07242:
Taekbeom Lee and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with HERE. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors present HERE , an active 3D scene reconstruction framework based on neural radiance fields, enabling high-fidelity implicit mapping.

Our approach centers around an active learning strategy for camera trajectory generation. Driven by accurate identification of unseen regions, which supports efficient data acquisition and precise scene reconstruction. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07742:
Teddy Koker and coauthors fine-tune machine learned atomic models so they give better forecasts of vibrations. Many traits of a solid depend on higher slopes of the potential energy surface. Standard training matches energies, forces, and stresses. Even then, the authors note, flaws in curvature remain and spoil forecasts of vibrations. Their 2026 preprint introduces phonon fine-tuning for interatomic potentials.

Phonons are the basic units of vibration in a crystal lattice. Getting them right matters for heat transport, stability, and superconductivity estimates. A fine-tuning stage aimed at curvature can fix what plain training losses miss. The method promises better materials screening without retraining models from scratch. Those who model solids on computers are the readers. The work addresses a known gap between fast learned potentials and the fine properties engineers actually need. The aim is plain: fast models that still get the fine traits of a solid right.
arxiv-2601-08142:
Dilki Wijekoon, Amine Mezghani, and Ekram Hossain study joint communication and sensing with a smart surface. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that shapes radio waves. The setting is physically consistent and includes mutual coupling between surface elements.

Coupling appears when elements sit closer than one element spacing apart. Ignoring it can make designs look better on paper than in hardware. The system pairs the surface with a multiple-antenna base station. Both monostatic and bistatic radar setups are explored. Readers in wireless research get a more honest model of what surface-aided sensing can deliver.
arxiv-2601-08242: Xinlin Cao, Ahcene Ghandriche, and Mourad Sini study light scattering by clusters of hybrid dimers. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats time-harmonic electromagnetic scattering in three-dimensional space. Each dimer pairs a high-contrast dielectric nanoparticle with a moderately contrasting plasmonic one. The two particles sit a subwavelength distance apart. Clusters of such dimers could shape light in ways single particles cannot. The analysis supports design of nano-optical devices, sensors, and metasurfaces built from coupled particle pairs.
arxiv-2601-08442: Kanta Asakawa and co-authors measure spin polarization of rubidium atoms desorbed from a cobalt surface by light. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a spin-polarized Co(110) surface and pulsed ultraviolet light. Desorption here runs through a non-thermal mechanism, not simple heating. The desorbed rubidium atoms came out spin polarized. That result implies spin transfer between the surface and the adsorbate during desorption. The effect could inform spin injection methods and surface science tools that read magnetic states with atomic probes.
arxiv-2601-08642: Martin Gairing, Adrian Vetta, and Zhanzhan Zhao model city investment as a neighborhood game. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks how cities should invest to improve welfare when residents respond strategically. The model builds on Schelling's bounded neighborhood model from game theory. Agents choose neighborhoods using concave, non-monotonic utility functions that reflect local population. The authors study how equilibria can be improved by city choices. The work speaks to urban policy, where a subsidy or amenity can shift sorting patterns in surprising ways.
arxiv-2601-08742:
Xin Quan and three co-authors test if large chat models can guess why a person acted. To work well with others, a model has to guess aims that are not said out loud. Old tests of logic in text do not check this skill. They ask what a text says, not what a person meant to do.

The team sets up tasks where a model must infer a hid aim from acts it can see. They call this skill attributional inference. It is key for groups of agents that must plan and talk. A reader who builds such groups gets a clear test of a weak spot. The work shows why plain text logic scores are not enough for team work.
arxiv-2601-08842:
Felipe Biava Cataneo tests if tuned chat models will take a hint from an out side guard. Safe AI plans use a guard tool to flag doubt in a model reply. The main model should then fix its path. Cataneo asks if a tuned model still lets a guard steer it in plain talk, or if it learns to shrug hints off.

He tests a small open model on grade school math tasks. Base forms of the model took hints well on direct tasks. The tuned form shows a pattern he calls context based push back. It takes hints in some frames and blocks them in others. A reader who builds guard stacks gets a warn. A guard is weak if the main model will not hear it.
arxiv-2601-09042:
Neelkamal Bhuyan, Debankur Mukherjee, and Adam Wierman tackle a learn task where each move can cost a vast, unknown fee. A learner picks a point each round and pays a hit cost. It also pays to move from its last point. In past work that move cost was capped. Here it is not, and the space is high in size, which breaks old plans.

Their method is called SCaLE. It is the first to prove a sub linear regret bound for this case, the authors say. Regret is the gap to the best fixed plan in hindsight. The proof needs no facts on the hit cost form. A reader in learn theory gets a plan for costly moves in the wild.
arxiv-2601-09142:
Shijian Ma, Yan Lin, and Yi Yang build a test set to catch firms that dodge hard asks on earn calls. On such calls, chiefs take asks from pros on sales and risks. A chief may dodge: talk round the ask, give a half reply, or shift theme. Those dodges can hide weak spots that share holders need to know.

Their set is called EvasionBench. It draws on a vast pool of call ask and reply pairs from a pro data base. A strict sieve keeps clear cases. Each case is tagged by dodge grade: direct, mid, or full dodge. A reader in finance gets a scale to grade dodge find tools, and to flag calls for a close read.
arxiv-2601-09342:
Ewelina Gajewska, Katarzyna Budzynska, and Jaroslaw Chudziak build a team of agents to spot hid hate speech. Hid hate does not use slur words. It hints, mocks by code, or praises harm in a sly way. A lone check tool oft misses it, since its sense rests on who is hit and what a group hears in the words.

Their team has a lead agent and group agents built on the fly. Each group agent speaks for a set of folk who may be the mark. The lead weighs their reads to make the call. A reader in net safety gets a check plan that hears a text as its marks hear it, not as a flat rule does.
arxiv-2601-09842:
Walid Maalej asks how to keep hundreds of programming students awake and engaged. His 2026 arXiv paper, bound for a software engineering education track at ICSE 2026, reflects on fun in large courses. Teaching coding basics in a big lecture is cheap and still common at universities.

The format bores students, who drift and disengage. It frustrates lecturers too, since interaction is hard to scale. The paper weighs playful methods that survive class sizes in the hundreds. Keeping student attention in the room is a precondition for any real learning at all.
arxiv-2601-09942:
Hunjun Shin, Hoonbae Moon, and Mohit Singhal ask how talks with a foe state shape talk at home. Views of a foe can limit what leaders can do in talks. Most past work used polls or mood scores. Those tools miss slow shifts in the story told about a foe.

The team tracks how North Korea is framed in US online talk. They look at high level summits as key events. The aim is to see if frames shift after such meets. They also ask if shifts last or fade fast. A frame that lasts can change the room leaders have to act.
arxiv-2601-10142:
Ruiran Su, Janet Pierrehumbert, and Markus Leippold track how money news talks about climate. Such news shapes vast sums in green funds. Yet talk in this elite field is not well mapped. The team reads two decades of Dow Jones news text.

They use large language models to pull three facts from each piece. Who speaks is the actor. How the theme is cast is the frame. What claims are made are the arguments. This actor frame argument chain lets them track shifts over time. It shows whose voice rose and which claims won ground in each era.
arxiv-2601-10242:
Guanxu Chen, Dongrui Liu, and Jing Shao ask if looped models can link inner sense to words. A model may hold a fact in its inner state. Yet its words may fail to state that fact. That gap is a known flaw. Looped models run the same layers again and again.

Each loop adds depth at no new weight cost. The team ask if loops act as a form of self look. A model could check its own state as it loops. They test this claim on set tasks. The work probes when loops help a model say what it knows.
arxiv-2601-10442:
Arwed Schütz, Lars Nolle, and Tamara Bechtold shrink finite element models with a physics led net. Finite element tools are a base of design work. But a full model is too slow for control or whole rig work. A shrunk model must run fast and stay true.

Shrink steps for curved laws need a next step named hyperreduction. The team use a net with physics terms built in. It is trained with a strong rule that checks first and second slopes. The net needs no mesh data from the trade tool. It learns from data alone, which keeps it of use with closed tools.
arxiv-2601-10542:
Kunal Dey and Reihaneh Safavi-Naini join two tools: mixed encryption and certified deletion. Certified deletion lets a user store data with a host. At a set time, the user can ask for a wipe. The host must prove the data is gone for good. Class tools can not do this. Quantum data can.

The team work in a preprocessing form. Some work is done up front, before the data is set. Their build adds mixed encryption to the wipe proof. Mixed means part class and part quantum. The aim is a store that can prove a wipe on call.
arxiv-2601-10642:
K. I. Smirnova and D. S. Wiebe compare two catalogs of HII regions in the galaxy NGC 628. HII regions are clouds of glowing gas around young, hot stars. They mark where stars are being born. The Kongiu and Groves catalogs list these regions in the same galaxy, but not in the same way.

The authors compare the traits of the interstellar medium drawn from each catalog. They look at star-forming regions and compare light fluxes across bands, including ranges near seven microns. Where the catalogs agree, values can be trusted; where they differ, users learn the limits. The study helps astronomers who mine catalog data for star formation work.
arxiv-2601-10742:
Amélie Gruel, Pierre Lewden, Adrien F. Vincent, and Sylvain Saïghi work on low-energy vision with event cameras. Neuromorphic vision records change, not full frames. It pairs well with spiking neural networks, the brain-like models that fire in pulses. The match brings gains in energy, latency, and memory for moving scenes.

Even so, cutting energy use further is a live challenge, above all for embedded devices. The authors present line-based preprocessing of event data as a step toward leaner pipelines. Preprocessing shapes what the network must handle at all. Their work targets cameras on drones, wearables, and sensors that must see clearly on a tiny power budget.
arxiv-2601-10842:
Abbas Dohadwala, Bryan Flores-Silva, Alicia Orozco-Moya, and Zoe Siegelnickel compute Betti numbers for powers of binomial edge ideals. Such an ideal is built from a graph, pairing variables along its edges. Its powers grow in algebraic complexity. The graded Betti numbers record the shape of the ideal's free resolution, a key algebraic portrait.

The authors give a closed formula for the Betti numbers in the linear strands of all powers. The graphs covered are closed graphs with no induced K4, the complete graph on four vertices. Closed formulas are prized in commutative algebra: they turn case-by-case computation into one clean rule. The result links graph structure to algebraic data in exact form.
arxiv-2601-10942:
Zitong Zhou, Matteo Paltenghi, Miryung Kim, and Michael Pradel present Change And Cover, a tool for the last mile of regression testing. Software changes arrive as pull requests. Testing the changed code is critical, yet even rich test suites leave some changed lines untested. That leftover gap is where regressions slip through.

The tool augments tests at the pull request stage, aiming at the exact code a change touches. Last-mile focus matters: broad suites waste effort on untouched code while missing the risky lines. Automated test generation for fresh changes could cut review burden and catch bugs before merge. The work targets teams that ship code daily and fear the one line no test watched.
arxiv-2601-11042:
Chi Zhang and co-authors study the collapse that hits large language models under sequential knowledge editing. Editing updates a model's facts one after another. After many edits, the model's general abilities can fall apart. Parameter-modifying edits are the riskiest kind. Past fixes lean on heuristic limits to how far parameters may move.

The authors characterize the collapse through spectral signatures, patterns in the model's weight matrices. A spectral view may show why edits pile up damage. It could also yield an early warning and a cleaner fix than heuristics. The work serves teams that must keep deployed models current without slowly breaking them.
arxiv-2601-11142:
Joris Koefler, Dmitrii Pavlov, and Rainer Sinn write on pure math in this 2026 preprint. Their topic sits in a young field called Positive Geometry. A key claim in that field says that amplituhedra are positive shapes. The claim draws strength from links to particle physics.

Forms tied to these shapes can give scattering amplitudes, the core numbers of particle theory. Brown and Dupont built a bridge for this work not long ago. Their bridge uses mixed Hodge theory, a deep part of modern math. It links the key forms to de Rham cohomology. Koefler and his coauthors build pairs of shapes with positive genus from that base.
arxiv-2601-11242:
Michael Sachs, Erin Gabriel, Robin Evans, and Arvid Sjolander study hidden variable models. Their 2026 preprint asks what such models force on seen data. A hidden variable is one the study can never observe. Graphs with hidden nodes are common in causal work.

Such graphs can force more than simple independence facts. The forced limits on seen data can be complex in form. Those limits can test parts of the model itself. Parts that looked untestable gain a test through the seen limits. The limits can also guide how data are used in fits. That guidance can make estimates sharper and more efficient. The work gives ways to derive the full set of such limits.
arxiv-2601-11942:
Qingyu Meng and Yangshuai Wang build a hybrid quantum-classical method for regression that is made to train well. Quantum neural networks draw much interest for science tasks. In regression, they often train poorly due to noisy gradients and ill-shaped loss fields.

Their frame uses geometric preconditioning, which reshapes the training steps. It also uses a staged curriculum, so tasks grow in steps. Both steps aim to ease the blocks that stall training. A more trainable quantum regressor could aid fits in physics and chemistry.  Both steps aim at a model that learns in a smooth way.
arxiv-2601-12042:
Xiaomei Zhang, Zhaoxi Zhang, Leo Yu Zhang, and their co-authors warn of a security gap in fast vision-language models. Such models shrink image tokens to run faster. That helps use in tight, low-latency settings. Most work so far checks speed and skill, not safety.

Token shrinking could open new attack paths or hide key proof. Their study maps those risks for the first time in depth. The title frames the point as less is more, until it breaks. Teams that shrink tokens need safety tests as well as speed tests.
arxiv-2601-12642:
Anahita Mobaseri and seven co authors study what happens when a drop of cornstarch and water hits a surface. Such mixtures are a premier example of shear thickening fluids. They flow like liquid until stressed, then suddenly act almost solid. The team combine high speed photography with direct force measurements.

They vary impact conditions across a wide range in their tests. The study identifies three distinct impact regimes. The title names the interplay that governs the behavior: inertia versus dilatancy. Dilatancy is the tendency of the packed grains to expand under shear. Knowing the regimes helps predict splashes, armor response, and industrial flows of such fluids.
arxiv-2601-13142:
Zhantao Ma, Quanfeng Lu, and co-authors lay ground work for agents that run a TV by remote. Big vision language models show skill at device control. Most past work used point and click acts, as on a phone or a desk screen. Day to day TV use, though, runs on a remote with a few keys.

The team built TVWorld to fill that gap. It is an off line graph form of real TV menus. Agents can be tested in it with no live set and in a way that can be rerun. For teams that build home agents, the set gives a fair yard stick for a mode of use that past sets skipped.
arxiv-2601-13342:
Anxhela Maloku, Alexandra Klymenko, Stephen Meisenbacher, and Florian Matthes put privacy where users meet the screen. In human computer work, privacy is a core care and is tied straight to how screens and flows are designed. A poor flow can leak data no back end rule can save.

The team sorts what past work says on privacy in screen design. They also ran fifteen semi structured talks with experts who do the work. From both, they draw the key picks and forces that shape if privacy is built in or bolted on. For design teams, the piece turns a vague care into picks they can act on at the draft desk.
arxiv-2601-14042:
Jiaze Li and a large team tackle a drift problem in federated learning in 2026. Federated learning trains one model across many clients who share parameters, not data. In the non-iid setting, each client's data differs in mix. The global model then suffers client drift, where local updates pull it in clashing directions.

Drift can seriously affect the final performance of the model. Their Federated Balanced Learning aims to keep local training in balance. Balanced updates could keep the shared model true to all clients. That matters for phones, hospitals, and banks that learn together in private.
arxiv-2601-14242:
Bertie Vidgen and a large team at Mercor built APEX-Agents, a test for AI agents, and report it in this 2026 paper. The test asks if an agent can do long jobs that cross many apps. The jobs were made by experts in three fields. They come from investment banking, management consulting, and corporate law.

Agents must work in real-like office settings, with files and tools at hand. Each job takes many steps, not one quick reply. The team ran eight agents through the test for a ranked board. They scored each agent by Pass@1, the share of jobs done right on the first try.
arxiv-2601-14742:
Ami Pandat, Kanyala Muvva, Punna Rajasekhar, Gopika Vinod, and Rohit Shukla build a drone dataset in this 2026 paper. Reliable drone detection is challenging for three reasons. Annotated real-world data are limited. Drones vary hugely in appearance. Visually similar distractors, such as birds, confuse detectors.

The team introduces SimD3, a large-scale, high-fidelity synthetic dataset for robust drone detection in complex aerial environments. Synthetic means the images are rendered, not photographed, so labels come free and exact. The dataset models payloads drones carry and bird distractors explicitly. Readers get training data for detectors that must tell a drone from a bird at a distance.
arxiv-2601-14842:
Jan Eyll, Jonas Fritsch, and Kai Zehmisch study shapes in contact geometry, a branch of math close to the study of motion. Their 2026 arXiv paper works in the standard Darboux space, a model space with a set contact form. The form they use is symmetric around a center ray.

The team looks at maps that keep the contact structure and fix the rim of a domain. They sort the domains that are straight in the vertical sense and round like a ball. Two such domains count as the same only under strict rules.
arxiv-2601-15042:
Andrea Protani, Riccardo Taiello, and co-authors locate brain tumors without pooling patient scans. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a hard fact of medical AI. Models need large, varied datasets, but scans sit locked in separate hospitals under privacy rules.

The team builds a federated learning framework instead. Each site trains on its own scans, and only model updates travel. Their design joins a transformer with a graph neural network. It also explains itself at the level of imaging modality, so users can see which scan type drove each single call.
arxiv-2601-15142:
Ji-Shun Lian, Jia-Xuan Li, and co-authors study the brightest kind of blazar, a galaxy with a jet aimed near Earth. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with extreme synchrotron blazars. Their light peaks once at very high frequencies and again beyond a tera-electronvolt.

Such sources make ideal labs for studying how jets speed up particles and emit radiation. The authors examine the properties of the gamma-ray emission in these blazars. They also weigh what physical origins could explain it. The work bears on how relativistic jets shine at the very highest energies seen.
arxiv-2601-15342:
Jingxu Wu, Chenjia Li, and Jie Shi map a phase change in a dark copy of the strong force. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dark QCD, a hidden twin of quantum chromodynamics. They study its chiral transition, where the vacuum's structure shifts.

The Polyakov loop part of the theory keeps a clear threefold structure. It couples to the chiral order parameter in one effective theory. The authors chart the landscape of uniform vacuum states. They find a window of metastability, bounded by points where a state loses stability. Metastable bubbles of the other phase sit at the heart of the story.
arxiv-2601-15842:
Gianluca Esposito, Simone Cepollaro, Luigi Cappiello, and Alioscia Hamma study quantum resources in gauge theories in a 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating quantum field theories is among the hardest tasks in particle physics. Classical computers generally fail on strongly coupled theories like QCD. Quantum computers may succeed where classical ones cannot. Lattice gauge theories are the standard discrete form of these theories. The authors study their magic.

Magic is a technical resource that marks quantum advantage. Classical simulation stays feasible when magic is low in the right sense. Mapping where magic sits in lattice gauge theories guides simulator design. It tells builders which parts truly need quantum hardware. For the quantum simulation program, such maps are strategic.
arxiv-2601-16042:
Nicola Spaldin calls for a fresh theory of how solids gain a twist. Her 2026 preprint draws on the known theory of charge shift in solids. That older theory gave a strict sense to the charge shift of a crystal. It also gave codes a clear way to work the value out. The shift theory changed how teams think of charged solids.
