Face coding in the female brain proved to use both sides, not one alone. That result revises a simple picture taught for years. Sex differences in brain organization matter for fair neuroscience: rules drawn from mostly male samples may not hold. The study encourages testing both sexes before general claims are made.
plos-pone-0011342:
Anna Christensen and co-workers examined plant versions of calreticulin in 2010, using the small weed Arabidopsis. Calreticulin is a protein found in the cell's inner workshop, where it helps fold new proteins and manage calcium stores. Animals have forms of it with clear jobs, but what the several plant forms each do was much less clear.

Arabidopsis carries three related forms, and the team tested how each one behaves and where it acts. The forms turned out not to be simple backups. Each had taken on distinct, specialized duties as plants evolved. That split helps explain how plants handle stress and growth with a partly shared toolkit. It also guides crop research, since calcium handling and protein folding both affect how plants cope with drought and disease.
plos-pone-0011442:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors tracked flu spread inside homes during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic in a 2010 study. Households were ground zero for transmission, and close contacts of patients were often given antiviral drugs in advance to prevent infection. Whether that drug shield held up inside a real home, with shared air and close contact, was an open question.

Following households where members took preventive antivirals, the team measured how often the virus still passed to contacts. Their transmission data let officials judge how much protection the drugs truly add at home. That judgment shapes pandemic plans: preventive drugs are costly and in short supply, so they must go where they work. The study gives planners household-level numbers instead of hopeful guesses for the next pandemic.
plos-pone-0011542:
Jia Hu, Karen Doucette, and Lisa Hartling gathered the world's evidence in 2010 on treating hepatitis C in children. The virus infects children as well as adults, mainly through medical exposure or from mother to child, yet nearly all treatment trials had been run in adults. A systematic review collects every eligible study, weighs its quality, and states plainly what is known and what is not.

Their synthesis tells pediatricians which treatments work in children, how safe they are at young ages, and where the evidence runs thin. Children are not small adults in drug handling or in the decades of life over which side effects and cures play out. A dedicated review prevents two errors at once: denying children treatments that would help, and giving them regimens whose risks were only ever measured in grown bodies.
plos-pone-0011642:
Carlos Goller and Patrick Seed screened for chemicals that strip a protective coat from E. coli bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This germ is the leading cause of urinary tract infections, and drug resistance is rising. Instead of killing the germ, so-called anti-virulence drugs aim to disarm it so the body can clear it.

The pair ran a high-throughput screen for blockers of the group 2 capsule, the sugary shield many harmful strains wear. The screen found candidate chemicals that stop capsule building. Such hits could lead to treatments that weaken infection while putting less pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance.
plos-pone-0011742:
Paolo Uva and co-authors set surface proteins of real tumours next to those of lab-grown cancer lines, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell lines are the workhorses of cancer research, yet how well their surface traits match the tumours they came from was poorly known. That gap matters, because surface proteins are prime drug targets.

From gene activity data, the team compared the full set of membrane proteins between tumours and derived lines. Their side-by-side test gauges what the lab lines keep and what they lose. The verdict helps researchers judge when results from a cell line can be trusted for therapy work.
plos-pone-0011942:
William Kelly and colleagues mapped in 2010 the sugar-processing toolkit of a bacterium that helps cattle digest grass. Butyrivibrio proteoclasticus lives in the rumen, the fermentation chamber of the cow stomach, and is skilled at breaking down plant polysaccharides, the tough sugars of fiber. It also makes butyrate, a useful energy product for the animal.

The team's survey of its glycobiome, the full set of genes for handling sugars, shows a microbe adapted in detail to a polysaccharide-rich home. Each enzyme cataloged is a candidate for improving feed digestion or industrial fiber breakdown. Better rumen science feeds directly into how much milk and meat a given pasture can support.
plos-pone-0012042:
Erik Meijaard and colleagues set in 2010 the ape counts of the age of Wallace next to counts from our own time, to gauge how far orangutans have fallen. Orangutans in Borneo now live thin on the ground, and to see one in the wild is a rare treat. Set by that, the old logs startle: collectors in the time of Alfred Russel Wallace could shoot apes day in, day out.

Working through those logs, the team found that the rate at which a searcher meets an ape has fallen steeply. The apes, they argue, were once spread far more thickly over their home woods. A long base line moves the goal for those who guard the apes: to raise today's thin counts back to health would still leave the apes far short of their old plenty.
plos-pone-0012142:
Dharanesh Gangaiah, Zhe Liu, Jesús Arcos, and co-authors studied a food-poisoning bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. Campylobacter jejuni is a leading cause of diarrheal illness, and it survives stress and infects people with the help of a stored chemical called polyphosphate. One enzyme builds that store, while a second one, PPK2, spends it to make an energy-rich signal.

The authors show PPK2 is a fresh factor in how this bacterium handles stress and causes disease. Blocking an enzyme the germ needs under stress is a classic drug strategy. Naming PPK2's role gives researchers a new target in a very common pathogen, one that grows harder to treat as drug resistance spreads.
plos-pone-0012242:
Serign Ceesay, Climent Casals-Pascual, Davis Nwakanma, and co-authors reported malaria's continued fall in The Gambia in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria cases had already dropped sharply in the country's west over several years up to 2007, raising a once-unthinkable idea: elimination. Since then, bed nets, spraying, and better treatment had been scaled up further with outside support.

Their report checks whether the decline held or bounced back as efforts expanded. A sustained fall strengthens the case that this once heavily burdened region could aim at zero local cases. It also supplies other African countries a worked example of which combined measures coincided with lasting gains.
plos-pone-0012342:
Jin Qian and Huajian Gao published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on how cells hold on to the surfaces around them. Single bonds between cell receptors and target molecules break fast, yet whole tissues stay firm for long spans. The authors asked how the softness of the surface under those bonds changes the way groups of bonds share the load.

Their model shows that soft surfaces weaken the teamwork among bonds, so clusters fail sooner than they would on stiff ground. The work helps explain why cells behave so differently on soft gels and firm tissue. It also gives engineers a rule of thumb for building soft materials that cells must grip, from wound dressings to lab-grown tissue scaffolds.
plos-pone-0012442:
Marcel Stoop, Vaibhav Singh, Lennard Dekker and colleagues compared proteins in spinal fluid from two forms of multiple sclerosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Most patients have the relapsing-remitting form, with attacks and recoveries, while others worsen steadily from the start in the primary progressive form. Whether the two are one disease or two is still argued.

Proteomics — reading hundreds of proteins at once — showed the fluids differ in measurable ways. Distinct protein profiles hint that the forms run on somewhat different biology. Such profiles could sharpen diagnosis and may explain why drugs that help relapsing patients often fail in progressive disease.
plos-pone-0012542:
Daria Gavriouchkina, Sabine Fischer, Tomi Ivacevic and colleagues studied a light-controlled repair switch in zebrafish embryos, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Light triggers many cell responses, and fish embryo cells literally sense light themselves, but how the signal reaches the genome was an enigma. One transcription factor, thyrotroph embryonic factor, responds to light.

The team showed the factor regulates light-induced transcription of DNA repair genes in embryonic cells. Coupling repair to daylight makes sense: sunlight itself damages DNA. The zebrafish system offers a clean model for how light, clocks, and genome protection are wired together in early life.
plos-pone-0012642:
Libby and Glass used maths to ask how big a judging committee should be, and who should sit on it. Hiring panels, juries, election counts and skating judges all face the same design problem. Too few judges gives noisy verdicts, while too many can add cost without adding truth.

Their 2010 paper works out how accuracy changes with the number of judges and their skill mix. The results give a rule of thumb for building panels in fields far apart. It is a neat case of one simple model serving many real decisions.
plos-pone-0012842:
Schuchmann and Siemers measured how loud the sonar calls of horseshoe bats are within one bat community. A bat's call strength sets the size of the world it can sense, since faint echoes from far prey get lost. Data on call intensity across species were only starting to gather when they wrote in 2010.

They asked whether species sharing one habitat split call strength to divide food resources, or use it to signal each other. Either answer links a physical trait to community life. Such work sharpens the ecology of night hunting.
plos-pone-0319542:
Joe D. Piper and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on young children in rural Zimbabwe who were exposed to HIV before birth but not infected. Worldwide, millions of such children exist thanks to treatment that prevents transmission from mother to child, yet they still face higher rates of illness and stunting than unexposed children. Piper's team measured body size and composition at age two in a subgroup of a large nutrition and sanitation trial.

Compared with unexposed children, the exposed group was shorter and lighter, with smaller arms and calves. Electrical measurements and skinfold tests showed they carried both less lean tissue and less fat. Lower birthweight did not explain the gap, and neither did stunting on its own. The authors suggest this early pattern of reduced body tissue may help explain why these children remain more vulnerable to sickness and slower development.
plos-pone-0327442:
Jiaxiang Zheng, Moxi Cao, and Chongbin Zhang built a computer system that can pick out the lead instrument in recordings of Chinese traditional music, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. In an ensemble, many instruments play at once, and telling them apart by ear or software is hard, especially when two flutes sound nearly alike.

Their method works in two stages: first it separates the mixed audio into single-instrument strands, then a classifier names the instruments present. On a new dataset they built, accuracy and related scores rose clearly over earlier approaches, with the biggest gains on sound-alike pairs such as the dizi and xiao flutes. They offer the tool for preserving and studying Chinese musical heritage.
plos-pone-0329042:
Snead and colleagues describe a 2026 study protocol set in rural Karonga, in northern Malawi. The team wants to learn what drives steady loss of kidney function in adults there. Kidney disease is rising worldwide and hits poorer countries hard. Blood tests based on creatinine, the usual marker, can miss cases in African populations.

Adults who took part in earlier health surveys will give new blood and urine samples and answer questions on risks at home. Samples from three points in time will be tested with both creatinine and cystatin C, a marker the authors note gives closer readings. The main outcome is a lasting drop of about a quarter in estimated kidney function. Findings should help Malawi aim screening and care at the people most at risk.
plos-pone-0341242:
Katja Bøhling Dybdahl and colleagues, including the DANCAVAS trialists, published this 2026 Danish cohort study of gout drugs and aortic aneurysms. A swollen belly aorta can rupture fatally, and urate-lowering gout medicines had been suggested to slow its growth. The team followed nearly a thousand screened men for five years through national registries.

Only a small share used the medicines, and their aneurysms grew no slower than other men's. Surgery, rupture, and death rates also showed no benefit. Dybdahl concludes these drugs should not be expected to protect men with aneurysms, whatever their value for gout.
plos-pone-0341642:
Denis Omara and colleagues provide step-by-step guidelines for making vaccine and gene-therapy vectors from a dog adenovirus. The usual human adenovirus used for such delivery is blunted by widespread prior immunity in people. The canine virus type 2 rarely infects humans and slips into airway and nerve cells well. It also keeps delivered genes switched on for a long time without inserting into the genome.

Their protocol covers growing the non-replicating vector, purifying it, and measuring its strength, the practical details a laboratory needs to reproduce the work. Because the vector provokes immunity on its own, it needs no added booster chemicals in vaccine designs. Sharing a vetted recipe lowers the barrier for groups wanting to build vaccines on this platform.
plos-pone-0341942:
Crystal Suei Cheng Wong and colleagues test whether a single dose of patterned magnetic brain stimulation sharpens vision when the eyes are deliberately blurred. A dozen adults with normal sight wore lenses that fogged their view, then received one of two stimulation patterns or a sham at the back of the head across separate visits. Sight and contrast tests ran right before and right after each session, under a registered plan with neither side knowing which session was real.

Neither active pattern changed contrast judgment or sharpness beyond the sham session. Sharpness did improve slightly over time in every session, a practice effect the authors flag. Wong and colleagues read the null result as evidence that one session cannot retune a healthy visual system under blur, whatever later sessions might do.
plos-pone-0343442:
Yuting Luo and colleagues build in 2026 a warning system for hidden stock manipulation in China's main share market. Past cases punished by the national regulator were labelled by month, then matched with company reports, online investor mood, and trading patterns. A learning model joined the text and number signals to score risk for each firm each month.

The joined model beat models using only one kind of signal, and it was far better at catching the riskiest cases early in a ranked list. The authors read this as proof that odd moves across disclosure, mood, and trading together reveal manipulation, giving regulators a practical screening tool.
plos-pone-0344142:
Xiaoqing Ye and seven colleagues published this 2026 cancer study testing a small peptide against stomach tumors. Drugs that block the growth factor VEGF can slow new blood vessels feeding a tumor, but the antibody versions are large and reach tissue poorly. A doubled peptide called D6, designed to grip VEGF, was their smaller alternative.

In cell tests and in mice carrying human stomach tumors, D6 slowed growth about as well as the standard antibody used for comparison. The catch was dose: the peptide needed repeated injections at higher amounts. Ye's group is now refining the molecule toward a more practical treatment.
plos-pone-0344742:
Claudia Nery Teixeira Palombo and colleagues interviewed just over five hundred mothers of young children in Salvador, Brazil, about their trust in vaccines. Most children there are registered with family health units, giving the team a clear window on everyday attitudes. Mothers answered questions on family circumstances, their children's vaccination records, and how safe and necessary they believe vaccines to be.

Confidence ran high overall, with more than four in five mothers trusting vaccines, yet about a quarter showed some hesitancy. Mothers with more schooling trusted more, while a poor or neutral relationship with clinic staff dragged trust down and pushed perceived risk up. Mothers who had refused a new vaccine were notably less confident overall. The authors urge services to invest in warmer, steadier relationships with parents.
plos-pone-0344942:
Parkpoom Chaisiriprasert and Apicha Deearom built a learning system to tell sea turtle species apart in underwater photos. Telling species apart supports counts and protection, yet murky water, poor light, and blocked views fool both people and models. Their system feeds both colour photos and edge maps that trace shell and flipper outlines into a shared network with smart blending steps.

The best blending version led on precision, recall, and overall detection scores, beating simpler fusions. Adding outline cues helped most where species look alike in colour alone. Automated, accurate sorting could let survey teams process far more dive and drone photos, building better maps of where each turtle species lives.
plos-pone-0345742:
Kathryn M. Yount and co-workers develop a short survey module that national statistics offices can use to measure women's empowerment. Countries lack routine data for tracking global gender goals. Their 2026 study builds the module for face-to-face surveys. It tests the module in Bangladesh, Malawi, and Nepal. The checks ask whether question groups hold together, and whether they mean the same thing across genders and countries.

Most question groups formed sound, distinct measures tied to empowerment ideas. A smaller set behaved the same across men and women, and fewer still across countries. Links with outside measures were mostly weak, though a few matched expectations well. The team concludes the module needs more refinement before scores can be compared fairly everywhere.
plos-pone-0346542:
Yan Zhang, Wei Chen, and Gang Yang published a study on virtual camera movement in PLOS ONE in 2026. Digital twins and AI-built 3D scenes need camera paths for tours and reviews. A poorly planned path swings and jerks, leaving viewers confused or even queasy.

Zhang's team guided path planning with how human vision works, aiming for views people can follow with ease. Their framework keeps tours smooth and readable at large scale. Designers of virtual site visits, training scenes, and city models face this need daily. Better camera paths mean reviewers spend their attention on the scene itself, not on fighting the viewpoint, which improves the value of every digital twin walk-through.
plos-pone-0347642:
HaoBo Yang and colleagues investigated how sodium nitrite, a preservative found in processed meats and a widespread contaminant, might help clog arteries. Hardening of the arteries kills millions each year, but the molecular route from nitrite exposure to disease was sketchy. Their 2026 study is a computer and data-mining exercise, stitching together gene databases, machine learning, and molecular simulations rather than new lab experiments.

The analysis singled out four suspect proteins, with an inflammation signal called IL-1 beta at the centre. Virtual docking showed nitrite binding stably to it, and diseased artery tissue showed heavier infiltration by immune cells. The authors frame the work as a hypothesis map for future laboratory testing, not proof of harm.
plos-pone-0348142:
Charuai Suwanbamrung and a multinational team studied in 2026 how households in southern Thailand understand dengue control and the surveillance system that tracks mosquito larvae. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes that breed in water containers around homes, so household practice decides much of the risk. Health workers use larval indices, counts of breeding sites found in surveys, to judge where outbreaks may ignite.

Their mixed methods study combined surveys with interviews of household representatives, the people who actually receive and act on dengue advice. Knowing what residents understand, and where the official message misses their reality, lets health programs teach more effectively. The study speaks for the household end of a surveillance chain that usually gets described only from the office end.
plos-pone-0348842:
Dong Yan and co-workers devise a smarter way to choose stitch lines when joining radar satellite images into one big map. Mismatched brightness and slight shifts between scenes can leave ugly seams. Their 2026 method first groups pixels into tidy super-regions. These regions stay consistent across overlapping images. Neighbors then merge by texture and edge evidence. Finally, the method picks the cheapest clean path through a network of candidate seams.

Tests on real radar scenes checked each step of the pipeline. Compared with two classic methods, the new route preserved whole objects and hugged their boundaries better. Cleaner mosaics matter for flood mapping, land monitoring, and any wide-area work built on radar imagery.
plos-pone-0348942:
Rehab Osman Taha and co-workers look for gene patterns in Thai patients with a bile duct cancer linked to a liver fluke parasite. The cancer is aggressive and common where the fluke infects people through raw fish. Their 2026 study compares just over a hundred cancer patients with fluke-infected people and healthy controls, reading a panel of cancer and stress-pathway genes.

Changes in one gene turned up in half the cancer patients, far more than in either comparison group, and carrying two copies raised risk most. Changes in a second gene appeared only in cancer patients. A famous cancer gene varied widely in everyone and told little. The pattern may be specific to this fluke-linked cancer and could sharpen screening in Thailand.
plos-pone-0349042:
Alahdal and colleagues screened a modified plant compound against lung cancer targets in a 2026 computer study. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, and tumors often stop responding to single-target drugs. Seven proteins tied to lung tumor growth were chosen as docking targets from a drug database search.

The compound, a phosphate form of a common plant pigment, was tested for fit against all seven targets, a multi-target strategy the authors call heptapharmacology. Strong fits would nominate it for lab testing. Computer docking cannot prove a drug works, but hitting several cancer pathways at once is a rational way to hunt for resistance-proof candidates.
plos-pone-0349142:
Emmanuel K. Sam and co-workers read the full genetic code of Salmonella bacteria taken from typhoid patients in Ghana. Typhoid fever still sickens and kills many people there, yet local data on which strains circulate remain thin. Their 2026 study works with isolates grown from blood and stool samples at Ghanaian care sites.

Sequencing showed wide variety among the strains. One typhoid type grouped closely with strains from nearby West African countries, which points to spread across borders. A type linked to severe invasive illness also turned up in stool. Many strains carried genes tied to harming the body, so the results give health teams a firmer base for tracking outbreaks and drug resistance.
plos-pone-0349242:
Yuhang Li and colleagues analysed fourteen years of Chinese news coverage of HIV and AIDS to watch the story change. From a large body of articles published between twenty ten and twenty twenty-four, computer methods extracted the main topic clusters. They pulled out the words used for people living with the virus and the metaphors wrapped around the disease. Then they mapped how these choices connect.

Coverage organised itself into five big themes, from prevention to medicine and society, and drifted steadily toward official, large-scale narratives and away from individual human stories. Neutral, de-identified labels for people with HIV became the norm, yet stigmatising terms survived in many forms. War, journey, and thing metaphors formed the core imagery. The authors describe media institutions adapting to a state-led system while old stigma quietly persists underneath.
plos-pone-0349442:
Yanping Feng, Yilin Wang, and Binyou Wang explored whether handgrip strength, a cheap bedside measure, mirrors brain activity in people living long-term in hospital with stable schizophrenia. Ninety-six patients squeezed a grip meter while a cap using near-infrared light tracked blood flow in the front of the brain during a word-naming task. The team compared grip patterns, including differences between the two hands, with the brain signals.

An uneven grip between hands lined up with stronger frontal brain responses in simple comparisons. Once age, sex, and other differences between patients were accounted for, that link faded and no grip group stood apart. The authors treat the work as exploratory: grip strength alone does not yet earn a place as a stand-in for brain function in this group, and larger studies would be needed.
plos-pone-0349942:
Anna J Dreyer and colleagues in Cape Town, South Africa, asked in 2026 what shapes thinking test scores before any HIV infection. Scores are often blamed on the virus, yet childhood poverty and schooling also leave marks that studies rarely measure.

Adults with and without HIV took a broad set of thinking tests, plus a knowledge test used as a stand-in for earlier ability. Life circumstances from childhood and adulthood were grouped into clusters. The analysis traced how those clusters feed into later scores, partly through earlier ability. The lesson is that fair reading of HIV and the brain must start with a person's whole history.
plos-pone-0350042:
Jing Liu and colleagues hunted for ageing signals in lungs harmed by radiation treatment for chest cancers. Radiation lung injury can scar lungs and spoil treatment gains. Gene data from injured lungs were crossed with known cell ageing gene lists, which flagged a growth factor called GDF15. Rat lungs exposed to radiation then showed damage, scarring, and ageing marks.

Blocking or boosting the factor in lung lining cells shifted ageing markers along a known signalling path. Injured tissue carried far more of the factor alongside DNA damage signals. If human work agrees, the factor could serve as both a warning marker and a drug target for easing radiation lung harm.
plos-pone-0350142:
Richard May and seven colleagues grade the evidence reviews published in behaviour analysis journals. Their 2026 umbrella review gathered every systematic review and meta-analysis in seven field journals up to 2023. Sixty-four reviews counted, sixteen with meta-analyses. Two standard tools scored how sound their methods were. The plan was logged in advance. The headline result is sober reading for the field.

Every single review rated critically low on the main quality scale. Plans were rarely logged beforehand. Risk of bias in the underlying studies was assessed badly. Publication bias often went unchecked entirely. A second, more forgiving scorecard showed adherence under half, though improving slightly each year. Reviews guide real clinical and educational decisions in behaviour analysis. This audit argues the field's synthesis machinery needs repair: registered protocols, honest bias checks, and fuller reporting before its summaries deserve full trust.
plos-pone-0350342:
Zhonglan Yin and four colleagues compare metabolic health between men whose jobs chain them to a seat and men whose jobs keep them moving. Their 2026 study enrolled over two thousand Chinese workers. Bus drivers formed the sedentary group. Sanitation workers formed the comparison. Questionnaires and clinical examinations ran between mid-2023 and late 2024. Metabolic syndrome was diagnosed under current Chinese diabetes guidelines.

Raw rates favoured the movers. The drivers showed more metabolic syndrome, far more high triglycerides, and more central obesity. Then adjustment complicated the story. Once other factors entered the model, sedentary work itself showed no significant link to the full syndrome. Specific components, though, still tracked with the sitting job. The nuance matters for workplace health programmes. Blaming the chair alone oversimplifies; the drivers' whole pattern of eating, schedule, and stress may carry much of the risk.
plos-pone-0350442:
Expression of Concern: the journal flags serious unresolved doubts about this article on a sugar coated molecule said to protect mice against the parasite behind visceral leishmaniasis. Readers should treat its claims as unverified.

Editors found control lanes in one figure that appear to match a figure in another article representing different conditions, and the methods omit how animals were euthanised. Raw data promised with the article were not provided. The first author disputes the image concern and says the originals are gone. With no source files, the journal states the reliability of the counted results cannot be checked.
plos-pone-0350642:
Ruijia Yang and three colleagues study what brief isolation does to soldier crabs in this 2026 behaviour paper. These crabs gather in huge, dense swarms on tidal flats. Their groups have no leaders or fixed roles. That makes them a clean system for testing how one separated individual rejoins the crowd. Isolation in the experiments lasted from five minutes to three hours.

Crabs kept apart for five to thirty minutes came back more active than controls. They also crowded closer to their neighbours. Three hours apart produced a stranger pattern. Those crabs first moved less, then became restless while staying poorly coordinated with the swarm. Short separations seem to energise returning crabs. Long ones disturb the timing that collective movement depends on, a finding relevant to any group-living animal.
plos-pone-0350742:
Catching melanoma early saves lives, and Yada Wuttithantawee and colleagues hunted for a blood signal of the disease. Their 2026 PLOS One study grew immune blood cells alongside melanoma cells and watched which genes the blood cells switched on in response to factors the tumor released.

Of seven candidate genes, one called RPLP1 rose clearly and early. The team then measured it in blood samples from eighty-five people, including melanoma patients, patients with other cancers, and healthy volunteers. Statistical curves checked how well the signal separated melanoma from the rest. The authors present RPLP1 as a candidate marker needing larger trials before any screening use.
plos-pone-0350842:
Efundem Agboraw and colleagues used primary care records for over twelve million adults in England from 2019 to 2024 to study referrals to social prescribing. Link workers connect patients to community help for loneliness, money strain, and housing woes. Offers and completed referrals were modelled by patient traits and area traits.

About four percent of patients were offered a referral, and over three quarters of offers became referrals. Women, older people, people in richer areas, and people with many long term conditions were more likely to be offered help. Among those offered, women, minority ethnic patients, and sicker patients accepted more. Growth since national rollout is real, but poorer areas lag in offers.
plos-pone-0350942:
Ligabaw Worku and a large team in Ethiopia studied the mosquitoes that spread malaria in 2026. They worked in two towns in the northwest, collecting young mosquitoes from breeding sites in the rainy season and after it, then raising them for tests.

Adults were checked for which species they belonged to, exposed to a common insecticide, and screened for gene changes linked to resistance. Some mosquitoes survived the spray, and the resistance gene appeared in the groups tested. Knowing which species are present, and how many shrug off the main spray, helps malaria programs choose tools that still work in each place and season.
plos-pone-0351142:
Yared Asmare Aynalem and colleagues looked at care before pregnancy in Ethiopia in 2026. The country issued its first national guide for such care in 2024, yet few clinics offer it, and most past work asked only about women's knowledge.

The researchers interviewed eighteen adults, women and men, at two public hospitals in Addis Ababa. People described patchy knowledge, often gained only after a problem in pregnancy. Husbands, faith, and clinic rules all shaped whether care was sought at all. The findings argue that services must work with local beliefs and family roles, not just hand out facts, if healthy starts to pregnancy are to become normal.
plos-pone-0351242:
Wasuwit Wanchaitanawong and five colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study of gallstones that slip out of the bile duct on their own before a planned endoscopic procedure. When a stone has already passed, the procedure becomes unnecessary, yet it can also be riskier than expected. The team reviewed more than four hundred patients at a referral center, recording who passed stones and who suffered complications afterward.

About twenty-eight percent of patients had passed their stone before the procedure. Younger patients, those with a single stone, and those with smaller stones were most likely to have done so. Unexpectedly, patients whose stone had passed developed inflammation of the pancreas after the procedure at about double the rate of others. The authors suggest confirming the duct is clear noninvasively before proceeding.
plos-pone-0351542:
Astronauts lose bone in weightlessness, which hints that bone-eating cells sense gravity itself. Natsuhiro Takahashi and colleagues spun mouse bone-eating cells in centrifuges to create stronger-than-normal gravity, in this 2026 PLOS One lab study.

Even half an hour of extra gravity disturbed the actin rings these cells use to seal onto bone and chew it. The rings dimmed and thinned, cell nuclei shifted, and the pits the cells normally dig grew shallower. Protein change scans after brief spinning pointed to the pathways involved. The authors say the cells' skeleton is a gravity sensor, which may explain part of bone loss in space.
plos-pone-0351642:
Muhammad Haider and seven colleagues trace the family tree of black kites in Pakistan's Punjab wetlands. Their 2026 genetic study samples birds at three wetlands, including two river barrages and a lake. Punjab sits at a migratory crossroads for this widespread raptor. The Milvus genus is taxonomically tangled, and Pakistan's birds were barely studied. Partial gene sequences from the kites were compared with reference sequences from around the world.

Local birds turned out genetically close, with tiny maternal distances between them. They form one freely mixing population across the wetlands. Across continents, structure was strong instead. Distances between far-apart lineages, such as West African and European birds, ran much higher. Statistical signatures suggested population expansion or steady purifying selection. For conservation, Punjab's kites can be managed as a single connected population, even while the wider species splits into distinct continental lines.
plos-pone-0351742:
Fabrizio De Massis and seven colleagues describe Italy's response to its first dog brucellosis outbreak. The 2026 report looks back to April 2020. A breeding kennel in central Italy housed over six hundred eighty toy-breed dogs. Brucella canis causes reproductive failure and spreads between dogs. Authorities restricted animal movement at once. Unusually, they chose a no-kill strategy for managing the outbreak.

A structured protocol combined neutering with repeated blood testing. Only dogs confirmed negative were cleared for adoption. More than three hundred dogs were successfully rehomed. Follow-up laboratory checks found no late infections among the adopted animals. The experience matters because culling is the default response in many countries. Italy's outcome shows that careful testing and staged rehoming can control an outbreak while keeping dogs alive and placed in homes.
plos-pone-0351942:
Isaac Osei and three colleagues untangle how heat and rainfall relate in Ghana. Their 2026 study uses weather station records from 1981 to 2020. Daily maximum and minimum temperatures move closely together. That overlap makes their separate links to rainfall hard to estimate. The authors apply a modelling method designed for such tangled predictors. Coastal and inland stations are compared as well.

Hotter days came with less rain, a clear negative link. Warmer nights came with slightly more rain. The idea that maximum temperature works through minimum temperature found no support. The model explained roughly a fifth of rainfall variation. Geography mattered. The negative link between hot days and rain was much stronger inland than on the coast. Such detail helps forecasters read temperature signals differently across Ghana's climate zones.
plos-pone-0352142:
Wen and Lim mined online posts about emergency care during South Korea's 2024 health crisis in a 2026 study. A mass walkout by trainee doctors left emergency rooms strained for months. More than a million posts and comments from major Korean platforms across that year were sorted by machine tools for feeling and themes.

Negative feeling clearly outweighed positive feeling in the posts. Beyond anger at outcomes, phrases about a medical void, being bounced between emergency rooms, and over-treatment stood out as core stressors. The analysis shows what frightened patients most during system failure. Such listening tools could warn officials early about which failures hurt public trust fastest.
plos-pone-0352242:
Christopher Campbell and Graeme Ackland rebuilt a classic model of party competition as a physics-style simulation to ask why modern politics polarizes. The classic model, with two parties chasing voters on one left-right line, predicts a rush to the center, the opposite of what many countries see. Their version spreads voters and parties across two policy dimensions and allows many parties at once.

Two-party contests still damped polarization, even when voters themselves were split into two camps. Multiparty fields did the reverse, pulling parties apart even when most voters were moderate. Adding abstention, activists, and turnout effects polarized even the two-party case. One comfort emerged: the winning party still ended up more moderate than its own supporters. The model blames the structure of competition, not just voter anger, for divided politics.
plos-pone-0352342:
Kim and colleagues built learning models to predict emergency visits in type two diabetes in a 2026 study. Records from five Korean institutions covered more than two hundred twenty thousand patients, including readings, labs, and prescriptions over time. Sudden diabetes complications often land patients in emergency rooms before worse outcomes follow.

Models trained on most of the records were tested on the rest to judge how well they flag a first emergency visit. Spotting high-risk patterns early lets primary care teams act before a crisis. Real-world records, with all their messiness, make the test more honest than tidy trial data, though care patterns differ between health systems.
plos-pone-0352442:
Goossens and colleagues set out a review plan in 2026 on injuries in padel, a fast-growing racket sport. Injury rates are high and the costs can be large, yet no full map of the evidence exists. Under the plan, the review will gather studies on injuries, risk factors, and prevention at every level of play.

A staged framework that moves from describing injuries to testing prevention will organize the work. Studies from any country, setting, or player group will count. The finished map should show where evidence is strong and where padel research is still blank, guiding coaches and health staff toward the prevention steps most worth testing next.
plos-pone-0353142:
Hakki and colleagues tracked blood counts through mild COVID-19 in a community study in a 2026 paper. Ninety-three recently exposed adults with no prior immunity or other illnesses gave blood over four weeks from first positive test. Hospital studies dominate blood knowledge, yet most infections are mild and managed at home.

More than three in ten cases showed a brief drop in a key white cell type early in infection, recovering by convalescence. Such dips could confuse doctors reading single blood tests. A timed picture of normal mild illness helps clinicians tell harmless swings from warning signs.
plos-pone-0353242:
Kim and colleagues held group talks with young Korean women about cervical cancer prevention in a 2026 study. Fourteen women in their twenties, split into those who screen and those who do not, discussed screening and vaccination. Shame around gynecology visits and sexually spread infections emerged in both groups.

Shared themes included negative views of clinic visits and stigma tied to infection. Other themes differed between screeners and non-screeners, showing where decisions diverge. Prevention fails when stigma keeps women away, even where services exist. The authors argue that shifting social views is as necessary as offering tests, and their themes point to messages that might help.
plos-pone-0353742:
Kim and colleagues reviewed research on drinking among Korean immigrant women in a 2026 paper. Drinking has risen among women in recent decades, yet this group's experience had barely been studied. The review covered work from five English-speaking destination countries and sorted the findings by theme.

All of the studies found came from the United States, leaving countries such as Canada unstudied. Three forces shaped drinking most often: adjusting to a new culture, faith life, and friendship circles. Stress from migration and Korean drinking customs appeared as well, though less steadily. The authors call for health programs that respect both culture and gender rather than treating all immigrants alike.
plos-pone-0354242:
Dongyue Wei, Zhe Ren, and Hongtao Yu study how a sports funding policy spread across China in a 2026 PLOS ONE mixed-methods paper. Provinces adopted sports industry development funds at different times between two thousand and six and two thousand and twenty-two. Standard diffusion theories stress wealth, markets, and pressure from above.

Combining adoption timing data for thirty-one regions with thirty stakeholder interviews, the authors found fiscal self-sufficiency and sports lottery sales raised adoption chances. Oddly, having more sports firms lowered them, suggesting funds answer perceived weakness. National pressure shaped the setting without deciding timing alone. Interviews showed local officials adapting the policy strategically, sometimes symbolically, a context-sensitive picture of how innovations spread.
plos-pone-0354342:
Taiga Noguchi led a team of eight authors who measured presenteeism with smartphones, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Presenteeism means working while sick, and it costs economies heavily while staying hard to measure. Surveys ask people to judge themselves, which is unreliable. This team instead used repeated phone-based behavioral responses.

Noguchi's signals, gathered many times from each person's phone, offer a passive and ongoing gauge of who is pushing through illness. Employers and health researchers could spot patterns without constant questionnaires. The work also raises fair questions about privacy that any user of phone sensing must answer. Handled openly, such measures could help target support before sickness becomes long absence.
plos-pone-0354742:
Jill Vögelin led a team of seven authors on this 2026 scoping review of feedback in medical and health professions training. Modern assessment programs lean on feedback about past work and feedforward, guidance aimed at the next attempt. The reviewers mapped studies from 2015 onward to see how both are actually used in assessment settings.

A small set of familiar methods dominated, and future-looking guidance usually stayed implicit or fixated on performance scores. Vögelin argues that naming feedforward plainly and making it actionable could strengthen how health students build competence over time.
plos-pone-0355042:
Yang Li and co-authors measure in 2026 how common severe short sight is among adults aged fifty and older in Fujian, southeast China. A population study enrolled more than eight thousand residents, who answered questions on schooling, income, and habits and received full eye and body checks. Severe short sight raises risk of serious eye disease later in life.

About one in twenty six adults had the severe form. Living inland lowered the odds, while higher pressure inside the eye and more schooling raised them. The authors call for better access to eye care for older inland residents and for closer watching of those with higher eye pressure or education.
plos-pone-0355242:
RETRACTED: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 retraction notice, withdrawing an animal study that had claimed a changed implant surface shape speeds bone growing onto implants. Readers should not rely on that study's findings. Concerns covered many figures, overlap with the group's earlier papers, and stability values that did not line up.

Editors noted near identical animal and implant counts, treatments, measures, and conclusions across papers that were never cited, plus images that matched after flipping or resembled each other inside the same paper. Timelines in the text and a figure also disagreed. The overlap left the work's originality and data in serious doubt.
plos-pone-0355742:
Zhe Liu and Dan Tian improved a well-known image segmentation model so it can pick out the most noticeable object in a scene. Adapting the general Segment Anything Model to saliency detection often leaves broken masks, fuzzy edges, and lost detail, especially when objects vary in size. Their 2026 design attacks three named weaknesses of earlier adapters.

A weighted multi-scale adapter learns how to calibrate features from different viewing scales instead of using fixed rules. A cross-fusion module ties levels together by meaning, not mere stacking. Wavelet processing rescues the fine, high-frequency detail that ordinary operations discard. Liu and Tian argue the three fixes together sharpen saliency maps for complex, textured scenes.
plos-pone-0355842:
Ella Barnum and seven colleagues use rats on a shift-work schedule to trace how circadian disruption reaches the gut, and whether the harm differs by sex, in this 2026 study. Earlier work from the team showed that shifted light cycles worsen stroke outcomes more in males. Two cohorts of rats lived for fifty days under either a fixed light-dark rhythm or one advanced by half a day every five days. The researchers then examined gut microbes, gut structure, and inflammatory signals.

Shifted males, but not females, lost microbial diversity, and the abundance of beneficial gut bacteria tracked with stroke survival. Their gut lining showed shortened, blunted villi, loosened barrier proteins, lower levels of a protective fatty acid, and higher circulating endotoxin and an inflammatory signal. Females were largely spared. The authors suggest this gut pathway helps explain why circadian disruption hits male stroke outcomes harder.
plos-pone-0356142:
Soyoung Kim and seven colleagues test whether gallstones quietly signal dangerous heart artery disease in people who feel perfectly well, in this 2026 study from South Korea. More than nine thousand adults with no heart disease history received both an abdominal ultrasound and a CT scan of their coronary arteries during health checkups. The team compared plaque types and narrowing severity between those with and without gallstones, adjusting for standard risk factors and matching patients on background traits.

About one participant in eighteen had gallstones. Those individuals were significantly more likely to carry noncalcified plaque, the soft, higher-risk kind, and to have a coronary narrowing severe enough to count as clinically significant. The authors conclude that finding gallstones should prompt attention to cardiovascular risk factors, since the same patients may harbor hidden, riskier plaque.
plos-pone-0356242:
Wenjie Zhao and three colleagues build an artificial intelligence system that spots Aspergillus mold in sample images, in this 2026 computer vision study. The fungus matters in medicine and food safety, but its tangled shapes, subtle features, rare strains, and partly hidden colonies defeat simple detectors. The team upgraded a current real-time detection framework with three new modules. One fuses complex structural features. One scores matches by shape to cope with blurred or blocked edges. A third adapts to colonies of different sizes.

The resulting model identified Aspergillus with precision above ninety percent and strong recall, while staying compact enough for practical deployment. The authors report that the shape-aware matching and multi-scale attention were key to handling occlusion and strain variety. They present the system as a faster, more reliable alternative to manual microscopic inspection for laboratories and screening programs.
plos-pone-0356542:
Pengfei Xu and five colleagues fine-tune a warm-up trick used by strength athletes in this 2026 experiment: doing heavy squats shortly before jumping to boost jump height. Twelve trained men each performed four squat protocols at a demanding load, varying depth, deep versus half squats, and whether the set stopped just short of failure or went all the way. Jump height was then measured at several points over the following twelve minutes.

All four protocols raised jump performance. Sets that stopped short of failure paid off sooner, lifting jumps by about four minutes, while sets taken to failure peaked later, around eight minutes. Half squats produced the stronger boost overall. The authors suggest a small set of heavy half squats, stopped before failure, as a time-efficient way to prime explosive performance before competition or training.
plos-pone-0356642:
Guillermo Puebla and five colleagues tested why people believe false health claims, using more than six hundred Chilean university students who judged true and false COVID-19 headlines. In their 2026 experiment, half the students held numbers in memory while judging, to load their working memory, and everyone completed measures of reflective thinking, pseudoscience belief, and tolerance for impressive-sounding nonsense.

The memory load slowed students down but did not make them more gullible. What predicted mistaking false headlines for true ones was a person's habits of belief: credulity toward pseudoscience and empty jargon, and weak reflective thinking. The results suggest that fighting health misinformation works better by strengthening how people evaluate claims than by simply slowing them down or reducing distractions.
plos-pone-0356742:
Huahan Zhan and seven colleagues test a gruesome-sounding claim in this 2026 study: can a common bathroom drain fly actually live inside the human gut? Larvae of this moth fly turn up in stool samples from time to time, raising fears of true intestinal infestation. The team raised the flies in the lab and confirmed their identity by shape and DNA.

Simulated stomach fluid proved lethal, wiping out eggs and nearly all larvae, and gut fluid finished off most survivors. Even when mice were fed live eggs and young larvae directly, nothing passed through, no tissue damage appeared, and no infestation took hold. The authors conclude that most supposed cases are probably contamination of samples or a brief false alarm, not a real infestation, which should reassure both patients and doctors.
plos-pone-0357042:
Teresa Kisi Beyen led a team of five authors mapping esophageal cancer in Ethiopia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. This cancer occurs in clusters in central Oromia, but the exact pattern was unclear. The team used spatial statistics, including autocorrelation and scan methods, to map where cases concentrate.

Beyen's hotspots give health officials concrete targets for screening programs. Clustering also guides research into local causes, such as diet or environmental exposures shared in one area. Esophageal cancer is often caught late, when treatment helps least, so targeted early screening in hotspots could save lives. Geographic evidence turns a vague regional worry into a list of places to act first.
plos-pone-0357142:
Jin Sothornwit and colleagues used Thailand's national hospital database from 2017 to 2024. They counted thyroid storm, the rare, life-threatening flare of an overactive thyroid. They also looked for what kills the patients it strikes. Their 2026 study compared more than a thousand storm admissions against several thousand admissions for thyroid overactivity without storm.

Storm cases grew steadily across the period. They roughly doubled per head of population. Death in hospital struck nearly one in five storm patients. Without storm, it struck one in a hundred. Storm itself multiplied the odds of death many times over. Septic shock, heart failure shock, and kidney injury were the strongest companions of death. The authors urge hospitals to treat those complications as the true battleground.
plos-pone-0357442:
Gregg E. Moore and coauthors published a 2026 ecology study in PLOS ONE revisiting a Massachusetts marsh six years after a winter storm buried it in sediment. Storm Grayson in 2018 dumped an uneven layer across the Great Marsh; one season later, buried plots showed thinner cover and shifted soil chemistry. Six seasons on, the team returned to test whether the sediment helped or harmed the marsh, measuring vegetation, soil chemistry, and living roots by depth.

Plant cover and height no longer differed by sediment amount, and species richness held. Salinity had fallen since 2018, while oxygen-related chemistry and sulfides shifted mostly in thinly covered plots. Roots told the most positive story: living density was strong in moderately covered plots, as if the marsh grew into its new elevation. Natural sediment deliveries of a few centimeters, they conclude, can feed marshes facing sea-level rise without lasting damage.
plos-pone-0358042:
Gary B Wilkerson, Mohammad Joghataee, and Ashish Gupta hunt for a measurable fingerprint of repeated concussion inside virtual reality, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Standard clinical tests miss subtle thinking damage after head injuries, especially as hits pile up. The team pooled data from two hundred two adolescents and young adults. They measured how fast and steadily participants turned, reached, and lunged at moving visual targets inside a headset.

Machine learning and theory driven statistics agreed on a leading signal. A neck movement score combining speed and correctness of response best separated people with several past concussions from those with one or none. Its variability partner moved the other way, as a decision model would predict. Together the pair may mark a cumulative, lingering deficit that ordinary symptom checklists pronounce healed. The authors propose such metrics for return to play calls that now rest on self report.
plos-pone-0358242:
Felistar Mwakasungura and colleagues published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE of people carrying both HIV and hepatitis B in Tanzania, drawing on a large national household survey from 2022–2023. Carrying both viruses speeds up illness even with treatment, yet country-level numbers were missing. The survey tested more than thirty thousand people aged fifteen and older across all regions of the country.

Each virus alone was fairly common, but dual infection was rare in the general population, at well under one percent. Among people living with HIV, however, about one in sixteen also had hepatitis B. Risk of the double infection rose with age and was higher for people not in a union, while having had only one lifetime sexual partner was strongly protective. The authors say Tanzania's overall burden is low, but screening people in HIV care for hepatitis B remains essential because that subgroup's risk is real.
plos-pone-0358342:
Ji Won Kim and four colleagues test whether an artificial intelligence reconstruction changes heart calcium scores, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The score, built from CT images, sorts patients into risk categories that drive statin decisions. A deep learning method promises cleaner images from the same scan. The team scored a cardiac phantom and one hundred thirteen patients three ways: the classic reconstruction, an iterative method, and the deep learning one at high strength.

In the phantom, all three agreed. In patients, the deep learning scores ran significantly lower than the classic method's, while matching the iterative method. Category agreement stayed high overall. Individual patients, though, could shift substantially between methods, with differences large enough to matter near the cutoffs where risk labels change. The authors' caution is practical: a score is only comparable when the reconstruction behind it is held constant.
plos-pone-0358742:
Wenwei Liu leads a team of eight shrinking a vision model until it can grade roses on a cheap device at the farm, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A rose's price depends on grade. Human grading is slow and inconsistent. The small computers in packing sheds cannot run heavyweight software. Their framework, Flora-YOLO, rebuilds a compact detector with four changes. The changes sharpen faint petal textures and protect detail under leaf clutter. They amplify weak signals from young buds and respect the irregular shapes of flowers.

Across cross validation on their rose dataset, the model reached accuracy near eighty-seven percent on the standard overlap measure. It beat its baseline while cutting computing load by more than a quarter. It needs under two million parameters, small enough for edge hardware. The work points toward grading lines where a camera, not a tired human eye, makes the call on every stem.
plos-pone-0358942:
Juan Hurtado, Carson Allan, Sergio Castrezana, Jeremy Bono, and Luciano Matzkin published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a catalog, a systematic list, of messenger RNAs that males pass to females when mating, in two fruit fly species, Drosophila arizonae and Drosophila mojavensis.

Messenger RNA carries instructions for making proteins, so molecules transferred in mating could affect the female after fertilization. Listing exactly which RNAs move across gives other biologists a reference set for studying reproduction and how species diverge. Work of this kind also feeds into understanding how new fly species form in the deserts these insects inhabit.
plos-pone-0359542:
Nickson Erick Otieno published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It uses GIS mapping, remote sensing from satellites, and linear models to fight erosion and sediment transport in the Lake Victoria watershed in Kenya. The aim is prioritizing spatially explicit action: choosing exactly where anti-erosion work should happen first.

Sediment washing into Lake Victoria clouds water, harms fish, and chokes the lake's bays. Maps built from satellite data and terrain models show which slopes and streams deliver the most sediment. Watershed managers with limited budgets need that ranking to place soil conservation where each shilling buys the most protection.
plos-pone-0360242:
Chen Li, Sijia Gao, and Meng Li reported in 2026 on blending laboratory paper analysis into the traditional craft of restoring ancient Chinese books. Their case study is a Chinese medical text named Yi Men Pu Du. Restorers have long judged old paper by eye and touch, choosing treatments by inherited experience.

The authors bring experimental analysis of the paper itself into that process, testing its makeup and condition before deciding how to repair it. Matching modern measurement with craft judgment aims to make restoration choices more precise and less likely to harm fragile pages. The study speaks to libraries and archives across China, where large holdings of ancient medical and scholarly books await careful repair.
pmc-13194242:
Shuyu Zhou is first author on a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of a combined treatment for sunken facial acne scars. Fractional carbon dioxide laser resurfacing is a standard option, and adding recombinant human epidermal growth factor, a lab-made skin growth protein, is increasingly practiced. Whether the pairing beats laser alone needed gathering.

Searching eight databases to July twenty twenty-five, the authors included twelve randomized trials with one thousand and forty-four patients, all in China. The combination improved scar scores more than laser alone and shortened crusting time. Side effects, especially darkening of skin, were less frequent with the combination. Evidence certainty, though, ranged from very low to moderate, so larger, stronger trials are needed.
pmc-13201942:
Ten years of using one gut-selective biologic are reviewed in a 2026 narrative review by Vipul Jairath, focused on vedolizumab for inflammatory bowel disease. The article traces how treatment of ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease changed over the decade, and where this antibody therapy fits among newer options.

Jairath and co-authors describe the shift from step-up treatment to early, target-driven strategies with endoscopic goals. Vedolizumab, the first approved drug blocking lymphocyte traffic into the gut, is assessed across that changing landscape of care. The review also weighs open problems, including how to sequence biologics and combine them, and points to decision-support tools as a promising direction.
pmc-13203942:
Wasted electricity in Bitcoin mining can be modeled rather than just lamented, and a 2026 study by Paolo Barucca builds that model around chain forks. The research article explains how competing miners, concentrated power, and slow block propagation create forks that discard work and weaken the network.

The authors model fork rates using miner numbers, hash power distribution, and propagation times across the peer-to-peer network. The model reproduces the empirical rule linking forks to the ratio of propagation time to mining time, and it flags anomalies around 2016 suggesting concentrated power or uneven delays. Their estimate of power wasted on stale blocks in the most recent year rivals half of United Kingdom generation.
pmc-13205642:
Smokers with HIV often get little help quitting, and a 2026 pilot report headed by Christof M Schönenberger checks whether offering a choice of nicotine products works in practice. The article reports the internal pilot of the Swiss RETUNE trial, which lets participants pick e-cigarettes, nicotine pouches, or patches instead of tobacco.

Among the first two hundred people randomized, about half were offered the product menu under the trial's cohort design. Just over half of those offered accepted a product, with e-cigarettes the most popular pick, patches second, and pouches rarely chosen. Most people who refused said they simply did not want to quit smoking.
pmc-13209142:
How deep is deep enough for sedation is the dispute in a 2026 letter headed by Yuanyuan Li about a dexmedetomidine dosing study. The letter responds to research reporting that the median effective sedative dose barely differs between men and women having upper limb surgery under a nerve block.

The writers argue the study's success threshold counted patients as adequately sedated at a depth many clinicians would call too deep for cooperative regional anesthesia care. They also note the trial then maintained a lighter level during surgery, undercutting its own definition in practice. Finally, they caution that finding no sex difference is not the same as proving the doses equivalent.
pmc-13210142:
Radar maps of sinking mining land are hard to unwrap, and a 2026 study by Baojing Zhang teaches a neural network to do it more faithfully. The research article presents MAPUNet, a multi-scale attention network for interferometric phase unwrapping where large ground deformation and noise defeat traditional algorithms.

The design adds pyramid pooling for wide context, a dual attention block, and a channel-attention residual module to suppress noise while keeping important features. On simulated scenes with heavy noise it beat rival methods on image similarity scores in the authors' tests. Applied to a real Shanxi mining district, it measured subsidence reaching roughly nine centimeters within one month.
pmc-13238242:
Kakeshita and colleagues report a rare cancer arising in a repaired aorta in a kidney transplant patient. The patient had earlier received a stent graft for an abdominal aortic aneurysm, then a successful living-donor kidney transplant. Graft function stayed stable on immune-suppressing drugs, the normal bargain that keeps a donated kidney alive.

Within the old aneurysm, doctors later found a spindle cell sarcoma, an uncommon cancer of spindle-shaped cells. Whether the stent, the immune suppression, or chance played a part is an open question. Single cases cannot answer it, but they put transplant and vascular teams on notice to watch repaired aortas for late, strange growths.
pmc-13241442:
Santana and colleagues in São Paulo pooled trials of curcumin for prostate swelling in a meta-analysis. Six studies covered six hundred ninety-seven men already taking standard prostate drugs. Symptom scores led the list, with prostate size and urine flow alongside. Random-effects models pooled the comparisons against placebo.

Curcumin users beat placebo groups by about four points on symptom scores. Prostate volume, residual urine, and a blood marker all shrank modestly while flow grew stronger. Benefit ran larger alongside alpha-blockers alone than with combination therapy. Santana urges bigger trials, citing wide variation between studies.
pmc-13242342:
Liu and colleagues at Qingdao Agricultural University correct a figure in their 2023 study of pig skin progenitor cells. The paper mapped gene activity in multipotent dermal fibroblast progenitors with germline potential. One fluorescence image in Figure 6 was the wrong one. The panel showed PRDM1 staining in lab-grown germ cell-like cells.

The proxy stands in for hand video, which the dataset lacks.

pmc-13244942:

Breeders gain a shortlist for heading experiments.
pmc-13246542:
Rybak, Ely, and Gustafson designed a future satellite network for Mars in this 2026 Journal of the Astronautical Sciences paper. Explorers and robots on Mars will need both communications and GPS-like positioning. Tilting the orbits helped only over long tracking times, while a six-satellite inclined constellation delivered much better fixes within shorter spans, with the best results at a fifty-degree tilt. A seven-satellite design added uniform polar coverage. The paper weighs those trade-offs to guide how a combined navigation and relay network for human Mars missions might be built.
pmc-13247042:
Shen, Lin, Lin, and co-authors created an exotic state of matter inside a quantum computer, in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. pmc-13247242:
Khan and co-authors comment on a striking anti-aging experiment in this 2026 brief report in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. pmc-13247642:
Yoo, Suh, and Kwon examined blood transfusion practice in septic shock across Korean hospitals, in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science study. Guidelines advise transfusing red cells only below a hemoglobin threshold, yet clinicians often transfuse earlier when lactate, a marker of tissue oxygen debt, runs high. About one patient in ten was transfused within six hours, and well over half of those transfusions happened above the restrictive threshold, especially where lactate was elevated. Transfused patients were sicker, with faster heart rates and higher lactate. After adjustment, transfusion showed no association with lower hospital mortality in any band, including the high-lactate group. The authors question lactate-driven transfusion habits.
pmc-13248942:
Nguyen and colleagues recount a misleading aneurysm case in a 2026 surgical report. A forty-eight-year-old man arrived after blunt trauma, and his swollen abdominal aorta was first read as a traumatic injury. A stent graft was placed, but the vessel then decayed rapidly, revealing the true problem: an infected, or mycotic, aneurysm.

Surgeons removed the infected graft and rebuilt the aorta with a cryopreserved donor vessel, which resists infection better in a contaminated field. Sixteen months later the man remained stable with the graft open and working. The authors use the case to show how infection can hide behind a trauma story, and why graft choice matters.
pmc-13249542:
Walker, Meeuwig, and Thompson counted the small fish and animals that ride along with sharks, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. These companions gain protection, food scraps, or free transport from their hosts, and losing a host can drag its companions down too. Using records from baited underwater cameras across three ocean basins, the team examined seven shark species.

Almost half of the individual sharks carried at least one companion. Australian blacktip sharks hosted companions most often, and scalloped hammerheads least. Warmth, salinity, wind, and distance from shore predicted companion presence best. Partly protected waters raised the odds of companions, while the strictest reserves held more companions per shark when they appeared.
pmc-13250842:
Xiaowei Sun and co-authors target the fat that hugs arteries in this 2026 study of abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the main belly artery. No drug treatment exists for it, only surgery once it grows large.

Scans and animal work showed that the fat layer around the aorta helps drive the disease. One of its proteins pushes white blood cells to cast out sticky DNA webs, which harm the artery wall. Tiny parcels released by stem cells, given into the belly, cut fat build-up, lowered that protein, and slowed aneurysm growth in animals. The team proposes them as a preventive approach worth further study.
pmc-13254442:
Obeidat and a large team survey how clinicians worldwide handle acute upper gut bleeding before the emergency endoscopy. Their 2026 Therapeutic Advances in Gastroenterology study collected five hundred thirty-three responses between April and November 2023. Death rates from this emergency have barely improved despite clear guidelines.

Fewer than half the clinicians used a triage system, and only about three in five applied risk scores at arrival. Fluid choices split evenly, and blood transfusion practice loosened sharply for unstable patients. A third never used stomach-emptying drugs routinely, while most gave acid blockers and, for suspected variceal bleeding, vessel drugs and antibiotics. Younger clinicians followed recent guidelines more closely than veterans, and the authors flag wide practice variation.
pmc-13260042:
Mykyta Fomin and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how excess fat in the body can break down autophagy, the cell's system for clearing damaged parts and surplus lipids. Cholesterol-rich particles such as LDL, often called bad cholesterol, can stress the cell's recycling compartments. By contrast, HDL, often called good cholesterol, helps move cholesterol out of cells. The review covers heart vessel disease, fatty liver disease, and disorders of thinking and memory.

Fat droplets then build up, energy-producing structures falter, and inflammation stays switched on. The authors propose treatments that combine lowering body fat load, lipid-lowering drugs, and tuning the recycling system. They frame autophagy failure as one shared mechanism linking metabolic stress to chronic inflammation.
pmc-13260542:
Eunseuk Lee and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of infection problems after CAR T-cell therapy, a treatment that engineers a patient's immune cells to attack B-cell cancers. Drugs used to manage treatment side effects add more risk.

Prevention combines antiviral drugs and pneumonia prevention, antibacterial and antifungal cover, antibody top-ups, and vaccines timed to immune recovery. The review sums up world guideline advice.
pmc-13260942: Piotr Długosz and Liudmyla Yuzva published a 2026 correction notice for their Scientific Reports article on mental health disorders and stress coping among forced migrants from Ukraine and Russia. The original article contained errors in its abstract about who was sampled and where they lived. The corrected text says people were gathered through invites on Telegram and Facebook. It states the sample as two hundred Ukrainian forced migrants living in Poland, and 164 Russian forced migrants living mainly in Serbia and other countries. The article has been corrected.
pmc-13262642:
Kendall Carpenter and colleagues study why United States clinicians do or do not join global child cancer and blood work in a 2026 journal article. Partnerships between rich-country and poorer-country centers can build care capacity and narrow survival gaps for children. Funding limits, lack of protected time, and family duties were the main barriers named. Interviews with 15 people pointed most strongly to workplace barriers, such as promotion rules. Suggested fixes include stronger center support and clearer funding guidance.
pmc-13263042:
Nayara Rubio Diniz del Nero leads a 45-year review of biopsied mouth lesions in older Brazilians in a 2026 journal article. Tissue diagnosis guides care for lumps and sores in the mouth and jaw, which grow more common with age. The team reviewed biopsy records for patients aged 60 and older, collecting sex, age, site, and diagnosis data across the full period.

Of 21,367 lesions diagnosed from 1978 to 2023, about one in eight came from older patients, mostly aged 60 to 79 and slightly more often women. Reactive lesions, growths from irritation, were the largest group. Fibrous hyperplasia was the most common single diagnosis, followed by oral squamous cell carcinoma, a mouth cancer. The authors call for stronger prevention and long-term oral care.
pmc-13263342:
Ahmed M. Eldosouky and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping where gold, fluorite, and barite may lie in the Dawi shear belt of Egypt. A shear belt is a zone of rock crushed by deep forces. The team combined satellite images, radar data, magnetic surveys, and field checks.

Radar imagery exposed surface cracks and lineaments, and the area split into three promising zones for exploration. Fluorite sat in pegmatite veins crossing older rocks. Gold occurred in quartz veins tied to the Najd fault system, though grades were low, from near zero to zero point six grams per ton.
pmc-13263642:
Cherie Wan-Yin Wong and co-authors report a 2026 journal article comparing two speech therapy models for aphasia, the language loss that often follows stroke. The intensive program packed therapy into two and a half weeks, three hours a day, mixing individual, group, and technology-based work. Conventional therapy spread one weekly two-hour session over months. The intensive model produced better language and quality of life outcomes at both individual and group levels. pmc-13263742:

Tumors exploit the same machinery, warping T-cell mitochondria to blunt the attack and slip away. The authors sketch metabolism-plus-immunity combinations designed to break that sabotage. Their map aims at the bottlenecks choking modern immunotherapy.
pmc-13264042:
Onur Baser wrote a 2026 validation study of MELD, a large health data set that joins Medicare claims with medical records, lab results, and patient surveys. The data cover 2020 to 2024 and hold about 60 million patients. Before such data can guide strong claims, its quality must be checked.

Baser used records from more than 32 million patients with at least a year of Medicare cover. Checks showed high inner consistency, and illness rates matched official counts with a mean error of 3.1 percent. Record linking matched 94.7 percent of cases. The data also predicted death and return to hospital fairly well. The author judges the set sound for real-world studies.
pmc-13264442:
Karoline B Bräuner, Hjalte L Berthelsen, and Anne G Vedel wrote a 2026 case report on a rare harm from a common bowel treatment. A phosphate enema, a fluid given through the rectum to clear the bowel, raised blood phosphate to a severe level. That surge then drove blood calcium down.

After the enema he developed the phosphate surge and low calcium. The authors note the risk is higher when kidneys work poorly. They stress fast spotting of the signs and prompt care for this rare event.
pmc-13264942:
Yacoub Abuzied and colleagues present a 2026 interview study on living with intermittent catheterisation after spinal cord injury in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. These patients cannot empty the bladder on their own and pass a thin tube several times a day. The study explored daily challenges and coping in Arab men at a large rehabilitation hospital.

Ten men took part; women who were approached declined, some citing privacy concerns about bladder care talk. Three themes emerged. The first covered daily routines: how often the tube is used, place and health hurdles, privacy, and fluid balance. The second covered cleanliness and leaks. The third covered body image and sexuality. The authors stress that local norms of modesty and privacy shape how patients manage and cope, and care should respect that.
pmc-13265842:

Adding just ten minutes of ultrasound after enzyme treatment reached about 93 percent. The treated protein dissolved, foamed, and held water and oil better than the control. Heat tests showed it also withstood higher temperatures before unfolding, and its amino acid mix was balanced. The authors back the pairing for food use.
pmc-13267542:

Etripamil is a self-given spray for sudden fast heart rhythms, the first of its kind approved in the United States. Other calcium channel blockers, given by vein or mouth, can drop blood pressure or cause fainting. The team asked whether the spray does the same.

The analysis pooled over 1,600 people treated across the drug's phase 3 trials from 2018 to 2023. Low blood pressure occurred in only about 0.4 percent of participants, and fainting in about 0.2 percent. Test doses given while the heart beat normally let the team watch pressure closely. The authors conclude the spray has minimal effects on blood pressure.
pmc-13268142:
Luiz Henrique Santos Cambrussi and colleagues report a 2026 study of wrist fracture repair with a locking plate. Breaks of the far radius bone are among the most common adult fractures. A plate fixed from the palm side locks bone angles and allows early movement. The team reviewed 135 fractures treated between January 2023 and August 2024, measuring three alignment angles on X-rays at three points.

The same held in the hardest fracture types under three different classification systems. Two blinded raters did the measuring and grading. The authors conclude the plate gives firm first correction and keeps it, even in complex breaks. They class the evidence as a case series.
pmc-13268642:
