It compares three ways to couple the two technologies, from tightly fused to loosely linked, weighing security, scale, and rule compliance. It reviews attacks specific to health care and defenses such as zero-knowledge proofs and privacy noise. A compliance framework covers US and European privacy law and device rules. Uses range from disease prediction to drug discovery.
pmc-13269742:

pmc-13269842:

pmc-13270242:

Temperature, feeding times, habitat complexity, and group membership kept changing for one group, while the other group lived in stable conditions. When their own learned information clashed with fresh social information, they chose the social side more often. The authors say unpredictability makes stored information lose value faster, pushing animals toward quick social updates.
pmc-13271042:

pmc-13271142:

The combined chart performed well in training and even better in outside checks, the authors report.
pmc-13271342:

pmc-13271442:

pmc-13271742:

The correction states that typesetting errors in the Results section printed extra numbers next to the upper limit of each confidence interval. pmc-13273242:

pmc-13273842:

pmc-13274142:

pmc-13275742:

pmc-13276342:

pmc-13277242:

pmc-13277542:

pmc-13277642:

pmc-13278242:

pmc-13278842:

pmc-13280342:

pmc-13280542:

pmc-13280742:

The team ran a forward-looking study at their center. Stool samples came from patients before drug care began. Germ profiles were read from gene traces in the stool. Outcomes tracked response to care and length of life.

In thirty patients with advanced cancer on drug care, gut germ mixes split by outcome. Some germ types were higher in patients who fared poorly, and others were lower. One germ type went with slower growth in the first six months. Tissue germ mixes did not split two cancer types apart. The authors say stool tests might one day help doctors guess how care will go.
pmc-13282042:
Charlotte Henningsen Hansen and co-authors offer a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on treating a severe form of dehydration in hospital patients. In hyperosmolar dehydration, the body lacks water and blood salts become too concentrated. It affects a large share of admitted adults and raises the risk of illness and death. Current guidance often fails to separate it from low blood volume, so patients may get the wrong type of fluid.

As a protocol, the work reports no treatment results yet. It sets out searches of major medical databases, plus checks of reference lists and trial records. Studies will be kept only if adults had proven dehydration of this type and were treated in hospital. The planned map of what fluid treatments have been tried should show gaps and guide later trials on safer, better-matched care.
pmc-13282842:
Kaori Inoue and co-authors present a 2026 study testing a novel internet advertising approach to raise awareness of fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. The disease, shortened to MASLD, can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer yet remains little known. The team first analysed what people search alongside the term fatty liver, then ran banner adverts. One group saw the advert after searching key terms; a control group saw it regardless.

Searches clustered on treatment and lifestyle, with diet, blood sugar, cholesterol, and visceral fat among the key terms. The targeted banners earned a higher click rate than untargeted ones, and far more survey responses. Targeted viewers also more often said they intended to seek medical care early, about sixty percent against about forty-two percent. The authors conclude that search-term based advertising may raise disease awareness and prompt earlier consultation.
pmc-13283442:
Shanthan R Ramidi authored a 2026 case of stubborn low oxygen from a heart flap opening, with breathlessness when upright. The opening, called a patent foramen ovale, occurs in about a fifth to a quarter of adults. It is usually silent, but rare shunting can starve blood of oxygen.

The patient was a 59-year-old woman with chronic low-oxygen breathing failure. Full checks ruled out main lung, vessel, and tissue causes of her problem. A bubble heart scan showed early right-to-left shunting through the opening. A catheter procedure closed the opening without open surgery for her. Oxygen rose at once and stayed better, freeing her from added oxygen. Position-linked symptoms are a key clue.
pmc-13284542:
Jing Li and co-authors report a 2026 clinical study of combined care for young and middle-aged adults with hypertension. One group got standard care, while the other added mindfulness-based stress reduction plus ear triple therapy for eight weeks. Each group had 115 patients treated at Jiangsu Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine.

After eight weeks, the added-care group did better on treatment effect, quick blood pressure lowering, symptom scores, anxiety scores, and mindfulness scores than the control group. Baseline traits and drug use were alike at the start. The authors conclude the combined approach eased symptoms and negative feelings, and may help patients manage their condition and stick with medication.
pmc-13284742:
European Food Safety Authority authors deliver a 2026 statement on a United States toxicology profile for mercury. The European Commission asked EFSA to judge whether the 2024 ATSDR profile should change EFSA advice from 2012. The statement was backed by the CONTAM Panel before approval.

EFSA found no need to update its weekly intake limits for either inorganic mercury or methylmercury based on the new profile. A new 28-day rat study was judged unfit to set a dietary reference point. Gaps in how ATSDR reported some methods were noted, but no major missed studies were likely. EFSA adds that newer methods and evidence since 2012 might still merit a fresh review in time.
pmc-13285542:
What do top heart-muscle centers in the United States do well, and where do they strain? Martin Maron, Barbara Steeves, and Andrew Wang survey staff, patients, and advocates in a 2026 study of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy centers. Chosen sites all offer septal surgery, defibrillator implants, and transplants.

Care teams and diagnosis steps looked much alike across centers, with shared habits for imaging and treatment picks. Teaching patients and staff about new drug classes, such as cardiac myosin blockers, proved key for smart choices and smooth flow. Gaps in funding and in dedicated staff, from office help to skilled scan readers, topped the strain list. The authors share habits that general heart clinics could adopt.
pmc-13285742:
Shuaiwei Song leads a 2026 multicenter cohort study on uric acid and new diabetes in people with coronary heart disease. High uric acid is best known for gout, but it also tracks with wider metabolic trouble. The study asks whether uric acid levels predict who goes on to develop diabetes, and whether inflammation carries part of that effect.

Patients were followed at five centers in China, and higher uric acid came with higher diabetes risk in a curved, dose-linked pattern. Risk rose past set levels that differed slightly for women and men. Adding uric acid to standard factors sharpened risk prediction a little. Blood markers of inflammation carried part of the link between uric acid and diabetes. The team suggests watching uric acid as one more warning sign in heart patients.
pmc-13286142:
Teresa Chen and co-authors scope smart software for finding deep vein clots in a 2026 review of imaging studies. Clots in deep veins demand fast answers, since delays raise the risk of a lung blockage or lasting leg damage. Reading scans takes scarce expert time, so the review asked how well computer models spot clots on ultrasound, CT, and MRI.

Seven databases yielded eleven studies from 2021 to 2025 that fit the rules, most of them built on ultrasound. Scores for catching clots and clearing healthy veins ranged widely on ultrasound, while the lone MRI model scored high on both counts. Models tested across mixed scan sets reached the strongest marks of the group. The authors place the tools as helpers beside experts, not stand-ins, and call for shared trials across hospitals plus proof the systems save time and money.
pmc-13287242:
Liuyi Luo and colleagues applied explainable computer vision in 2026 to face and skull images from 130 adults, half with sleep apnoea confirmed by overnight testing and half matched controls. Their goal was to find shape traits linked to the condition without starting from a fixed list of expected features.

The model separated the groups well, with an accuracy measure the authors report as 0.87. Highlight maps pointed to the jaw and chin, as expected, but also to the forehead, brows, and upper eyelids. Direct measures then confirmed narrower brow spacing and greater forehead projection in patients. The authors say larger groups must confirm the upper-face traits.
pmc-13287542:
Daiki Nakajima and co-authors describe in 2026 a man aged 84 with a stiffened spine condition who fell two metres and broke a lower chest vertebra. Scans also showed blood filling the right chest, yet no ribs were broken and lungs looked unbruised.

Chest drainage rose past 2400 millilitres within ten hours, forcing emergency camera surgery. The main injury site was not bleeding. Blood came instead from a hidden break in a bony spur several levels higher. Heat sealing and clotting agents stopped it, and spine fusion followed later. The authors urge teams to hunt for distant spur breaks when chest bleeding keeps growing in such patients.
pmc-13287842:
Do Young Shin and co-authors reviewed records in 2026 for 113 Korean children treated for Graves disease, an overactive thyroid condition, between 2004 and 2023. They hunted early signs that predict who will settle off drugs, who will relapse, and who will need lasting high doses of the standard tablet.

About four in ten children reached remission, on average after roughly three years. Lower hormone and antibody levels at diagnosis, and faster antibody falls, marked the remission group. Relapse struck about a quarter of those who remitted, more often boys. A simple ratio drawn from antibody change at six months gave cut-off values for both remission and dose needs.
pmc-13288042:
Jun-Ming Lin and co-authors present four older patients in 2026 whose spine fractures were first read as simple bone-thinning breaks, a common call in the elderly. Each case in fact hid another cause: two carried spinal infections of differing germs, one a further infection type, and one a blood cancer of the marrow.

The team lists warning signs in blood tests, covering inflammation markers, protein balance, and antibody screens. They also show that taking a small bone sample during the cement repair procedure can reveal infection or cancer in time. The authors urge biopsy whenever lab or scan features look even slightly unusual.
pmc-13288542:
Amir Hossein Taghiparast and colleagues adapt an AI learning scale for Iran in 2026. The scale gauges will to learn AI. It was turned into Persian with care. The team then surveyed 800 students. All studied medical sciences at Babol University.

Tests backed a four-part scale. Parts cover knowledge, attitudes, and support. One part covers mind and behavior outcomes. The parts explained 44.55 percent of answer spread in tests. Fit checks passed at a fair level. Scores held steady on retest. The scale worked the same for men and women. Schools can use it to plan AI courses.
pmc-13289142:
Sarun Srikhom and colleagues plan a 2026 study of quality-of-life tools in trials. Such tools weigh health states by patient values. Trials often skip them in reports. The team will track use over 50 years. Four databases will be searched.

Trials in English since 1976 will count. Adult generic tools form the core set. The EQ-5D family leads that set. Short Form tools also count. AI tools will screen and pull data. Language models may do the same work. The team will test which path is more exact. Trends will split by disease and region.
pmc-13289242:
Maryam Schütte Saem and colleagues offer a 2026 estimate of new cases and remission for endometriosis in Germany. Endometriosis is a long-term gynecologic condition where tissue like the womb lining grows elsewhere and can limit daily life. Direct counts of new cases are rare, so the team worked backward from prevalence data.

They used statutory health insurance data covering more than 35 million girls and women aged 10 or older in 2012 and 2022. An illness-death model with 5000 bootstrap resamples turned age-specific prevalence into incidence and remission rates. The median incidence peaked near age 32 at about 1.73 per 1,000 person-years in the estimates. Remission peaked much later, near age 52, giving planners a fuller picture of how the condition starts and fades.
pmc-13289342:
Jaclyn N Portelli Tremont, Charlotte Blythe Smith, and Jared Robert Gallaher wrote a 2026 patient guide on ostomies for trauma and emergency surgery care. An ostomy is a surgical opening in the belly that lets stool leave the body into a bag. It may be needed when bowel is damaged or sick from injury, cancer, or bowel inflammation.

Gentle text first traces food through stomach and intestines, where nutrients are taken up and waste remains. Two main types are explained: a colostomy from the large intestine and an ileostomy from the last part of the small intestine. The opening itself is called a stoma, and a pouch sticks to skin around it. Hospital steps for making an ostomy are also laid out for new patients.
pmc-13289742:
Min-Yuan Liu and Nai-Hsin Chi describe a 2026 case of a giant fatty tumor of the heart sac in a 57-year-old man. He had two years of intermittent right chest tightness and repeated fainting before imaging. Scans showed extensive fatty tissue around the heart, and magnetic imaging pointed to a benign fat growth, called a lipoma, as the likely diagnosis for the mass.

Open surgery through the breastbone found a well-bordered mass arising from the right ventricular outflow tract, and it was fully removed. The specimen measured 4 × 20 × 18 cm and weighed 2850 g in the lab record. Microscopy showed mature fat cells with fibrous bands and no cancer signs, confirming a lipoma. Recovery details follow in the report.
pmc-13289942:
Borbála Német and coauthors validate a 2026 Hungarian version of Skindex-Mini, a three-item survey on skin disease burden for quality of life. Skin conditions harm mood, social life, and daily function well beyond visible symptoms, and a fast screening tool helps busy clinics. The brief survey was tested against longer established measures in 578 patients with inflammatory and noninflammatory skin diseases in one cross-section.

Factor analysis supported a single dimension, and item analysis showed strong separation power with fairness across groups. Links with stigma and distress were moderate, as hoped for a related but distinct measure, while separation from well-being was acceptable. Short length plus solid performance suit the tool for rapid screening in clinics and studies alike.
pmc-13290642:
Two years of on-and-off weakness in all four limbs traced back to an adrenal tumor, Javed Shakir and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. The 37-year-old woman had been evaluated repeatedly, with her episodes written off as general weakness.

A fuller workup finally found the pattern: her potassium kept running low, bottoming at 2.1 mmol/L, while aldosterone was high at 100 ng/dL and renin was suppressed, the signature of primary aldosteronism. Scans located a right adrenal adenoma. After laparoscopic removal of the gland, she left the hospital within a week, and follow-up showed normal potassium and no more episodes. Shakir and colleagues use the case to push endocrine and metabolic causes up the list when limb weakness comes and goes.
pmc-13290942:
Outpatient Parkinson's care in Germany runs on habit more than evidence, Ingmar Wellach and colleagues find in a survey study from 2026. Nearly all Parkinson's treatment happens in local practices, yet detailed data from that setting are scarce. So the team surveyed specialist neurology practices online, as groundwork for a registry pilot.

Practices assessed patients in strikingly similar ways, centering on motor exams, especially rigidity checks tied to drug-treatment monitoring. Non-motor symptom checks and broader testing, by contrast, were patchy. Time pressure and regional variation stood out as open questions. Wellach and colleagues call for outpatient-specific evidence and guidelines, plus long-term studies across sectors. They argue this baseline map is the first step toward precision care in everyday practice.
pmc-13291042:
Konstantin Hennis leads a 2026 mouse study of a heart rhythm gene change. The change makes the HCN4 channel overactive. In people, such changes link to a fast resting heartbeat. Chronic fast rhythm is feared as a heart harm driver.

Mutant mice showed higher resting heart rates. Their electrical conduction also ran faster. No rhythm faults appeared on their own. Heart tissue showed no harm from the fast rate. Under pressure load, mutant hearts resisted bad remodeling. That result defies the simple fear story. A fast pacemaker need not damage the heart, it seems.
pmc-13291242:
Local population trends may hint at global extinction risk. Laura H. Antão leads a 2026 study linking field counts to world red list grades. Most species lack any formal risk review. Long field records offer an untapped clue.

The team used over 60,000 populations of 2,362 species. Sites spanned sea and land, each watched for twenty years or more. Each population trend was sorted into five classes. Few local groups rose or fell in a steady line. Most trends looked random over time, above all at sea. Still, higher global risk matched more local falls. Steady local drops could thus flag future risk rises earlier.
pmc-13291442:
Anemia is common yet missed in Ethiopian cancer care. Frezer Kedir leads a 2026 review and pooled analysis of the problem. Low blood counts worsen fatigue and survival. Low-resource clinics face the burden with few tools.

Eleven studies from across Ethiopia were pooled. About two in five treated cancer patients had anemia. Late stage disease raised the risk a lot. Women, older patients, and rural residents also ran higher risk. Poor nutrition and other illness added to the load. Many chemo cycles and bone spread mattered too. Past bleeding was a further flag. Clinics can use these flags to test and treat sooner.
pmc-13291542:
Video games have become a lab for testing artificial minds. Stephen Ornes reports this trend in a 2026 feature article. One project set 25 virtual players loose in a town called Smallville. Each player was driven by a large language model.

Each agent got a short written identity at the start. One ran a pharmacy and loved helping people. Over two game days, agents woke, worked, and socialized. One threw a Valentine’s party with no further prompting. Others asked dates and planned their trips. A mayoral run spread by word of mouth. Bigger tests put a thousand agents in Minecraft. Whole virtual societies emerged there too.
pmc-13292342:
Farhan Haq and co-authors examine a 2026 twist in bladder cancer treatment: the tumor-killing complex alpha1-oleate also rewires tumor metabolism. Samples came from patients in a placebo-controlled trial of the drug instilled into the bladder. Cells shed into urine at each treatment and biopsies after six instillations went through RNA sequencing, and urine was screened on adipokine arrays.

Treated tissue switched off broad sets of metabolic genes compared with placebo. Networks for building glucose and lipids quieted, including the genes for adiponectin and leptin, two hormone-like regulators of fat and sugar. Leptin appeared to sit upstream of the adiponectin response, and the two networks intertwined strongly in treated tumors. Shed cells showed the metabolic shift happened fast, and urine levels of both proteins rose after treatment.
pmc-13294042:
Zengliang Guo and colleagues update a pig virus test in a 2026 methods study. Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus keeps recombining, so older PCR assays miss new strains. The team targeted the variable nsp2 gene to tell apart classical, highly pathogenic, and NADC30-like strains in one multiplex reaction, using fresh sequences from databases and their own lab.

Standard curves stayed linear from high to low copy numbers, with detection near 8 to 10 copies for each strain and no cross-reaction with other common pig pathogens. Repeat variation stayed under 2%. Among 588 samples, the new test found 15.5% positive, above the older method rate, with strong agreement overall.
pmc-13294242:
James A Blake heads DebrisWatch II, a 2026 reanalysis of geosynchronous debris watched with the 2.54 m Isaac Newton Telescope. Faint debris near the crowded ring is hard to census because coverage trades against sensitivity. Better star trail centering, distortion fitting, and blind image stacking were applied to old survey frames and to a matching small telescope dataset.

Stacking recovered 25 object tracks missed before and pushed detection one magnitude fainter. Position accuracy fell under one arcsecond, enough for starter orbits from short arcs. A modest 36 cm astrograph was benchmarked against the big scope, showing what cheap gear can recover. Light curves hint at object spin and shape.
pmc-13294342:
Marwa Mohamed Farag and colleagues watch brain and gut blood flow around transfusion in preterm babies for a 2026 prospective study. Stable anemic infants born at 32 weeks or earlier, aged at least 3 weeks, with hemoglobin under 9.5 were studied in Alexandria from March to December 2023. Thirty babies got packed red cells while light sensors tracked oxygen in brain and belly.

After transfusion, major flow speeds and vessel measures fell, while tissue oxygen in brain and gut rose and oxygen extraction dropped. Flow changes tracked gut oxygen shifts, and heart rate tracked both regions. Transfusion thus eases oxygen strain even as high pre-transfusion flow settles down.
pmc-13294442:
Johanna P. Müller, Matthew Baugh, and Bernhard Kainz build a backpropagation-free anomaly finder for medical scans in a 2026 study. Radiology needs detectors that stay sharp, readable, and cheap under shifting real-world data. Their convolutional forward-forward method learns layer by layer with local goals, and goodness scores naturally flag images that break the learned pattern.

The self-adaptive version tunes its own depth, learning pace, and score scaling, even under tight budgets and one-shot training. Across several imaging benchmarks it matched or beat standard trained rivals on anomaly and out-of-distribution detection in the reported tests. Local learning could suit hospitals lacking big compute clusters.
pmc-13294842:
Lorena González-García and co-authors study what supports life satisfaction in healthy older adults in a 2026 article. Resilience and feeling well supported by others are both thought to protect well-being in later life. The authors ask whether support changes how strongly resilience links to satisfaction.

Forty-two volunteers, mostly women and averaging about 67 years old, completed standard questionnaires on all three topics. Both resilience and support predicted greater satisfaction, together accounting for a large share of the differences between people. The link between resilience and satisfaction proved strongest when perceived support was low, though the small, selective sample limits how far findings travel.
pmc-13295842:
Fulin Zhou and colleagues offer a 2026 review of how physical forces and the immune system interact as bones, joints and muscles age. The field, called mechano-immunology, asks how load and tissue stiffness shape immune cell behaviour.

With age, people move less, tissues stiffen and immune cells sense force less well, which weakens infection clearance and repair. The authors link that breakdown to osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and other wasting conditions. They also survey possible remedies, from exercise and controlled loading to engineered materials, that might restore balance in ageing musculoskeletal tissue.
pmc-13298842:
A citrus-scented edible coating bought fish fillets about three extra days of freshness, report Jiaxin Han and co-authors in a 2026 food science study. They coated seasoned white snakehead fillets with a lemon essential oil, rutin, and chitosan film and stored them near the freezing point.

Compared with cold storage alone, coated fillets oxidized less, kept firmer texture, and grew microbes more slowly. On day ten the coated group's bacterial count sat at 4.98 log CFU/g, just under the national limit the control group had crossed by day seven. Chemical profiling found 2,267 metabolites, with shifts in amino acids and aroma compounds tied to slower spoilage.
pmc-13299542:
The strain of answering crisis calls comes less from the topics than from how the service itself is organized, finds Radka Čopková in a 2026 pilot study of anonymous helpline workers. Seventy-three workers in Slovakia and the Czech Republic completed burnout and job-demand measures.

Overall demands correlated with burnout at rs = 0.41, while job resources pulled the other way, and together they explained half the variance in burnout scores. Service-related demands, covering workload structures and organizational conditions, were the strongest single predictor across exhaustion, mental distance, and cognitive and emotional impairment. Topic-related demands did not predict burnout. The author urges helpline managers to fix structural pressures first.
pmc-13301542:
High blood pressure follows most kidney transplant patients home, and Alicja Danieluk with colleagues review what is known, and what is missing, in a 2026 survey of post-transplant hypertension. Between seventy and ninety-five percent of recipients live with it, and heart disease remains their leading killer. The authors scan guidelines, drug evidence, and the transplant-specific drivers of pressure.

Calcium channel blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers still lead treatment, though the trials behind them are old. The 2024 KDIGO guidance skips transplant blood pressure entirely, leaving targets borrowed from other populations. Trimming calcineurin inhibitors or steroids, or switching agents, can help some patients. Fresh randomized trials in recipients top the authors' wish list.
pmc-13303342:
A lung infection that mimicked cancer killed a man within ten days, Seigo Miyoshi and colleagues report in a 2026 case of spread-out nocardiosis. The sixty-four-year-old arrived with appetite loss and breathlessness; scans showed a five-centimeter lung mass plus diffuse nodules, and cancer with pneumonia was suspected. Blood and sputum cultures grew Nocardia on day three, prompting targeted drugs, but his breathing kept failing.

Autopsy found squamous cell carcinoma in the lung plus necrotizing pneumonia and matching sores in the thyroid, a rare site. The germ proved to be Nocardia otitidiscaviarum. The authors stress early suspicion and fast lab testing when such lung patterns appear.
pmc-13303442:
Leman Tuba Karakurt leads a 2026 study of sleep and skin-related quality of life in children with cutaneous mastocytosis. In this condition mast cells build up mainly in the skin, and the course is often mild, but daily effects are poorly mapped.

Thirty-five affected children were compared with 50 healthy controls. Disease severity was scored with the SCORMA index, sleep with a parent questionnaire, and quality of life with a skin-specific index. Affected children had worse sleep overall, with more bedtime resistance, night waking, and daytime sleepiness. Skin-related quality of life was only mildly reduced and tracked disease severity more than sleep scores.
pmc-13304742:
Kawther Zaher and co-authors propose a design framework for immune-reprogramming nanomedicines in a 2026 review. Many immune treatments fail late because immunity is handled as one output rather than a timed, placed network of cell states.

Their immunoscape model links outcome to delivery route, release timing, first-contact cells, lymph routing, surface coating, and safety checks. Two strategy families are compared: natural products such as beta-glucans and plant compounds, and smart carriers such as lipid particles and cell-like vesicles. Practical design rules aim at cancer, infection, inflammation, and tissue repair uses.
pmc-13306942:
Shan Ning coated brittle coal with flexible polyurea to tame violent breaking in a 2026 study. Stored strain energy in coal can burst out under high stress, so a surface skin that holds sides in may steady failure.

Pressed samples wore layers from 0 to 1.25 mm thick while sound emissions and surface imaging tracked cracks and energy flow. Coatings curbed sideways bulging and shifted failure from sharp splitting toward slow, ductile damage in reported results. Thicker skins also pushed microcracks from shear toward tension types and raised energy soaked up before the peak load.
pmc-13307142:
Banu Esencan Türkaslan added eggshell particles to a self-healing gel for soft tissue uses in a 2026 study. Polyvinyl alcohol and graphene oxide gels were cast by freeze and thaw cycles, then checked by X-ray, microscopy and infrared tools.

A 1 percent eggshell share lifted tensile strength to 0.326 MPa while keeping high stretch in reported tests. Healing recovered about 67% of strength for that mix, close to the plain gel's 69% in the given figures, and all gels healed fast at room temperature without outside triggers. Swelling behaviour added to the biomedical promise.
pmc-13308342:
Christopher L Coe and co-authors probe in 2026 whether a stronger early swelling response to a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine in rhesus monkeys tracks with stronger immunity. The vaccine joined a spike binding part to a human antibody tail, with an added booster agent to wake the immune system.

Monkeys with bigger drops in blood iron at 24 hours and higher white cell ratios made antibodies that blocked virus binding more strongly. That edge held for the Wuhan, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta forms, but it faded for the Omicron form tested here. Early reaction size also foresaw how long cell based defence lasted, which backs a view that brief swelling can help.
pmc-13308942:
Bethlehem A Bekele and co-authors argue in 2026 that fair mentorship is core infrastructure for neuroscience, where Black scholars stay scarce at each career rung. Black trainees form just 6 percent of neuroscience doctoral students in the United States, yet 14.7 percent of the whole population there.

Fair mentorship, in their frame, joins craft training with career maps, identity backing, and doors into closed networks of peers. Group, kin like, and cross site models share the load that now falls hard on few Black staff. Paid, planned schemes, such as the Black in Neuro programme, build belonging and keep talent in the field. Schools must fund that work as a base need.
pmc-13309142:
Natalia Chalupczak and Shari R Lipner test in 2026 whether onychogryphosis, a thick curved ram horn nail, links to later leg and foot harms in a large United States data network. They matched 174,537 patients with the nail state to an equal set without it on age, sex, race, weight, diabetes, kidney state, and smoking.

Over five years, the nail group faced far higher risk of foot or toe removal, ulcers, skin infection, bone infection, and gangrene in the matched data. Hazard ratios ran from about 1.5 for gangrene to near 2.8 for removal work in those five years. The links held in diabetes and artery disease subsets, so a horn nail should prompt a close leg check.
pmc-13309442:
Jule Adriaans and colleagues track pay fairness views in Germany across 2009 to 2023 in a 2026 study. Workers in the east long rated their pay as less fair than workers in the west. The team asked whether that east-west gap had closed over time.

Long-running household survey data showed a large early gap that shrank across the study years. The change came mainly from low-paid eastern workers, whose pay moved closer to western pay and whose fairness views improved. Western views grew slightly less fair at the same time. The authors read the pattern as real convergence, even after accounting for age, schooling, and job traits.
pmc-13309542:
Lukas Hupe and co-authors build a cleaner computer model of dividing disk-shaped cells in a 2026 study. Cell division drives growth in bacterial colonies, embryos, and tumors, yet many particle models jerk or spike forces when a cell splits. Those glitches spoil the physics the models are meant to show.

Each modeled cell is a pair of overlapping disks that pull apart during division, passing through a dumbbell shape. Rules for motion keep forces smooth at every moment, for the splitting cell and its neighbors alike. Runs confirm smooth forces, and an older rod-cell model is recast in the same framework for comparison. The authors offer the model for studies of growing tissues.
pmc-13309642:
Patrick-Pascal Strunz and colleagues test a therapy app for spinal arthritis in a 2026 companion study. The condition, axial spondyloarthritis, stiffens the spine and limits movement. A nationwide trial of the Axia app had already shown gains in patient-rated activity, function, and life quality among 200 patients.

Thirty-two patients at one center spent 12 weeks in standard care, then 12 weeks using the app, while staying on stable drug therapy. Spine movement scores barely moved during standard care, setting the base for judging the app phase. Muscle strength, disease activity ratings, safety, and joint scans were also tracked. The authors use the design to check whether patient-rated gains match body measures.
pmc-13309942:
Sarah Mai Viebahn and co-authors chart hospital care for multiple sclerosis in Germany from 2019 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Care has been shifting from hospital wards to outpatient clinics as strong long-term drugs spread. Full data on ward use and its drivers had been thin.

National hospital billing data covered all ward cases coded for multiple sclerosis across the six years. Ward admissions fell by 28 percent, from 45,067 cases in 2019 to 32,670 in 2024 in the national count, while day care cases rose from 4,127 to 5,627 over the same span. Drops varied widely by region and disease subtype. The authors link the shift to therapy and care changes and map where ward use persists.
pmc-13310442:
Qiqi Zhang and co-authors build a single-cell gene regulation map for pig muscle in a 2026 study. Gene effects on traits often depend on cell type, which bulk tissue data blur. Pigs offer both farm value and a model for muscle biology, so a cell-level map carries weight.

Forty-two single-cell data sets from pig skeletal muscle were used to tune a workflow for reading variants and filling gaps from sparse cell data. The resulting atlas charts muscle cell types and growth paths, with 5,020 gene regulation sites found at single-cell level in the analysis. Joining farm trait data flagged three sites tied to meat quality and growth in a cell-dependent way. The authors offer the framework for other tissues and species.
pmc-13310642:
Zhanwei Zhu and co-authors uncover how cooling therapy saves threatened brain tissue after stroke in a 2026 study. The penumbra is the at-risk ring around the stroke core, and saving it improves outcomes. Cooling protects the brain, but the molecular route behind penumbra rescue was murky.

In mice with temporary artery blockage, cooling shrank the dead core and slowed penumbra loss. Protection came mainly by curbing cell suicide rather than other death routes. Cooling cut the eat-me signal that dying neurons display, by lowering a scramblase protein called Xkr8 that flips that signal outward. Blocking Xkr8 copied the benefit, while forcing Xkr8 up erased it. The authors name the pathway as a drug target.
pmc-13310742:
Alessandro Zampogna and colleagues used wearable sensors to track walking in advanced Parkinson disease in a 2026 pilot study. Pills give the key drug in bursts, which can cause swings in movement and stray motions. A gut gel gives the drug in a steady flow, but its effect on daily walking had not been measured well.

Forty three patients took part, with 15 on the gel and 28 on best oral care. A waist sensor logged step length, speed, rhythm, freezing, and stray motion through the day. Gel users showed steadier steps and fewer swings, while stray motion time was alike. Sensors may help guide dose and follow up.
pmc-13310942:
Thibault Mazard and colleagues test blood messenger RNA signs for bowel cancer in a 2026 study. Early bowel cancer is far more curable, yet stool tests are often skipped and lack sharp accuracy. Free floating RNA in blood plasma may offer a kinder screen if the right mix is chosen.

Six RNA signs were measured in 178 patients across all stages and 171 healthy people. Four signs ran higher in patients, though one rose only in late stage disease. A three sign combined score split patients from healthy people best, even at stage I, and the split grew stronger in later stages. Assay checks backed the method for wider study.
pmc-13311142:
Helen F Gloege led a 2026 study that pairs two targeted drugs against Ewing sarcoma. The aggressive bone and soft tissue cancer strikes youth, and spread or returned disease resists standard chemo. A cell cycle drug and a growth path drug were tested together across cell and mouse models.

In five cell models the pairing killed far more cells than either drug alone. Protein and gene reads confirmed the growth path was shut down. The cycle drug froze cells in a rest phase and deepened drug driven death. In two mouse graft models the pair extended survival clearly. Human trials are the next test.
pmc-13312242:
Cassandra Elias and co-authors describe a 2026 project at Women's College Hospital, a Canadian hospital for outpatients, aimed at antibiotic choices for surgical patients carrying penicillin allergy labels. Such labels are common yet usually wrong, and they push teams toward second-line drugs instead of cefazolin, the preferred agent for preventing surgical infections.

An audit had shown that 20 percent of patients given second-line prophylaxis might have qualified for cefazolin. So the team built education modules and a workflow for sorting patients by risk. In pre and post surveys of 61 clinicians, the first module changed little, but modules two and three improved readiness to take allergy histories, judge severity, and prescribe prophylaxis. Clinicians rated the supporting tools highly, with the paperwork aid accepted by 92 percent of respondents.
pmc-13312542:
Lonsako Abute Woiloro and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a cluster randomized trial testing couple-based maternity education in rural central Ethiopia. Maternal deaths remain a heavy toll in poor settings despite proven interventions. How much a husband's involvement changes use of maternity care along the whole continuum has rarely been tested rigorously in rural areas.

Sixteen kebeles, the smallest administrative units, will be assigned by lot, eight to the program and eight to control, with 248 couples in each arm. Couples join in the early second trimester for group maternity education plus home visits designed to draw husbands into antenatal, birth, and postnatal care. Analysis will follow intention-to-treat principles with models that account for clustering. The authors expect the finished trial to give policymakers firm evidence on educating couples together.
pmc-13312842:
Carla Schröpel and colleagues ask, in a 2026 multicenter study, how entering medical school with prior qualifications shapes German students' satisfaction with their studies. Students who arrive with a degree or vocational medical training add diversity to the cohort. Whether that background changes how they learn or how content they feel had gone unexamined internationally.

Surveying students at five medical schools from the third semester to the final year, the team modeled links among background, deep learning strategies, part-time work, and three kinds of satisfaction. Deep strategies behaved the same for everyone: elaboration lifted contentment with course content while critical thinking lowered it. Pre-qualified students more often worked alongside their studies, and that work slightly dented satisfaction with study conditions while slightly improving their sense of coping with the load.
pmc-13312942:
Lonneke Bos and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether lifestyle and other changeable factors age the brains of people with multiple sclerosis. A second question is whether that brain aging explains their disability and thinking problems. The gap between a brain's predicted and actual age is a recognized wear marker in this disease, but its ties to habits were unexplored.

Scanning 242 patients and 117 healthy controls, all near age 53, the team computed each person's brain-age gap and tested smoking, alcohol, activity, diet, leisure, education, and body mass at age 18. Lifetime smoking, heavier drinking, and higher teenage body mass each went with an older-looking brain, while more physical activity pointed the other way. Mediation analysis then asked how much of each habit's link to walking, hand function, and cognition runs through that gap, sharpening targets for prevention advice.
pmc-13314442:
Zeyu Liang and colleagues test blood-fat and body-shape indexes for heart risk in sleep apnea patients in work published in 2026. Adults with obstructive sleep apnea face high rates of coronary heart disease, yet which simple index sorts their risk best was unclear.

The team studied 1122 adults who had both sleep testing and coronary imaging at one center. Of these, 533 patients had heart disease and 589 did not, as counted in the report. They compared the triglyceride-glucose index alone with blends that fold in waist and body shape measures. Each index was scaled per standard step and run through adjusted models for both current disease and later major heart events. They also probed whether body fat spread explains part of the link. The results can help clinics triage apnea patients for heart checks.
pmc-13314742:
Ana Cláudia Cavalcante Espósito and co-workers test how washing wears down the sun guard of protective shirts, in a letter published in 2026. Sunscreen creams fail when people skip or skimp them, while clothing gives a steady shield that needs no reapplying.

The team took sun shirts from the Brazilian market and washed them through 50 cycles, by the count in the title, then measured how much UVB, UVA, and blue-violet light passed through. Top-rated garments, classed UPF50 or more, let through at most a share of 2 percent of UVB as the standard cited states. Rules exist for UVB grades, but none yet govern UVA or visible light cover, the authors note. American testing mimics about two years of use, including checks after 40 washes, as cited. Their data show whether the guard survives real laundering.
pmc-13315442:
Juan P Barrera and colleagues typed gut parasites from dogs and cats in central Spain in a 2026 study of spread risk to people. Stool samples that tested positive for Giardia or Cryptosporidium were checked at several gene sites to name the exact types present and judge their zoonotic potential.

Host-adapted Giardia types ruled in pets. Types C and D were most common in dogs, and type F in cats. Types A and B, which can infect people, appeared at moderate rates. Cryptosporidium canis led in dogs and Cryptosporidium felis in cats, with rare finds of types tied to people. The results add One Health data for the region.
pmc-13315642:
Irwan Susanto and co-authors combined a meta-analysis with computer docking in 2026 to judge tannins as silage additives. High-protein forage often loses protein during air-free storage, forming ammonia and lowering feed quality, and tannins bind protein, so they might slow that breakdown.

Pooling published trials showed tannin addition clearly lowered ammonia nitrogen, non-protein nitrogen, and soluble nitrogen in silage. Docking tests then checked how tannin-derived compounds bind glutamate dehydrogenase, an enzyme tied to breakdown pathways in Clostridium germs common in silage. Together the two lines of evidence support tannins as natural guards against protein loss during storage.
pmc-13315742:
Shanpeng Xu and colleagues built a deep learning counter in 2026 for petals in cut chrysanthemum flower heads. Petal count helps judge quality and identify cultivars, but hand counting is slow and error-prone on such packed, partly hidden flowers, limiting large breeding programs.

Images from many varieties formed a training set, with density maps made by hand marking and smoothing. A congested-scene network strengthened with a squeeze-and-excitation attention block estimated petal density across the head. Counts agreed strongly with true petal numbers in their checks. Fast automatic counting could make flower phenotyping practical at scale.
pmc-13317542:
Zhao-Xiang Dong and colleagues tell, in a 2026 case report, of a vaginal leiomyoma, a rare benign muscle growth. Every scan misread it as a neck-of-womb growth in a woman of childbearing age. Fewer than a few hundred such cases exist in print worldwide.

Ultrasound and MRI both called the front vaginal wall lump a cervical myoma. Hands-on examination, confirmed during surgery, placed its origin in the vagina instead. The authors argue that careful palpation can beat high-tech imaging at pinning down where a lump truly starts, and that knowing imaging's blind spots prevents confident mistakes. Combining touch and technology, they say, gives the truest preoperative picture.
pmc-13318242:
Shihui Guan and colleagues report a 2026 case of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, a multi-system disorder of eye and tooth development, in a young boy whose missing chromosome stretch also shut down growth hormone. Pairing the case with a literature review, they test whether deletion size predicts hormone failure.

Family gene sequencing in the 5.4-year-old found a fresh 3.824 megabase deletion at chromosome band 4q25, removing PITX2 and neighbors. His growth hormone peak was just 4.22 in stimulation testing, with bone age lagging by a year and a half. Twenty months on long-acting hormone therapy gained him 16.5 centimeters and restored a normal height range. Ten reviewed cases supported the size link. Growth checks, they urge, belong in routine care for deletion carriers.
pmc-13318542:
Tahereh Varmazyar and co-authors report a 2026 rat study of metformin and exercise. They asked whether either treatment, or both together, protects memory. The disease model used D-galactose to mimic Alzheimer's disease. Animals were divided into eight groups for comparison.

Learning and movement were tested with a water maze and an open field. Brain tissue from the hippocampus was examined under the microscope. Expression of the BDNF gene was also measured. The combined group performed better on maze measures. Those rats received 100 mg/kg of metformin plus exercise. They showed less nerve cell damage than untreated model rats. Their BDNF expression was also higher. Movement did not differ, so the benefit centred on learning.
pmc-13318642:
Jia Li and colleagues describe a 2026 fatal case of aortic dissection. A tear in the main artery was classed as type B3. Poor blood flow hit several organs at once. Gas also appeared in the liver's portal vein. Their patient was a 64-year-old man with high blood pressure. He had eight hours of severe belly pain.

Scans showed the tear running from the aortic arch to the iliac arteries. Gut arteries were blocked, and gas filled the bowel wall and liver vein. Those signs point to dead bowel tissue. Blood tests showed extreme inflammation, with IL-6 reaching 14,001.98 pg/mL in the reported results. Stubborn acid build-up added to the picture. The family chose comfort care, and he died 47 hours later.
pmc-13319042:
Hongli Sun and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study of family income and preschool children's mental health in Western China. The sample is large: 21,366 children aged three to six, plus their parents. Standard questionnaires measured child difficulties and prosocial behaviour. Parents reported their own depressive symptoms.

Higher income families had children with fewer difficulties. Against low-income families, middle-income odds of difficulties were 27 percent lower, and high-income odds were 39 percent lower in their analysis. Prosocial behaviour odds rose by 9 and 30 percent for those groups. Parental depression carried a large share of the income link. It accounted for 30.5 percent of the difficulties link in middle-income families, and more for other outcomes. The authors stress parent mental health in policy thinking.
pmc-13319742:
Yu Yu and co-authors build a chip sensor for trace hydrogen gas in a 2026 study on safe use of a clean fuel. Hydrogen burns with ease and can catch fire from a tiny spark, so leaks must be caught at very low levels. Their chip joins four tiny switches in a bridge layout with a built in heater on a thin floating film.

Two switches sense the gas while two shielded ones cancel drift, and a metal coat splits hydrogen to shift the signal. At the best heat setting the chip found gas down to a tenth of a part per million in the tested range and answered in seconds at high levels. It mostly ignored other common gases and held steady across repeats.
pmc-13320242:
Daniele Vetrano and co-authors pool studies on an overactive neck gland hormone after kidney transplant in a 2026 review. The hormone often runs high in kidney illness and may stay high after a new kidney is placed. Whether that pattern forecasts death or graft loss stayed murky, due to mixed study designs and timing.

Twenty three studies entered the review, and 19 with 26266 recipients fed the pooled counts. High hormone before transplant showed no clear link to death and only a shaky link to graft loss. High hormone that stayed high after transplant tracked with clearly higher death and graft loss risks, and the risk rose further when blood calcium also ran high. Lasting hormone excess after transplant marks a group needing close watch.
pmc-13320342:
Danni Xu and co-authors weigh clean air policy costs and gains across five Chinese mega city clusters in a 2026 study. Cutting smokestack and traffic fumes costs firms and cities dearly, and whether growth can rise while fumes fall at varied local paces was the core puzzle. A curve model that links fume output to income was fitted for each cluster and each main pollutant.

Three clusters showed fumes falling in a straight line as income rose, while two showed a rise then fall curve for most fumes. One gas class rose then fell against income in all clusters without fail. Health linked money losses from fine dust and ozone also split sharply by cluster, tied to local growth paths. Tailored local plans beat one size rules, the team argues.
pmc-13320442:
Christophe Glorieux and co-authors review a pro harm pairing of vitamin C with quinone compounds against cancer in a 2026 article. Quinones are natural ring compounds found across living things that help move energy in cells. Vitamin C can shield cells or harm them by dose and setting, and with quinones it speeds a cycle that pours out harmful oxygen forms.

Cancer cells already run high on such forms and hold weak shields, which may leave them open to a push past the edge while healthy cells cope. Natural and lab made quinones are weighed for how they spin that cycle with the vitamin and what that does to tumor growth, spread traits, and death paths. Dose and cell setting decide the line between help and harm.
pmc-13320542:
Jin Peng and co-authors present a 2026 computer framework that sorts cyber threat reports into a shared attack catalogue. Analysts must map free text reports to the MITRE ATT&CK catalogue, a slow task that also needs clear reasons and coverage of rare attack types. The system, CSEM-CTI, mixes a security tuned language model with large model guidance.

Across three report sets, the system scored 0.939 for broad tactic sorting and 0.481 for finer technique sorting on macro F1 measures. Rare class scores rose sharply, explanations scored high on faithfulness checks, and trick attacks fooled it only 5.5 percent of the time. The authors link those gains to how evidence, prototypes, and loss design work together.
pmc-13322142:
İnci Menekşe and Ümit Begüm Efes test whether plaque revealing dyes stain dental filling materials in a 2026 laboratory study. Dentists use disclosing agents to show plaque, but dyes might discolour restorations. Discs of four filling materials, 20 per material, were treated with two agents, Mira-2-Ton or a ProPind gel with erythrosin dye.

Colour change passed the visible threshold in every group. Mira-2-Ton caused changes classed as clinically unacceptable across materials, worst in Charisma Diamond and mildest in Z250. The ProPind gel kept changes within acceptable limits for all materials, with no clear gap between them. Choice of disclosing agent thus matters for keeping fillings looking clean.
pmc-13324442:
Zijing Yu and colleagues quantify deaths and disability from lip and oral cavity cancer caused by tobacco in a 2026 analysis. They track both smoked and chewed tobacco over 1990 to 2021 and project trends to 2050.

Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, the team compared rates by sex, region, and development level. Total deaths from this cancer nearly doubled, yet the age-standardized death rate fell from 1.07 to 0.94 per 100,000 people. The drop came from smoking alone, while chewing tobacco harm rose slightly, hit women hardest, and stayed highest in South Asia. Forecasts to 2050 show smoking harm still falling but no gain for chewing tobacco.
pmc-13325442:
Yuan-Chih Chen and colleagues build a wider net for urine markers of toxic chemical exposure in a 2026 study. Mercapturic acid conjugates form when the body detoxifies reactive compounds, but standard screening misses many of them.

A new workflow pairs enzyme deacetylation with high-resolution mass spectrometry and a home-built library of 734,170 possible structures. Spiked tests on 11 standards validated the method. Applied to urine from 15 people before and after eating deep-fried food, it mapped 847 features to candidate structures, far above the roughly 100 in earlier work. After the meal, 59 markers rose and 11 fell, pointing to shifts in aldehyde handling.
pmc-13325942:
Wanling Huang and colleagues build a 3D bioprinted home for primary leukemia cells in a 2026 study. Acute myeloid leukemia cells fade fast in flat dishes, which makes drug testing unreliable.

Patient bone marrow cells were printed inside a gelatin and hyaluronic acid gel tuned to feel like real marrow. Inside the gel, the cells lived longer, kept dividing, and held onto stem-like groups. Their drug responses also matched clinical behavior more closely than dish cultures. Gene profiles showed MYC and mTORC1 programs switched on, with both energy routes running hot. The patient-specific setup could sharpen preclinical drug screening.
pmc-13326942:
Hugh D Simpson and co-authors chart how seizures start in the thalamus and cortex in drug-resistant focal epilepsy in a 2026 study. Brain stimulation helps such patients. Which thalamic hubs join seizures was still fuzzy.

Thirteen patients with implanted wires gave recordings from cortex, deep temporal areas, and thalamus. Firing in the thalamus showed in 89 percent of seizures caught on the recordings. Over half of those events showed locked starts in both regions. Four clear patterns ran from sharp spiking to broad quieting. Which nuclei joined depended on the brain network in each patient. Wider thalamic targeting may improve stimulation choices.
pmc-13327542:
Tigran P Norekian and Robert W Meech map the nerve system that coordinates swimming in a colonial jellyfish relative in a 2026 study. Nanomia septata carries many swimming bells on one stem, and the bells must pulse together for forward or reverse escape swims. Signals pass between each bell and the colony at cone-shaped junctions in the stem.

Staining revealed two giant axons, a spread-out nerve net, and paired tracts linking bells on opposite sides. Giant axons spread excitation fast, but they reach each bell only through the nerve net and a small terminal cluster of nerve cells. One route triggers reverse swimming through a skin impulse, another feeds forward swimming, and the net shows facilitation and summation.
pmc-13328342:
Meng-jiao Li and co-authors review mesenchymal stem cells for bile duct diseases in a 2026 article. These versatile cells calm immunity and fight scarring, making them candidates for disorders inside and outside the liver's bile network. The review gathers animal and clinical evidence across several diseases.

Conditions covered include primary biliary cholangitis, biliary fibrosis and cirrhosis, biliary atresia in infants, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and bile duct cancer. Four action routes recur: immune calming, antifibrotic effects, bile acid handling, and shielding of duct lining cells. Results still vary widely between studies, and the mechanisms stay partly murky, so the authors call for tighter trials before routine clinical use.
pmc-13333342:
Wangting Li and colleagues assessed a gentle laser treatment for pigment epithelium detachment, a fluid blister under the retina that clouds vision, in a 2026 retrospective study. Subthreshold micropulse laser promises help without burning tissue, but results across the blister's three forms had rarely been compared.

The study covered 42 patients, one eye each, treated between January 2017 and April 2023: 27 with the serous form, 10 drusenoid, and 5 polypoidal. Vision improved modestly overall, by a mean of 0.07 LogMAR, though no single group improved significantly on its own. Only the serous group shrank its blister area significantly. Starting vision was the strongest predictor of both vision gain and area loss. Serous cases often needed repeat sessions, while 60.0 percent of polypoidal eyes also needed anti-VEGF injections. With no control group, the authors call for larger controlled trials.
pmc-13333542:
Klaudia Walczak and colleagues inspect the power plants of cells from patients with mucopolysaccharidosis in a 2026 study. The inherited disorders clog lysosomes with undegraded sugar chains, and earlier work disagreed about the mitochondria, reporting anything from extra organelles to broken respiration to no change at all.

The team used skin fibroblasts from patients across MPS types. They photographed mitochondrial networks under fluorescence microscopy and counted mitochondrial DNA against nuclear DNA by PCR. Network shape looked normal in patient cells compared with controls, an answer to one branch of the dispute. Mitochondrial DNA levels did fall in several types, I, II, IIIA, IIID, and VI, but not in the others, suggesting mild harm tied to types rather than damage everywhere. The authors stress the study is descriptive and hypothesis-generating: it shows quantity changes, not proven dysfunction, and they call for functional tests to settle what the mitochondria can do.
pmc-13335342:
Yuhong Qin and co-authors built a machine learning tool to spot infectious mononucleosis from routine blood cell data in a 2026 detection study. Mono's symptoms are vague, so it is often missed or caught late, while proof tests take time.

The study gathered 234 proven mono patients from April 2024 to December 2025 and 478 controls, mixing other infections showing reactive lymphocytes with healthy people. Recursive feature pruning with cross-checks ranked blood measures, and eight machine learning algorithms were trained and weighed on accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and related measures. The goal is a fast lab flag that raises suspicion of mono from tests already drawn, shortening the path to proof and cutting complications from delayed recognition.
pmc-13337042:
Han Chen and co-authors mine wrist wearable data from about 90,000 UK Biobank participants in a 2026 health study. They asked whether the daily alignment between movement rhythms and device temperature rhythms predicts future disease. Week-long records from people with a median age of 63 years were split into three alignment features.

Over 7–11 years of follow-up, stronger 24-hour coupling tracked with lower risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, depression, sleep apnea, and death. A larger phase shift from the expected opposite pattern tracked with higher cardiometabolic risk. A 12-hour rhythm feature linked to lower gut and psychiatric risk. A Scottish cohort check supported the method, suggesting rhythm alignment as a cheap population health signal.
pmc-13337842:
Krisztián Havanecz and colleagues track directional movement in elite youth soccer in a 2026 season study. Under-15 male players wore motion sensors through training and matches. The focus was whether the dominant leg changes how often and how hard players turn each way.

Counts of direction changes and movement load were split by dominant and non-dominant sides. Results showed clear interactions between side and leg dominance for directional load in the reported analysis. Left-footed and right-footed players also differed. Coaches who only count total turns may miss uneven strain, so side-aware tracking could guide training and lower injury risk for young athletes.
pmc-13338142:
J. Benita Evangalyne leads a 2026 survey of family helpers in cancer hospitals in Tamil Nadu, India. These helpers plan care and support patients each day, yet their views of service quality are rarely studied. The study links helper background to how quality shapes contentment.

A total of 480 helpers across cancer hospitals answered a set of questions covering six quality areas. Clean wards, fast response, and kind staff each tied to higher contentment in the reported models. Together the areas explained a large share of the gaps in scores. Age and schooling also mattered, while income did not. The results point managers to wards and staff response first.
pmc-13338942: Adriana Oliveira Manfiolli and colleagues issued a 2026 correction for a study of stress kinases in the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus. Only Figure 4A was wrong: matching images were used by accident for two strains under Congo Red, the test was repeated, and the corrected panel now shows the true growth results.
pmc-13339642:
Hélio M. T. Albuquerque and colleagues settle a fifty-year-old structure dispute in a 2026 chemistry study. Burning of 3-amino-1H-indazole with oxygen was reported by Hünig and Pozharskii as an azo product, but proof was thin. Repeating the work in basic conditions gave two products.

Which product formed depended on how much tert-butyllithium was used as reported. Magnetic resonance and X-ray methods pinned both structures. The deep-red Hünig compound is an imine form. The orange Pozharskii compound is truly an azoazole, with bond layout opposite to the 1977 claim. One framework now reconciles both old reports.
pmc-13342242:
Haobin Peng and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare crisis during kidney stone surgery. A 63-year-old woman having percutaneous nephrolithotomy for several right kidney stones suddenly bled into both chest cavities and her abdomen while the operation was under way.

Airway pressure spiked, oxygen fell, and blood pressure dropped before bedside ultrasound revealed fluid around both lungs and inside the abdomen. Doctors drained both sides of the chest and the abdomen, gave fluids, blood, and pressure-raising drugs, and the patient steadied. She went home after 10 days and was well at three months. The authors urge quick ultrasound checks when breathing trouble strikes during such surgery.
pmc-13347942:
Katherine W Eyring and co-authors map DNA methylation cell by cell. Their study was published in 2026. It covers autism brain tissue. A paired method read two signals at once. One signal was methylation. The other was gene activity. Over 60,000 nuclei were read in total. All came from the front brain cortex. The donors numbered 49 in all.

Over 30,000 regions differed in methylation. They clustered at promoters and control sites. Those sites stay active across life. Shifts were small beside ageing effects. They barely tracked gene activity levels. Age marks centred on excitatory neurons. Age-varying autism marks pointed elsewhere. They flagged growth of neuron projections as a disturbed path. Autism effects thus shift across the lifespan.
pmc-13348142:
Pragadeesh Ayyamuthu Rajarathinam Uma and colleagues report the complete genome of a leaf bacterium that helps tomato plants grow, in an announcement from 2026. Strain MtTm-13 was picked from tomato leaves in Coimbatore, India, where a pink colony grew on methanol feed. The strain is known to bear stress while aiding plants through hormones, mineral freeing, and protective compounds.

The genome spans 5,231,310 base pairs with a G plus C share of 69 percent and 4,660 protein-coding genes in the reported assembly. A full gene set lets researchers find the exact paths behind growth help and stress cover, guiding use as a living farm aid.
pmc-13348242:
Hongran Moon and colleagues test whether kidney stones speed decline in polycystic kidney disease, in a prospective cohort study published in 2026. A total of 410 patients had entry scans within a year that separated true collecting-system stones from cyst wall crusts, then were followed for a median of 5.18 years toward dialysis start and a wider decline marker set.

Dialysis start hit 51 patients and the wider marker hit 96 in the reported counts. Stone carriers faced a hazard ratio of 2.84 for dialysis after full adjustment, with a smaller lift for the wider marker. Links looked stronger in men, giving stone checks a sharper role in watching this inherited disease.
pmc-13349842:
Shaoqiu Chen wrote a 2026 editorial introducing a collection on finding biomarkers and drug targets with both traditional methods and artificial intelligence. Careful lab work built on clear hypotheses has produced many markers now used in precision medicine.

Modern biomedical data, though, are now too large and mixed for older analysis pipelines to handle comfortably, leaving gaps in repeatability and in joining different data types. AI tools can pull compact signatures from such data and carry lessons across diseases. The editorial frames the two approaches as partners: machine methods can rank candidates fast, while classic experiments supply the depth needed before a target reaches patients.
pmc-13349942:
Muhammad Wasif Saif and colleagues commented in 2026 on a network meta-analysis ranking targeted drug combinations for advanced pancreatic cancer. The work they discuss pooled 13 phase III trials with 5,759 patients, comparing gemcitabine-based combinations against gemcitabine alone.

Network methods compare many treatments at once by mixing direct trial results with indirect links, useful when head-to-head trials are missing. The commentators value that reach for guidelines and policy, but warn that indirect comparisons rest on shaky ground when trials differ in patients or design, a common problem in cancer research. Their piece weighs what such rankings can and cannot tell doctors choosing therapy.
pmc-13351642:
Jennifer J Salinas and colleagues report beta testing in 2026 of the 50K4Life phone app, built to run walking challenges. Health apps often fail because people find them hard to use, so early testing matters. Twelve public school office staff in El Paso County, Texas used the app, built on the Pathverse platform, for a 2-week challenge.

All 12 finished the challenge, and ratings were high for design, layout, and battery use. Problems still appeared: over half struggled with navigation and slow step-count updates, and some could not find all features. Every user opened the leaderboard and challenge pages. The results guide fixes before wider rollout to school staff.
pmc-13352142:
Kwon and colleagues build a tool that picks out peptides able to cross cell walls. These short chains can carry drugs into cells. Yet no one can spot good ones by eye. The team fed a data set of known chains into a group of learning models. A method called SHAP ranked which traits mattered most. Five traits rose to the top. They cover shape, charge, and how atoms link.

The tool was right in just over four cases out of five on test data. It beat older tools on the same test. Since the five key traits are clear, chemists can use them to design new chains. The same method may suit other peptide types.
pmc-13358342:
Amene Ghaderi and co-authors present a 2026 study of electronic prescribing in Iran. The program lets doctors send prescriptions to pharmacies by computer instead of on paper. The team asked doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and office staff what helps the program work and what holds it back.

Through interviews sorted into strengths, weaknesses, chances, and threats, the study maps the program's real state on the ground. The findings can guide health leaders who want to fix weak spots, train staff well, and spread the system more widely. Clear evidence like this matters as more countries move prescribing online.
pmc-13358542:
Huanhuan Yang and co-authors pool past research on a simple blood score in esophageal cancer in a 2026 review. The score, called HALP, joins four routine measures: hemoglobin, albumin, and counts of lymphocytes and platelets. Together they reflect blood health, nutrition, and immune strength. The team asked whether a low score warns of worse outcomes.

They combined 11 studies and compared survival across score levels. Patients with low scores died sooner and saw their cancer return earlier than those with high scores. Because the score comes from cheap, standard blood tests, it could help doctors spot patients who need stronger support and closer follow-up.
pmc-13358842:
Gilson Gabriel Viana Veloso and co-authors question a key lung cancer test in a 2026 commentary. For most patients with non-small cell lung cancer, treatment hinges on a score called PD-L1, which gauges a protein tumors use to hide from the immune system. High scores favor immune drugs. Yet the score is an imperfect hero, the authors argue.

About a fifth to a third of patients score negative, and they tend to respond less well, but some still benefit. The authors discuss new ways to read the marker, including blood-based tests. Their piece urges doctors not to let one score alone decide who receives immune therapy.
pmc-13359942:
Xiaomeng Hu and co-authors build a simple survival model for advanced liver cancer in a 2026 study. Patients at middle to late stages now often receive a triple mix: targeted drugs, immune therapy, and procedures that block the tumor's blood supply. Results still vary widely between patients. The team sought a forecast from facts already in the chart.

Using data from 184 patients, they built a model on three items: sex, a liver function grade called ALBI, and a blood ratio called ALR. The model split patients into clearly different outlook groups. A tool this simple could help doctors stratify risk and tailor how aggressively each patient is treated.
pmc-13361842:
M Alfawaz and co-authors tested a plant compound in tiny carriers against colon cancer in rats in a 2026 study. Paeonol, from peony root, fights oxidative stress and inflammation, two drivers of colorectal cancer. The team loaded it into biodegradable nanoparticles to help it reach tissue. Sixty male rats were split into six groups, including healthy controls and groups given a cancer-triggering chemical for ten weeks.

Some triggered rats got plain paeonol, others the nanoparticle form. Blood markers of tumors, stress, and inflammation were measured, along with gene activity for cell death and clean-up paths. Tissue from colon, liver, and kidney was examined closely. The focus was a protective pathway called NRF2/HO-1. Better delivery could turn a promising plant compound into a real shield.
pmc-13362342:
Mukhlid Alshammari explored nurses' views on medication safety in Saudi hospitals in a 2026 qualitative study. Medication errors remain a major threat to patients. Nurses, who give most medicines, see the system up close. Alshammari found they frame safety as a shared process built on communication, workload, staff skill, and teamwork with technology, not as lone personal slips.

Barcode scanners and electronic records did improve safety in the nurses' eyes. But their value depended on nurse vigilance, good training, and teamwork, above all under heavy workload. The study urges bundled fixes: standard communication habits, enough staff, ongoing training, and reporting cultures that do not punish honesty. Technology should support clinical judgment, the nurses insist, never replace it.
pmc-13364042:
Nayanne Lima Dos Santos Ferreira and a large team present a 2026 study on food packaging films made from okra mucilage and corn starch, strengthened with liquid smoke. The smoky liquid, rich in phenolic compounds, was cast into the films at up to three percent. The team tracked thickness behavior, water traits, strength, structure, antioxidant power, and how fast the films rot in soil.

Liquid smoke thickened the casting mix, made the film surface more water-shy, and cut vapor passage, while the film dissolved a bit more readily in water. Stretch strength rose by over half at the top dose, with a small loss of stretch. The smoke supplied nearly all the antioxidant action. Soil burial ate most of each film, backing their use as active, compostable packaging.
pmc-13364742:
Jeong Lee and co-workers report in 2026 the first case set of a rare drug side mark: seed fluid that turns blue or green on a gut drug named upadacitinib. Six men with gut swell disease at four Korea care sites noted the change a mid span of two months into high dose care.

No man had pain, germ signs, or odd lab tests of the seed fluid. The tint faded when the dose fell and cleared when the drug stopped for some. The team casts it as a rare, dose tied, soft harm that fades, and asks for more study.
pmc-13365342:
Jie Li and co-workers check in 2026 if soft glass micro grains, prized as drug ships, harm mice when fed by mouth. The team made three grain types, with pure glass frames and two that break down more fast. Mice got high doses, up to a top dose, with repeat feeds.

No mice died, and blood, chem, and flesh checks showed no clear harm. The fast break type left liver, spleen, and kidney more quick than its kin. Immune cell counts held calm for all types. The work guides safe grain design for mouth drug ships.
pmc-13369742: Gebreyohannes and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their 2024 study of anticholinergic burden, the cumulative effect of drugs that block a key nerve signal. Quality of life in a resource-limited setting. The counts of medicines by burden score were wrong: sixteen, not fifteen, medicines scored one point, and five, not four, scored three points, with trihexyphenidyl added to the top group. Furosemide, warfarin, and morphine remain the most used one-point medicines, and a corrected first figure replaces the original in the journal record.
pmc-13378342:
Miguel E Domínguez-Romero and colleagues published a 2026 study on spinal cord injury in frogs that can no longer regrow the cord. Young frog larvae can repair such injuries, but after they change into adult form they lose that ability, much like mammals. The team looked at energy systems inside the injured cord.

Using imaging, energy measurements, and gene activity tests, they found that mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy, became fewer, larger, and abnormal after injury. Even so, energy levels rose, because the cord switched on sugar-burning pathways and used stored fats instead. That switch may help cells survive when their normal energy system is damaged.
pmc-13382042:
Roscoe Lim and colleagues present a 2026 study testing whether ultrasound signs of a stiff heart can flag early disease in a transplanted heart's arteries. That artery disease develops early after transplant and causes much later harm. The team reviewed 136 heart transplant recipients treated between 2018 and 2023.

Heart ultrasounds provided several measures of how the heart relaxes. The outcome was artery disease seen on imaging one year after transplant, found in about fifteen percent of recipients. Only one measure, a short relaxation timing value, was clearly linked with the disease. A model combining that measure with age and sex separated patients fairly well, suggesting a non-invasive early warning sign.
pmc-13384042:
Lauren De Bruyn and colleagues test cholesterol top-ups during long sepsis in mouse studies in 2026 work. Blood cholesterol falls sharply in sepsis and low levels track with worse outcomes, but cause and effect were unclear. Septic mice received five days of infusions rich in LDL or HDL cholesterol, or a placebo.

Infusions raised the targeted blood fractions and eased cholesterol loss in the adrenal glands. Muscle mass, force, and fiber cholesterol did not improve, though, and adrenal structure and hormone response stayed impaired. The authors conclude that repletion alone does not fix the adrenal and muscle problems of prolonged sepsis.
pmc-13384242:
Sumit Kumar and colleagues review why guideline-based care for esophageal cancer often falls short in North East India in 2026 work. The region carries one of the country's heaviest loads of this deadly cancer. Modern care calls for staging, nutrition checks, combined drug and radiation steps, surgery, and steady follow-up.

The review traces gaps along the whole care path, from late arrival to loss during follow-up. Distance, weak transport, language range, money strain, and scarce specialist centers all push patients off the guideline path. The authors argue that fixing delivery systems matters as much as new drugs for closing the outcome gap.
pmc-13385442:
Bowen Zhang and colleagues find surface markers that can isolate platelet-biased blood stem cells in 2026 work. Such stem cells favor platelet output and matter in aging and blood cancer, yet no markers could pick them out alive. The team combined gene, chromatin, and surface protein data from single mouse stem cells.

Machine learning settled on a four-marker pattern that isolates the biased cells to high purity, proven by single-cell transplants. A compact gene panel also split biased from balanced stem cells in a chip-based test. Both tools tracked the known rise of biased cells with age and their selective wake-up after platelet loss.
pmc-13390642:
Friedrich Krohn leads a 2026 imaging study asking whether a small midbrain region degenerates in Alzheimer's disease and tracks thinking ability. Post-mortem work shows varied damage in the substantia nigra alongside classic Alzheimer's pathology, but its link to symptoms during life was unclear.

Using a prospective German study of cognitive impairment and dementia, the team tested whether magnetic resonance measures of this region differ in Alzheimer's patients and relate to general cognition. The region's markers were lower in Alzheimer's disease and linked to cognitive function. Dementia researchers gain a candidate imaging signal outside the usual memory circuits, suggesting that Alzheimer's decline involves more brain systems than the classic ones.
pmc-13390742:
