Maria Paniagua-Garcia leads a multi-country 2026 cohort study of Campylobacter bacteria found in the bloodstream, comparing patients with intact and weakened immunity. Bloodstream infection with this gut bacterium is uncommon, and its course across immune states has been hard to summarise from single hospitals.

Cases collected from 2009 to 2024 across many centres let the team compare presentation, treatment, and outcomes between immunocompetent and immunodeficient patients. Doctors who treat such infections gain a fifteen-year, multi-country picture. It shows who gets this bloodstream infection. It shows how hard it hits when immunity is low. It also shows where care should differ. The scale also helps separate consistent patterns from local quirks. Most past work came from one site at a time, so this shared pool counts for much.
pmc-13392342:
Haiyan Yu and colleagues show, in 2026, that gut bacteria-derived compounds can inflame and kill bile duct cells, a finding relevant to an autoimmune liver disease. Primary biliary cholangitis destroys small bile ducts, but the effects of p-cresyl sulfate and p-cresyl glucuronide in it were unclear.

Human bile duct cells treated with either compound showed increased cell death by flow measurement. Mice given the compounds developed portal inflammation with lymphocyte infiltration, alongside changes in death-related proteins and inflammatory signals in blood. Liver researchers gain a mechanistic link between microbial waste products and bile duct injury that may help explain disease triggers.
pmc-13392642:
Pramono and co-authors report a 2026 genetics study of 710 Indonesian Friesian Holstein cows on a commercial farm in West Java. They examined four single-letter DNA variants in two genes: leptin, a hormone gene tied to fertility, and IGF-1, a growth-factor gene. Each cow's variants were matched against milk records, such as 305-day yield, and reproductive records, such as calving interval and days open.

One leptin variant, g.820 C>T, showed moderate diversity and real associations with days in milk, calving interval, first insemination after calving, days open, and conception rate. Cows carrying the CC type reproduced better than TT carriers, marking the variant as a candidate for marker-assisted selection, where breeders use DNA tests to choose animals. The second leptin variant showed little variation and no associations. One IGF-1 variant was identical in every cow tested, so it cannot guide breeding here.
pmc-13393142:
Takayuki Gyoten and Akihiro Yoshitake report a giant clot floating in the aortic arch. It was traced to a deep vein thrombosis that crossed into the arterial side through a hole between the heart's upper chambers. Scans suggested clot fragments had already reached the brain, and ultrasound confirmed the opening, a patent foramen ovale, with flow in both directions. The heart team judged the picture a paradoxical embolism alongside a lung clot.

Because the arch clot resisted heparin and threatened further strokes, surgeons removed it urgently under circulatory arrest. They pulled out a fresh cast thirty centimetres long, then cleared the lung arteries and closed the hole directly. Later testing pointed to protein C deficiency as an underlying driver. Six months on, scans showed no remaining clot and the patient stayed free of nerve complications on blood thinners.
pmc-13394342:
Gabriela Arenas and co-authors offer a 2026 first look at fat-carrying proteins in human breast milk. Milk from 22 healthy women was spun at very high speed to pull out these particles. The team measured their density, fat content, and marker proteins, and watched how they moved in a gel. The work asks whether milk carries the same kinds of particles that move fat through blood.

The particles matched the density of the lighter blood lipoproteins, but not the high-density kind. They held far less fat than whole milk and moved much like blood particles. The authors present this as early evidence that milk fat transport is wider than once thought.
pmc-13394642:
Saara Otonkoski and co-authors report, in 2026, a year of follow-up after sound-wave treatment for uterine fibroids. Fibroids are benign growths that cause heavy bleeding or a sense of pressure. Guided by magnetic scans, focused sound heats and kills fibroid tissue with no cuts. The study enrolled 163 women picked as fit for the treatment at one centre.

Women with bleeding and women with pressure both felt much better by three months. Gains held at twelve months, and quality of life scores rose in both groups. About three fifths of each fibroid lost its blood supply. The authors call the method a fast, knife-free relief when it works.
pmc-13395242:
Fabian Patauner and co-authors review, in 2026, trials of drugs for Gram-negative bacterial infections since 2000. These germs cause many grave hospital and community infections. The team gathered 68 trials in adults covering belly, lung, urinary, and blood infections. They read each trial's design, aims, and patient mix.

Belly and urinary infections drew the most trials. Most studies tested whether a new drug was no worse than standard care, and few aimed to prove better. New drugs featured often, yet resistant germs were rare in the patient pools. That gap weakens use of results in real wards. The authors call for more funding and rule changes to aid real-world trials.
pmc-13395342:
Belle Tamir Brahms and co-authors compare, in 2026, two blood pressure drug families for long-term cancer risk. Both families are widely used and guard heart and kidneys well. Records from Israel's largest health fund covered hundreds of thousands of adults who stayed on one family only. Follow-up ran from 2002 to 2024.

Overall cancer odds came out lower for the ACE inhibitor group than for the blocker group. The gap varied by cancer type, with lower odds for several common cancers. Leukaemia showed no real gap. Age at diagnosis and time to diagnosis also differed. The authors stress that records alone cannot prove cause. They call for forward studies and lab work.
pmc-13395442:
Kaoru Okano and colleagues scan, in 2026, the knee cushions of young rugby players for early wear signs. A cushion that slips outward, called extrusion, tracks with later knee arthritis. The team used ultrasound on 94 college rugby men with no past knee harm and 42 student controls. Both knees were checked lying, bent, and standing on one leg.

Rugby players showed more cushion slip in every pose. The gap held after body size was weighed in. No player had clear knee injury, so the shift looks like an early change from hard play. Ultrasound proved handy for checks under load. The authors urge longer studies and early guard steps for contact athletes.
pmc-13396342:
Kavya Raveendran and co-authors uncovered how a guardian protein reaches unsynapsed chromosomes during meiosis, the cell division that makes eggs and sperm. Their 2026 study focuses on HORMAD2, a checkpoint protein that flags chromosome sections that have failed to pair, and SYCP2, a scaffold protein of the chromosome axis.

Deleting a short binding motif in SYCP2 broke its grip on HORMAD2 and kept HORMAD2 off the axes, while the axes themselves still formed and pairing machinery stayed intact. Without that recruitment, the silencing of unpaired chromatin and the alarm signal to the cell weaken. The result clarifies a surveillance step that guards fertility and genome quality.
pmc-13396542:
Yiying Gao and co-authors rebuilt the radiation dose from a lab accident after the fact, using small dosimeter chips read minute by minute. Their 2026 study reconstructs an incident with a wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence spectrometer, a machine that identifies elements in samples, where no personal dose records existed.

The team replayed the event: dosimeters were placed at seven spots matching head and hand positions, and the machine ran at its recorded settings of 40 kilovolts and 7 milliamps. Minute-level dose rates at each spot were combined with estimates of how long each body part stayed there. The method offers a template for the many accidents where nobody wore a meter.
pmc-13396642:
Madeleine Bloomfield and co-authors explored how people feel about taking low-dose lithium as a daily supplement, in a 2026 qualitative study. Lithium is a proven drug for mood disorders at full doses, and small doses have been sold as supplements for decades, yet research on the supplement form is nearly absent.

The team ran a focus group with people who had never taken it but worried about their own or a relative's mood, and a second study with current users. Conversations covered willingness, hopes, and worries. With hints that micro-doses might help mood and thinking at lower risk, the authors argue that user attitudes should shape the trials now being planned.
pmc-13397342:
Adam Yasgar and co-authors paired mass screening with computer learning to find chemical probes for an enzyme that manages the cell's inositol phosphate signals, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, ITPK1, keeps the balance among those signal molecules, and its pathway is tied to human disease.

First the team shrank the enzyme's test to plates with 1,536 wells and screened about 19,000 known and varied compounds. That haul of real results then trained a machine learning model to predict which further compounds would block the enzyme, raising the hit rate beyond blind screening. Good probes for ITPK1 would let biologists switch the pathway off cleanly and watch what happens.
pmc-13399342:
Bianca Lopes Cunha and colleagues comment on a three-year comparison of pacemaker patients, in a 2026 editorial written in Portuguese. The study under discussion followed people who received pacemakers for one of two rhythm problems. Cunha's group argues the results point beyond the pacing wire itself to the health of the atria, the heart's upper chambers.

Serial ultrasound scans showed that sinus syndrome patients developed progressive enlargement of the left atrium and left ventricle plus worsening mitral valve leakage. Block patients stayed comparatively stable, even though their ventricles were paced more than 90 percent of the time. The editorial notes the study's limits: it was retrospective, single-center, and small, with no detailed data on lead position or atrial strain. Even so, the authors float the idea that sick sinus syndrome itself marks an underlying atrial muscle disease.
pmc-13399542:
Schwarzmüller and co-authors show, in 2026, that the kinase PAK1 drives resistance to two hormone therapies in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, but through different wiring. Up to 40 percent of late-stage patients resist endocrine therapy and relapse. Using MCF7 cell models made resistant to tamoxifen or to estrogen loss, the stand-in for aromatase inhibitors, they found PAK1 levels high and hyper-responsive to growth factors.

Blocking PAK1 cut proliferation in both resistant models, yet the mechanisms split. In tamoxifen-resistant cells, inhibition switched on the pro-death protein BAD and triggered apoptosis. In estrogen-deprived cells it suppressed growth-related kinases instead. Proteomic profiling mapped the substrate networks behind the split response. Earlier data found high PAK1 levels in 19 percent of premenopausal ER+ patients. The authors propose blocking PAK1 to outflank endocrine resistance in luminal breast cancer.
pmc-13400342:
Ethan P Rogers, Parker D Sperstad and Erik D Holmstrom study, in 2026, how two parts of the hepatitis C virus genome bind each other. One part, called 3 prime X, sits at the genome end and is needed for the virus to copy itself. It pairs with a second conserved part inside the coding region.

The team watched single molecules using a light-based method that reports when RNA parts come close. They measured binding strength across many conditions. The partner part bound the two shapes of the first 55 letters of 3 prime X unevenly, favoring one shape. That bias may help the virus switch between making proteins and copying its genome.
pmc-13400442:
Proczka, Zagzoog, and Haulon describe, in 2026, a move to stop endografts from being squeezed during endovascular repair of the aortic arch in chronic dissections. Retrograde branches can compress the graft's lumen in the tight true channel of a dissected arch, creating a pseudocoarctation that risks cardiac failure. Their example patient got an arch endograft with three branches, placed for an anastomotic false aneurysm with dissection reaching the supra-aortic trunks.

Preoperative imaging showed distal arch narrowing with a true lumen of 21 millimeters against a false lumen of 25 millimeters in the affected zones. After wiring the left subclavian artery, they performed kissing angioplasty, inflating balloons simultaneously in the endograft and the left common carotid branch. That branch carried a 9 by 75 millimeter bridging stent. The maneuver disrupted the dissection flap. By postoperative day three, imaging showed the true lumen expanded and the graft at its 28-millimeter nominal diameter.
pmc-13400542:
Yaojun Peng and team show, in 2026, that an enzyme called MMP8 helps sepsis pry open lung blood vessels. Sepsis can wreck the vessel lining, letting fluid leak into the lungs and other organs, a major driver of death. The enzyme was known to rise in sepsis, but its role at the barrier was unclear.

MMP8 rose in treated vessel cells and in lungs of septic mice. Raising or lowering it in cells changed how leaky the lining became under inflammatory attack. Blocking it in mice eased lung leakage, organ injury and death. Mechanistic work traced a chain: the enzyme activated a signaling protein, which freed cutting enzymes that destroyed a key cell-to-cell anchor. Patient blood levels also ran high, especially with chest fluid.
pmc-13401242:
Panhui Yu, Kang Liu, and Fang Chen describe a 2026 case of MOG antibody-associated disease, an immune attack on the nervous system, that looked like a brain infection in a teenager. The patient was a previously healthy 13-year-old boy with headache, fever, vomiting, and double vision.

His spinal fluid showed inflammation, and brain MRI scans revealed patchy lesions across the right temporal lobe, basal ganglia, and other areas that changed over time. Extensive microbe testing found nothing. Blood tests repeatedly showed MOG antibodies by a live cell-based assay, while aquaporin-4 and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies were negative. He improved during overlapping treatment that included intravenous immunoglobulin. The case warns that MOG disease can closely imitate central nervous system infection in children.
pmc-13401342:
Jean Jacques Nenba Sambo and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of tuberculosis lesions in cattle slaughtered for food in Ngaoundéré, Cameroon. Bovine tuberculosis can pass to people, and control measures in Cameroon are weak, raising the stakes for meat inspection.

Between April and October 2024, veterinary inspectors examined 1,256 slaughtered cattle at two slaughterhouses for tuberculosis-like lesions, and lesion samples were stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method to look for acid-fast bacilli. A structured questionnaire gathered information on possible risk factors, and the team analysed links with lesion prevalence using logistic regression. The study gives an estimate of how common such lesions are in cattle entering the local food supply, and which animal or management factors travel with them.
pmc-13401542:
Dai Maruyama and co-authors report a 2026 Japan subgroup analysis of the phase III SUNMO trial in relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. The trial tested subcutaneous mosunetuzumab, a T-cell-engaging bispecific antibody, plus polatuzumab vedotin, an antibody-drug conjugate, against a standard rituximab chemotherapy pairing.

In the full trial, 208 patients were randomized two to one, 138 to the new pairing and 70 to rituximab with gemcitabine and oxaliplatin. Sixteen patients came from Japan, nine on the new pairing and seven on the standard arm. Every Japanese patient on the new pairing responded, a 100 percent response rate, against about 57 percent on standard treatment. Progression-free survival was strongly prolonged as well. The authors frame the fixed-duration outpatient regimen as a new option that is easy to reach for this hard-to-treat lymphoma.
pmc-13401942:
Benster and team compare, in 2026, how quickly two approved treatments work in treatment-resistant depression, using UC San Diego Health records from 2017 to 2025. Adults received either repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, 279 patients, or intranasal esketamine, 93 patients. Response meant at least a 50 percent drop on the PHQ-9 depression scale, with weighting to balance the groups on age, trauma, anxiety, drug use, and baseline severity.

Esketamine acted faster: median time to response was 36 days against 49 days for magnetic stimulation, with a hazard ratio of 1.62 for response speed in the weighted model. Suicidal ideation improved faster too, at a median of 9 days versus 26 days for the stimulation group. Final response and remission rates also favored esketamine, 68.8 and 45.2 percent against 59.4 and 40.1 percent, converging by about 90 days. In the stimulation cohort, anxiety and benzodiazepine use predicted slower response.
pmc-13402442:
Farah Ismail leads a team that pooled every published case of neurobrucellosis, infection of the nervous system by Brucella bacteria, into one patient-level picture. Searching PubMed Central and Google Scholar through November 2025, they kept 23 articles covering 34 confirmed patients with brain involvement. Average age was 35.7 years, and about two in three patients were male.

Headache led the symptoms at 67.64 percent, ahead of fever and vomiting. Weakness, seizures, and hearing loss each appeared in roughly a quarter of patients. MRI was the favored scan, most often showing frontal lobe lesions, and blood antibody testing confirmed most diagnoses, while spinal fluid culture rarely grew the germ. Diagnosis took 8.83 months on average, a delay the authors blame on vague early signs. Most patients recovered on medicines alone; about a third also needed surgery. Brucella melitensis was the species named most often.
pmc-13402642:
Jones, Lilly, and Cole explore, in 2026, how Australian health promotion practitioners use theories of the policy process, the frameworks for understanding how policy gets made and changed. Influencing policy is a core professional function, yet engagement with the theory behind it was unstudied. They interviewed practitioners working in Queensland online, using semi-structured conversations analyzed by reflexive thematic analysis.

Ten practitioners took part, eight recruited purposively and two by snowball sampling, with a median of 18 years of industry experience spanning one to 24 years across the group. Four themes emerged. Practitioners grasp policy complexity but barely know the theories by name; they nonetheless apply the theories' constructs implicitly in daily work. Organizational context decides how far they can engage policy, and industry-level factors gate their involvement. A cited United States study echoes the gap, with 78 percent of students valuing policy action but 76 percent lacking understanding of the process.
pmc-13403642:
Tatiane Cristina da Silva and colleagues asked in 2026 how people without homes reach mental health care in a São Paulo state town. They spoke with 21 people living without housing in July 2024. Care runs through a local network of linked services.

People moved between care points when blocks in one place pushed them onward. A street outreach clinic stood out as a bridge that eased entry into care. Some felt welcomed, while others met bias that cut care short. Their hopes were plain: equal access for all. The authors urge warmer welcome, better training, and steadier support.
pmc-13404242:
Ravindra S Bohra and co-authors compared two ways in 2026 to find germs behind ventilator lung infections in intensive care. Their North Indian center enrolled 106 patients with the infection. One group got a rapid gene panel plus standard culture, while the other group got culture alone.

Patients tied to the rapid panel left intensive care sooner, with a median stay of nine days against thirteen for culture finds. Breathing tubes also came out within a week more often in the panel group. Death at 28 days ran lower with the panel, though not by a firm margin. Odd, test-negative panel patients fared worse than test-negative culture patients.
pmc-13404842:
Wonjeong Yoon and co-authors trace smoke-free rules and smoking behaviour in South Korea from 2005 to 2020, in a 2026 report. The country tightened bans over two decades, but links between wider bans and everyday behaviour were rarely tracked together. Five national survey waves supply the data.

The analysis covers 10,028 adults who smoked at least weekly. Restrictions in bars, restaurants and workplaces grew sharply across the period. Seeing smoking in those venues fell from very high levels to between 5.8 and 12.4 percent in the reported figures, while support for bans climbed. Voluntary smoke-free homes and quit motivation were tracked alongside, using weighted models that account for repeat respondents.
pmc-13405342:
Yingcui Li and colleagues delete a cartilage gene in mice to learn what keeps joints healthy, reporting in 2026. Hyaluronan, a slippery matrix sugar, fills cartilage and joint fluid. The enzyme Has2 makes most of it in skeletal tissue, but its adult role was undefined.

Twenty male mice carried a switchable Has2 deletion in cartilage cells, triggered by tamoxifen at three weeks of age. Within a week, hyaluronan had nearly vanished from joint cartilage and growth plates, confirmed by specific staining. Later tissue checks trace how cartilage and joints cope without their main lubricant and scaffold. The model isolates adult maintenance roles that embryo studies could not separate.
pmc-13406942:
Dong Hoon Suh and Dong Soo Han, in a 2026 perspective piece, consider how researchers should use generative artificial intelligence when writing scholarly papers. Surveys show many academics already lean on such tools for drafting help and error checking, yet rules for proper use remain unsettled.

Submission records from large journal groups show far fewer authors declaring AI help than survey figures would predict. That gap suggests confusion about what must be reported, or quiet underreporting. Views also differ on AI help with drafting itself and with peer review. The authors argue for shared, explicit disclosure rules so readers can trust how a paper was produced and judge the work fairly.
pmc-13408342:
Ritchel Gannaban and colleagues report in 2026 that fatty sugar-coated lipids act as organisers of a key membrane supply route. The cancer protein KRAS must sit in the cell's outer membrane to signal, and that seat depends on a lipid called phosphatidylserine delivered to the membrane's inner face. Two transport proteins ferry it there from the endoplasmic reticulum at contact points between the organelles.

High-resolution imaging showed that blocking production of certain glycosphingolipids scattered the transport proteins, displaced a kinase needed to prime the exchange, and cut membrane phosphatidylserine sharply. Other machinery stationed at the same contact sites, including calcium channels, also failed. The findings recast these lipids as structural organisers of membrane contact sites and suggest a fresh angle on controlling KRAS in cancer.
pmc-13409042:
Erika Maharani and co-authors pool the published trials in 2026 on whether a standard heart tracing can separate a dangerous inherited heart muscle disease from a benign rhythm nuisance. Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy can kill suddenly, while outflow tract arrhythmias with a similar tracing pattern are usually harmless, and advanced imaging is not available everywhere. Ten studies covering over seven hundred patients were combined.

Inverted T waves across the right chest leads were the most studied sign, catching just over half of true cases while rarely appearing in the benign condition. The rare epsilon wave almost never appeared in benign cases but missed most disease. Measures of signal width across the chest leads performed strongly, one ratio approaching excellent discrimination. The authors offer the pooled figures to help clinicians decide who needs referral for definitive imaging.
pmc-13412142:
Ghyslaine Giselle Ramírez and colleagues review in 2026 how heat stress damages cattle eggs and early embryos down to the molecular level. Hot seasons already cut fertility on farms, and warming climates widen the risk. The review gathers studies done in living animals and in laboratory dishes, tracing effects from the ovary through fertilization to the first days of embryonic life.

Heat disrupts follicle growth and hormone output in the ovary, leaving eggs in a poorer setting. Inside eggs it stirs oxidative stress, strains mitochondria, tangles the division spindle, and leaves lasting epigenetic marks. Embryos then cleave and implant less reliably, and effects may reach offspring. The authors map these weak points as targets for protective interventions.
pmc-13412542:
Matiullah Alimzai and colleagues run a 2026 case-control study of scabies risk among dermatology patients in Kabul province, Afghanistan. Scabies, a contagious mite infestation, burdens poor communities heavily, and Afghan data on its drivers were scarce. Clinics enrolled 410 participants between March 2024 and May 2025: 210 confirmed cases and 200 controls, compared on housing, hygiene, and sharing habits.

Bathing only two or three times a week carried the strongest link, with odds over twenty times those of frequent bathers in adjusted models. Sharing blankets or clothes, weaker personal hygiene, and living in a mud house each raised risk several-fold. Brick housing, employment, female sex, and older age appeared protective. The authors urge control programs that pair treatment with better water and housing.
pmc-13412642:
Carina Braeutigam and co-authors report in 2026 a quality improvement project that taught a children's cancer unit to score nausea with a faces scale. Chemotherapy nausea in children is hard to assess, and poor documentation blurs whether anti-nausea drugs are working. The Baxter Animated Retching Faces scale, showing cartoon faces from calm to retching, was introduced stepwise with staff teaching and a slot in the electronic record.

The share of patients with at least three documented nausea scores on chemotherapy days jumped from 5 percent at baseline to 75 percent in the first month after the record change. Scores peaked at 94 percent that September and stayed above goal for two years. Nurses adopted the tool readily, the authors conclude.
pmc-13413242:
Seoyoung Choi and co-authors report a 69-year-old man whose kidney damage came from crystals of antibody light chains. He presented with weight loss and protein in his urine, and blood and urine tests showed high levels of kappa light chains. His history included thyroid cancer. Their 2026 case report describes the diagnostic path and the biopsy findings.

Bone marrow examination revealed plasma cell myeloma of the IgA-kappa type. Kidney biopsy found crystal inclusions inside both podocytes, the cells that filter blood, and proximal tubule cells, and staining was positive for kappa light chain and for the IgA heavy chain. The team diagnosed light chain crystalline podocytopathy with proximal tubulopathy. They note two unusual features: heavy-chain staining alongside the light chain, and the absence of Fanconi syndrome or a scarring pattern often seen with this condition.
pmc-13414442:
José Diogo da Rocha Viana and co-authors optimize in 2026 the microfiltration of coconut water, a drink that spoils within hours of leaving the nut. Crossflow through a silicon carbide membrane can clarify it gently, provided pressure and temperature are tuned. Classical response-surface modelling and a neural network steered by a genetic algorithm each searched the settings, scoring flow rate and fouling while tracking how many minerals and metabolites survive.

Each method won on different ground: the network described flow best at the points tested, while the classical model predicted unseen settings better in their comparisons. Both settled on the same window, validated at 60 kilopascals and 35 degrees with strong flow and high nutrient passage. Fouling proved mostly a surface cake that cleaning reversed well.
pmc-13415342:
Jingyu Yang, Stefan Gründer, and Dominik Wiemuth uncover a new role for a bile acid sensing channel in the pancreas, reporting in 2026. The channel, called BASIC, sits mainly in glucagon making alpha cells of mouse islets. Glucagon raises blood sugar, so alpha cell health matters for glucose balance.

Mice lacking the channel had fewer alpha cells, made less glucagon, and showed lower glucagon levels in blood. Genes that define alpha cell identity were disturbed as well. The channel belongs to a sodium channel family related to acid sensors. Its loss reshapes the cell rather than merely muting one signal, suggesting a guardian role for alpha cell identity.
pmc-13415742:
Lanya Yu, Zhe He, and Guibin Qiao recount a breast cancer case in 2026 where stopping hormone therapy preceded a fast, invasive return. A woman aged forty-one had a fully removed intraductal papillary carcinoma, an in situ tumor type usually classed as low risk. Her tumor carried strong hormone receptors and a high growth index of twenty percent.

Adjuvant toremifene damaged her liver, so the drug was withdrawn. The cancer soon came back as invasive disease on the chest wall. Toxicity management, patient education, and closer surveillance for patients who interrupt therapy are the lessons the authors press.
pmc-13415842:
Sengan and Shieh propose, in 2026, a federated intrusion detection system for hospital Internet of Things networks spanning many sites. Patient data cannot legally be pooled there, yet attacks must be caught jointly. Their design confronts two problems at once. Each hospital's data distribution differs, the non-IID problem that cripples federated averaging. And some participants may be Byzantine, submitting poisoned updates to corrupt the model.

Hospitals are clustered by how alike their data distributions are, using a Wasserstein-distance affinity matrix, with gradient divergence correction before a Byzantine-tolerant consensus protocol secures the combining step. On test traffic the system reached accuracies of 93.17 percent on the IoT-Flock dataset and 89.84 percent on CICIoT2023 in non-IID conditions. It still held 83.61 percent accuracy with four Byzantine attackers, converged within 29 to 67 rounds, and met a 16-millisecond real-time constraint the authors set. They frame it as ready protection for device-dense wards.
pmc-13416042:
Xinyue Liu and a large team build a deep learning system that grades non-small cell lung cancer from scans and clinical data, in 2026. Their system, MM-DLS, reads PET and CT images taken before treatment alongside patient variables. It predicts tumor subtype, stage, and survival risk in one framework, trained and checked on 4,164 patients from several centers.

External validation gave accuracy scores near 0.86 for subtype and for early and middle stages, and 0.88 for stage four disease. Survival discrimination held strong at one, three, and five years across treatment types. A single noninvasive score could support guideline based care where tissue answers stay uncertain.
pmc-13416642:
Angela M. Moosmann and co-authors externally test a treatment algorithm for fractures of the upper arm bone near the shoulder, in 2026. The St. Gallen Algorithm, proposed in 2019, aims to cut failures and second surgeries for these common elderly fractures. Their hospital reviewed isolated cases treated from 2010 to 2020.

About forty-three percent of 730 patients had in fact been treated along the algorithm's path. Overall failure reached thirteen percent at a mean follow-up of twenty-two months. Failure was eleven percent in the algorithm group versus fourteen percent outside it, a nonsignificant gap. Shoulder self scores were nearly identical. Multivariable modeling hinted at protection, cautiously interpreted.
pmc-13417742:
Xiaotian Zhang, Xiaoran Gong, Shanshan Di, and Miaomiao Teng review environmental DNA as a tool for judging water pollution risk, in a 2026 article. Traces of DNA shed by organisms can reveal many species at once without catching them. Older methods rely on chemical tests, single species lab exposures, or visual surveys, which miss community level harm.

Uses now span biodiversity checks, pollution diagnosis, restoration tracking, and early warning. Pairing with RNA methods, machine learning, and water flow models adds power. Drawbacks include false detections, thin reference libraries, and weak counting ability. Standard methods and better databases are the main needs, the authors argue.
pmc-13418142:
Özer and colleagues report a 2026 ancient DNA study of hunter-gatherers who lived in what is now western Russia thousands of years ago. The Sakhtysh burial ground held eastern hunter-gatherers, whose genes form part of many Europeans' ancestry today. The team read genomes from 36 people buried across about two thousand years, and called immune gene (HLA) types for 27.

The Sakhtysh people stayed genetically stable over that long span, with no sign of mixing with western hunter-gatherers or early farmers nearby. Their HLA variety was low, likely because the group was small; no true HLA calls from ancient hunter-gatherers existed before these. One type, B*27:05, appeared in about half of those tested, though it is rare today. Screening found a narrow set of past infections, including a possible animal-linked bacterium and two long-lasting viruses.
pmc-13418842:
Iannuzzi and colleagues trial two blood and milk measures as stress gauges in dairy goats, hunting welfare markers a farmer could use without disturbing the herd. Telomeres, the caps that protect chromosome ends, shorten under stress, while cortisol is the stress hormone. Their 2026 pilot follows twenty Alpine goats on pasture across three samplings spaced fifteen days apart. It reads telomere length from milk DNA and cortisol from serum, alongside weather records.

At the middle sampling, which fell in a spell of adverse weather, cortisol doubled from its level before settling back. Telomeres dipped, then recovered most of the loss by the final check. Telomere length moved against humidity and dew point but rose with rainfall, a mixed weather fingerprint. Short dips, the authors conclude, mark passing strain rather than lasting damage. Pairing the fast hormone signal with the slower genomic one gives a fuller welfare picture for pasture herds.
pmc-13419442:
Siwakan Phuetphaichit and colleagues evaluate a Hemo-Alert program meant to speed the right antibiotic to hospital patients with bacteria in the blood. Their quasi-experimental study ran at Siriraj Hospital and compares care before and after the alert system began. The main measure was time from the blood result to therapy that matched the germ.

That time fell from 81.38 hours before the program to 66.17 hours after it in the reported group means, a trend that fell short of firm statistical proof. Clinical outcomes were tracked beside the timing gain. Even a soft trend matters here, since each day on the wrong drug raises risk in bloodstream infection. The authors set out what a larger rollout would need to prove the gain.
pmc-13420242:
The Royal Society of Chemistry retracts a 2021 paper by Mudassar Sher and colleagues on a mixed catalyst used against germs and water pollutants. Editors found that three X-ray patterns shown for fresh and reused material looked the same in one figure. A second figure held a signal trace with a repeating pattern that should not appear in real data.

Sher and the co-authors sent a reply with fresh data, yet the reply did not settle either concern. The team also could not supply the raw files behind the published figures. Five named authors oppose the editors' choice, while the rest gave no reply. With trust in the data gone, the journal treats the findings as no longer sound and marks the paper as withdrawn.
pmc-13420342:

The repair treats repeated front shoulder dislocations when a dent in the ball of the joint, a Hill-Sachs lesion, catches on the socket rim. During remplissage, surgeons fix back-of-shoulder muscles into the dent to keep the joint stable.

Here, ultrasound scanning during surgery shows the infraspinatus and teres minor muscles and the lesion in real time. Needle placement and anchor insertion are guided by the live image rather than by feel. Fixation uses a double-pulley suture method that presses tissue firmly into the dent. The authors say ultrasound helps surgeons place portals safely and aim anchors better, which is most useful for less-experienced surgeons. They present the method as a safer, more exact add-on to standard arthroscopic Bankart repair.
pmc-13420842:
Only and colleagues analyze healing after a kneecap-realigning bone operation in this 2026 study of tibial tubercle osteotomy, a procedure that cuts and shifts the shinbone bump where the patellar tendon attaches. They examined what happens at the cut bone's lower edge, where it meets the front of the shin shaft, using measurements on serial X-rays.

The cohort covered 101 knees operated between 2009 and 2015, mostly in young women with a mean age of 21 years. By four months, 62 percent of knees showed radiographic healing at the interface in the films available. Eleven percent developed gap resorption, the cut edge dissolving back by more than two millimeters, and four tibial fractures occurred between 18 and 201 days after surgery. No measured factor, including starting gap size or how far the bone was shifted, statistically predicted fracture, leaving gap resorption as the one warning sign.
pmc-13421242:
Luis F. S. Castro-de-Araujo and co-authors use twin and sibling data from the ABCD Study to ask, in a 2026 paper, whether ADHD symptoms lower school grades or whether the arrow runs the other way. The ABCD Study follows thousands of American children, and its family design lets researchers separate genetic from environmental influence.

ADHD symptoms came from a standard behaviour checklist, and grades were reported by caregivers for the previous school year. Genetically informed direction-of-causation models, extended with polygenic scores for ADHD and educational attainment, could not settle which trait drives the other. Estimates pointed both ways with differing precision, and sex did not change the pattern. The authors leave the causal question open.
pmc-13421542:

Sixty-six German shift workers from various industries took part. The comparison group kept sleep diaries only, during a four-week wait. Both groups improved in sleep efficiency, insomnia symptoms and depression scores, yet the counselling group did not improve significantly more, so superiority was not shown. Daytime sleepiness changed in neither group. The authors suspect that keeping a diary and joining a study were themselves therapeutic.
pmc-13421742:

They used arterial spin labeling, an MRI technique that measures cerebral blood flow without injected contrast, in sixty patients with gliomas, mostly aggressive grade 4 tumours.

Patients whose enhancing tumour volume later grew had clearly higher tumour blood flow before surgery than those whose tumours stayed stable or shrank. The link survived adjustment for age, scan interval and a key genetic marker, while changes in the surrounding non-enhancing tissue showed no such relationship. Flow in tissue around the tumour simply mirrored whole-brain values. The authors propose the measurement as a practical prognostic marker.
pmc-13422942:
Rachel House leads an eight-author team mining Australian pharmacy records, in a 2026 study, for dispensing patterns that warn of asthma and COPD flare-ups. Pharmacies see reliever inhalers fly out long before an emergency visit, so long dispensing histories might betray risk that clinics miss.

Reliever inhalers dominated, and over a third of records showed three or more dispensed in a year — a recognised danger sign. Nearly half the steroid-tablet records reached a gram cumulatively. Preventer adherence was poor, with under eight percent of records hitting sixty percent. The authors argue these patterns can flag high-risk patients.
pmc-13423042:
Kiran Paudel heads a large team studying suicidal thoughts among clients of a syringe services programme in New Haven, Connecticut, who use opioids. Between April and June 2024 the group surveyed 199 programme clients about recent thoughts of death or self-harm, their use of mental health care, and the obstacles that kept them from care.

Roughly 84% of those surveyed were opioid dependent, and more than two-thirds were receiving medication for it. Over a third reported recent suicidal ideation on a standard depression questionnaire item. The authors connect such risk with gaps in mental health service use, arguing that harm-reduction sites are a practical place to offer screening and referral.
pmc-13423142:
João Loja and four colleagues describe patients aged 90 and older admitted to an internal medicine department at a Portuguese tertiary hospital during 2025. Numbers in this age band keep rising, yet recent Portuguese data on their condition and hospital course were scarce, so the team reviewed 89 consecutive admissions.

Eighty patients were in their nineties and nine were centenarians; most were women, with a mean age of 94 years. Before admission, 77% lived at home, but 54% were fully dependent in daily activities. Nearly every patient took long-term medication. The study records diagnoses, length of stay, discharge destination, and deaths in hospital, giving planners a grounded picture of very old inpatients.
pmc-13423942:
Michaela J. Gibson and six colleagues build a grading system for cartilage loss on the front-upper surface of the long pastern bone in Thoroughbred racehorses. That bone often fractures on race day in New Zealand. Fetlock joints endure huge motion and compression at the gallop, yet the wear pattern on this surface had never been formally described.

Scores used a four-step scale from no damage to severe. Fracture and control horses scored alike. Scores climbed with age and career starts, and ran higher on the inner side of the limbs that bear more load in counterclockwise racing.
pmc-13424142:
Saihui Li and six colleagues report a glass that bends like rubber yet stays clear deep into the infrared, a pairing long thought out of reach. Their chalcogenide glass, sixty parts sulfur to forty selenium, is built as a dual network of chains and rings with cross-links that can move, letting the solid flex without clouding.

The material transmits light out to 21 micrometres while stretching to about 650% of its length and springing back near 80%. It also heals cuts and remembers shapes at room temperature. As a demonstration, the team built infrared lenses whose focus can be tuned live, correcting image distortion on the fly. Soft infrared optics for sensing and imaging are the target.
pmc-13424342:

This acute myeloid leukaemia carries the CBFB::MYH11 gene fusion and answers well to cytarabine chemotherapy, yet up to 30% of patients relapse because traces of disease, measurable residual disease, survive treatment.

Transplant can cure such patients but many lack donors or fitness for it. Earlier hints that this fusion type carries high levels of the blocked survival protein give the approach a mechanistic foothold, the authors note.
pmc-13424542:

Electron microscopy found the two membranes' average pore sizes nearly identical, about 23 nanometres, while surface openness differed, 14.5% against 10.2%, without reaching significance. pmc-13424842:
Yu and colleagues test whether stimulating the breathing nerve can hold the airway open during sleep. Stimulating this nerve engages the diaphragm and possibly sensory feedback routes, and the team examined timing during drug-induced sleep endoscopy in 19 patients.

The authors conclude end-expiratory stimulation improves airway openness and ventilation, with repeated delivery sustaining the benefit.
pmc-13426942:

The fungus causes illnesses that range from surface infections to life-threatening spread through the body. Its toxin is cut from a larger protein, released as the fungus grows in thread form, and then breaks into cell surface layers of the mouth and other tissues.

When myeloid cells are removed in animal studies, the fungus grows more freely and death rates rise. Giving GM-CSF has helped some patients with weak immune systems, such as those lacking the CARD9 protein. The review maps this two-way traffic and where it might be used in treatment.
pmc-13427342:

Such networks map how signals and chemicals inside cells guide cell choices, but building them by hand from the literature is slow. The team asked general-purpose models to rebuild known signal networks for heart cell growth, scar-type cell activation, and force sensing, plus a core metabolic network from a gut bacterium.

Tewari found the models recovered between a quarter and about two-thirds of the reactions in the curated signal networks. Logic models built from those networks then predicted responses to changes with low accuracy, between 6 and 33 percent. For metabolism the models did better on coverage, reaching up to 91 percent of reactions, though accuracy at predicting food use varied a lot. The authors supply benchmarks to guide later gains.
pmc-13427442:
Christiane Barthel and colleagues compared a standardized bone reduction technique with conventional methods for upper arm fractures near the shoulder in a 2026 matched cohort study. Seventy-two patients in matched pairs at one center were compared on X-ray outcomes, especially anatomical reduction and rebuilding of the medial calcar support. Consistent technique could narrow outcome variation in a fracture notorious for uneven results. Wire holds are brief and are drawn out at the end, so the added steps add care and time but leave no gear in the bone for good.
pmc-13427542:
Paul D. Ferrell and a large team report in 2026 on a blood marker that may flag heart damage years after radiation. pmc-13427642:
Baikété and colleagues map how water gathers around pyridine, a ring compound whose nitrogen atom makes it a stand in for many drug and solvent molecules. The team catalogs every arrangement: 326, from three for the smallest cluster to fifty five for the largest.

Near matching arrangements multiply so fast that at room temperature no single form rules. By seven waters the shell closes into cages around the ring. Step by step growth stays uphill in free energy, and a bond by bond audit finds five weak contact types knitting the shell.
pmc-13427842:

Eleven patients, or 21 percent, experienced recurrence, while the 12-month disease-free survival rate stood at 90.5 percent overall. Patients whose tumors scored high on PD-L1 recurred far more often, 44 percent versus 5 percent for low scorers in this series. pmc-13428442:

The sweet spot was 450 degrees for one hour, where graphene oxide reduced in place and the framework partly converted to magnetic iron oxide, forming a three-part composite. pmc-13428542:

Zhang found leaf and stem microbe groups resembled each other and differed clearly from the root's. Total variety stayed similar across organs. Two bacterial and two fungal phyla ruled, but the leading genera changed by organ. Chance, rather than strict sorting, mainly built these groups. pmc-13433342:

Outcomes include knowledge, practical skill, satisfaction, competence, and confidence. Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently, with standard tools for bias checks, and a common software package will pool results. At writing, screening was under way, with the finished review planned for submission by June 2026.
pmc-13433842:
Shaoshuai Zhao and co-authors flew drones in 2026 over wheat fields to weigh crop bulk from air reads, then took apart which read drives the calls in learning models. True bulk checks wreck the crop, so air reads rule growth watch and yield calls. The team fused hue reads, green marks, and canopy height across four growth stages.

Four learning kinds faced off, and a boosted tree set won with room to spare. A break-down tool that splits credit per read crowned canopy height as the top driver, with two hue marks close behind. Lone and whole-set reads showed shape and hue play twin roles that back each other. The frame gives growers a clear map of what each read buys.
pmc-13433942:
Dicle Buyuktaskin and co-authors probed sense handling in 2026 in teens with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, a brain growth state marked by loose focus, restless drive, and snap acts. Sense faults in this group deepen daily conduct and feeling strain, yet hard lab reads stay scarce. The team joined forms with touch lab tests in 26 teens with the state and 29 peers.

Form reads split the groups on touch care and touch dodge. Hard touch clocks, for first feel and for tell-apart speed, showed no firm split. The authors urge care: soft trends in hard reads may hide faint shifts that big groups must settle.
pmc-13434042:

Plant cuts proved both the compound and its twin sit in the herb, with gene reads to match their birth path. Six bubble builds faced off, and one won on size, charge, and calm shelf life. That build killed near all test cancer cells in dishes by tripping cell suicide and halting the cell cycle. Aim tags on the bubbles point the load at tumor ports.
pmc-13434742:

Benchmarks covered two fake data sets and four real ones. They included branching development and varied responses to gene tweaks. GRNvelo beat tools in the reported tests. The authors frame it as an approach for predicting and steering cell fate.
pmc-13436242:

Treated films also load their vesicles with fewer matrix building proteins. Cargo shifts mean the vesicles that do escape carry less of what the film needs. pmc-13437242:

Clinic readings were modeled over time, pre-pregnancy levels estimated from matched non-pregnant women, and labor readings came from 11,836 vaginal births.

Pressure followed the classic curve, dipping lowest near week twenty-five and rising toward term. Early pregnancy readings already sat above the estimated pre-pregnancy level. After birth, pressure climbed again, peaked around days five to seven, and eased back by about five weeks. The authors offer these curves as a normal reference, so doctors can tell harmless shifts from early signs of a pressure disorder.
pmc-13437442:

About twenty-six percent of patients saw the disorder return during follow-up. A combined model that mixed shape complexity, texture traits, and two standard clinical scores sorted returning patients far better than any part alone. Its accuracy score in the check group clearly beat the clinical scores and the texture models by themselves. Remodeling of the atrium leaves structural fingerprints plain scores miss, the authors argue, and reading them sharpens risk sorting.
pmc-13437642:

Ammonia alone cut worm numbers by about seventy-six percent, a strong kill. Left alone it also raised nitrous oxide output, a real climate cost. Adding the two inhibitors curbed that gas release. Bacterial diversity held steady throughout, a reassuring sign for soil health. The authors present ammonia fumigation as a workable tool that can be tuned: with inhibitors, it protects crops while trimming its own footprint. Field tests remain before farm advice can follow.
pmc-13439242:

Untangling that web matters because the three problems usually arrive together and reinforce each other in later life, especially where healthcare is scarce.

Subjective sleep quality, how rested people felt their sleep was, emerged as the most influential predictor node in both time intervals studied. Cognitive components proved the most vulnerable targets, especially orientation, attention and calculation, and language. Networks for men and women stayed moderately similar in structure across the periods. Che argues that improving perceived sleep quality is the most central, modifiable lever available, with potential knock-on benefits for both mood and cognition in rural aging programs.
pmc-13439442:

All-solid-state lithium batteries promise more stored energy, yet their solid electrolytes oxidise at the voltages rich cathodes need. Those precursors yielded halide and sulfide electrolytes loaded with fluorine while keeping ions moving well. At the cathode, a sturdy fluoride-rich skin formed and limited further decay. A test cell with a lithium-rich oxide cathode kept over three quarters of its capacity after two thousand fast cycles at a five-volt cutoff. The authors offer the exchange route as a general platform for fluorinated battery materials.
pmc-13439642:

A 66-year-old man arrived with sudden double vision on vertical gaze, slurred speech, and unsteady walking.

Examination showed the full classic pattern of the syndrome. Brain scans and vessel imaging, though, showed no fresh lesion or blockage. Treating the picture as a likely back-of-brain stroke, the team gave clot-busting medicine within three and a half hours of onset. Recovery was complete within a day, and later scans confirmed no lasting damage. The authors urge clinicians to trust the eye signs when imaging stays silent.
pmc-13439742:

This team added amide side chains, which form hydrogen bonds like those in protein beta sheets, forcing the layers to stack in opposite directions.

Their two materials, named aCOFamide-1 and aCOFamide-2, trapped large amounts of iodine from vapour. They also pulled iodide, a charged form of iodine, out of water, which is a hard task in molecular capture. Computer maps showed positive electric patches near the amide groups that attract the negative iodide ions. pmc-13441042:

The authors present the pairing as a candidate step toward regenerative care for demyelinating disease.
pmc-13442442:
Holly Aitken and colleagues survey bone and joint patients about phone-based motion capture in a 2026 study at a rural referral center. The tool, OpenCap, reads 3D joint motion from videos shot on two iOS devices. Three groups took part, with 200 child patients, 200 sports patients, and 200 joint replacement patients in the pool.

Shares with the needed gear ran from 65.5 percent to 83.5 percent across the groups. Home place, town or country, did not shift access in a clear way. pmc-13442542:
Xuelian Wang and colleagues review how smart computer models merge life exposure and gene-scale data to find liver cancer marks in a 2026 paper. Liver cancer kills many people worldwide, and the cell type called HCC leads the count. Known drivers span virus liver illness, drink-linked liver harm, and fat-linked liver disease, each shaped by life exposures.

The review weighs mark hunts that join exposure records with gene, protein, and fuel data, plus maps of where cells sit in tissue. Clear models that show their logic get praise for early catch, outlook sorting, and care choice. Gaps get blunt talk: exposure records stay thin, data tools vary, most work looks back, and few models face outside tests. New layers such as single-cell reads may sharpen marks, the authors say, if checks grow stricter.
pmc-13442642:
Wenjing Wu and colleagues track United States lung illness deaths across 1999 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Death records came from the CDC WONDER system, with rates checked by sex, age, race, and region. Raw death counts rose from 227,985 in the first year to 263,209 in the last, a gain of 15.5 percent across the span.

Men carried higher rates than women, though male rates fell faster. The West cut rates most, while the South logged the largest rise in raw counts. Older adults bore the heaviest load, and adults aged 25 to 34 years saw a slight rate rise. The authors urge plans aimed at those groups.
pmc-13443042:
Todo Bom Luís and colleagues grade infection risk in hospital adults across Portugal in a 2026 study. Germs caught in care raise harm, cost, and stay length, yet risk checks stay loose in many wards. A high band held 11.4 percent of adults in the same count. Curve tests helped set the split marks. The authors say a shared scale can steer wards to guard the highest-risk beds first, a step many sites still skip in daily care.
pmc-13443542:
Yuchen Yang and colleagues spin layered fiber mats that guard lungs while they spare plastic in a 2026 paper. Throwaway filter media strain to catch the finest dust, and their waste piles up in landfills. Their multi-level splitting spin method weaves three fiber scales, from ultrafine threads to submicron strands, in one mat.

The woven maze traps dust through twisty paths while air slips through open channels. Mats held top-grade capture of PM0.3 dust, the hardest size class, with low breath drag in their tests. Polymer use fell by 99 percent next to market N95 masks in their count. The fibers also break down after use, unlike standard mask plastics. The authors pitch the mats for masks and vents that must protect without waste.
pmc-13444142:
Zhe Xian Koong and colleagues gain clean control of quantum-dot spins while keeping their light links pure in a 2026 paper. Dot spins can hold quantum data and spit single photons, a dream pair for quantum nets. The snag: spin control and one-shot reads once fought each other in the same dot.

A flip pulse hit a contrast mark of 97.4 percent, while light loops kept a cyclicity mark of 471 in the runs. Both GaAs and InGaAs dots took the scheme. The authors show the setup can pair with a nuclear memory for repeater nodes.
pmc-13446042:
Codey E. Dueck and colleagues set out a method to grade how well a solids-based extraction pulls viral material from wastewater, in a 2026 paper for surveillance labs. Wastewater tracking of disease leans on extraction, yet each lab needs a yardstick for its own losses. A cattle coronavirus, spiked into samples on purpose, serves as the stand-in.

Heat-based release measured the starting stock more truly than a machine method. The team also found the cattle virus already present in wastewater at low levels, a background any grade must subtract. Sixteen hours of soaking gave the best recovery in their runs. A paired test that reads the cattle virus and a pepper virus at once matched the single tests, which saves time in routine checks.
pmc-13446342:
Hongtu Cui and colleagues build a platform that forecasts cancer drug response from which genes a tumor cannot live without, in a 2026 study. Matching drugs to tumors is the heart of precision oncology, yet standard molecular reads predict response unevenly. Their system, DrGee, reads gene activity and infers sensitivity through gene essentiality instead.

Four drugs flagged for one lung cancer line were tested in dishes and mouse grafts, and two held up, with a like check in ovarian cells. Patient groups split by its calls also split in survival.
pmc-13447742:
An, Lee, and Kim published a 2026 study on how young children judge their own eating. Most past work asked parents, not children, about daily food habits. The team surveyed 243 preschoolers and their parents at daycare centers in Cheonan. Both sides filled out the same healthy eating practice questionnaire.

Children rated their eating habits higher than their parents rated them. The gap ran wider for nutrition than for hygiene habits like hand washing. Hygiene ratings matched more closely between children and parents across the board. Boys showed a bigger gap with parents than girls did in scores. The authors say diet checks should ask both children and parents. Daycare meal programs could use both views to plan better lessons.
pmc-13448042:
Nazar and colleagues used Sweden's nationwide spine registry in 2026 to compare long-term reoperation risk after two neck operations for worn discs. One, fusion, welds vertebrae together; the other, disc replacement, preserves motion. Fusion may shift load onto neighboring levels and wear them out, a problem called adjacent segment disease. Earlier trials disagreed on whether implants prevent it.

The analysis covered 9,338 patients, most fused and a few hundred with disc replacements, followed for up to about nineteen years. About one in ten patients needed another operation at a neighboring level by ten years, with 509 such reoperations in all. After adjustment, disc replacement carried a lower risk, but the gap vanished in a matched comparison. Younger patients and single-level surgery carried higher risk, and the authors counsel caution in claiming a protective effect.
pmc-13448642:
Samuel Wright and a large team profile blood proteins and immune cells across melanoma treatment to explain immunotherapy resistance in 2026 work. Many patients gain no lasting benefit from checkpoint blockade, and blood markers that flag early resistance could spare toxicity and redirect care sooner. Serial sampling during treatment, rarely combined with matched tumour tissue at scale, was the study's distinctive asset.

Over twenty-nine hundred plasma proteins and deep immune cell profiling tracked two hundred fifty patients with metastatic melanoma, alongside ninety-two matched tumours. Proteins rising after treatment in responders tied to effector immune activation, while non-responder proteins traced to suppressive myeloid cells and tumour cells themselves. Proteins linked to side effects in responders appeared to come from damaged healthy tissue. The dataset maps how tumours and the wider immune system interact under therapy.
pmc-13449042:
Yuk Kam Yau and colleagues study in 2026 whether the pandemic-era breakup of regular primary care harmed Hong Kong patients with diabetes. Their cohort held 123,403 adults whose continuity was scored by how consistently they saw their usual clinic before the outbreak, from 2017 to 2019, and during it, from 2020 to 2022. Outcomes were then followed from June 2022 to June 2024.

Patients whose continuity score fell by twenty to thirty percent faced a 33 percent higher risk of cardiovascular disease than those whose score fell least. The largest drops carried similar excess risk, and the same pattern showed for coronary disease and heart failure separately. Kidney failure risk also rose once continuity fell by more than a fifth. The authors urge health systems to build contingency plans that keep chronic care continuous through future public health crises.
pmc-13449342:
Pasko and colleagues compared in 2026 how exactly knee replacement surgery hits its planned plastic insert thickness.  They reviewed 815 patients of one surgeon treated between 2018 and 2022. About half had robotic help and half had the standard method, with a nine-millimetre insert planned for all.

Robotic cases landed far closer to the plan, with a mean error of about a third of a millimetre. Standard cases overshot by well over a millimetre and a half on average. About 72 in 100 robotic patients got exactly the planned thickness, against only 16 in 100 standard patients. Spread around the target was also much smaller with robotic help. The authors say robotic tools execute the plan more faithfully and balance knee gaps more evenly.
pmc-13452142:
Caixeta, Chen, and Miura published a 2026 letter on tongue-tie checks in young children. A Brazilian task force had set advice on lingual frenulum disorders, the tongue-tie group. Their letter answers critics of that task force document point by point. The exchange centers on how well the screening tools were truly validated.

The authors say their review screened over 300 papers for the document. They argue no tool had passed full, proper validation checks yet. One test was validated backward in time, not forward as rules require. Only 36 of 100 babies were rechecked, and half had surgery between checks. Photo-based scoring between raters also drew their methodological fire in the letter. Uniform rules, they stress, were applied to every instrument reviewed alike.
pmc-13453742:
Jaime A Teixeira da Silva writes a letter urging journals to face how generative AI is slipping into peer review and editing. His 2026 letter notes that some editors still dismiss AI's role, while AI written work already circulates and risks being cited as if human checked. He also flags the unpaid labor that props up human review as a pressure point.

Cheap AI review could ease the reviewer shortage, he allows, but its biases must be weighed first. The deeper crack, he argues, is hidden use: authors quietly polish with AI and reviewers cannot spot it, a failure already surfacing in post publication retractions. He doubts the keep it human stance can hold as use spreads. The letter asks how widely reviewers themselves now lean on AI to do their reviews.
pmc-13454142:
Xin Sun and fourteen co-authors uncover an autoimmune loop in the spleen that helps drive cerebral malaria, the deadliest form of the disease. Protein scans fingered CD36, a host protein packed on infected red cells, as the trigger for self attacking antibodies. Their 2026 study spans patient material and mouse work to trace the circuit.

The antibodies help clear infected cells, yet they also strike other CD36 bearing cells, cutting platelets, wounding vessel walls, and stoking body wide inflammation. Infection draws a special macrophage type into the spleen, where pumped up protein shredding fires B cells to make the antibodies. The team built a drug, Glutoborin, that targets those macrophages through their sugar transporter. In animals it cut antibody output and eased the disease, marking the cells as a drug target.
pmc-13454342:
Rongfu Xu and nine colleagues report, in 2026, a way to turn cellulose, the fiber in plants, into a better glue for water-based batteries. Such batteries are safe and cheap, but their electrode glues grip poorly and let active material drift away. The team reshaped cellulose chains by opening their stiff rings, which raised polarity and flexibility.

The reshaped fiber formed a tight net that coated battery particles and held iodine in place. An iodine electrode built with the new binder delivered strong capacity even at very high current. Pouch cells kept about 98 percent of their capacity after 3,000 hours of use. The binder also worked for layered, heavy electrodes and for vanadium oxide cathodes. The authors offer the method as a green route to better aqueous batteries.
pmc-13455042:
Lingling Xuan and Yali Lv hunt, in a 2026 study, for blood-free markers of asthma tied to stress inside the cell's protein factory, the endoplasmic reticulum. Such stress feeds airway inflammation, yet it lacked clear signature genes. The pair mined sputum gene data from 118 patients with moderate to severe asthma and 21 healthy controls.

Network and machine learning screens narrowed the field to two genes. One, ERN1, ran high in patients, while the other, TMEM129, ran low. Together they separated asthma from health with solid accuracy, and an outside dataset scored even better. Mouse asthma models echoed both shifts, and added irritants deepened the stress signal. The authors propose the gene pair as a diagnostic signature worth testing in clinics.
pmc-13457042:
Peng Shi and seven colleagues weigh, in a 2026 study, how much doctors can trust gene sequencing of spinal fluid when hunting brain infections. The test, metagenomic sequencing, reads all DNA in the fluid at once, a boon when standard cultures stay silent. The team reviewed 46 patients tested for suspected encephalitis or meningitis at their center.

An expert panel graded each case as definite, probable, or unlikely infection, forming the reference truth. Sequencing found a germ in about 28 percent of patients. Its hit rate climbed steeply with certainty, from none in unlikely cases to about 73 percent in definite ones. Overall sensitivity was modest, near 41 percent, while every positive call was correct. Herpes viruses led the finds. Read counts added meaning: higher counts matched surer diagnoses. The authors cast the test as a strong rule-in tool that cannot rule infection out.
pmc-13458642:
Baez and colleagues built in 2026 dye probes that paint one Brassica chromosome at a time, to tame a crop clan with a tangled past. Brassicas mix three base genomes, and cross breeds swap bits in ways eyes can't track. Their chromosomes are small and look near the same. The team mined code for spans found on one chromosome alone. Short dye strands were built from those spans, in two grades of build.

The paints lit one pair each, clean and bright. Each was proven on the clan's main crops, from turnip kin to oilseed rape. The probes caught real swaps: one whole swap line in rape seed, and a bit of one chromosome tucked in a mate in a six set cross. Breeders can now watch swaps plant by plant, the team says. Trait hunts gain a map.
pmc-13458742: A fix notice — the authors amend their mixed-methods instrument for measuring organizational health. Abad Alzuman, Muath Jaafari, and others issue the fix. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is a published erratum. It fixes the record on the organizational health habits index, keeping the validation study accurate.
pmc-13458842:
Lucia Ledererová and four colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient with an intradural disc herniation, where disc material slips inside the cord membrane. The condition accounts for under 1 percent of disc herniations. It is hard to spot on scans, often looking like a tumour. Their patient was a 70-year-old woman with acute back pain, pain radiating to the thighs and leg weakness.

Scans showed a herniation at the L1/2 level, high in the lower spine where this condition is rarest. During microsurgery, ultrasound helped locate fragments that had migrated inside the membrane, and these were removed. A tear in the membrane front was sealed with an absorbable collagen pad, not stitches. At seven weeks and at 18 months, she was pain-free, with no new nerve problems and no spinal fluid leak. The authors suggest ultrasound guidance and collagen repair as useful options.
pmc-13459442:
Jasmin B. Kuemmerle-Deschner leads a global expert group reviewing in 2026 how patients with familial Mediterranean fever should be monitored over the long term. This inherited condition causes repeated attacks of fever and inflammation, and quiet inflammation between attacks can still damage organs. Their proposed schedule rests on three aims: charting each patient's disease pattern, detecting hidden inflammation, and watching how drugs are borne and their side effects. Guidance across sources largely agrees on core measures, though little advice rests on validated evidence. Clinics are encouraged to adapt the schedule to their own patients and resources rather than follow one rigid template.
pmc-13460142:

The choice matters because mechanical valves last but demand lifelong blood thinning, while tissue valves wear out sooner. Searching nine databases through the end of 2025, the team found eight retrospective studies covering 1,504 patients, most receiving tissue valves.

Mechanical valves, however, carried about double the risk of clot-related events and nearly five times the bleeding risk, reflecting the anticoagulation they require. No randomized trials were available, so the authors base their comparison entirely on observational cohorts from mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan.
pmc-13460742:
Miao and colleagues traced in 2026 how a tapeworm infection scars the liver, linking the damage to a sugar-burning enzyme and a chemical tag on DNA packaging proteins. Alveolar echinococcosis, caused by the fox tapeworm, grows through the liver and stiffens it with scar tissue. The tag, called lactylation, comes from lactate, a by-product of fast sugar burning, and had been tied to scarring in other settings.

In infected mice, lactate ran high in liver and blood, and one enzyme, hexokinase-3, rose sharply. The tagged form of a packaging protein sat on scar-related genes in infected livers. The authors name the enzyme as a drug target for this neglected disease.
pmc-13461542:

Four papers examine how gendered norms, identities, and inequalities shape attitudes to nature and behaviour rather than leaving them neutral. Settings range from diets across countries to climate denial in Sweden.

One line of work links gender identity to pro-environmental behaviour, Tiberio summarises, with diet intentions that differ by gender and culture. A Swedish study ties climate denial in men partly to threatened masculinity when green concern is coded as feminine. The second line covers how gender shapes views of nature and the restful feel of city spaces. The editors argue identity, norms, and cultural roles must enter future models of how humans relate to nature.
pmc-13461842:
Hiromitsu Domen, Takumi Nakaya, and Hidehisa Yamada share safety tips, in a 2026 technique article, for handling small lung artery branches during robotic chest surgery. The robot gives a view and nimble tools, yet sealing these vessels is one of the riskiest steps. Heat-sealing tools can leak or burn nearby tissue, while clips alone are fiddly in tight fields. Their method joins both: clip first, then heat sealing.

Care goes into clip position, the spacing before the seal, and easing the clip tool out safely. pmc-13461942:

They trace the plausible human routes: eggs from tainted environments or larvae in raw offal.

Humans elsewhere catch it by exactly those routes, and Australia's wildlife livestock human interface sustains the cycle across the continent. pmc-13462042:

He also had cardiogenic shock, a state where the weakened heart cannot supply the body. He had diabetes and high blood pressure, and a stent placed six months earlier. Back in hospital with chest pain, he collapsed into repeated ventricular fibrillation, a chaotic heart rhythm, during an emergency artery-opening procedure.

The blocked right coronary artery was then opened. His early course was rough, with weak pulse pressure, high lactate, lung infection, and suspected brain injury from oxygen loss. Yet he left hospital on day ten with brain function scores, and recovery held at one year.
pmc-13462242:
Anna Carlsson and colleagues improved and tested BioRID P50F, a prototype crash test dummy built to average female size for rear impacts. Rear crash testing still relies on male dummies, though women face higher risk of lasting whiplash injury than men.

The upgrade softened the upper torso, refined the spinal curve, and simplified how the hip point is measured. Head, hand, and foot contours were also reshaped to match female anatomy more closely. In sled tests, the new dummy's upper-back rearward tilt matched female volunteer response ranges better than before. Carlsson judges the dummy faithful enough, alongside the male dummy, to reveal sex differences in rear-impact response.
pmc-13462342:

Boosted ALOX12 made cancer cells more sensitive to ferroptosis, in a form needing active p53 and oxygen stress. The chain works: p53 suppresses a partner gene, SLC7A11, freeing ALOX12 to act. The authors propose ALOX12 as a marker of better outlook and a treatment lever for colon cancer.
pmc-13462842:

The team searched three sources for studies checked against tissue or cell results, the gold standard. Sixty-nine studies covering over 350,000 nodules qualified.

In head-to-head comparisons they matched or beat experienced radiologists. Adding AI to the standard scoring system lifted its specificity at equal sensitivity. The authors back AI as a support tool, not a replacement.
pmc-13463142:

Only about 600 cases have been reported since the syndrome was described in 1975.

A kidney biopsy showed diabetic damage alongside interstitial inflammation and acute tubule injury. After other causes were excluded, doctors settled on TINU with diabetic nephropathy. pmc-13463942:

pmc-13464242:

Soon after placement the plug broke loose and lodged in the mitral valve gear.

The man recovered well after the retrieval. Fast imaging and a ready retrieval kit, the authors note, make such saves possible.
pmc-13464742:
Ciliberti and co-authors examine the microbial safety of ornamental edible flowers in this 2026 study. Such flowers decorate plates, yet they are nearly impossible to wash without bruising. They are eaten raw. So the bacteria and fungi riding along reach the person who eats them.

Petal color even shaped which microbes thrived in some flowers.
pmc-13464942:
Kaboyi and colleagues surveyed adults in the Nyanzale displacement camp in North Kivu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, in late 2025. Their 2026 report covers the mental health toll of forced displacement. Among 385 residents, they screened for anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress with standard questionnaires. Clustering statistics grouped people by the pattern of traumatic events they had lived through.

The burden was heavy. About 56 of every 100 adults met the threshold for moderate-to-severe anxiety. About 44 met it for depression, and about 47 for probable PTSD. What people were still enduring mattered most. Exposure profiles marked by continuing insecurity inside the camp itself carried the highest odds of all three conditions. The authors press for mental health care built into camp services.
pmc-13465342:

CPAP, which blows gentle air pressure through a mask to keep airways open, is the main treatment for obstructive sleep apnea. It only works while worn, and many patients quit early, so the authors searched studies from 1995 onward for strategies that hold up in everyday clinics.

Problems during the first night and first month best predicted later quitting, they found, so early attention matters most. Explaining the condition and its benefits helped. So did fitting the right mask and personalizing settings. Counseling approaches helped too, along with scheduled follow-up by visits, phone, or telemedicine. Long-term habits were largely set by how the initial treatment period went.
pmc-13465442:

The starting resistance at the A1 pulley also declined across the four weeks. That starting value tracked symptoms well, correlating strongly with pain scores and moderately with triggering severity. Sessions producing bigger resistance drops were followed by bigger pain improvements the next week. The authors propose it as an objective companion to symptom scales.
pmc-13465642:
