The study enrolled 308 people at Mettu Karl hospital, with and without HIV. Stool samples were cultured, and drug tests used standard disk methods.

Enterococci grew from about 57 percent of the people tested. Roughly nine percent of those isolates were likely resistant strains. Carriage ran higher in HIV-positive patients, about 11 percent against about 7 percent in HIV-negative patients. The gap was not firm, though. Nearly half of all isolates resisted many drug classes at once. A hospital stay in the past six months was the one factor clearly tied to resistant carriage after adjustment. The authors frame such carriage as a quiet reservoir to watch.
pmc-13465742:
Junjing Jia, Qianying Lu, Yingyi Zhang, and Yanmei Zhao review an oxygen-sensing protein in type 2 diabetes, published in 2026. The protein, HIF-1 alpha, helps cells adapt when oxygen runs low. In diabetes it can protect tissue in some settings yet drive harm in others, depending on cell type and disease stage.

Lasting overactivation may feed unwanted blood vessel growth, scarring, inflammation, and poorer insulin response, while brief activity can aid repair. The authors argue that future drugs need to target the protein selectively rather than switch it fully on or off. Most support so far comes from lab and animal work, so proof in patients remains thin.
pmc-13465942:
Miaoran Zhang and colleagues examine a flower disease that weakens honeybees during jujube bloom, using combined chemical and gene-activity profiling in a 2026 study. Sick bees showed two clear molecular shifts. Compounds tied to tryptophan metabolism rose, while sugars and related building blocks fell.

One enzyme gene, HK, stood out with the strongest downward trend among sugar-handling genes and matched the pattern in follow-up lab checks. The authors keep it as a candidate for later work rather than a proven cause. Their results give bee researchers concrete leads for a problem that hits pollinators at a busy season.
pmc-13466042:
Wei Xue, Tianyi Chen, Yang Xiang, and Junjun Yang review a gene defect that condemns some women to repeated molar pregnancies, writing in 2026. A molar pregnancy grows abnormal tissue instead of a healthy embryo and can turn into a form of cancer. Faults in both copies of the NLRP7 gene explain many of these recurring cases.

pmc-13466342:
Liu and colleagues studied in 2026 how the diabetes drug alogliptin could rescue dental implant success in diabetes, where implants often fail to bond with bone. The team first compared bone loss around implants among patients on different blood sugar drugs. They then ran cell and diabetic rat experiments. Finally they tested a gel that delivers the drug right at the implant site.

pmc-13467842:

pmc-13469042:

pmc-13469242:

pmc-13469642:

pmc-13470142:

pmc-13471342:

pmc-13471942:

pmc-13472542:

pmc-13473442:

pmc-13474542:

pmc-13474842:

pmc-13475342:

pmc-13477842:

pmc-13478342:

pmc-13480042:

pmc-13492042:

pmc-13499142:

pmc-13499642:

Their patient was a woman in her seventies presenting with advanced disease who underwent extensive surgery to remove visible tumour, followed by chemotherapy given into the bloodstream. She responded partly at first, yet the disease later progressed with recurring abdominal fluid and spread across the abdominal lining. The authors use the case to weigh cancer control against quality of life in older patients when standard regimens fail and choices narrow.
pmc-13500442:
Filip Opaterny and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a simple switch for waking silent antibiotic-making gene clusters in a Streptomyces bacterium, a genus prized as a source of medicines. The strain studied carries 36 such clusters, nearly all cryptic or silent under lab conditions. Their strategy replaces a cluster's own weak promoter, the DNA on-switch, with a strong standard one through targeted recombination, first proven by switching on vivid blue pigment production from a dormant gene.

Applying the switch inside a silent cluster for chain-building enzymes produced two distinct antifungal compounds depending on exactly where the promoter landed. Both showed the spectral signature of polyenes, a class of antifungal molecules, and structural work identified them as strevertene relatives, one an intermediate on the path to the other. The intermediate proved roughly twice as potent against fungi in the reported tests, supporting promoter swapping as a discovery tool.
pmc-13502842:
Kasahara and colleagues tracked quality of life, nutrition, and fatigue in malignant lymphoma patients from the start of chemotherapy through a year after discharge. Twenty-one patients who received exercise therapy were assessed at admission, at discharge, and at six and twelve months afterward. Assessments used quality-of-life surveys, grip and knee strength, a six-minute walk test, a nutrition screen, and a fatigue inventory.

Kasahara found health utility scores rose by twelve months, and most quality-of-life domains improved over time, including physical and social functioning and mental health. Fatigue scores improved at follow-ups, and nutrition scores improved at six months, while physical function did not change but stayed stable rather than declining. The authors argue the pattern supports continuous rehab and nutritional support during and after chemotherapy, and they offer the utility data for planning long-term survivorship care, pending confirmation.
pmc-13503142:
Yuzhen Shu leads a seven-author team reviewing a 2026 platform that weds ultrasound with nanozymes, particles that mimic enzymes. Ultrasound contributes delivery and activation: cavitation, sonoporation that opens cells, phase changes, and piezoelectric effects. Nanozymes contribute control over reactive oxygen species, generating them to kill or scavenging them to heal, while adjusting oxygen supply. The review sweeps across tumours, drug-resistant and biofilm infections, atherosclerosis, brain disease, bone and cartilage damage, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and tendon repair.

Running through the survey is a methods problem. Effects credited to the nanozymes often blend with sonodynamic activation or ultrasound-triggered drug release, and papers rarely separate them cleanly. Ultrasound settings go unstandardized, and exit routes from the body get little study. The authors argue progress should be judged by credit for what the enzymes did and designs matched to each disease. It should not be judged by piling functions onto particles.
pmc-13503942:
Busra Aslan Akyol leads a team that built a single test for five worm drugs in cattle tissues, in a 2026 paper. The drugs, from the macrocyclic lactone family, kill parasites at tiny doses, but traces can linger in meat, liver, kidney, and fat. Food rules cap those traces.

Their method pulls the drugs out with a quick extraction mix, then reads them with a liquid separation tool and a glow detector. Recovery across tissues ranged from about 74 to 96 percent, with detection limits near one part per billion. Of 168 real samples, 18 held traces, and just one meat sample broke the legal cap. The test uses one gram of tissue and little solvent, which cuts cost and waste.
pmc-13504742:
Rami Bou Khalil leads a team testing whether low vitamin D tracks with depression in people with eating disorders, in a 2026 study. Both problems are common in this patient group, yet their link had barely been studied. The work took place at a specialist unit in Montpellier, France.

The team assessed 481 outpatients with standard psychiatric interviews and routine blood tests. Those short on vitamin D had about twice the odds of a current depressive disorder. The link survived checks for illness severity, other mental conditions, and season of testing. It did not vary by eating disorder type. The authors advise checking vitamin D in such patients who show low mood, while noting that only follow-up studies can show which problem comes first.
pmc-13505142:
Deng and He translate and validate an oral health outcome set for Chinese patients, part of an effort to measure dentistry by results patients feel. The ICHOM Adult Oral Health Standard Set asks about pain, function, and appearance, but a questionnaire only travels if its language version measures the same thing. Their 2026 study followed cross-cultural adaptation steps, then gave the Chinese version to 224 dental patients and checked its statistics.

One item, aesthetic satisfaction, misbehaved and was dropped, leaving eleven items that hung together well: internal consistency reached a strong level and split-half reliability stayed acceptable in the reported coefficients. The items organised into two factors that together explained well over half the variation in answers. Scores also correlated moderately with a general oral health question, supporting that the set measures what it claims. The authors approve the version for Chinese practice.
pmc-13505342:
Di Paola and colleagues probe whether burosumab, a drug for a rare bone disease in children, also calms immune cells. The disease, X linked hypophosphatemia, stems from a faulty gene that leaves blood phosphate low and bones soft. Burosumab blocks a hormone that wastes phosphate and is known to ease bone pain. Their 2026 study compares macrophages, immune cells that drive inflammation, from untreated patients, treated patients, and healthy donors.

The sample was small: four untreated children, eight treated, and five healthy donors. Untreated children's macrophages leaned to the M1 state, a pro inflammation mode, and carried more TRPV1, a protein tied to pain signaling. Treated children's cells leaned to the calmer M2 state with less TRPV1. The same shift appeared when healthy macrophages were inflamed in a dish and then exposed to the drug. Pain relief from burosumab may thus come partly from immune calming, not phosphate alone.
pmc-13507142:
Keqian Du leads a 2026 team that designs fat particles to deliver circular RNA for treating high uric acid and its complications, such as gout and kidney damage. Humans lack uricase, an enzyme that breaks down uric acid, and injected enzyme fades fast and provokes immunity. Their particles use lipids built from malic acid, a mild natural acid with calming effects.

Screening picked a lead particle that entered cells well, stirred little immune response, and added antioxidant action. In male mice, the system gave lasting uric acid cuts, eased joint pain and tissue scarring, and protected kidney function. Circular RNA lasts longer than standard RNA, which supports durable effect from each dose.
pmc-13507642:
Rashmi Venkatesh and four co-authors compare jawbone structure in healthy people, gum disease patients, and patients who have both gum disease and type 2 diabetes, in 2026 work. Standard X-rays often miss early bone loss until much mineral is already gone. The team instead used fractal analysis, a math method that scores how complex a bone pattern looks. They applied it to dental X-rays from 120 people split evenly into three groups.

Bone pattern scores differed clearly between groups in the spaces between teeth near the first molar. Scores in the deeper root-tip region, though, did not differ in a meaningful way. Scores also fell in the between-teeth region as disease and diabetes entered the picture. The results suggest that blood sugar status shapes bone quality in gum disease, and that this scoring method may catch change earlier.
pmc-13508242:
Dennis Bardoe and five co-authors explain why symptom-free malaria in pregnancy differs across trimesters in Ghana's Kintampo South District, in 2026 work. Such hidden infections can harm both mother and newborn. The team studied 462 pregnant women at health facilities, testing blood under the microscope for malaria parasites. Surveys captured social, clinical, and home environment details. A decomposition method then split the trimester gap into parts explained by those measured traits and parts left unexplained.

Overall, about one in seven women carried malaria parasites without symptoms. Burden peaked in the second trimester, and one parasite species caused most infections. Measured traits explained nearly three quarters of the trimester gap. Low uptake of preventive malaria doses in pregnancy was the biggest single contributor. Evening time outdoors, rare repellent use, and living near overgrown plants also weighed heavily.
pmc-13508342:
Apurva Dixit and five co-authors study the spread of a remote heart failure care program from a specialist center into community settings in Ontario, in 2026 work. The program, Medly, pairs a digital therapy tool with defined clinical roles and had already proven itself in specialty care. One-time provincial funding let three community organizations try it for the first time. The team judged rollout success with standard outcome measures and interviewed twenty team members three months after the first patient joined.

All three sites stayed faithful to the program design and saw it as fitting and welcome. Yet only one site met the tests for feasible, adopted rollout. Interviews praised the program's design and edge over usual care everywhere. Differences in local setting, staffing, and outside support explained the split in success. The cases show that a proven program still needs local groundwork before community spread can be assumed.
pmc-13509342:
Shatalov and colleagues profiled inherited gene variants in 275 Russian patients with triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype lacking the usual drug targets, in a 2026 study. Such cancers often carry inherited faults in DNA repair genes, but whether testing beyond the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes adds value was unclear in this population. Most patients received exome sequencing, while others had a repair-gene panel.

Shatalov found about two fifths of patients carried a harmful or likely harmful variant. BRCA1 and BRCA2 together accounted for about one fifth, dominated by BRCA1 and one recurring founder variant found in 23 cases. Wider testing added a modest number of carriers in other breast cancer and repair genes. It also produced a large burden of variants of uncertain significance in nearly two thirds of exome-tested patients. The authors support broader testing for risk assessment but warn non-BRCA findings should not drive therapy choices.
pmc-13510642:
Tan and colleagues in Singapore gave in 2026 a short course of a lung cancer drug to thirteen patients, then read how their tumors reshaped in the first weeks. The drug blocks a growth switch that the tumors carry in flawed form. All had early stage lung tumors set for cut out. Pills ran a month or more pre cut. Tumor and rim tissue then got deep gene and place reads, set against drug free tumors.

All tumors shrank or held still, and near half dropped a stage. No known drug proof flaw showed up in that span. The tumors grew less pure, with more sound rim in the mix. Immune and flare genes woke, and the fuel path flipped from fast sugar burn to slow air burn. The team sees fresh weak spots to pair with the drug.
pmc-13514642:
Jurairat Jongthawin and colleagues present a systematic review, published in 2026. A meta-analysis accompanies it. The question is how well a stool test device finds gut parasites. The device is the Mini Parasep concentrator. It makes stool processing simpler and safer in the lab. The team pooled past studies of its detection rate in human samples. Reference methods were the benchmark.

The overall detection rate was good. The device did especially well for roundworm and tapeworms. It also did well for the blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni. Detection was weaker for whipworm and hookworm. The liver fluke Opisthorchis viverrini was harder to find too. Results thus depend on the species sought. The authors judge it fit for routine screening and surveys. Stronger accuracy studies are still needed.
pmc-13515842:
Arjun Balmiki Prasad leads a twelve-author team presenting StxTyper, free software that names Shiga toxin genes in E coli genomes, in a 2026 article. These toxins drive bloody diarrhoea and kidney failure, and some subtypes are far more dangerous than others, so naming must be exact. The team first mapped every known subtype by family-tree relatedness, keeping the historical naming. They then built that scheme into a tool and database, also folded into a national reference program.

Checks against lab PCR assays and a Danish surveillance workflow showed the tool typed isolates correctly. Running it over more than 111,000 public E coli genomes gave a census of toxin subtypes at scale. The authors add a naming procedure for newly found subtypes, so future discoveries slot into the scheme rather than splintering it. For labs, the gain is a shared, automatic standard for a high-stakes label.
pmc-13516142:
Ayşe Kaya and four colleagues develop inhalable dry powders of a zinc compound for lung cancer therapy in a 2026 formulation study. The compound, zinc diethyldithiocarbamate, barely dissolves in water, which fights against deep-lung delivery. The team packaged it inside ring-shaped sugar carriers of two kinds and made powders by freeze-drying or spray-drying, adding the amino acid leucine at three levels.

Spray-dried powders came out lighter, flowed better, and launched far more of their dose into the fine particles that reach deep lung. Leucine improved matters further, wrinkling particle surfaces and lifting the fine-particle share dramatically at the top dose. Impact testing confirmed more particles in the breathable size band. Kaya's team names the spray-dried, leucine-rich powders as the lead candidates and calls for animal studies of benefit and safety.
pmc-13516642:
Mendes and colleagues designed and tested a new family of candidate Alzheimer's disease compounds built on a curcumin-like scaffold. Their 2026 study spans synthesis, computer modeling, enzyme tests, and animal experiments. Current Alzheimer's drugs only ease symptoms, so the team targeted the two cholinesterase enzymes whose activity deepens the brain's shortage of a memory-related chemical messenger.

Mendes made the compounds through a standard condensation reaction and showed by docking simulations that they fit the active sites of both target enzymes well. Laboratory assays confirmed inhibition of both enzymes, with selected derivatives improving on the parent scaffold. In rats given a drug that mimics Alzheimer's-like damage, chosen compounds showed neuroprotective effects suggesting preserved nerve tissue. One distinct lead from a screening library expanded the chemotype's diversity, and the authors position the family as multitarget candidates needing potency and selectivity work.
pmc-13517342:
Udara Rathnayake and three colleagues review a crippling bone disease of fast-growing broiler chickens in a 2026 article. Bacterial chondronecrosis with osteomyelitis starts when heavy young birds stress immature leg growth plates into tiny cracks. Germs from the gut or airways ride the blood into those cracks, settle, form biofilms, and kill bone from inside, leaving birds lame.

Breeding, housing, feed tweaks, and antibiotics each blunt the disease somewhat, none solves it. The review's focus is vaccination, especially a newer method: germs inactivated by electron beams rather than chemicals. Beam-killed vaccines keep the microbes' shape intact, which may train immunity better. Rathnayake's team lays out the causes and disease course, grades the current controls, and argues beam-based vaccines could anchor antibiotic-free prevention. The stakes span farm income, bird welfare, and food safety.
pmc-13517942: Enos Moyo and nine colleagues publish a short correction to their 2025 study of HIV risk among girls and young women in Namibia. The study covered how far the DREAMS scheme reached them. The notice restores an Acknowledgments section the paper left out. The added text credits earlier in-house work under the PHN DREAMS scheme, some done with paid consultants, as shaping the study design and the reading of results. The authors say the findings stand unchanged. The editor approved the fix, and the paper now carries the missing section.
pmc-13518042:
Yasuda and Ito reported a 2026 case in which noisy breathing and swallowing trouble in a one-year-old girl traced to an artery taking a wrong route behind her food pipe. She arrived with two days of breathing difficulty and a history of choking episodes while eating, with the high-pitched sound and chest retractions of upper airway narrowing. Croup treatment with inhaled epinephrine helped only temporarily.

Yasuda explains that imaging first suggested windpipe narrowing. Contrast CT then showed an aberrant right subclavian artery crossing behind the esophagus and squeezing it. Trapped food residue sat above the squeeze, and the swollen food pipe pressed the windpipe. Because she kept struggling and could swallow only liquids despite medical care, surgeons rerouted the artery onto the nearby carotid artery. After surgery she ate food and the noisy breathing resolved, a reminder that vessel anomalies can hide behind common croup.
pmc-13518642:
Eline Alons leads a seven-author team testing MyCommunication-Children, a questionnaire bank built to measure how well children take part in everyday communication. The children involved had speech, language, or voice disorders, or hearing loss. Earlier tools for adults did not fit children's lives, and parent reports cannot capture a child's own view.

In the 2026 study, 310 children answered all 49 draft items plus comparison questionnaires. Careful item reduction removed 17 items, and factor analysis supported one underlying trait. Two short forms emerged, one with 10 items for all settings and one with 9 items for school. Reliability was high for the full bank, giving clinicians a child-reported outcome measure.
pmc-13518942:
Angelita Liang and four colleagues chart how alternative splicing, the remixing of gene messages, unfolds as human bone marrow stromal stem cells become bone-forming osteoblasts in 2026 work. Splicing lets one gene yield many messenger RNAs, yet its choreography during bone differentiation was incomplete. The team paired deep short- and long-read RNA sequencing in a model cell line.

Early commitment stages showed splicing shifts in genes tied to known bone regulators such as RUNX2 and TEAD1. Later maturation stages shifted splicing in skeleton, matrix, and shipping-vesicle genes. Protein and phosphate-tag data confirmed matching protein changes across many functional domains. Together the layers describe a coordinated program guiding the bone-building transition.
pmc-13520142:
Ya-bei Li, Zhong-wen Zheng, and Man Zuo probe in 2026 whether total body water relates to stomach and intestinal illness, using United States survey data plus genetic causal analysis. Body water marks fluid balance and tracks with metabolic disease, yet gut links were untested beyond observation. The survey arm covered 36,043 adults from NHANES waves spanning 2001 to 2018.

Within a mid-range of body water, roughly 24.9 to 38.5 liters, odds of gut symptoms ran lower, while values above that range tied to higher odds. Formal tests did not confirm a curved pattern, and the authors warn body size and fatness may drive the signal. Genetic analysis gave suggestive support for a causal link to gut and abdominal diseases.
pmc-13520242:
Kristen Uskovich and six colleagues chart in 2026 how often young American children accidentally swallow recreational drugs, using poison center records from 2000 through 2024. Earlier studies covered narrower slices. The national file held 41,612 unintentional ingestions in children under six, mostly toddlers, almost all at home and involving a single substance.

Half the children had no or minor effects, yet 5 percent suffered major effects and six died. Cannabis products drove 84.7 percent of cases, followed by stimulants and psychedelics. Opioid and stimulant ingestions reached intensive care most often. The yearly rate exploded 3,307 percent across the study window, accelerating after 2013 with edible marijuana and psilocybin products. Prevention efforts are overdue, the authors argue.
pmc-13520342:
Jakkrit Juhong and colleagues study in 2026 raised eye pressure in people with inflammation linked to an implanted eye device, using records from a Thai tertiary clinic. High pressure can damage vision, so the team searches for features that mark higher risk.

Ninety affected patients were found over eight years, with 30 high-pressure cases matched to 60 controls. A misplaced lens implant and a long eyeball each carried much higher odds of raised pressure in adjusted analysis. Further risk factors follow in the full results. For eye clinics, the findings support close pressure checks when device position or eye length already raises concern.
pmc-13520542:
Jiarun Song and colleagues engineer in 2026 a nanoparticle treatment that delivers a channel-blocking drug directly to retinal ganglion cells in a rat model of chronic high eye pressure. Glaucoma kills those cells slowly, while pressure lowering alone often fails to stop loss.

Prior work showed that overactive TRPV4 channels disturb calcium balance and jam cellular recycling, pushing cells toward death. Particles use a toxin subunit for selective cell entry, with a shell that opens only where reactive oxygen is high. Treatment restored recycling flow and cut cell injury in the model. Precise, on-demand release may reduce dose and side effects compared with free drug.
pmc-13521542:
Mantri and colleagues reviewed the evidence in 2026 on autologous platelet concentrates, meaning healing products made from a patient's own blood, in regenerative dental procedures and root-end surgery. Their systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 39 clinical studies comparing platelet-rich plasma or fibrin against standard scaffolds and treatments.

In young teeth with open roots, platelet products healed no better than a simple blood clot scaffold, and root growth was similar. In mature teeth, X-ray healing also showed no clear gain. The clear benefit appeared in periapical surgery, where platelet products nearly doubled the rate of good radiographic healing as an added material. Pain relief after surgery trended lower but was not proven, so the authors frame these products as helpful add-ons, not replacements.
pmc-13521942:
Qaisar Ali and colleagues simulate in 2026 whether a zinc oxide nanocage can pull the antibiotic ciprofloxacin out of drinking water, using quantum chemistry calculations. Antibiotic residues in water foster resistance, so low-cost capture materials are actively sought.

Five binding layouts were optimised, with the strongest layout showing highly favourable adsorption energy and no cage distortion. Binding ran through fluorine and oxygen atoms on the drug meeting zinc and oxygen sites on the cage. Charge transfer, energy gap narrowing and bonding analyses all supported firm attachment. Binding was spontaneous, although very strong grip limits cage reuse after capture.
pmc-13522342:
Aniket K. Shahade and Priyanka V. Deshmukh introduce in 2026 a custom neural layer for spotting apple leaf diseases from photos, targeting black rot, rust, scab and healthy leaves. Hand inspection is slow and error-prone, while standard networks can miss location-specific disease patterns.

Their spatially adaptive layer modulates features with trainable Gaussian shapes and penalises irregular kernels during training. A balanced set of 3,164 images was built by upsampling smaller classes. Held-out accuracy reached just over 98 percent, with class scores near perfect and most confusion between rust and scab. Baseline comparisons support the custom layer for precision farming in controlled settings.
pmc-13523342:
Haoyue Yu and co-authors report a rare lung complication of hepatitis B therapy in a 2026 case report. A middle-aged non-smoking Asian woman received weekly injections of pegylated interferon-alpha for chronic hepatitis B. One month into treatment, after the fifth dose, she developed breathlessness on exertion, dry cough, and low fever. Detailed scans showed thickened lung tissue partitions with hazy patches, and lung tests showed reduced gas transfer.

Infection, autoimmune disease, and heart causes were excluded, leading to a diagnosis of interferon-induced interstitial lung disease, a complication reported mostly in hepatitis C treatment. Stopping the drug and starting steroid treatment brought marked improvement within a day and full symptom resolution within a week. Imaging and lung function recovered gradually, with no recurrence at follow-up.
pmc-13524142:
Harsh Shah and colleagues describe a digital support suite, Ni-kshay SETU, built to help Indian health workers follow fast-changing tuberculosis guidance. The suite pairs an AI chatbot with role-specific decision support and a knowledge hub in several languages.

The platform reports 46,379 active subscribers and over 1.63 million visits, reaching users in 35 of 36 states and territories. Over 70 percent of users are frontline workers, such as treatment supervisors, health visitors, and lab technicians. Knowledge test scores rose clearly after use, from about 14.5 to about 20.5 on average across some 18,900 tests. Users rated the tools highly, and 96.4 percent said they would recommend the suite to peers, Shah reports.
pmc-13526742:
Shirin Hui Tan and others pull together, in a 2026 systematic scoping review, what is known about the gene origins of digestive system cancers between 2013 and 2025. These cancers account for over a quarter of cancer cases and about a third of cancer deaths worldwide. Sequencing gains have bred many more findings, yet none spanned the whole group.

Fifty-seven studies from three data banks were mapped. Colorectal and gastric cancers led, while esophageal, pancreatic, and rarer types such as gallbladder cancer were little studied. Recurrent gene changes hit TP53, KRAS, PIK3CA, and CDKN2A, with repair deficiency and microsatellite instability prominent in colorectal and gastric disease. Epigenetic shifts and single cell and spatial methods exposed how varied tumors are. Germline variant work stayed narrow, mostly in colorectal, pancreatic, and select liver cancers.
pmc-13526842:
José Ignacio Guzman Montoto and others validate, in a 2026 study, a portable VR simulator for laparoscopic camera navigation. The skill gets little dedicated training, because high-end simulators cost much and assessment is sporadic. Their platform, SECMA, mimics the pivot of a surgical port and records hand movements at high frequency in six dimensions.

Twenty surgeons and eighteen medical students performed a six-target navigation task across four sessions. Machine learning separated experts from novices reliably, with execution time, path length, and depth movement as leading signals. Hidden-state modeling found an expert coordination pattern built on deliberate pitch exploration, while novices showed scattered yaw and roll noise. Statistical models confirmed expert advantages and practice gains. The authors pitch the device for proficiency-based training.
pmc-13527542:
Jack and colleagues wrote a 2026 editorial championing a new imaging measure for Crohn's disease, a chronic bowel inflammation that damages the full wall of the intestine. The editorial discusses a study by Dong and co-workers. That study used dual-energy computed tomography to measure creeping fat. The scan separates tissues by how they absorb two X-ray energies, and creeping fat means the fat wrapping around inflamed bowel segments.

Jack reports that the measured fat volume matched clinical, endoscopic, tissue, and molecular signs of disease activity, tracking both inflammation and scarring. The fat measure also stayed high in patients whose symptoms had settled, suggesting it detects hidden ongoing disease that standard activity scores miss. The editorial argues this turns a once-qualitative observation into an objective monitoring tool, while noting that larger multicenter studies must confirm it changes decisions and improves patient outcomes.
pmc-13527942:
Heber Isac Arbildo-Vega and seven colleagues publish a 2026 review asking a dental question. When gums recede and worn notches form at the tooth neck, does adding restorative work to gum surgery help? The team searched nine databases through December 2025. They looked for randomized trials with at least a year of follow-up, and they pooled the results.

Only four trials qualified from 199 records screened. Across nine gum measurements, combined treatment and gum surgery alone performed much the same. One exception was a small rise in probing depth, which stayed within healthy limits. The combined approach did reduce tooth sensitivity. Because certainty was rated low and trials were few, the authors want larger multicenter studies before firm guidance is given.
pmc-13528042:
Xinyuan Wang and five colleagues trace how long-term acid-blocking drugs can harm the gut in a 2026 mouse study. Proton pump inhibitors are widely used against reflux. The team gave mice rabeprazole for four weeks. The drug worsened gut injury from a chemical irritant and from radiation. Crypts and villi shrank, and gut stem cells thinned out.

Gene, microbe, and metabolite scans told a linked story. The drug disturbed gut microbes and lowered bile acids in the ileum. One acid, called 7KLCA, normally keeps stem cells renewing through Wnt signals. A gut microbe that makes that acid restored renewal when fed to mice. Blocking a bile sensor also eased injury. The authors name the microbe-to-acid-to-Wnt chain as the key route. They suggest it as a treatment target for drug-related gut damage.
pmc-13528142:
Caifang Chen and nine colleagues run a practice project to sharpen fall awareness among high-risk hospital patients in a 2026 paper. Falls are a top harm in hospitals. The project ran in seven wards of a Changsha hospital with the worst fall records. It enrolled 420 high-risk patients, split evenly before and after, plus seventy nurses. Twenty audit points were built from best practice advice.

A baseline audit exposed gaps between advice and ward reality. The team then acted on five fronts: leadership support, system fixes, staff training, patient teaching, and record alerts. Work ran for three months. A follow-up audit compared rule compliance, fall rates, and patient knowledge and habits. The paper reports the design and early audit machinery in detail. It aims to show awareness training adds value beyond standard fall bundles.
pmc-13529142:
Jia and colleagues charted deaths from duodenal ulcer across the United States from 1999 to 2023 using national death registry data. A duodenal ulcer is a sore in the first section of the small intestine. Their 2026 analysis counts 34,520 such deaths and breaks trends down by sex, race and ethnicity, age, region, and urban or rural residence. It uses statistical models that detect turning points in rates over time.

Jia found the overall age-adjusted death rate fell across the period, dropping through about 2009, then flattening with signs of a rebound afterward. The decline-then-rise pattern was clearest in men, adults over 65, and several racial and ethnic groups, and appeared in all four census regions. Rural areas consistently carried higher rates than cities. The authors call for targeted prevention aimed at older adults and people on stomach-harming medications to close the persistent gaps.
pmc-13530142:
Noy Rosental Vazani leads a 2026 mapping study of how mouth lining becomes tough and keratinized in some regions but stays soft in others. Tissue came from the border zone where gum meets cheek lining in two healthy donors. A high-resolution spatial method read gene activity spot by spot across each slice.

Sixteen tissue clusters mirrored the real anatomy and split gum from lining programs clearly. Both tissue fates branched from one shared starter layer. Collagen signals from supporting tissue engaged switches on surface cells, while strong cell-to-cell adhesion locks reinforced the tough program from within the surface layer itself.
pmc-13530242:
Songling Huang and co-authors present a 2026 system that reads tobacco box labels automatically for factory quality tracking. Manual label checking is slow and error-prone under real plant conditions. Their framework fuses the label words with the label picture instead of trusting either alone.

Several tuned language models vote on the text side, while optical character reading handles the image side with a spelling-distance repair step for digits. A dynamic weighting scheme settles disagreements between the two sides. On nearly ten thousand real labels the fused system beat text-only, image-only, and several known document systems.
pmc-13530742:
Rosenberg and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 192, a Statcast-based check on whether elbow ligament surgery with internal bracing leaves professional pitchers subtly diminished. The check goes beyond what traditional statistics show. The ulnar collateral ligament is the elbow ligament torn by throwing.

The matched study followed 23 Major League pitchers operated on between 2016 and 2024 against 1,569 age-matched controls, using pitch-tracking data from full seasons before and after surgery. After surgery, batters hit the cases' pitches harder: exit velocity, barrel rate, and hard-hit share against them all rose clearly. Their own fastball velocity dropped by about two miles per hour in the post-surgery seasons analyzed here. Workload fell too, with fewer innings and strikeouts, and batters swung and missed less often. The declines exceeded the changes seen in matched controls over the same span.
pmc-13531742:
Hongxia Liu and co-authors pinpoint in 2026 a tiny RNA that worsens heart attack injury by silencing a protective gene. Blood from 77 heart attack patients and 82 healthy people was compared, and rat heart cells underwent oxygen-starvation injury in the lab. The RNA, named miR-324-3p, rose sharply in patients.

Raising the RNA in injured cells fanned inflammation and stress, while blocking it calmed both. Its target gene STAT3 fell as the RNA rose. Removing STAT3 erased the benefit of blocking the RNA, proving the pairing drives the effect. The RNA also showed strong diagnostic value.
pmc-13531842:
Ruiqi Li and co-authors ask in 2026 when a blood test can stand in for lung wash fluid when hunting pneumonia germs after stem cell transplant. Paired samples from transplant patients and healthy-immune patients underwent DNA sequencing, with a larger transplant group used to validate markers. Lung sampling is invasive, so a blood shortcut would help fragile patients.

Microbe patterns differed sharply between blood and lung fluid only in transplant patients, whose lung fluid carried richer growth. Far more blood sequences matched lung sequences in that group, tied to leakier lung barriers. Hundreds of blood sequences predicted lung presence with over 70 percent certainty.
pmc-13532942:
Nasimi A Guluzade, Gordon S Mitchell, and Daniel A Keir study in 2026 how breathing matches carbon dioxide output during exercise while blood levels stay steady. Twenty healthy young adults cycled at four steady levels below the point where breathing surges. The team measured airflow, gas exchange, blood carbon dioxide, and response to added carbon dioxide.

A model split the drive to breathe into a forward signal tied to effort and a brake from carbon dioxide sensing. The forward signal rose steeply with effort, while the sensing response also rose. Readers see how both drives balance to limit swings in blood gases.
pmc-13533242:
Zhengru Liu and colleagues report in 2026 a tiny electronic sensor array that screens for opioids with help from machine learning. Fast, cheap, portable screening matters as fentanyl drives the opioid crisis in the United States. Their sensors use carbon nanotubes decorated with gold and platinum particles.

Hundreds of samples of fentanyl, codeine, hydrocodone, and morphine were tested by hand and by an automated rig. Simple models sorted the drugs with moderate accuracy, while a deep network reached much higher accuracy on manual tests. Readers learn which signal in the data matters most for telling these drugs apart.
pmc-13534442:
Yi Chen, Fangming He, Ai Liu, and Yujun Shi study in 2026 what patients with knee osteoarthritis know and do about acupuncture. The joint disease causes pain and stiffness with no cure, and acupuncture is a common added therapy. A survey across hospitals in Beijing in spring 2025 gathered 532 valid responses.

Scores showed moderate knowledge, positive attitudes, and fairly high use of acupuncture. Knowledge linked directly to both attitude and practice, and attitude carried part of the knowledge effect into practice. Structured teaching plus clear expectation setting may help patients decide and stick with care plans.
pmc-13536542:
Rong-de Zhong and colleagues combine in 2026 MRI radiomics with gene data to predict IDH mutation status and outlook in glioma, a major brain tumour type. Scan traits may mirror tumour genetics, saving invasive sampling. Training and check sets came from public MRI files, plus an outside hospital group for validation.

A nine-feature scan model predicted mutation status strongly and also tied to survival. Eight key genes linked to tumour growth and mutation status were confirmed at protein level and mapped to cell types. Two scan features tracked gene levels in opposite directions, aiding interpretation.
pmc-13536642:
Shanshan Li and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a portable rapid test device for monkeypox and related poxviruses. Fast field testing matters where lab access is thin and rash diseases look alike. The suitcase-sized unit runs eight samples in about an hour from raw swabs, with no separate DNA extraction step.

Against stored clinical samples the test matched earlier results closely, with full sensitivity on the main set checked. A second panel also separated monkeypox from chickenpox correctly in a small group. Cross-reactions were rare across twenty virus types, supporting field use.
pmc-13536742:
Uchenna Igbokwe leads a 2026 assessment of malaria testing readiness in public clinics across Kaduna and Kano States in Nigeria. Global guidance requires a test before malaria treatment, using rapid tests or microscopy. Staff visited 418 public facilities in August 2025 and scored readiness on five points covering tests, microscopy, trained staff, written procedures, and recent stock levels. Links between facility traits and full readiness were also tested.

Every facility held rapid tests and trained staff, and none reported recent stock-outs of tests or key medicines. About nine in ten facilities met all readiness points, while microscopy was present in under one quarter. Larger hospitals, city sites, regular supportive visits, a named malaria lead, and free supplies each raised the odds of full readiness. The authors urge steady supply and support, with extra help for rural sites.
pmc-13537742:
Hernando Gaitán Duarte and colleagues reflect on Colombia general health social security system from 1993 to 2026 in a Spanish-language editorial written from a medical viewpoint. The system faces a deep crisis marked by late access to care, growing underfunding, insurer interventions and closures, weaker provider capacity, and dissatisfaction among patients and health workers. The authors call for a broad social agreement to rebuild trust.

A short history traces Law 100 of 1993 and later turns that eroded money, institutions, and confidence. Insurers gained a dominant middle role under market and managed competition rules, with surplus and vertical growth distorting prices and rivalry. Public hospitals suffered in that setting. The editorial urges learning from early coverage gains and later errors to protect the right to health.
pmc-13538342:
Ke Chen and colleagues split bowel adenomas, the growths that precede bowel cancer, into immune types in a 2026 data study. Standard grading reveals little about immune surroundings that may drive progression. Gene data from several adenoma groups were clustered by immune genes, checked with cell mixture tools and single-cell data, and contrasted for gene activity and pathways between types.

Two types emerged, one rich in lymphocytes and immune genes and one quiet with suppressed activity. The rich type showed heightened presentation and signaling pathways, while single-cell data revealed early signs of tired killer T cells even at the adenoma stage. The quiet type carried tissue features hinting at forward change. The authors propose immune typing for risk sorting and early prevention planning.
pmc-13538542:
Khairunnisa Makmon and co-authors trial a theory-based flood education module for teenagers in Selangor, Malaysia, in a 2026 randomized study. Floods strike Malaysia often and adolescents are especially exposed, yet readiness can blunt harm. A single lesson built on a threat-and-coping model reached 140 students across eight schools, while 147 peers waited as controls. Readiness index scores were taken before, right after, and three months later.

Readiness scores jumped in the taught group right after the lesson and stayed clearly higher three months on. Waiting controls showed no such gain. The authors credit the theory frame for designing teaching that converts risk awareness into action rather than fear. School programs of this kind are offered as a route to tougher adolescent resilience against recurring floods.
pmc-13538742:
Rabbi Swaby, Julia Townson, and Rachel E J Besser interview UK health professionals about monitoring children with early-stage type 1 diabetes in a 2026 qualitative study. Screening now finds children before symptoms appear, yet frontline views on follow-up monitoring were unclear. Fifteen professionals across the pediatric diabetes team gave semi-structured interviews, analyzed thematically for barriers and needs.

Three themes emerged around uncertainty in managing early stages, hunger for guidance and consistent messaging, and the work of folding monitoring into routine care. Knowledge gaps left clinicians unsure which tests to use and how to explain progression risk to families. Professionals backed monitoring in principle but demanded training, clear pathways, and expanded services before national rollout.
pmc-13540042:
Albayrak and colleagues profiled in 2026 the emotional patterns of adolescents with ADHD across several Turkish centres. Emotion regulation trouble and inner distress, such as anxiety and low mood, are core features for many of these teens. The study enrolled 109 clinically referred adolescents aged eleven to eighteen.

Emotion regulation difficulties tracked closely with anxiety and low mood. They also carried a significant indirect link between resilience and anxiety-depression burden. One subgroup stood out: teens who bounce back poorly yet carry quiet emotional strain despite modest outward symptoms. The authors call this a low-resilience silent profile, easily missed in routine care. Brief self-report scales of regulation and resilience, they argue, can guide assessment and follow-up beyond standard ADHD symptom counts. Profile-based planning could help clinicians tailor support to each teen's emotional pattern.
pmc-13540442:
Dongming Liu and eleven colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, a little-known enzyme called SSU72 as a promoter of colorectal cancer growth. Colorectal cancer is often found late and resists treatment, so new drivers and drug targets carry weight.

Tissues with high SSU72 levels fared worse, and laboratory work showed the enzyme quieting two self-destruct programs in cancer cells. The mechanism ran through a stress sensor called PERK inside the cell's protein-folding compartment: SSU72 stripped a phosphate from it and switched off the stress response. Animal work confirmed more aggressive tumors when this pathway was silenced. Blocking SSU72's enzyme activity is proposed as a treatment angle for high-expressing tumors.
pmc-13540842:
Yu-Qi He and five colleagues follow, in a 2026 prospective study, whether a wider-than-usual angle between an infant's thighs predicts slower gross motor development. The adductor angle is measured during routine neurological checks in the first two months of life.

Records covered 1,132 infants born between mid-2020 and mid-2023 at one large hospital, with milestone ages drawn from the child health system. A wide angle appeared significantly oftener in preterm babies. Statistical modelling, however, found no significant effect of the finding on motor outcomes for either preterm or full-term infants. Wide confidence intervals leave small effects possible, and the authors want a better normal range defined.
pmc-13540942:
Yizhuo Shen, Jianpeng Sheng, and Pengcheng Yan present, in a 2026 software paper, a lightweight system for governing and sharing research data files before publication inside an institution. Core facilities juggle unreleased genomics files of many types, while public repositories only serve finished work.

Their open-source tool, MetaServe, registers varied assets from sequencing output to documents without demanding repository-grade formatting. Automatic file recognition, hand-supplied project annotations, and faceted search make holdings findable. Access runs through authenticated downloads, handoffs to viewer services, and export lists for analysis pipelines, all under role-based permissions with an audit trail. The system already runs at a Beijing medical research institute.
pmc-13543342:
Julia M van Beekum's team asked in a 2026 interview study why occupational hygienists and occupational physicians in the Netherlands so rarely work side by side on chemical hazards. Hygienists measure exposure while physicians judge health effects, and that split can delay spotting work-related disease. Seventeen people from both fields were interviewed at length, and the answers were sorted with a behaviour framework of capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Both groups said they had limited knowledge and skill for spotting chemical health effects early. Each side struggled to translate the other's findings: exposure data rarely became health calls, and symptoms rarely fed back into exposure checks. Existing tools deepened the divide by serving one field only. Traits of Dutch occupational care added further friction. The authors urge joint training and shared tools so that exposure science and health care finally meet over the same worker.
pmc-13543542:
Hai-Hua Zhou and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a hidden abscess found at the join left by rectal cancer surgery, eight quiet years after the operation. A 43-year-old woman with no symptoms had a routine surveillance colonoscopy, which showed a small lump inside the rectal wall at the old join. Ultrasound from within the bowel showed a defined lesion under the surface, and its appearance could have been mistaken for returning cancer.

Rather than major surgery, the team cut into the lesion endoscopically and found a cavity holding pus and yellow plaque-like material, the signature of a chronic abscess rather than a tumour. They washed the cavity out and closed the opening with clips. Follow-up ultrasound showed the mass gone, and recovery was uneventful. Deep, late abscesses can masquerade as recurrence, and skilled endoscopy can both unmask and treat them.
pmc-13544842:
Aghajanzadeh and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a parathyroid tumor hiding in the chest. Their patient, a 19-year-old woman, had four years of bone pain and weakness. Blood tests showed high calcium and sky-high parathyroid hormone levels. Neck scans, though, found no tumor in the usual spots.

A tracer scan pinpointed a large growth inside the thymus gland in her chest. A first keyhole attempt could not reach the deep lesion safely. Surgeons then opened the breastbone partway and removed the tumor fully. Tissue tests confirmed a parathyroid adenoma, a benign but hormone-pumping growth. Her calcium and hormone levels fell to normal after surgery. Tailored surgical routes, they stress, cure even deep chest cases.
pmc-13548542:
Fernando Cruz and colleagues present an improved chromosome-level genome assembly for the jaguar, in a 2026 data description. Jaguar numbers have fallen with habitat loss across the Americas, and conservation work depends on a reliable reference genome. Earlier assemblies were more fragmented. The team sequenced two animals with long-read and short-read methods, then used chromosome contact data to order the pieces.

Nearly all of the assembled sequence landed on chromosomes, and the team annotated more than twenty-five thousand protein-coding genes. Contiguity improved markedly over the existing reference. The authors position the new assembly, named mPanOnc3.5, as a firmer base for tracking jaguar populations, comparing individuals, and studying how this big cat evolved. Such a resource also helps planners judge genetic health when designing protection programs.
pmc-13548642:
Zhenping Wu and colleagues blend a blood gene signal with clinical course data to forecast short-term death in sepsis, in a 2026 prospective intensive care study. Sepsis kills many critically ill patients, and immune gene activity might sharpen prognosis beyond bedside scores. Of 249 enrolled patients, 198 had gene measurements from a panel of thirty-five candidate transcripts, narrowed by statistical selection to one immune transcript, PAX5, plus four clinical variables.

Five modeling methods competed at predicting death by one, two, and four weeks. A random survival forest won, with discrimination scores in the mid-zero-point-eight range, clearly beating the classic regression approach and matching a top boosting method. Blood disease, sex, organ failure score, and positive blood cultures carried most weight, while the gene added a modest extra. The authors offer the framework as a step toward biologically informed triage.
pmc-13551542:
Gilberto Sánchez-González, Luz del C Hernández-Hernández and Elaine Gallagher published this 2026 systematic review of what dengue fever costs Mexico. Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, is entrenched in Mexico and strains public budgets through treatment, prevention and lost productivity. In the first review of its kind for the country, the authors gathered cost studies from 2010 to 2020, in English and Spanish, including ministry reports and grey literature.

Seven articles met the inclusion criteria, all reporting national costs and three focusing on particular states. The burden peaked in 2013, when annual costs reached 176.82 million dollars as reported, or 281.60 million in present value. Studies counted direct care, prevention and surveillance spending plus indirect losses such as missed work. The authors warn that methods differed so much between studies that comparisons are shaky. They conclude dengue's economic burden in Mexico is high and swells further in outbreak years.
pmc-13551942:
A 2026 study by Daniel Egger and five colleagues followed a drug switch in a serious eye disease. The disease is wet age-related macular degeneration. Some eyes stay active despite standard injections. Clinics switched 43 eyes from 38 patients to a newer drug, faricimab. All had failed to stretch visit gaps beyond eight weeks on older drugs. The team tracked vision, retinal thickness, and fluid for up to two years.

Vision held steady through follow-up, with no firm change at any visit. Retinal thickness fell and stayed lower. A pigment layer swelling also shrank over time. Fluid under the retina dropped at every check. The share of dry maculas rose from zero to about a quarter. Visit gaps lengthened from under six weeks before the switch.
pmc-13555642:
Young-Min Kim and three colleagues watch a memory switch change at the nanoscale after its first firing in a 2026 study. These threshold switches select cells in dense three-dimensional memory stacks. What physically changes during first firing has stayed murky. A sharp microscope tip applied voltage to tiny targeted spots, confining the action.

After local switching, electron microscopy revealed tiny crystals forming where the top contact meets the switching layer. That crystal growth thinned the glassy layer, easing later switching. The voltage needed for repeat firing dropped well below the first-firing level. The authors show the crystal-glass boundary carries the local current, clarifying a mechanism long argued from indirect evidence alone.
pmc-13556042:
Yuchen Cui and six colleagues built in 2026 a deep learning system that reads pathology images to diagnose oral squamous cell carcinoma, a common mouth cancer. Diagnosis today leans on a pathologist's eye, which takes time and varies between observers. Their network, PGMA-Net, was designed to work across microscope magnifications, to cope with images from different hospitals, and to explain its decisions.

Guide maps drawn from pathology knowledge steer the model's attention to the tissue features that matter. Extra modules align features across magnifications, rebalance rare classes during training, and adapt the model to new centres. On an internal test set the system scored high on both discrimination and accuracy, and it held up well on an outside set after adaptation. Visualisations show which regions drove each call, a step toward tools clinicians can trust.
pmc-13558542:
Lana Salloum and nine colleagues widened in 2026 the picture of dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, a scarring inflammatory disease usually described as a condition of young Black men. Their retrospective cohort covered 29 patients across a large Boston-area health network over ten years. A parallel scoping review gathered seventeen published cohorts holding 710 patients. Records supplied background details and histories of metabolic, psychiatric, and autoimmune conditions, plus smoking.

The local group was mostly male with an average age in the mid thirties, yet racially mixed. Nearly half had another disease from the same follicle-blocking family, over eight in ten carried a metabolic condition, and about four in ten had a psychiatric diagnosis. Published cohorts agreed on male predominance and metabolic company while under-reporting mental health. The authors argue the disease is global and tied to metabolism, not confined to one population.
pmc-13559342:
Stasiak and colleagues review what happened when patients taking oral or targeted drugs for blood cancers underwent major lung surgery, in a 2026 retrospective case series. Anatomical lung resection, removing a lobe or more, is standard for early lung cancer but carries a bleeding risk. Blood cancer patients face extra danger because both their disease and their medicines disturb clotting. The series examines postoperative hemorrhagic complications in this small, specific group treated at one center.

Median operative blood loss was 100 milliliters, yet median drainage on the first postoperative day reached 1,040 milliliters, signaling substantial bleeding after surgery in these patients. The authors describe the incidence of hemorrhagic complications as unexpectedly high for lung resection. Notably, the two patients who had stopped oral chemotherapy before surgery did not bleed afterward. Stasiak stresses causality cannot be proven from so few cases, and urges multidisciplinary planning plus larger studies of perioperative drug management.
pmc-13560042:
Rahmadi Budiman and colleagues surveyed members of an Indonesian hydrogen and fuel cell association on how energy knowledge links to saving behaviour. The study asked whether personal values and attitudes carry part of that link.

Data came from 195 members, split into three kinds of saving: cutting use, buying efficient gear, and acts that help others save. Energy literacy predicted saving behaviour directly and also through values and attitudes, with a strong total effect in the model. The indirect routes worked better for cutting use and helping others than for efficiency buying, which costs money upfront. Budiman suggests literacy campaigns should build values and attitudes, while efficiency gains may need price or policy help too.
pmc-13560142:
Haixia Wang and three colleagues review neutrophil extracellular traps in diseases of the central nervous system. Their 2026 article explains these web-like structures of DNA, histones, and antimicrobial proteins that neutrophils cast out to snare pathogens. Helpful in infection, the traps turn harmful when they form excessively or clear too slowly inside the brain.

The review covers how neutrophils cross the blood-brain barrier, what triggers trap release there. The webs then contribute to stroke, traumatic brain injury, bleeding around the brain, Alzheimer's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators feature among the triggers discussed. Emerging treatments aim either to stop traps forming or to dissolve them faster, and the authors survey that neuroprotective pipeline. They frame the synthesis as a guide for researchers hunting new targets in neurological disorders.
pmc-13560242:
Huaxing Zhao and colleagues identify interleukin 17D as a follicular fluid protein that helps eggs acquire developmental competence during maturation. Their 2026 study begins with proteomic comparison of pig follicular fluid, then tests the protein across roughly twenty thousand pig and mouse oocytes and over thirteen thousand embryos. Failed maturation underlies much subfertility in animals and humans.

IL17D rose sharply in follicular fluid as maturation proceeded. Adding it strengthened the two-way communication between egg and surrounding cumulus cells by raising the junction protein CX43 and the projections linking them. Treated eggs kept better redox balance and tighter synchrony between nucleus and cytoplasm. Embryos from treated eggs developed better in dishes and to full term in animals, aided by shifts in fat metabolism and histone marks. The protein works through the receptor CD93, and relatives IL17A and IL17F helped as well.
pmc-13560342:
Yulu Qiu and colleagues build a mouse model of how autoimmunity against TRIM21, the target of anti-Ro52 antibodies, can seed interstitial lung disease. Their 2026 in vivo study immunizes mice with the full protein, then challenges them with a viral mimic to imitate infection triggers. Anti-Ro52 antibodies are the commonest marker tied to lung involvement across connective tissue diseases.

Immunized mice produced systemic autoantibodies and activated B cells, with inflammation that oddly concentrated in the lungs and IgG deposited there. The viral mimic then sharply worsened matters, drawing in CD8 T cells and myeloid cells and switching on chemokine pathways. Gene sequencing flagged Ccl6 as a top-rising gene, and its protein was confirmed in the inflamed tissue. The authors conclude TRIM21 autoimmunity primes the lung for CD8-driven inflammation, offering targets for anti-Ro52 positive disease.
pmc-13560542:
Sham Mohamad Farouq Alkhateeb and colleagues test whether a carbon dioxide laser boosts fluoride uptake into tooth enamel beyond varnish alone. Their 2026 in vitro split-tooth study uses six human upper premolars extracted for orthodontic reasons, each crown halved so one side serves as its own control. Every specimen received five percent sodium fluoride varnish; experimental halves then got fifteen seconds of one-watt laser light.

Under the electron microscope, varnish-only enamel kept its etched, microporous look. Laser-treated enamel melted and fused into a smoother, recrystallized surface. Elemental analysis showed significantly more fluoride locked into the laser side, with the paired comparison favoring the combined treatment. The authors read the laser as a genuine adjunct that drives fluoride deeper into enamel structure. The work is bench science on extracted teeth, a proof of mechanism ahead of any clinical testing.
pmc-13560742:
Stephen P. Becker, Alison E. Pritchard, and Jessica R. Lunsford-Avery review behavioral sleep treatment for children and teenagers with ADHD, a group where sleep problems may reach seventy percent yet long went untreated. Their 2026 review organizes recent findings by developmental stage, from early childhood through adolescence. Sleep is framed as a twenty-four-hour dimension of a disorder usually treated as a daytime problem.

Across age bands, behavioral sleep interventions proved feasible and improved parent- and self-reported sleep in the studies surveyed. Evidence on weaving sleep strategies into standard ADHD behavioral care remains thin, and the authors map both the opportunities and the friction there. They call for treatments tailored to development and to mechanism, with new attention to circadian rhythm and sleep regularity. Digital and integrated care delivery could widen reach for families.
pmc-13562342: Bariatric surgeons report comprehensive multicenter experience with revisions of one-anastomosis gastric bypass featuring 250-centimeter biliopancreatic limbs. The team with care test complex revisional surgery results. The 2026 Europe PMC paper fully presents multicenter results. It provides essential guidance for difficult reoperations. Obesity surgery sometimes requires revision. Accumulated experience informs technical refinements. Patients benefit from shared knowledge.
pmc-13563942:
Shengwei Du and colleagues test, in a 2026 laboratory study, whether blocking an enzyme called TrxR1 makes liver cancer cells more sensitive to the drug motesanib. They paired motesanib with auranofin, a drug that inhibits that enzyme, across several experimental models of hepatocellular carcinoma.

The pair killed cancer cells far more strongly together than either approach suggested alone. Blocking TrxR1 let harmful oxygen molecules build up through a self-digestion process in the cells, triggering stress responses that damaged DNA and slowed growth. Removing a key self-digestion gene reduced that damage, supporting the proposed chain. The work points drug developers toward a paired strategy for advanced liver cancer.
pmc-13569542:
Agnès Aubry and co-authors examine, in a 2026 biographical study, how legal guardians in Switzerland cope with work the authors frame as dirty work. Their clients are vulnerable adults who often refuse the imposed help, and the tasks can be coercive. Life-history interviews reveal two broad coping styles shaped by class and gender upbringing.

One style leans into care, recasting guardianship as noble work, at the cost of heavy emotional labor. The other leans on law and administration, treating coercion as legitimate and keeping emotional distance. Social work researchers get a lens on how personal history quietly organizes professional survival.
pmc-13572542:
S Anandaraj, with seven colleagues, presents a 2026 study that predicts the strength of green concrete with a neural network. The mix swaps part of the fine aggregate for marble dust and adds luffa, a plant fibre, as reinforcement. Lab tests alone cannot cover every blend, so a model that learns from past mixes can guide new ones.

Marble dust ran from 0 to 40 percent and luffa fibre from 0 to 2 percent across the test mixes. The best blend, 20 percent dust with 1 percent fibre, hit 34.5 megapascals in compression. It also reached 6.2 in bending and 4.25 in split tension. The authors credit tight particle packing from the dust and crack bridging by the treated fibre. A two-layer network then learned to predict all three strengths at once.
pmc-13573442:
Nisa Nur Ayhanci, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study that brings a child migraine disability questionnaire into Turkish. The PedMIDAS form asks how much migraine cuts into school, home, and play life for children and teens. A sound Turkish version lets local clinics and studies gauge that burden the same way others do.

Sixty young patients with migraine took part. The form was translated forward and back to guard meaning. In a first session, children gave background and migraine details and filled in the form plus a quality-of-life scale. Fifteen days later, they filled in the migraine form again. Scores held steady across the gap, with a repeat correlation near the top of the scale. Internal consistency reached an acceptable level, and scores tied to migraine traits and quality of life as expected. The authors deem the version fit for use.
pmc-13574742:
Daniel A Ermann, with 12 colleagues, reports a 2026 real-world study of a drug class for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia in older Americans. The drugs block Bruton tyrosine kinase, a signal the cancer needs, and several near twins compete with no head-to-head trial between them. Routine care data can fill that gap for patients who start treatment.

The team used a de-identified Medicare fee-for-service database, which covers most Americans over 65. Patients who began one of the rival drugs as first treatment were compared on outcomes that matter in practice, such as survival and staying on therapy. Trial patients skew younger and fitter than Medicare patients, so real-world gaps may emerge that trials miss. The comparison aims to guide first picks for a cancer of older age. The authors frame the data as a partner to trial results, not a swap.
pmc-13575142:
Sagar Changela and four colleagues ask whether COVID-19 raises the later risk of obstructive sleep apnoea in a 2026 records study. Sleep apnoea, where the airway repeatedly closes during sleep, links to heart, metabolic, and thinking problems. Whether infection triggers new cases was unclear.

Health records came from the Montefiore system in the Bronx, covering adults tested between March 2020 and August 2024. Among 910,393 eligible patients, those hospitalised with COVID-19 had a 41 percent higher adjusted risk of new sleep apnoea than test-negative controls. Non-hospitalised cases also carried higher risk, at 33 percent. Findings held against a pre-pandemic comparison group. The authors support targeted screening after infection for people at high risk.
pmc-13576342:
Joung Min Choi, Yat Fei Cheung, and Liqing Zhang present CancerSubtyper, a 2026 deep learning framework that sorts tumours into subtypes using DNA methylation data. Methylation, a chemical tagging of DNA, carries rich signals about a tumour's type. Yet the data are vast, noisy across batches, and hard for non-specialists to handle.

Their system runs the whole pipeline automatically: cleaning, feature picking, batch correction, and subtype calling. Two models cover two jobs, one sorting cancers with known subtypes under light supervision, the other mixing supervised and unsupervised learning to hunt for new subtypes. An interactive web interface lets users explore and check results visually. Code is freely shared. The authors aim to lower the entry bar for large-scale methylation analysis in precision cancer research.
pmc-13578342:
Mohammad Javad Zarei and Somayeh Davoodabadi Farahani test plasma devices as a way to lift the output of straight bladed wind turbines, in a 2026 computer study. Such turbines spin around an upright shaft and work at any wind direction, yet their blades stall easily at low spin rates. Plasma actuators are strips that push air along the blade surface with an electric field, with no moving parts.

The team varied voltage, strip length, and placement on the blade in fluid flow models. Under the best settings a three blade rotor nearly doubled its average power score, and gains were largest at slow spin where stall bites hardest. Output also swung less across the working range, which steadies the machine. Rotors with two to five blades were checked under the same best setup.
pmc-13578542:
Maren Friederike Balks and colleagues ask whether a meal changes blood flow in the chest aorta enough to skew scan studies, in a 2026 study. Twenty young healthy adults, half of them women, had flow scans of the aorta after fasting and again after eating. The scanner tracks flow in three directions over time, giving beat by beat measures of volume, speed, and peak flow.

Eating nudged every measure up by a small but real margin. Peak flow rose in about three quarters of the group, and the top speed climbed the most of the set. The shifts were modest next to person to person spread. Still, the authors warn that mixed fasting states across visits or sites could tilt study results, so meal timing deserves a note in scan protocols.
pmc-13578742:
Cheikhouna Gaye and colleagues map the chemistry of three mangrove species in Senegal's Sine Saloum Delta, in a 2026 study. West African mangroves are little studied for their drug like compounds, despite harsh coastal lives that push plants to make strong defenses. Leaves were extracted in water and in alcohol mixes, then read by a high precision mass tool that groups related compounds into families.

The scan named about one hundred fifty compounds, led by plant acids, pigment flavonoids, and tannins. Two of the three species carried the richest phenolic loads and the strongest power against damaging oxygen forms. A live test during the scan pinned the main protective compounds, among them ellagic acid and two flavonoid families. The third species leaned on a different compound class and scavenged weakly.
pmc-13579742:
Yonas Wondie and colleagues ask how many medical students in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, have tested themselves for HIV, in a 2026 survey dated to 2024 fieldwork. Self testing is a core route to early detection, yet students face exposure risks at work and in private life with little targeted support. A questionnaire went to 375 students at a government medical college, and every form came back.

About one in five had used an oral self test. Students who had joined HIV programs were far more likely to have tested, as were men, students with a recent risk exposure, and those with a past sexually transmitted infection. The authors say the rate is low for a group this exposed, and they urge campuses to fold self testing into program work and counseling access.
pmc-13580042:
Truong and Tran describe in 2026 a survey dataset on Vietnam's local civil servants. It was collected just after the country's July 2025 administrative amalgamation, which merged units and pushed digital transformation. The dataset links digital skills to motivation and performance in this reshaped workforce.

The online questionnaire drew 380 responses from local government staff spread across Vietnam's six socio-economic regions. It measures digital literacy, digital competence, public service motivation, satisfaction with the job, and intention to leave, using scales the authors show to be reliable and valid. Because the survey ran right after the restructuring, it captures the workforce at a moment of unusual change. The authors offer the data to practitioners managing the digitalization drive and to scholars studying how digital skill and public service motivation shape performance outcomes.
pmc-13581442:
Viktor J Oláh and a large team of co-authors locate a little studied receptor at the release sites of calming brain cells, in a 2026 study. The receptor variant, built with a part called GluN2D, sits on the sending tips of a key interneuron type in the hippocampus. Its tail carries the address label that parks it there. Background glutamate levels switch it on, and it then dials the release of the calming signal GABA up or down.

Drugs that tune this receptor family, plus low dose ketamine, lost their grip on GABA release in mice missing the part in those cells. One selective blocker copied ketamine's lasting gains: stronger memory wiring and restored reward drive in a depression model, without ketamine's side effects. The authors nominate the receptor as a drug target.
pmc-13583342:
Şeyda Kaya, Zeliha Selamoglu, Sevgi Durna Daştan, and three co-authors turn to Kazakhstan's beekeeping sector and ask what its hive products might offer drug research. Bee products carry plant compounds called flavonoids, and the team picked four of them: myricetin, galangin, kaempferol, and quercetin. Using a web tool named SwissADME, they predicted how each compound would behave inside the body.

All four scored alike for likely uptake, and none was expected to reach the brain. Galangin, kaempferol, and quercetin were predicted to absorb well from the gut and passed every common drug-likeness rule the team applied. Myricetin lagged on gut uptake, which the authors link to its more polar shape. Galangin came out as the most balanced candidate for later lab work.
pmc-13583542:
Brison A Shira, Alana K E Thomas, and R Graham Cooks study a curious cluster of the amino acid serine. Eight serine units can lock together into a charged cluster that strongly favors partners of the same handedness, left or right. Such clusters interest chemists who probe how life's molecules came to favor one handedness over the other.

Using an ion trap mass spectrometer, the team swapped single amino acids into the cluster and watched which swaps it accepted. Swaps kept the same-handed preference in most cases, though two swaps at once, or swaps with less common amino acid forms, weakened or even flipped that preference. Their reading is that the cluster forms first, then trades units one at a time, guided by weak forces that can sense handedness.
pmc-13584342:

McMurdie and Holmes argued in 2014 that a common step in microbiome work should be dropped. Studies of microbe communities produce count data, and labs must adjust those counts before they compare samples. Many labs thin counts down to an equal size, a step called rarefying.

pmc-5310842:

pmc-5899442:

pmc-6119242:

The review traces how poor insulin response harms blood vessels over time. High sugar, pressure, and fats injure vessel walls and favor clots and plaque. The authors connect cell-level changes to the heart attacks patients actually suffer. Their account helps explain why diabetes care puts so much weight on early metabolic control.
pmc-6357742:

pmc-6629542:

pmc-7146642:

smith-antiquities-1842:
William Smith published his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities in 1842, the first of his great classical reference works. Smith was a schoolmaster turned publisher's editor with a genius for organizing knowledge. The dictionary was built for students and teachers who needed the ancient world explained in English.

Entries cover the laws, gods, games, dress, houses, and daily tools of Greece and Rome, all in alphabetical order. Smith gathered a team of scholars and illustrated the articles with images of real objects. Victorian schoolboys learned their antiquity from these pages, and the book set the standard for a generation. It was the great dictionary-maker's first triumph. Later editions grew still larger, but the 1842 volume shows the moment when classical reference in English came of age.
stephanos-alexandria-magna-arte-ideler-1:
Stephanos of Alexandria lectured at Constantinople in the early seventh century, under the emperor Heraclius. No English version in the public domain exists.

Stephanos blends the furnace with the stars, teaching that the work on metals mirrors the order of the heavens. He addresses the emperor as a pupil and calls alchemy a sacred, God-given science. His lectures carried the Alexandrian art into Byzantium whole. From there it passed, in time, to the Islamic world and back to Europe.
teste-transactions-magnetisme-1842:
